en: The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume One.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Northern Wei Dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.
Chapter One: The Six Matters Requested by Brahmā (1) **Chapter One: The Six Matters Requested by Brahmā**
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was at the Excellent Enlightenment Site in the kingdom of Magadha.
Having first attained Buddhahood, he reflected upon all sentient beings who were entangled in the net of delusion and inverted by false views, making them difficult to transform and guide.
"If my remaining in this world were of no benefit to sentient beings, it would be better for me to pass away into *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

At that time, Brahmā, knowing the Buddha's thought, immediately descended from heaven, approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, knelt with palms joined, and entreated him:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Turn the Wheel of Dharma; do not enter Parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha replied to the Brahmā:
"The various classes of sentient beings are shrouded by defilements and dust; they delight in and cling to worldly pleasures, and possess no heart of wisdom."
"If I were to remain in the world, it would be a vain labor of merit; as I contemplate, only extinction is true bliss.
At that time, Brahmā again prostrated himself and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Today the ocean of Dharma is full and the banner of Dharma has been raised; to provide moisture, relief, and guidance, now is precisely the right time.
Furthermore, those among all sentient beings who are ready to be delivered are also exceedingly numerous. Why then, World-Honored One, do you wish to enter nirvana?
This would cause these living beings to lose their protection forever.

In the past, throughout incalculable eons, the World-Honored One constantly gathered the medicinal herbs of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; he sought them even through a single verse, offering his own body, wife, and children as the price.
"Why do you not reflect upon this and instead wish to abandon me alone?

Long ago in the distant past, there was a great king in Jambudvīpa named Śūraprabha, who ruled over eighty-four thousand small kingdoms and towns, sixty thousand mountains and rivers, and eight billion villages; he had twenty thousand queens and ten thousand ministers."
At that time, King Wondrous Form possessed incomparable power of virtue; he nurtured all people and things, and their abundance and joy were boundless.
The king thought to himself:
"As for me now, I provide for all beings solely with wealth and treasures, yet I do not establish them in the Way and its teachings. This is my fault; how bitter it is!"
"Now I must seek the wealth of the Dharma that is firm and substantial so that all may attain liberation.
He immediately issued a proclamation throughout Jambudvīpa:
"Whoever is able to provide me with the Dharma, I shall grant whatever they require; I dare not go against their wishes."
He issued a proclamation throughout the entire city, but there was no one who responded. At that time, the king was filled with sorrow, his grief so piercing and poignant.

King Vaiśravaṇa, seeing him in such a state, wished to test him; he immediately transformed himself into a yakṣa, with a dark blue-black complexion, eyes red as blood, canine fangs protruding upward, and hair standing on end, with flames issuing from his mouth. He came to the palace gate and proclaimed aloud:
"Who wishes to hear the Dharma?"
"I shall explain it for you.

Upon hearing these words, the king was overcome with joy; he went out in person to welcome him, prostrated before him, prepared a high seat, and invited him to be seated. He then assembled his ministers and officials to surround him on all sides, desiring to hear the teaching.
At that time, the yakṣa spoke again to the king, saying:
"The study of the Dharma is difficult; how can you wish to hear and know it so casually?
The king joined his palms and said:
"I dare not refuse anything you require.
The yakṣa replied,
"If you give me your beloved wife and children as food, I shall grant you the Dharma."

At that time, the Great King offered his beloved queen and his most excellent son as an offering to the yakṣa; having received them, the yakṣa took them and ate them in the midst of the assembly upon a high throne.

At that time, the various kings, high officials, and ministers, seeing the king in such a state, wept and lamented in distress; they rolled upon the ground and entreated the Great King to desist from this matter.
For the sake of the Dharma, the king’s mind remained firm and did not waver.
At that time, after the yakṣa had devoured his wife and children, he spoke this verse for him:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; All that is born is subject to suffering."
"The five aggregates are empty and signless; there is no self, nor anything belonging to a self.

Having spoken this verse, the king was filled with great joy; his heart was free from regret even as much as a hair’s breadth. He immediately committed it to writing and dispatched messengers to proclaim it throughout Jambudvīpa, causing all to recite and study it.
Then King Vaiśravaṇa restored himself to his original form and praised him, saying:
"Excellent! How most marvelous and extraordinary!"
"The lady and the crown prince still exist as they were before.
The king of that time was none other than the present Buddha’s body.
If even for the sake of the Dharma he acted thus in the past, why would you now wish to abandon sentient beings and enter nirvana prematurely without providing them deliverance?
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, I was a great king in Jambudvīpa named Kṣemadatta. I ruled over eighty-four thousand villages and districts across various nations, with twenty thousand consorts and court ladies, and ten thousand ministers."

The King possesses compassion and extends his pity to all; the people rely upon him for their livelihood, and as grain is abundant and cheap, they are moved by gratitude for the King's benevolence, regarding him as a loving father.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"I am now most honored, standing at the head of the nobility, and my subjects each enjoy peace and happiness under me.
Although this is so, it does not yet satisfy my heart; I shall now seek out the treasure of the sublime Dharma to benefit them."
Having reflected thus, he dispatched his ministers to issue a proclamation to inform everyone:
"Whoever possesses a sublime Dharma and will explain it to me, I shall provide whatever they require, according to their every wish."
At that time, there was a brahmin named Raudrākṣa who came to the palace gate and said, "I possess the Dharma.

Upon hearing this, the king was delighted; he immediately went out to welcome him, prostrated before him, prepared a fine seat with bedding and cushions, and invited him to take his place. The king, together with his attendants, joined their palms and addressed him, saying:
"We pray only that you, Great Master!"
"Please take pity on this ignorant and lowly person, reveal and expound the wondrous Dharma, and allow me to hear and know it.
At that time, Raudrākṣa replied to the king, saying:
"My wisdom was sought in distant lands; it was not easily attained through years of study. How can you wish to hear it so simply and without effort?"
The King replied again, "Whatever you require, please inform me of it all;
I shall provide it all. Raudrākṣa said:
"Great King, if you are able today to carve out your own body and light a thousand lamps as an offering, then I shall speak to you.
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with redoubled joy. He immediately dispatched a man riding an elephant that could travel eighty thousand *li* to proclaim throughout all of Jambudvīpa:
"The Great King of the kingdom of Kien-she-po-li (Kāñcīpura) will, seven days from now, for the sake of the Dharma, carve his own body to light a thousand lamps."

At that time, the various minor kings and all the people, having heard these words, each harbored grief and distress. They all came to the king; upon arriving and completing their prostrations, they addressed him together, saying:
"All living beings in this world rely upon Your Majesty, just as the blind rely on a guide or a child looks up to its mother. After the King’s passing, whom shall we have to depend upon?"
If one were to carve a thousand lamps into one's own body, it would certainly not be fully saved; why then, for the sake of this single Brahmin, abandon all sentient beings of this world?
At that time, twenty thousand ladies of the palace, five hundred crown princes, and ten thousand high ministers joined their palms in supplication, and did so in exactly the same manner.

Then the King replied, "You all must take care not to obstruct my unsurpassed resolve for the Way. For this purpose I vow to seek Buddhahood; when I later attain Buddhahood, I shall first deliver you."
At that time, seeing that the king’s resolve was firm, the multitude wept and lamented, throwing themselves upon the ground in distress.
The king’s mind remained unshaken, and he said to the brahmin:
“Now you may gouge out my flesh and light a thousand lamps.”
He immediately carved them out for him, placing a wick of fat in each.
When the assembly saw this, they fainted and then revived; they threw themselves to the ground like a great mountain collapsing.
The king spoke again, saying:
"I only pray that the Great Master will deign to show compassion and accept my request;
please preach the Dharma first, and only afterwards light the lamps. Should my life be cut short, I would not have time to hear the Dharma."
Then Raudrākṣa proclaimed these words of the Dharma:
"That which is eternal must come to an end; that which is high must surely fall; what is joined must be separated;
and all who are born must die."
Having spoken these verses, he then lit the fire.
At that moment, the king was filled with great joy; his heart was free from regret, and he made this vow:

"I now seek the Dharma for the sake of attaining the Way of the Buddha. When I later attain Buddhahood, I shall use the light of wisdom to illuminate and awaken sentient beings from the darkness of their fetters."
Having made this vow, heaven and earth shook violently, even causing the palaces of the gods in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens to tremble; they all looked down from above.

Seeing the Bodhisattva performing ritual offerings by mutilating his own body and disregarding his life, they all descended together, filling the void of space. Their weeping tears fell like torrential rain, and they also rained down celestial flowers as an offering.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, descended before the king and, after offering various praises, asked him:
"Great King!
Your suffering is now at its utmost limit; do you have any regrets in your heart?"
The King replied, "No. Śakra spoke again:
"Observing the King's body now, it trembles and is not at peace; though he says for himself that he has no regrets, who would believe him?
The King made another vow:
"If from the beginning until now my heart has felt no regret, may all the sores upon my body immediately heal."
Having spoken these words, he was immediately restored to health.
That king of that time was none other than the Buddha himself.
In the past, the World-Honored One sought the Dharma through bitter and painful means solely for the sake of sentient beings.
"Now that you have fulfilled [your vows], why do you abandon us to enter parinirvāṇa, causing all beings to forever lose the great light of the Dharma?
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

In a past life, he was a great king in Jambudvīpa named Vimalakīrti, who governed eighty-four thousand villages and settlements across various kingdoms. He had twenty thousand wives and court ladies, five hundred crown princes, and ten thousand ministers; the king possessed great compassion and regarded his subjects as his own children.
At that time, the Great King’s heart was inclined toward the True Dharma; he immediately dispatched his ministers to proclaim to all:
"Whoever possesses the sutras and teachings and will expound them for me, I shall provide them with whatever they require, according to their wishes."
There was a brahmin named Raudrakṣa who came to the palace gate and said:
"There is a Great Dharma; whoever wishes to hear it, I shall explain it for them."

Upon hearing these words, the king was overcome with joy; he went out in person to welcome him, prostrated at his feet in salutation, and inquired after his well-being. Leading him to the great hall, he prepared a high seat and invited him to take it, then joined his palms and said:
"I pray only that you, Great Master!"
"I shall preach the Dharma for you.
Raudrākṣa said, "As for what I know, I have pursued my studies in all four directions, enduring toil and hardship for many years; why does Your Majesty wish to hear it so casually?"
The king joined his palms and said, "Whatever may be required, I pray you will graciously issue the command; regarding the Great Master, I dare not have any stinginess.
He then replied to the king:
"If you can have a thousand iron nails driven into your body, I shall grant you the Dharma.
The king consented, saying,
"In seven days from now, I shall prepare for this matter."
At that time, the Great King immediately dispatched a man riding an eighty-thousand-li elephant to proclaim throughout all of Jambudvīpa:
"In seven days from now, King Vileṅkeli shall have a thousand iron nails driven into his body."
When the ministers and citizens heard this, they all gathered like clouds and said to the Great King:
"We from all directions have received the King’s benevolence and virtue, each attaining peace and happiness."
"Only we pray, Great King!
For our sake, do not drive a thousand iron nails into your body.
At that time, the queens, court ladies, crown prince, and ministers—all those gathered in the palace—simultaneously entreated the king with piteous pleas:
"O Great King!
For our sake, do not bring about the end of your life on account of one person, thereby abandoning all sentient beings under heaven.
At that time, the king replied to them in gratitude:

"Throughout the long course of birth and death, I have sacrificed my body countless times; whether out of greed, hatred, or delusion, were one to pile up these white bones, they would exceed Mount Sumeru; the blood from my severed heads would surpass the waters of the five rivers; and the tears from my weeping would be more than the waters of the four seas. In such various ways, I have pointlessly squandered my life and body, never once for the sake of the Dharma."

I am now driving in these nails to seek the path of the Buddha; when I later attain Buddhahood, I shall use the sharp sword of wisdom to sever the disease of your fetters (saṃyojana). Why, then, do you wish to obstruct my resolve for the Way?
At that time, the assembled multitude remained silent and spoke no word.
Then the Great King said to the brahmin:
"I pray only that you, Great Master!"
"Please bestow your grace by speaking first, and only then drive in the nails; if my life should end then, I shall not have the opportunity to hear the Dharma.
At that time, Raudrākṣa spoke this verse:
"All things are impermanent; All who are born possess suffering."
"All phenomena are empty and unarisen; truly, they are not mine.
Having spoken this verse, he immediately drove a thousand iron nails into his own body.

At that time, the multitude of minor kings and ministers, along with the entire great assembly, threw themselves to the ground like a collapsing mountain; they rolled about in weeping, unable to distinguish the cardinal directions.

At that time, the heavens and earth shook in six ways, and the devas of the realms of desire and form, marveling at the cause, all descended together. Seeing the Bodhisattva undergoing such hardship for the sake of the Dharma and having his body mangled and broken, they wept simultaneously, their tears falling like torrential rain, and they rained down celestial flowers as an offering.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came before the king and asked him:
"Great King!
Now that you are so courageous and diligent, undaunted by pain for the sake of the Dharma, what do you seek to obtain?"
"Do you wish to become Śakra or a Cakravartin king?
Or do you seek to become a Māra king or a Brahmā king?
The king replied to him:
"What I am doing does not seek the pleasure of receiving retribution within the three realms; all my merit is used to seek the Buddha-way.
The Heavenly Emperor spoke again:
"The King now destroys his body and undergoes such suffering; do you have any regrets or remorse in your heart?"
The King replied,
"There is none.
The Lord of Devas spoke again:
“Now observing Your Majesty’s body, it cannot support itself; yet you claim there is no regret. What can serve as proof?
The King immediately made a vow:
“If my sincerity is true and my heart is free from regret, may my body now be restored to its former state.”
Having spoken these words, they were immediately restored to health.
The devas and the people were filled with immeasurable joy and vigor.
"The World-Honored One’s ocean of Dharma is now full and his merits are entirely complete; why do you wish to abandon all sentient beings and quickly enter nirvana without preaching the Dharma?"
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In the distant past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a great king of this Jambudvīpa named Brahmādeva. He had a crown prince named Dharmakīrti who delighted in the True Dharma; he dispatched messengers to search everywhere throughout the four quarters, yet they were completely unable to find it."
"At that time, the Prince, having failed to obtain the Dharma, was filled with grief, distress, and vexation.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing his utmost sincerity, transformed himself into a brahmin and went to the palace gate, saying:
'I know the Dharma; whoever wishes to hear it, I shall explain it for them.'"

Upon hearing this, the Prince immediately went out to welcome him, prostrating at his feet as a mark of respect. Leading him to the great hall, he prepared an excellent seat and invited him to sit, then joined his palms and said:
"I pray only that the Great Master..."
"Have compassion for me and explain it. The Brahmin said,
"The task of study is extremely difficult!"
Only after following a teacher for a long time does one finally attain it.
How can you wish to hear it so abruptly?
This is logically impossible.
The Prince spoke again:
"Great Master, whatever you require, please command me; my person, as well as my wife and children, I shall not begrudge at all.
The Brahmin said:
"If you can now create a great pit of fire, ten fathoms deep, filled with blazing flames, and cast yourself into it as an act of offering, I shall then grant you the Dharma."
At that time, the Crown Prince immediately acted according to those words and constructed a great pit of fire.

When the King, the Queen, the ministers, and the court ladies heard these words, they could not find peace of mind; they all gathered together and went to the Prince’s palace to admonish him and explain to the Brahmin:

"We pray only that you will show us compassion; for our sake, do not cause the Prince to throw himself into the fire pit. If he has any need—whether for the kingdom, the city, his wife and children, or even our own bodies—we shall serve as his attendants."
The brahmin said, "I do not coerce you;
it shall be according to the prince's own will!
If you can act thus, I shall preach the Dharma for you."
"If it is not so, do not speak.
Observing that their resolve was firm, they each remained silent.
Thereupon, the Great King immediately dispatched a messenger riding an elephant that could travel eighty thousand *li* to proclaim throughout all of Jambudvīpa:
"Prince Dharmagandha, for the sake of the Dharma, will cast his body into a fire pit seven days from now.
Those who wish to see him should come to the assembly early."

At that time, the minor kings, the officials, and the people from the four distant regions, supporting one another regardless of their strength, all gathered like clouds and went to where the Crown Prince was. Kneeling for a long time with palms joined, they spoke to the Crown Prince with one voice:
"We, your ministers, look up to and rely upon you, O Crown Prince, as we do our own parents."
"If I were to throw myself into the fire now, the world would lose its father, and forever be without one to rely upon.
I pray that you will have pity on us; do not, for the sake of one person, abandon all.
At that time, the Prince spoke to the multitude, saying:

"Throughout the long course of birth and death, I have lost my body countless times. Among humans, I was slain by others out of greed; in the heavens, when my lifespan ended, I suffered the grief and pain of losing my desires; and in the hells, I was scorched by fire, boiled in cauldrons, sawn with axes, cut by blades and spears, and cast into the River of Ashes and the Forest of Swords. In a single day, the number of times I have lost my body is beyond reckoning; the pain pierced to my very marrow and cannot be fully described."
Among the hungry ghosts, a hundred poisons pierce their bodies.
Among the animals, there is suffering as they provide for the mouths of many; bearing heavy loads and eating grass, their hardships are likewise beyond counting.
"In vain you have borne manifold sufferings and wasted your lives, never having used a single virtuous thought for the sake of the Dharma.
Now that I offer this foul and impure body as an offering to the Dharma, how can you wish to turn back my unsurpassed resolve for enlightenment?"
"I shall relinquish this body to seek the path of the Buddha; when I later attain Buddhahood, I shall bestow upon you all the fivefold Dharma-body.
The multitude remained silent.
At that time, the Prince stood upon the fire pit and said to the Brahmin:
"I pray only that you, Great Master, will preach the Dharma for me;
should my life suddenly come to an end, I would not have the opportunity to hear the Dharma."
Then the brahmin immediately spoke this verse for him:
“Always practice a mind of loving-kindness, Eliminating thoughts of anger and harm;
With great compassion, have pity for sentient beings, And shed tears out of sympathetic sorrow.”
"Cultivating a heart of great joy, sharing the Dharma one has attained with others,
and providing protection through the intention of the Path— this is what accords with the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
Having spoken this verse, he then intended to throw himself into the fire.
At that time, Śakra and Brahmā, each grasping one of his hands, further challenged him, saying:
"All living beings within Jambudvīpa rely upon the grace of the Prince; there is none who does not find their proper place."
"Now that I am about to cast myself into the fire pit, the world will lose its father; why do you obstruct me, causing me to sink alone and abandon all beings?
At that time, the Prince replied to the Heavenly King and the various ministers and citizens:
"Why do you hinder my unsurpassed resolve for the Way?"
The devas and the assembly of humans immediately fell silent.
They then each cast their own bodies into the fire pit.
Heaven and earth shook violently, and the devas in the void simultaneously wailed, their tears falling like heavy rain.
Immediately, the fire pit was transformed into a lotus pond, and the Prince sat upon a lotus pedestal within it, while the devas rained down flowers until they reached his knees.
At that time, the Great King Brahmā was none other than the present Father King Śuddhodana;
at that time, the mother was none other than the present Māyā.
At that time, the Crown Prince Dharmakīrti was none other than the World-Honored One of today.
At that time, the World-Honored One sought the Dharma in this manner for the sake of teaching sentient beings;
now that he has attained full perfection, he ought to nourish those who are withered and parched. Why, then, do you wish to abandon them by entering nirvana and refuse to preach the Dharma?
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
In the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there were five hundred rishis in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, the teacher of these sages was named Uttara; he constantly contemplated the True Dharma and, desiring to practice and study it, sought it out in all four directions, proclaiming to everyone: "
"Who possesses the True Dharma? If there is anyone who can preach it for me, I shall provide them with whatever they desire.
A brahmin came forward and replied to him, "I possess the True Dharma;
whoever wishes to hear it, I shall preach it for them."
Then the rishi-teacher joined his palms and said:
"I only pray that you will take pity on me and, out of compassion, explain this for me.
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"The study of the Dharma is difficult!
It is only after enduring long-term hardship that it is attained; how can you now wish to hear it so casually?
This is not possible according to principle."
"If you wish to obtain the Dharma with utmost sincerity, you must follow my instructions.
The rishi replied,
"I dare not disobey what the Great Master has commanded."
He then immediately said to him:
"If you can now flay your skin to make paper, split your bones to make pens, and use your blood to mix with ink to transcribe my Dharma, then I shall speak it to you."

At that time, having heard these words, Uttara was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. Respecting the Tathāgata’s instruction, he immediately flayed his own skin, broke his bones apart, and mixed his blood with ink. Looking up, he addressed him, saying:
"Now is the very time; I only pray that you will speak quickly!"
Then the brahmin spoke this verse:
"One should always restrain one's bodily conduct, Refraining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
Avoiding double-tongued speech, harsh words, Falsehoods, and frivolous chatter."
"The mind does not crave various desires, It harbors no thoughts of the poison of anger, And abandons all false views; This is the practice of a bodhisattva.

Having spoken these verses, he immediately committed them to writing and dispatched messengers to proclaim and transcribe them. He ensured that all people throughout Jambudvīpa would recite them and practice according to what was taught.
World-Honored One, at that time you sought the Dharma in this manner because your mind was free from regret for the sake of sentient beings;
why now do you wish to abandon all things and enter nirvana without preaching the Dharma?
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a great king in Jambudvīpa named Śibi. The city where the king resided was called Devavatī, which was infinitely prosperous and joyful."

At that time, King Śibi ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kingdoms, sixty thousand mountains and rivers, and eight hundred billion villages within Jambudvīpa. He had twenty thousand queens and court ladies, five hundred crown princes, and ten thousand ministers; he practiced great compassion and took pity upon all beings.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, was bereft of the five virtues; his life was about to end, and he was distressed and unhappy.
Viśvakarman, seeing him thus, came forward and said:
"Why are you so despondent, with such a sorrowful countenance?"
Śakra replied: "I am about to reach my end;
the signs of death have already appeared. Just as in this world the Buddha-dharma has now perished and there are likewise no great bodhisattvas, I do not know upon whom my heart may rely."
"For this reason, I am sorrowful.
Viśvakarman said to the Lord of Devas:
"In Jambudvīpa there is a great king who practices the path of a bodhisattva; his name is Śibi. His resolve is firm and his diligence is intense; he will certainly attain the Way of the Buddha."
"You should go and seek refuge with him; he will surely be able to protect you and deliver you from this perilous distress.
The Heavenly Emperor replied again:
"If he is indeed a Bodhisattva, we must first test him to see whether he is truly sincere or not."

"You shall transform yourself into a pigeon, and I will change into a hawk; I shall pursue you closely from behind until we both arrive at the place where that great king sits. There, you shall seek his protection; by this means, we shall test him and be able to discern the truth."
Viśvakarman replied again to the Lord of Devas:
"O Great Being, Bodhisattva!
It is not fitting to inflict suffering; you should instead offer worship. There is no need to press him with such difficult tasks."
At that time, Śakra spoke these verses:
"I have no ill intent; just as true gold must be tested, so I test this Bodhisattva to know whether he is truly sincere."
Having spoken these verses, Viśvakarman transformed himself into a pigeon and Śakra became a hawk; the hawk pursued the pigeon from behind, intending to seize and devour it.
At that time, the pigeon, terrified and trembling, flew toward the Great King and entered beneath his armpit, taking refuge in the King.
The hawk soon arrived behind him and stood before the palace, addressing the Great King:
"This pigeon is my food; having come to your side, O King, you ought to return him to me quickly, for my hunger is most urgent."
King Śibi said, "My original vow was that I would deliver all beings; since this one has come to rely upon me, I shall never give him to you.
The hawk spoke again, saying:
"Great King!
You now claim to deliver all beings; yet if you cut off my food, my life cannot be sustained.
Am someone like me not also 'all'?"
The king then replied,
"If you were given other meat, would you be able to eat it?
The hawk immediately said:
"I shall eat only freshly slaughtered, warm meat.
The king reflected again:
"Now, to seek freshly slaughtered, warm meat is to harm one being in order to save another; this is of no benefit in principle."
He reflected within himself:
"Except for my own body, all other living beings cherish and protect themselves.
He then took a sharp knife, cut flesh from his own thigh, and offered it to the hawk to ransom the life of this pigeon.
The hawk reported to the king:

"Your Majesty is a patron who regards all beings with equanimity; though I am but a small bird, it is not right for you to be partial or unjust. If you wish to trade this dove for meat, you should weigh them so that they are equal."
The King commanded his attendants:
"Quickly bring a scale.

A hook was placed in the center with a pan attached to each end. He immediately took the pigeon and placed it on one side, then placed the flesh he had cut from his own body on the other side. Although he exhausted the flesh of his thigh, it remained lighter than the pigeon.
He further cut off both his arms and both his sides until the flesh of his body was entirely exhausted; thus, he did not equal the weight of the pigeon.

At that time, the Great King raised his entire body and attempted to step onto the scale himself, but his strength failed him; he slipped from his stance and fell to the ground, losing consciousness and feeling nothing for a long while. Only after a long time did he revive, and he reproached his own heart:
"For a long time I have been tormented by you, transmigrating through the three realms and experiencing every kind of bitterness and poison, yet I have never performed meritorious deeds."
"Now is the time to establish practice through diligence; it is not the time for indolence.
Having thus rebuked himself in various ways, he exerted himself to stand up. Reaching the upper scale of the balance, his heart was filled with joy, and he considered himself virtuous.

At that time, the earth and heavens shook in six ways, and all the celestial palaces trembled and swayed. Even the gods of the Form Realm descended simultaneously, and beholding from the midst of the void the Bodhisattva practicing such difficult austerities—wasting away his physical frame while his mind was fixed upon the Great Dharma, disregarding even his own body and life—they all wept together, their tears falling like heavy rain, and they rained down celestial flowers as an offering.
At that time, Śakra returned to his original form and stood before the king, saying to the Great King:
"Now that you have performed such an unsurpassed deed, what do you seek?"
"Do you now wish to seek the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, Śakra, or the Māra King?
Among the three realms, what is it that you seek?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"What I seek," he said, "is not the honor and glory of the Three Realms; the merit and reward of my deeds, I desire to use to seek the Buddha-way.
The Lord of Devas spoke again:
"Now you have broken your body, even to the marrow of your bones; do you have any sense of regret?"
The King replied,
"There is none.
The Lord of the Devas spoke again:
"Though you say there is no regret, who can know it for certain?
I observe your body trembling incessantly and your speech faltering; when you claim there is no remorse, what proof do you have?"
The king then made this vow:
"From my very beginning until now, I have not harbored even a hair’s breadth of regret; the aspiration I seek shall surely be fulfilled."
"If my words are true and not false, may my body be restored to its former state immediately.
As soon as he had finished making this vow, his body was restored, appearing even more robust than it was before.
The devas and the people of the world marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; they were so filled with joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves.
King Śibi was none other than the present Buddha.
In the past, World-Honored One, for the sake of sentient beings you disregarded even your own body and life to such an extent;

now, the World-Honored One’s ocean of Dharma is full, the banner of Dharma is raised, the drum of Dharma is struck, and the torch of Dharma shines forth, providing moisture and benefit until its fulfillment. Now that the proper time has arrived, why do you wish to abandon all sentient beings and enter nirvana without preaching the Dharma?

At that time, the Brahma King, before the Tathāgata, joined his palms in praise and spoke of how the Tathāgata, in his previous lives, had sought the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings on a thousand occasions.

At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation of the Brahma King and immediately proceeded to the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to turn the Wheel of Dharma; it was because of this that the Three Jewels first appeared in the world.
At that time, the assembly of the eight classes of beings—humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others—hearing this teaching, were all filled with joy;
they received it upon their heads and practiced it accordingly. 2. Chapter Two: Mahāsattva Gives His Body to the Tiger. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
At that time, when it was time for the World-Honored One to beg for food, he donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg alone with Ānanda.

At that moment, there was an old woman who had only two sons; they committed theft without restraint, and the owners captured them and brought them before the king. According to the legal statutes, their crime merited death, so they were handed over to the *caṇḍālas* to be taken to the place of execution.
From afar they saw the World-Honored One!
The mother and her two children all approached the Buddha together, prostrating themselves and entreating him with piteous words:
"We only pray, O Celestial Honored One!"
"To descend upon us and deliver us from this bitter calamity, to save the life of my son.
His sincerity was profound and earnest, truly worthy of compassion.
Out of compassionate pity, the Tathāgata immediately dispatched Ānanda to the king to request his life.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, the king immediately released him; having escaped this calamity, he was filled with boundless joy and gratitude for the Buddha’s kindness.
He then went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated himself at his feet, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
“By the grace of the Buddha’s compassion, I have been saved from death. I only pray, O World-Honored One!”
"Have compassion for us and allow us to join the ranks of those on the Path.
The Buddha consented and said to them,
"Welcome, Bhikṣus!"
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and the garments he wore were transformed into *kāṣāya* robes. A heart of reverence arose within him, and his resolute faith became even more firm.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him; all defilements were forever exhausted, and he attained the path of an Arhat. His mother, having heard the Dharma, attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
At that time, Ānanda witnessed this event with his own eyes and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, extolling the various virtuous qualities of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, he sighed in praise:

"What auspicious merit did these three—the mother and her two children—possess in their past lives, that they encountered the World-Honored One, were spared from grave retribution, and attained the peace of Nirvāṇa?"
"To have received such singular benefit within this single body—how joyful it is!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"These three people did not merely receive life through me today; in the distant past as well, they were saved and sustained by my grace."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not understand, World-Honored One!
Regarding the three people you saved and brought back to life in past lives, what were those events like?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Mahāratanananda (Aqin: 'Great Treasure'), who ruled over five thousand small kingdoms."

The king had three sons: the eldest was named Mahāpunya, the second was named Mahādeva—which in the language of Qin means "Great God"—and the third was named Mahāsattva. This youngest son had practiced compassion since childhood, feeling pity for all beings as if they were his own infants.
At that time, the Great King, together with his ministers, consorts, and crown prince, went out for an excursion. The king, becoming weary, paused for a short while to rest.
The king’s three sons wandered together through the forest and saw a tigress who had just given birth to two cubs; she was so overcome by hunger that she was about to devour her own offspring.
The king’s youngest son said to his two elder brothers:

"This tigress is now at the height of her suffering; she is emaciated and on the verge of death, and moreover, it is her first time nursing. From my observation of her intent, she wishes to devour her own cubs."
The two elder brothers replied,
"It is as you have said.
The younger brother questioned his brothers again:
"What shall this tiger eat now?
The two elder brothers replied,
"If it could obtain fresh, warm flesh and blood from a recently slaughtered animal, its desire would be satisfied."
Again he asked:
"Is there now anyone capable of accomplishing this task to save these lives and ensure their survival?
The two elder brothers replied:
"This is a difficult task.
At that time, the king’s youngest son reflected within himself:

"Throughout the long course of birth and death, I have sacrificed my body countless times, pointlessly discarding my life—sometimes for the sake of greed, sometimes for anger, and sometimes for ignorance—but never for the sake of the Dharma."
"Now that we have encountered this field of merit, where is this body of ours?
Having settled their plan, they continued forward together.
Before they had gone far, he said to his two elder brothers:
"Brothers, you may go for now; I have a private matter to attend to and shall follow after you.
Having spoken these words, he quickly took the original path and reached the place where the tiger was. He threw himself before the tiger;
the famished tiger’s jaws were clenched so tightly that it could not eat him.

At that time, the Prince took a sharp piece of wood and pierced his own body to draw blood; when the tigress obtained it and licked it, her mouth opened, and she immediately began devouring the flesh of his body.

The two elder brothers waited for him for a long time, but he did not return. They searched for his tracks and sought him out; remembering his former resolve, they knew he must have reached that place and been devoured by a starving tiger.

When they reached the riverbank, they saw Mahāsattva lying dead before the tiger; the tiger had already eaten him, and his flesh and blood were smeared all over. They threw themselves to the ground, losing consciousness and dying; after a long time, they regained their senses. They wailed and rolled about, fainting from confusion and distress, and then regained consciousness once more.

While the lady was sleeping, she dreamed of three pigeons playing together in the forest wilds; suddenly a hawk seized and devoured the smallest one. Upon waking, she was struck with terror and spoke to the King:
"I have heard a popular proverb:
'The pigeon is the offspring of the dove.'"
"Now that my little dove, my beloved son, has perished, there must surely be some ill omen.
He immediately dispatched people to search for him in all directions.
Before long, the two sons arrived, and their parents asked them:
"Where is my beloved son now? The two children choked with sobs;
their voices were stifled and cut off, unable to sound forth. After a long time had passed, they finally spoke again:
"The tiger has already eaten him."

Upon hearing this, the parents fell to the ground in a faint, losing consciousness; after a long while they revived and immediately rushed with their two sons, the lady, and the court ladies to the place where the corpse lay.
At that time, the starving tiger had finished eating the flesh, leaving only the bones scattered in disarray upon the ground.
The mother supported its head while the father grasped its hand; they wailed in grief until they fainted, only to regain consciousness again.
After a long period of time had passed in this manner, once the Mahāsattva’s life had come to an end, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, whereupon he immediately formed this thought:
"By what conduct did I come to receive this retribution?"

With his divine eye, he saw clearly and surveyed the five realms of existence; he beheld the corpse from before still remaining in the mountains, while its parents grieved and lamented, writhing in bitter agony and weeping excessively out of pity for their own delusion.
"Perhaps they might even lose their lives here; I shall now go and admonish them to change their minds.
He then descended from the sky, hovered in mid-air, and used various words and phrases to explain and persuade his parents.
The parents looked up and asked,
"Who are you, O deity?
We pray that you will inform us."
The deva immediately replied, "I am Prince Mahāsattva;
because I sacrificed my body to relieve the hunger of the tigress, I have been reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven."
"Great King, you should know this!
There is a law that what exists returns to non-existence; that which is born must necessarily end.
Through evil one falls into hell; through goodness one is reborn in heaven."
"The path of birth and death is constant; why now alone have you sunk into the sea of sorrow, grief, and affliction, failing to awaken yourself and diligently cultivate all manner of goodness?
His parents replied, "You practiced great compassion and took pity on all beings, yet you abandoned us to meet your end."
"My heart thinks of you, yet my grief is so profound that it severs me to the core;
my suffering is beyond calculation. You have cultivated great compassion—how could you be like this?

At that time, the heavenly being further offered various verses of wondrous goodness to express his gratitude to his parents. Thereupon, the parents attained a slight awakening. They fashioned a casket of the seven precious gems, placed the bones within it, and after completing the burial, erected a stupa above the site. The heavenly being then vanished.
The king and the great assembly returned to their palace.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Was that Great King Mahārathaṇḍana anyone else at that time?"
The father-king of my present life is King Śuddhodana.
The queen of that king at that time was my mother, Mahāmāyā.
He who was Mahāpunarvasu then is now Maitreya.
The second prince, Mahādeva, is none other than the present-day Vasiṣṭhamitra.
Who else could the Prince Mahāsattva of that time have been?
I am that very person.
The tigress mother of that time is this old woman here.
The two cubs of that time are these two people here.
In the distant past, I rescued those in urgent distress and perilous straits, enabling them to attain safety.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood, I likewise rescue them from their calamities, causing them to forever leave behind the great suffering of birth and death.
At that time, Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter Three: The Two Brahmins Receiving the Fast (Uposatha). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, during the first watch of the night, two devas came to where the Buddha was. The celestial radiance of the devas’ bodies illuminated the Jetavana Grove, making it all appear like gold.
The Buddha, according to their capacities, expounded the sublime Dharma;
their minds were awakened and enlightened, and they both attained the fruit of the Path. They prostrated themselves before the Buddha with their heads at his feet and returned to the heavens.
At dawn the following day, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Last night two devas came to visit the World-Honored One; their majestic marks were brilliantly manifest, and their pure radiance was dazzling."
"What merit did he plant in the past to obtain such a wondrous fruit?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, when his bequeathed Dharma was nearing its end, there were two brahmins who observed the eight precepts. One of them made a vow to be reborn in heaven;..."
The second man sought to become a king.
The first man returned to his home, where his wife called out to him to eat together.
The husband replied to his wife:
"I have just received the Buddha’s fast and shall not eat after midday.
His wife spoke again, saying:
"You are a brahmin; you have your own system of precepts. For what reason do you receive the fast of a heterodox path?"
"If you now act contrary to this and do not share a meal with me, I shall report this matter to the other brahmins, so that they may expel you and refuse to associate with you.
Having heard these words, he was deeply struck with fear and immediately ate with his wife at an improper time.
The two followed their respective lifespans and each met his end.
He who had wished to become a king, having observed the fast perfectly, was reborn into a royal family.
He who had wished to be born in heaven, because he broke the fast, was instead reborn among the nāgas.
At that time, there was a man who served as the king’s gardener, daily presenting various fruits and melons to him.
Later, while at a spring, this man found an extraordinary pear, its color and fragrance being most exquisite. He then thought to himself:
"Whenever I enter or exit, I am always seen and rebuked by the gatekeeper; I should give this to him."
"As soon as he thought this, [the king] gave it to him.
Having received it, the gatekeeper reflected again:
'When I serve as a messenger, I am always held back and constrained by the eunuchs; I shall give this to them.'"
He then took this mango and presented it to the eunuch.
After the eunuch had received it, he passed it up to the lady.
When the lady obtained the mango, she in turn offered it to the King.
The king ate this mango and found it exceedingly sweet and delicious;
he then asked his consort, "Where did you obtain this?
The consort immediately answered truthfully, and as they passed the blame back and forth, it eventually reached the garden superintendent.
The king summoned him again and questioned him, saying:
"In my garden there is this exquisite fruit; why did you not offer it to me, but instead give it to another?
Thereupon, the garden superintendent explained the matter from beginning to end.
The king spoke again, saying:
"From this day forward, you must constantly send these mangoes; do not let the supply cease.
The park superintendent replied:
"These mangoes have no seeds; they were obtained from a spring. I have commanded that they be sent regularly, but there is no way to provide them.
The king spoke again, saying, "If you cannot obtain them, your life shall be taken."
The park keeper returned to the garden, where he was overcome with grief and distress, raising his voice and weeping bitterly.
At that time, a dragon heard the sound of his crying, transformed itself into human form, and came to ask him:
"What is the matter that you are weeping so piteously?"
At that time, the garden keeper recounted everything in detail.
The dragon returned to the water and, placing many exquisite fruits upon a golden platter, gave them to the man and said to him:
"Take these fruits to present to your king, and convey my message to him as well."
He said, "I and the king were originally close friends. In a former life, we were both brahmins who together observed the eight precepts of the fast, each seeking his own wish.
Because your observance of the precepts was complete, you became a human king;
because my observance of the precepts was incomplete, I was born among the dragons."

I now wish to practice the dharma of the fast and seek to cast off this body; I pray that you grant me the eightfold precepts of the fast to bestow upon me. If you refuse, I shall submerge your kingdom and turn it into a great ocean.
The park keeper then presented the fruit to the king and recounted the transformation as instructed by the dragon.
Upon hearing this, the king was deeply displeased.

Why is this? Because there is no Buddha in the world at this time and the Dharma has also been extinguished; the text for the Eightfold Precepts of the Fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) cannot now be obtained. If one does not recite it, I fear one will meet with harm.
Reflecting upon this principle, I am therefore filled with sorrow and anxiety.
The King has a chief minister whom he holds in the highest esteem; the King said to the minister:
"A divine dragon has come to me seeking the method of the *śīla* (fasting observances). I look to you to obtain it, for I shall entrust it to you."
The minister replied, "In this world there is no such dharma; how could it be obtained?
The king spoke again, saying:
"If you do not obtain it now, I shall put you to death.
Upon hearing this, the minister was deeply distressed and returned to his own home.
This minister had a father who was aged and elderly; whenever he returned from outside, the son would greet him with a peaceful countenance and a cheerful expression to comfort his father's heart.
At that time, the father, seeing that his son’s facial expression had changed from its usual state, immediately asked him:
"By what cause has it come to this?
Thereupon, the minister related the matter in detail to his father.
His father replied, "The pillars in our hall frequently emit light; let us try breaking them open to see if there might be some extraordinary object within.

Following his father’s instructions, he had others drag the wood out, fell it, and split it apart, whereupon they obtained two scrolls of scripture: one was the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, and the other was the *Text on the Eight Precepts of the Fast*.
The minister immediately took it and presented it to the king.
The king was filled with such joy that he could not contain himself; he placed this sutra upon a golden platter and personally delivered it to the dragon.
When the dragon obtained this sutra, he was filled with great joy and celebration;
he then presented precious jewels as gifts to the king, observed the eight precepts of the fast, and practiced them with diligence. After his life ended, he was reborn in a celestial palace.
The King of Men also practiced and upheld the precepts of the fast; when his life ended, he was reborn in heaven to dwell together with us.

Last night, we all came together to inquire about and receive the transformation of the Dharma. At that very moment, he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, forever ceasing rebirth in the three miserable realms and wandering through the heavenly paths. From this point forward, he shall ultimately attain Nirvāṇa.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the entire assembly rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
**Chapter Four: The Offering of the Poor Man of Vārāṇasī** Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, there was a great elder in the country who had a son born to him. The boy’s countenance was upright and handsome; having been born for only a few days, he was already able to speak, asking his parents, "Is the World-Honored One present?"
He replied,
"It is still there.
He asked again:
"Are the Venerable Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the others all present? He replied, "They are all here."

When the parents saw that their son was able to speak as soon as he was born, they considered him to be no ordinary human being. Deeply wondering at the reason for this, they went to question the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "This child possesses great merit; there is no need for doubt."
The parents were filled with joy and returned home.
The son addressed them again, saying:
"I only pray, my dear parents!"
"Please the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus on my behalf.
His parents replied,
"To invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha, we require provisions that cannot be prepared all at once."
The boy spoke again, saying:
"Simply sweep and sprinkle the hall and chambers, and prepare the seats and mats; set up three high thrones, and food and drink of a hundred flavors will arrive spontaneously."
Furthermore, my mother from my previous life still exists; she resides in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. Summon her for me.

His parents followed his words and dispatched a man on an elephant to gallop and fetch her. As for why three high seats were prepared: the first was for the Tathāgata, the second for his mother from his previous life, and the third for his mother of the present life.
When the Buddha and the assembly of monks had entered his house and were seated in order, sweet delicacies and fine flavors were provided in abundance and at their disposal.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them; the father, the two mothers, and all members of the family, hearing the Dharma with joy, all attained the first fruit of the path.
As this boy grew older, he took leave of his family to renounce the world; through diligent application to the right practice, he attained the state of an Arhat.

Ānanda said to the Buddha, “What merit did this śramaṇa plant in past lives that he was born into a noble and wealthy family, could speak at such a young age, and furthermore studied the Path to attain supernatural powers?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In a previous life, this person was born in Vārāṇasī as the son of an elder.
After his father passed away, the family estate declined and was exhausted, gradually leading them to poverty."

Although he encountered the era of a Buddha, he had nothing with which to make offerings; reflecting on this with displeasure, his mind could not find relief. He therefore abandoned his noble lineage and sought employment as a laborer, working for a full year until he had earned one thousand taels of gold.
A man of noble lineage asked,
"Do you wish to take a wife?
He replied:
"No," he replied.
The nobleman asked again,
"What would you do with gold?"
He replied,
"I wish to use it to provide a meal for the Buddha and the noble Sangha.
The man of noble lineage said:
"If you wish to invite the Buddha, I shall provide the gold and assist you in organizing the gathering at my residence.
The poor man agreed, and he immediately prepared a variety of delicacies and invited the Buddha and the Sangha.
"By virtue of these causes and conditions, after his life ended, he was born into the family of an elder; now he has again invited the Buddha, and having heard the Dharma, he has attained the Way.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The poor man of the past is none other than this son of an elder, the śramaṇa, here today."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the entire assembly was filled with joy; they received it upon their heads and practiced accordingly.
5. Chapter Five: The Sea Deity’s Interrogation of the Ship’s Crew. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants in this country who went to sea to gather treasures. They deliberated among themselves, saying:
"We must seek out a wise man to serve as our guide."
He then invited a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who observed the five precepts to enter the great ocean with him.

Once they had reached the middle of the sea, the sea deity transformed his body into that of a yakṣa—hideous in form, dark blue-black in color, with long fangs protruding from his mouth and flames burning upon his head—who came and pulled at their ship, asking the merchants:
"Is there anything in this world more terrifying than I?"
The wise man replied,
"There is something even more fearsome, many times worse than what you have described.
The Sea God asked again:
"What is it? He replied:

"In the world there are foolish people who commit various unwholesome deeds—killing, stealing, and committing sexual misconduct without restraint; they engage in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter; they harbor covetousness and malice, and are submerged in wrong views."
Upon death, they enter hell and undergo ten thousand forms of suffering.

The hell-wardens, such as A-pang, seize these sinners and subject them to various punishments; some are hacked with knives, others are torn apart by chariots, their bodies dismembered and cut into thousands of pieces.

Furthermore, they may be pounded in mortars or ground by stones; they undergo all manner of sufferings, such as the mountains of knives and trees of swords, the burning chariots and boiling cauldrons, the freezing ice and the seething excrement.
"Enduring such suffering for many tens of millions of years—this is truly terrifying and far more severe than what you have experienced.
The Sea God released him, vanished his form, and departed.
After the ship had traveled several li, the Sea God again transformed himself into a man whose body was emaciated and skeletal, with his sinews and bones appearing to be joined together;
he came once more to pull the boat and asked the people, "In this world, is there anyone more haggard and thin than I?"
The wise man replied,
"There are others who are even more emaciated and severely afflicted than you.
The Sea God asked again:
"Who else is more miserable? The worthy one replied:

"There is a foolish person whose nature is base and evil, who is stingy, greedy, and envious, and who does not know how to practice giving. Upon death, he falls among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). His body is as large as a mountain, yet his throat is like the eye of a needle; his hair is long and disheveled, and his form is black and emaciated. For many tens of millions of years, he knows nothing of water or grain."
"A form such as this is even more hideous than yours.
The sea deity released the ship and vanished.
After the ship had traveled several *li*, the sea deity again transformed himself into another man, exceedingly handsome, who came once more to pull the boat and asked the merchants:
"Is there anyone among men as exquisite as we are?
The worthy one replied,
"There are those who surpass you by hundreds of thousands of millions of times."
The Sea God asked again,
"Who is the victor?
The Wise One replied:

"In this world, there are wise people who practice all manner of goodness, constantly purifying their actions of body, speech, and mind. With faith and reverence toward the Triple Gem, they make offerings at all times. When such a person's life ends, they are reborn in the heavens, with a countenance so bright and pure, and a beauty so peerless, that they surpass you by many thousands of millions of times."
"Comparing you to her is like comparing a blind monkey to a beautiful woman.
The Sea God took a handful of water and asked him,
"Is the water in my hand more, or is the water in the ocean more?"
The wise man replied, "The water in my cup is more; it is not the water of the ocean.
The Sea God asked again:
"What you have just said—is it spoken with sincerity?
The worthy one replied, "These words are the ultimate truth; they are not false."
How is this clarified?
Although the waters of the ocean are vast, they must inevitably be exhausted.
When the kalpa is about to end, two suns appear simultaneously, causing all springs, pools, and streams to dry up completely.
When three suns appear, all the small rivers dry up completely;
when four suns appear, all the great rivers and oceans are utterly parched;
when five suns appear, the great ocean begins to diminish.
When six suns appear, two-thirds [of the waters] are diminished;
when seven suns appear, the ocean waters are completely exhausted, Mount Sumeru collapses and is destroyed, and everything down to the adamantine foundation is scorched and consumed by fire.

Furthermore, if there is anyone who, with a heart of faith, can offer even a single handful of water to the Buddha, or give it to the Sangha, or present it to their parents, or bestow it upon the poor and destitute, or provide for birds and beasts—the merit of this will not be exhausted throughout kalpas.
"By this it may be known that the ocean is small and the water held in my cupped hands is much more.
The Sea God was filled with joy and immediately presented precious jewels as gifts to the worthy man, while also entrusting him with exquisite treasures to be offered to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Then the merchants, having obtained sufficient treasures from the worthy man, returned to their own country.

At that time, the worthy man and the five hundred merchants all went to where the Buddha was; they bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and having completed their prostrations, each offered the precious goods along with those entrusted by the sea deity to the Buddha and the Sangha. They then knelt down with palms joined and addressed the Buddha:
“We wish to become your disciples and receive your pure transformation.”
The Buddha immediately granted his consent,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
Whereupon his beard and hair fell away naturally, and the Dharma robes were upon his body.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, tailoring it to their dispositions; they attained immediate awakening, purified all desires, and realized arhatship.
At that time, those present in the assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with great joy; they received it upon their heads and practiced it accordingly.
Chapter Six: Gaṅgāda (6). Chapter Six: Gaṅgāda. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove Monastery.
At that time, there was a chief minister in the kingdom whose family was immensely wealthy, yet he had no son.
On the banks of the Ganges, there was a temple dedicated to Maṇibhadra, which all the people of the land revered and worshipped.
At that time, this minister went to the place of sacrifice and prayed, saying:
"I have no offspring. I have heard that the heavenly deity possesses immeasurable merit and protects all living beings, being able to grant their wishes; I now therefore take refuge in him."
"If my wish is granted, I pray that you grant me a son; I shall adorn his celestial body with gold and silver, and treat his divine shrine with famous incense.
If there is no efficacy, I shall destroy your temple and smear your body with excrement."
Having heard this, the deva reflected to himself:
"This man is wealthy and powerful; he is no ordinary person, for whom it is fitting that I become his son."
"My virtue is meager and I cannot grant your wish.
If your wish is not fulfilled, you will surely suffer humiliation.
The temple deity then went back and informed Maṇibhadra.
Maṇibhāra was unable to accomplish this by his own power, so he went in person to King Vaiśravaṇa and informed him of the matter.
Vaiśravaṇa said, "It is not within my power to cause you to have a son; you should go to the Lord of Devas and seek this boon from him."
King Vaiśravaṇa immediately ascended to heaven and informed Śakra, saying:
"I have a minister named Maṇibhadra who recently told me:

'In the city of Rājagṛha there is a prime minister who has made a solemn vow to me regarding his request for a son. He swore that if his wish is granted, he would increase his offerings twofold; but if his wish is denied, he shall destroy my temple and bring it into disrepute.'"
"That man is fierce and violent; he will surely be able to do so. I hope that Your Majesty will grant him a son.
Śakra replied, "This matter is extremely difficult; we must seek the necessary conditions."
At that time, there was a deva whose five virtues had departed from his body and whose life was about to end. Śakra addressed him, saying:
"Your life is drawing to a close; would you wish to be reborn into the family of that minister?"
The devaputra replied:

"I desire to leave the household life and cultivate right practice; however, if one is born into noble and honorable status, it is difficult to renounce the secular world, and thus my aspiration to remain in the middle stream cannot be fulfilled."
Śakra replied again:
"Simply go be born there; if you wish to study the Way, I shall assist you.
When the son of the deva reached the end of his life, he descended in spirit to take conception in the family of a high minister.
Immediately after being born, he was of handsome and upright appearance; the king then summoned a physiognomist to bestow a name upon him.
The physiognomist asked:
"From where was this child originally obtained?"
The prime minister replied,
"I previously requested him from the deity of the Ganges.
For this reason, he was given the name Gaṅgāda.
As he gradually grew older, his aspirations were set upon the Way and the Dharma; he then addressed his parents, requesting to leave the household life.
His parents told him, "We are now wealthy and noble, with vast and extensive estates. You are our only son and must succeed to the family lineage."
"If they allow me to remain alive, they will never grant my request.

The son did not follow his father's will and felt deep sorrow within himself; he then intended to sacrifice his life to seek another ordinary place, believing that from there it would be much easier to find a way out.
Thereupon he departed in secret and threw himself down from a high cliff;
having fallen to the ground, he was not injured at all.
He then went to the riverbank and cast himself into the water.
The water washed him out again, yet he suffered no pain.
He further took poison and swallowed it;
the toxic vapors did not take effect, and there was no way for it to cause his death.
He further thought to himself:
"I shall violate the laws of the state and be put to death by the king.
It so happened that the king’s consort and her maidservants had left the palace to bathe in the garden pond; they had all removed their garments and left them among the trees.
At that time, Gaṅgāda secretly entered the grove, took his garments and belongings, and carried them out.
The gatekeeper saw him and went to inform King Ajātaśatru.
When the king heard of this matter, his wrath flared up; he then took up his bow and arrows and shot with his own hand, but the arrow turned back and flew directly toward the king’s body.
This happened three times, yet he could not hit his mark.
The king, struck with fear, cast aside his bow and asked the man:
"Are you a deva, a nāga, or a yakṣa? Gaṅgada replied:
"Grant me one wish, and only then shall I dare to speak my mind.
The King said,
"I shall grant it."
Gaṅgāda said, "I am neither a deva, nor a nāga, nor a ghost; I am the son of the prime minister of the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
I wish to leave the household life, but my parents will not permit it; therefore, I intended to take my own life so that I might be reborn in another place."
I have thrown myself from cliffs, leaped into rivers, and drunk poison, yet I did not die; thus I committed crimes against the king’s law in the hope of ending my precarious life.
Now that Your Majesty inflicts further harm upon me, you still cannot wound me. Such is the state of affairs—how exceedingly cruel this is!
"I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and grant me permission to enter the Way.
The King immediately replied,
"I grant you permission to leave the household life and cultivate the Noble Path."
Thereupon, he took him along and went together to the place where the Buddha was. He informed the World-Honored One of the matter as it had occurred previously.
At that time, the Tathāgata granted him admission as a śramaṇa; with the dharma-robes upon his body, he immediately became a bhikṣu.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and his mind was opened and clarified; he attained the path of Arhatship, possessing the three insights, the six supernatural powers, and the eight liberations.
King Ajātaśatru then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As for this Gaṅgika, what roots of goodness did he plant in previous lives that he did not die when thrown from a mountain, did not drown when falling into water, suffered no pain from eating poison, and sustained no injury from being struck by arrows? Furthermore, how did he encounter the Holy Honored One to attain deliverance from birth and death?"
The Buddha said to the king:

"In the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī. Its king was named Brahmadatta; taking his palace ladies with him, he was sporting in a grove, while the court ladies sang with resonant voices."
Outside, there was a man who joined in with a loud voice. When the king heard this sound, he became filled with anger and jealousy; he dispatched men to capture him and ordered that he be executed.
At that time, a high minister came from outside and saw this man being held in captivity, so he asked those around him:
"For what reason has this come to pass?"
The people standing nearby detailed the circumstances of the matter.
The minister said,
"Stop for a moment!"
"Wait until I have seen the King.
The minister entered and addressed the King, saying:
"That man's crime does not reach the level of being extremely grave; why would you put him to death?"
"Though we harmonize our voices, your form remains unseen; since there has been no illicit or lewd intercourse between us, I pray that you will show compassion and grant us our lives.
The King could not refuse and pardoned them, sparing them from execution.
Having escaped, he entered the service of a high minister, serving with diligence and care without fail.
Having served in this manner for many years, he reflected to himself:
"Lust harms a person more than a sword; my current distress is entirely due to desire."
He then said to the great minister,
"Please grant me permission to leave the household life and follow the path of spiritual practice.
The minister replied:
"I dare not go against your wish; once my studies have led me to realize the Way, I shall return to see you.
He then departed for the mountains and marshes, where he concentrated his mind on the subtle principles until his spirit was awakened and he attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
Returning to the city, he went to the house of the high minister.
The minister was filled with joy and invited him to receive offerings; he provided him with delicious food and exquisite clothing, so that the four requisites were never lacking.

At that time, the Pratyekabuddha manifested supernatural transformations in the midst of the air, emitting water and fire from his body and radiating great light. When the minister saw this, he was immeasurably delighted and immediately made a vow:
"By virtue of my kindness in saving your life, may I be wealthy, noble, and long-lived in every lifetime, surpassing others by many millions of times, and may my wisdom and virtue be equal to yours."
The Buddha told the king:
"The great minister of that time who saved one person and enabled them to attain the Way is none other than this present-day Gaṅgāda.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, in every place where he was born, his life was never cut short prematurely; and now, having encountered my era, he has attained the state of an Arhat."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, all those present in the assembly believed, revered, and rejoiced;
they received them upon the crowns of their heads and practiced accordingly. Chapter Seven: Sujāta Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with Ānanda, donned his robes and took up his bowl to enter the city for alms.
At that moment, there was an old man and an old woman who were both blind; they were impoverished and destitute, having no place to dwell, and were staying overnight beneath the city gate.

He had only one son, seven years of age, who constantly went begging to support his parents. Whenever he obtained fine fruits and vegetables, he would offer those that were most delicious to his parents; as for the leftovers—those that were sour, astringent, foul-smelling, or unpalatable—he would eat them himself.
At that time, Ānanda saw this young boy; although he was of tender years, he was respectful and filial, and Ānanda’s heart was filled with affection for him.
After the Buddha had finished his almsround, he returned to the vihāra.
At that time, as the World-Honored One was expounding the Dharma for the great assembly, Ānanda knelt with palms joined and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:

"Just now, while accompanying the World-Honored One into the city for alms, I saw a young boy who was compassionate and filial. Together with his blind parents, he stayed beneath the city gate; whatever he obtained by begging from east to west—whether it were food, drink, vegetables, or fruit—he would first offer the finest and most delicious portions to his aged parents, while he himself ate what was broken, decayed, foul-smelling, and utterly unpalatable."
"Day by day it was thus, and he was most worthy of love and respect.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"Whether one has left the household life or remains at home, if they practice loving-kindness and filial obedience, making offerings to their parents, the merit calculated from this is exceptionally superior and immeasurable."

Why is this? I recall that in past lives, I practiced loving-kindness and filial piety, making offerings to my parents, even using the flesh of my own body to save them from the peril of their desperate distress.

"By virtue of these merits, one becomes a Lord of Devas above and a Holy Sovereign below, even until attaining Buddhahood as the uniquely honored one within the three realms—all of which arises from this merit.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not understand, World-Honored One!"

In a past life, he was compassionate and filial toward his parents; not sparing even his own body or life, he was able to save his parents from a perilous situation by offering them his own flesh. What were the details of that event?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively and reflect well!
I shall explain it to you."
Ānanda replied,
“Indeed, I shall listen well!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In the distant past, immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, there was a great kingdom in this Jambudvīpa named Takṣaśilā.
At that time, there was a king named Deva."

At that time, the king had ten crown princes, each governing their own respective kingdoms. The youngest prince was named Śubhavyūha (修婆羅提致), which in the Jin language means "Excellent Abiding. The territory he governed was the most prosperous and joyful of all, as observed by its inhabitants.
At that time, there was a high minister in the service of the father king named Rāhu, who harbored treacherous and rebellious intentions and murdered the great king.
Once the great king had died, he seized the throne and became king; he immediately dispatched his troops to various kingdoms to kill all the crown princes.
This youngest one was revered by ghosts and spirits; at one time, he entered a garden intending to go for a stroll.
A yakṣa emerged from the ground and knelt prostrately, saying:
"The minister Rāhu has rebelled and murdered his father, the King. He has dispatched various troops to kill your elder brothers, and now he has sent men again with the intent to come and kill you."
"Your Majesty should devise a plan to avoid this calamity.
When the king heard this, his heart collapsed in terror; by that night, he had devised a stratagem and intended to flee in haste.

At that time, there was a son named Sujāta—translated into Chinese as Shansheng (Well-Born)—who, upon reaching the age of seven, was handsome, intelligent, and very lovely. The king cherished him dearly; whenever he went out and returned, he would embrace the boy, weeping and sighing with grief.
Seeing the king enter and exit in a state of agitation and fear, his wife immediately questioned him:
"Why are you so hurried, appearing as if in terror?
Her husband replied:
"It is not for you to know," [the husband replied].
The wife pulled him again, saying, "I now give myself to you; let us share our lives and deaths together and face this peril as one. Do not abandon me."
"What matter is there now that you would inform me of?
The king replied, "Recently,
when I entered the garden, a yakṣa demon emerged from the earth, knelt before me, and said to me:"

"Minister Rāhu has now raised a rebellion; having already slain the father-king, he has dispatched his troops to kill your elder brothers, and now he has sent soldiers again to come and kill you, O King. You ought to flee from him."
"Upon hearing these words, my heart was filled with terror; fearing that such a host of soldiers might arrive, I fled in haste for that very reason."
The wife knelt upright and addressed the king, saying, "I pray that I may attend upon you; do not leave me abandoned.
Thereupon, the king immediately took his wife and son, and together they departed, intending to go to another country.
At that time there were two paths: one required seven days and the other fourteen days.

When he first set out, filled with trepidation, he prepared provisions for only seven days, intending to wait for but a single person. Once they had left the city, his mind became confused and agitated, and he proceeded along the fourteen-day path.
