Having already been gone for several days, their provisions were exhausted; overcome by hunger and despair, with no other recourse remaining, he felt such compassion and love for his son that he intended to kill his wife in order to sustain himself and keep his child alive.
He ordered his wife to carry the child in front while he followed behind, drawing his sword with the intent to kill her.
At that moment, the child looked back and saw his father drawing his sword to slay his mother; the child then joined his palms and addressed the King, his father, saying:
"I only pray, Great King!"
"I would rather have my own body killed than harm my mother.
With earnest entreaty, he admonished his father to save his mother's life, saying to him:
"Do not kill me all at once; cut me into pieces and eat me little by little, and it may last for several days."
"If my life were to end, this flesh would soon rot and decay, and could not be kept for long.
Thereupon, his parents, wishing to cut off their son's flesh, wept and wailed in anguish as they carved and ate it.

Day after day he cut off flesh to eat until his meat was nearly exhausted and only bones remained; before he could reach another country, the famine grew even more severe, so the father again took up a knife, dismembered him at the joints, and peeled away the flesh bit by bit to obtain a small amount.
Thereupon, as his parents were about to depart and abandon him, the boy reflected to himself:
"My life is short; I only pray that my parents will grant me a small portion of the flesh they have with them to give as alms."

The parents did not refuse; they immediately divided it into three portions. They ate two portions themselves, and as for the remaining one portion, along with the leftover flesh, bones, eyes, tongue, and so forth, they gave it all to him as an offering.
Thereupon they departed.
The son then made this vow:

"I now offer my own flesh to support my parents; by means of this merit, I seek the path of the Buddha to universally deliver all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, causing them to leave behind all suffering and attain the bliss of Nirvāṇa."
When this vow was made, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; the gods of the realm of form and desire were all struck with amazement, wondering for what reason their palaces were trembling.

He immediately observed the world with his divine eye and saw that the Bodhisattva was offering the flesh of his own body to his parents, vowing to attain the Way of the Buddha and pledging to deliver all sentient beings; for this reason, heaven and earth shook greatly.
Thereupon, all the devas descended and filled the void of space, weeping with tears that fell like heavy rain.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, came wishing to test him; he transformed himself into a beggar and approached him to beg for alms. [The Bodhisattva] took the meat from his hand and gave it to him as well.
He then further manifested himself as lions, tigers, and wolves, coming to devour him; the boy thought to himself:
"If these various beasts wish to eat me, I shall give them all my remaining flesh, bones, marrow, and brain."
His heart was filled with joy, free from any regret.
At that time, the Lord of Devas, seeing that his resolve was firm and his mind would not waver, returned to his form as Śakra, stood before the boy, and said to him:
"With such filial compassion, you have been able to offer your own flesh to support your parents."
"With these merits, what do you seek?
Is it the status of a Heavenly Lord, a Māra King, or a Brahmā King?
The boy then replied:
"I do not seek the happiness of the three realms; I take these merits to seek the path of the Buddha, vowing to deliver all immeasurable sentient beings.
The Heavenly Emperor spoke again:
"Since you are able to offer your own body as a gift to your parents, do you feel no regret toward them?"
The son replied, "I now serve my parents with utmost sincerity; I have no regrets even as great as a single hair.
The Lord of Devas spoke again:
"I now look at you and see that your flesh is already gone; yet you speak without regret. This is difficult to believe.
The son replied, "If I have no regrets and my vow is to surely attain Buddhahood, may my body be restored to its former state."
Once the vow had been uttered, his body was immediately restored to health.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the other devas, with one voice and in unison, praised him, saying, "Excellent!"
The child’s parents and the people of the kingdom all went to where the child was and marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.

At that time, the king of the country, seeing the extraordinary deeds performed by his crown prince, redoubled his reverence and felt immeasurable joy. He took the child’s parents and the prince into the palace to provide for them, honoring them with the utmost respect and feeling deep compassion for the prince.

At that time, the king personally led his army together with King Susīma and Prince Sujāti back to their own country. There they executed Rāhu, installed [the rightful heir] as the sovereign king, and the father and son succeeded one another. The kingdom became prosperous and joyful, eventually attaining a state of great peace.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"The King Supratiṣṭhita of that time is none other than my father, King Śuddhodana, who lives today.
The mother of that time is none other than my mother, Mahāmāyā, who lives today."
"The Prince Sujāta at that time was my very self.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"Because in past lives I practiced compassion and filial piety, making offerings to my parents and saving them from their distress by giving them my own flesh, through the merit of these deeds I was constantly born into noble and honorable positions among gods and humans, receiving immeasurable blessings. By virtue of this merit, I have now attained Buddhahood myself."

At that time, when the assembly heard the Buddha recount his own past karmic origins, those present were each moved to lament with sorrow. They were deeply impressed by the Buddha’s extraordinary conduct of filial piety and compassion; among them, some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, some *sakṛdāgāmin*, some *anāgāmin*, and some *arhat*. Some resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, while others established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression.
The entire assembly was filled with great joy; they received [the teaching] upon their heads and practiced it accordingly.
*The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume One.
*The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Two.
Translated by the Śramaṇas Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Northern Wei Dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.
Chapter Eight: The Daughter of King Prasenajit, Vajra Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the principal consort of King Prasenajit, named Mālī, gave birth to a daughter called Vajrā—“Vajra” meaning “Diamond” in the Jin language. This girl’s face was extremely hideous; her skin and flesh were coarse and rough like camel hide, and her hair was stiff and coarse like horsehair.
The king observed this woman and felt not the slightest inclination toward pleasure; he then issued an edict to the palace:
"Guard her with diligent care, and do not allow any outsider to see her."

Why is this? Although this girl is ugly and her appearance does not resemble that of a human, she is the daughter born of Queen Mallikā; despite her ugliness, you must secretly dispatch people to protect and nourish her.
As the girl grew older, it became time for her to be married.
At that time, the king was filled with sorrow and anxiety; having no other means or plan, he addressed his minister:
"Go and search for one who was originally of a noble family of householders, but who is now impoverished and possesses no wealth or property; bring such a person here."
The official immediately followed these instructions and went to search for one; he found the son of a wealthy family who was living in poverty.
The official then summoned him and brought him before the king.
The king, having found this man, went with him to a secluded place and related the circumstances in detail, saying to him:
"I have a daughter whose facial features are hideous; I wish to find a husband for her, but as yet no suitable match has been found."
"I have heard that you belong to a noble clan; though you are poor at present, I shall provide for you. I trust you will not refuse me, for I wish to take you as my wife.
At that time, the son of the elder knelt on his right knee and said:
"I shall obey the King's command. Even if the Great King were to grant me a dog, I would accept it; how much more so this daughter who is the very personification of the Great King?"
"If you now grant her to me, I shall receive her by your command.
The king then gave his daughter as a wife to that poor man, and for him he constructed palaces, residences, gates, and pavilions, arranged in seven tiers.
The king commanded his daughter’s husband:
“Take charge of the door keys yourself; whenever you wish to go out, close them yourself.
My daughter is so hideous that she is without peer in this world; do not allow outsiders to see her face.”
"She shall always keep the doors and gates firmly secured, confining herself within.
The king provided wealth and goods, as well as everything she required, to supply her husband so that he would never lack for anything.
The king immediately prostrated himself and appointed him as a high minister.
Possessing abundant wealth and treasures, he held banquets together with the various noble clans, taking turns month by month.
At the time of the assembly, husbands and wives would both attend; men and women gathered together to enjoy themselves.
When people came to the assembly, they all brought their wives with them, yet that minister alone always attended by himself.
The crowd was filled with doubt and wonder:
"Is that man's wife perhaps so exceptionally beautiful that she shines with a brilliance beyond compare?
Or could she be so utterly hideous that she cannot be shown?"
"For this reason, that man did not bring her here.
Now we must devise a plan to go and see that woman.

Thereupon, they all agreed with one mind and spoke secretly among themselves; they encouraged him with wine until he lay down drunk, took the keys to the door, and sent the five men to his house to open the gate.
At that time, her heart was filled with distress as she reproached herself for her transgressions, saying:
"What sin have I sown that I am so loathed by my husband?
I am constantly confined and dwell in a dark chamber, beholding neither the sun nor the moon, nor any other person."
He further thought to himself:
"Now that the Buddha dwells in the world, he benefits all sentient beings; those who encounter suffering and distress all receive his deliverance.
He then paid homage from afar with a sincere heart to the World-Honored One, saying: "I only pray that you will look upon me with compassion, come before me, and briefly grant me your instruction."
The girl’s sincerity was such that her heart of reverence was pure and profound.
The Buddha, knowing her resolve, went immediately to her home and manifested by leaping forth from the earth before the girl, appearing in the form of his deep-blue hair so that she might see it.

When the girl raised her head and beheld the appearance of the Buddha’s hair, her joy redoubled; with such rapturous devotion and a most profound heart of reverence, the hair on the girl’s own head naturally became fine and soft, like the color of deep blue.
The Buddha again manifested his face;
when the woman saw it, she was filled with joy, her own face became upright and handsome, and her evil features and coarse skin naturally vanished.
The Buddha again manifested his body, causing the woman to see it from the waist upward, its golden hue radiating brilliantly.

Upon seeing the Buddha’s body, her joy increased all the more; because of this joy, her unwholesome features immediately vanished, and her body became upright and majestic, like a celestial maiden, so wondrous and peerless that none could equal her.
Out of compassion for the woman, the Buddha manifested his entire body.

The woman scrutinized him with unblinking eyes; she leaped for joy, unable to contain herself. Her entire body was likewise upright and graceful, with marks and signs of excellence beyond the ordinary and rare in the world; all her unwholesome features were completely extinguished, leaving nothing behind.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, whereby she immediately exhausted all evils and, at that very moment, attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Once the woman had attained the Way, the Buddha departed.
Then those five men opened the door and entered within; seeing their wife’s extraordinary and peerless beauty, they said to one another:
"I wonder why this man does not come and go; his wife is so exceptionally beautiful that it has even reached such an extent.
Having finished observing her, he closed the door and returned the key to the person where it belonged, fastening it back onto its original strap.

The man awoke and, having finished his business, returned home. Upon entering the gate, he saw his wife; she was upright and wondrously beautiful, her features so outstanding that they were rarely found among men. Seeing her, he was filled with joy and asked, "Who is this person?"
The woman replied to her husband,
"I am your wife. The husband asked his wife:
“You were previously most hideous; for what reason are you now so upright and handsome?
His wife answered her husband in detail regarding the aforementioned matter:
“It is because of the Buddha that I have received such a body.”
The wife spoke again to her husband:
"I now wish to meet with the king; you should convey this intention to him for my sake.
The husband accepted her words and immediately went to inform the king.
"The young lady wishes to come and see you now.
The king replied to his son-in-law:
"Do not speak of this matter; you must quickly and securely lock her up and take care that she does not escape."
The groom replied to the king: "Why is this so?
This maiden has now received the divine grace of the Buddha and has attained such exquisite beauty that she is no different from a celestial nymph."
Having heard this, the king replied to his son-in-law, "If it is truly so, go quickly and bring her here.

Immediately, he prepared the carriage and welcomed his daughter into the palace. Seeing that his daughter’s appearance was exceptionally beautiful and distinguished, the king leaped for joy, unable to contain himself; he then ordered the chariots to be readied, and the king, together with the queen, the daughter, and her husband, went as one to the place where the Buddha was.
Having finished paying homage to the Buddha, he stood to one side. At that time, King Prasenajit knelt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wonder what merit this woman cultivated in her past lives that she was born into such a noble, wealthy, and prosperous family?"
"What further transgression have I committed that I must receive such an ugly form, with coarse and tough skin and hair, as severe as that of a beast?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to reveal this to me."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"When people dwell in this world, whether they are handsome or ugly, it is entirely due to the retribution of their past deeds—whether of merit or of transgression.

Long ago, in the distant past, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī. At that time, there was a great elder in that country whose wealth was immeasurable. His entire family constantly made offerings together to a Pratyekabuddha, who had a coarse body, an ugly appearance, and looked withered and haggard."
At that time, the elder had a young daughter who saw the Pratyekabuddha coming every day; with a malicious mind, she treated him with contempt, reviling and disparaging him, saying:
"How loathsome! Your face is ugly and your skin is coarse and foul."

"Even unto this. At that time, the Pratyekabuddha frequently went to his house to receive his offerings. Having remained in the world for a long time, he desired to enter nirvana; for the sake of his donor, he performed various miraculous transformations: he flew through the air, emitting water and fire from his body, leaping up in the east and sinking down in the west, leaping up in the west and sinking down in the east, leaping up in the south and sinking down in the north, and leaping up in the north and sinking down in the south; he sat and lay upon the void, manifesting all manner of transformations so that the entire family might behold his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). He then descended from the sky and returned to their home.
Upon seeing this, the elder was filled with redoubled joy, and his daughter immediately repented and reproached herself, saying:
"I only pray that the Venerable One will grant me forgiveness!
My former evil intent was a transgression of profound gravity; may you kindly not hold it against me, so that I shall remain free from guilt."
"At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted her repentance.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"The woman at that time was none other than the King's daughter now."

Because at that time he harbored an evil and unwholesome mind and reviled the noble ones and pratyekabuddhas, he committed a verbal transgression; consequently, from that time until now, he has constantly suffered an ugly form.

Later, upon witnessing his supernatural transformations, he repented of his own ways and consequently regained his physical comeliness. His brilliant talent surpassed that of all others, such that none could equal him.
Because he had made offerings to the Pratyekabuddha, he enjoyed wealth and honor in every lifetime, and through those conditions, he attained liberation.
"Thus it is, Great King! All sentient beings who possess form should guard their bodies and speech; do not recklessly commit wrongs, nor revile others.

At that time, King Prasenajit, along with his ministers and the entire great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on causes, conditions, and karmic retribution, all gave rise to faith and reverence. Moved by this, they stood before the Buddha; through such faith, some attained the first fruit up to the fourth fruit of the path, some resolved upon the unsurpassed, impartial mind, and others attained the stage of non-retrogression. All harbored deep longing and veneration, respectfully receiving the Buddha’s teachings, joyfully following them, and together putting them into practice.
Chapter Nine: The Causes and Conditions of Suvarṇadhana (9). Chapter Nine: The Causes and Conditions of Suvarṇadhana. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty venerable disciples.
At that time, there was a great elder in the city; the elder’s wife gave birth to a son named Suvarṇadatta. This boy was exceptionally handsome and distinguished, with few equals in the world.

In a previous life, this child was born with his hands curled up. His parents were startled and marveled at it, deeming it an ill omen; they immediately opened the child’s two hands to examine his auspicious marks. They saw two gold coins in the child’s hands and rejoiced, taking them at once.

As soon as they took them from one spot, they grew back again; they sought out and took them again, and they grew back just as before. Thus, they diligently gathered the gold coins until their storehouses were full, yet the child’s hands never became empty.
As the boy grew older, he addressed his parents, requesting to leave the household life.
His parents did not oppose him and immediately granted his wish.
At that time, Suvarṇadhana went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
“May the World-Honored One deign to show compassion and grant me permission to leave the household life, so that I may enter the ranks of the Path.
The Buddha addressed Kancana:
"Listen, you may go forth.
Having received the Buddha's permission, at that time Suvarṇadatta immediately shaved his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and became a śrāmaṇera.
When his years were fully met, he was permitted to receive the full precepts; the assembly of monks was then immediately ordered to confer the *upasampadā* upon him.

As the monks at the ordination platform performed the rites in succession, whenever he prostrated with both hands striking the ground, there were two gold coins at the spot where his hands struck. Thus he proceeded in succession, prostrating to all, and wherever he prostrated, there were always gold coins.
Having completed his reception of the precepts, he practiced with diligent effort and attained the path of Arhatship.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I venture to ask, World-Honored One!"
"What merit did this bhikṣu Suvarṇadatta originally create, that from the time of his birth his hands have held gold coins?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to reveal this to us."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should reflect upon this well!"
"I shall now explain it.
Ānanda replied, "So be it;
I shall listen attentively!"
The Buddha said:

"In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin who appeared in the world. He transformed beings through the true Dharma and taught them, delivering and liberating sentient beings in numbers beyond reckoning."

The Buddha, together with the community of monks, was traveling through the realms of various countries; at that time, wealthy householders, elders, and their sons prepared meals and provided offerings to the Buddha and his assembly of disciples.

At that time, there was a poor man who lacked wealth and property; he would regularly gather firewood in the wild marshes to sell. On one occasion, having gathered wood and sold it for two coins, he saw the Buddha and the Sangha accepting an invitation from the royal family. With a heart of joy and reverence, he immediately offered those two coins to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Out of compassion for this man, the Buddha accepted them.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Because that poor man gave these two coins as an offering to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, for ninety-one kalpas he constantly held gold coins, possessing wealth and treasures at his own disposal without end.”
The poor man at that time was the bhikṣu Suvarṇadatta.
Even though that person had not yet attained the Way, his future retribution will likewise be immeasurable.
"Therefore, Ānanda!
All sentient beings should diligently take the practice of giving as their primary activity.

At that time, Ānanda and the members of the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, all believed and understood it. Some attained the fruit of Srotāpanna; some attained the fruits of Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat; some resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path; and others attained the stage of non-retrogression.
The entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter Ten: The Causes and Conditions of Puṣpadeva (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great community of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, within the kingdom, there was a wealthy and eminent householder who begot a son with a most handsome and upright countenance.

Once the boy was born, celestial flowers rained down naturally from the sky, filling the interior of the house. He was immediately given the name Pūrvadeva, which in the Jin language means "Flower Heaven."
As the boy grew older, he went to where the Buddha was. Seeing that the Buddha’s countenance and marks of excellence were peerless, he was filled with joy upon seeing him and thought to himself:
"I have been born into this world and have encountered the Holy Honored One; I shall now invite the Buddha and the assembly of monks."
He immediately stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One,
together with the assembly of monks, will deign to visit my humble home tomorrow and accept a modest meal of vegetables.”
Upon seeing this auspicious omen, the Buddha, knowing her spiritual faculties, immediately accepted her invitation.
Thereupon, Puṣyadevī returned to her home.

At the time for the morning meal the following day, the Buddha and the assembly of monks went to her house; Puṣyadevī then manifested precious couches and seats throughout the interior of her residence, arranging them with solemn adornment, and the Buddha and the assembly of monks sat upon those seats.
When Puṣyadeva desired various kinds of food and drink, they were spontaneously provided through the merit of that person.

After the Buddha and the assembly of monks had finished eating and set aside their bowls, the Buddha extensively expounded the various Dharmas for Puṣyadeva. Puṣyadeva and his entire household attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
At that time, Puṣyadeva took leave of his parents and sought to go forth from the household life to become a disciple of the Buddha.
His parents granted him permission.
He then went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and requested to become a bhikṣu in order to receive the Buddha’s teachings.
The Buddha granted them entry into the Path and praised them, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣus!

Their hair and beards fell away naturally, the kāṣāya robes were donned upon their bodies, and they immediately became śramaṇas. They followed and practiced the Buddha's teachings, attaining the state of Arhat.
At that time, Ānanda, having witnessed this event, went to where the Buddha was, knelt down with his right knee on the ground, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What merit did this bhikṣu Puṣpadatta originally plant, such that he obtained these natural celestial flowers and was further able to manifest beds, seats, food, and drink?"
“World-Honored One!
You should resolve and dispel this doubt for us.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen well if you wish to know!
In the past, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin who appeared in the world to deliver and liberate sentient beings.
At that time, the community of monks traveled through villages and arrived at various noble families, all of whom made offerings to them."

At that time, there was a man who was poor and possessed no wealth. Seeing the Sangha, he rejoiced; regretting his lack of offerings, he immediately went into a wild marsh to gather various grasses and flowers to scatter over the monks. With a sincere heart, he paid them homage and then departed.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The poor man who scattered flowers upon the Sangha at that time was this very Bhikṣu Puṣpa-deva.

Because he used a heart of faith and reverence in the past, gathering flowers to scatter over the Sangha and making his vow with a sincere mind, for ninety-one kalpas, in every place where he was born, his body has been upright and handsome; and whatever he required—whether food and drink or bedding and furniture—arrived spontaneously and immediately according to his thoughts."
By virtue of this merit, one shall personally attain the Way.
Therefore, Ānanda!
Let no sentient being disregard a small gift as being without merit; just like Puṣpadeva, they shall now all obtain it for themselves.
At that time, Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
11. Chapter on the Causes and Conditions of Ratnadeva (Eleven) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an elder who fathered a son; at that very moment, the heavens rained down the seven treasures, filling the interior of his house until they were heaped high.
He immediately summoned a physiognomist to examine the boy's features.
Upon seeing him, the physiognomist observed his extraordinary marks and replied to the elder:
"The boy’s features are most exceptional."
Having heard this, the elder was filled with joy and immediately said to the physiognomist,
"We shall establish a name for him.
The physiognomist asked:
"What auspicious signs occurred when this child was born?
The elder replied,
"When this child was born, it rained the seven treasures from the heavens, filling my house."
The physiognomist replied, "This child possesses such merit that he shall be named Raṇatīva; in the Jin language, this means 'Jewel Heaven' (Bǎotiān).

As the boy grew older, his talents and arts became widely renowned. Having heard of the Buddha’s divine and holy virtues, which were peerless and rare, he felt a deep yearning and longing for them. Desiring to leave the household life, he immediately took leave of his parents, went to the Buddha's dwelling, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May the World-Honored One graciously grant me permission to leave the household life.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent.
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
At these words, his beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and the Dharma robes appeared upon his body. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he immediately attained Arhatship.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“I do not understand, World-Honored One!

What merit did this Bhikṣu Ratnadeva create in a former life, such that at the time of his birth, the heavens rained down various treasures, and food and clothing appeared spontaneously, so that he lacked for nothing?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In a past age, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin who appeared in the world and liberated sentient beings beyond counting."

At that time, the community of monks was traveling through the villages. Then, in one of those villages, there were several lay devotees who together invited the monks and provided them with various kinds of offerings.

At that time, there was a poor man who, though harboring a heart of joy, lacked the wealth or offerings to provide for the Sangha; he therefore took a handful of white stones resembling pearls and scattered them among the monks, making a great vow.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The poor man who at that time made an offering of beads is this present bhikṣu Ratnadeva.

Because in the past he used a heart of faith and reverence to scatter white stones resembling beads among the assembly of monks, for ninety-one kalpas he has enjoyed immeasurable merit; he has been abundant in wealth and treasures, with food and clothing provided spontaneously, never lacking anything."
"Because at that time you possessed a heart of faith and reverence, now that you have encountered my world, you have attained the realization of the fruits of the Path.

At that moment, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those in the assembly spontaneously gave rise to faith; some attained the first fruit, up to the fourth fruit, while others resolved their minds to abide in non-retrogression.
At that time, the assembled multitude, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter Twelve: Kṣāntivādī (12) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having first attained the Way, delivered Ājñātakauṇḍinya and his companions; next, he delivered the thousand brothers of the Kāśyapa clan, including Uruvilvākāśyapa. As those he delivered gradually increased, the number of those who attained liberation became vast.
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha were filled with immeasurable joy and could not help but praise him, saying:
"The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is truly extraordinary!
All classes of sentient beings shall receive his grace and be delivered from suffering."
Furthermore, he praised Kauṇḍinya and the rest, as well as the group of Uruvilvā:

"Venerable bhikṣus, what karmic conditions did you share with the Tathāgata in the past, that when the Dharma drum first resounded, you were the very first to hear it, and you alone were the first to taste the nectar-flavor of the Dharma?"
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the people were proclaiming, went at once to inform the World-Honored One of the matter in full detail.
The Buddha told them:
"In the distant past, this multitude and I made a great vow together."
"If I attain the Way, I shall first deliver them.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"He has long shared a vow with you; what was the nature of that matter?"
“Please deign to show us compassion and explain this for us.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!”
Reflect upon this well.
In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī; at that time, the king’s name was Kali.
At that time, there was a great rishi in the kingdom named Kṣāntivādin, who dwelt with five hundred disciples in the mountain forests, practicing patience.
At that time, the king, together with his ministers, queens, and court ladies, entered the mountains for a tour and excursion.
The king, becoming weary, lay down to rest.

The court ladies left the king and wandered about, observing the flower groves, where they saw Kṣāntivādī sitting upright in contemplation. A sense of reverence arose within them, and they immediately scattered various flowers over him; they then sat before him to listen to the Dharma he was preaching.
The king awoke and looked around; not seeing his daughters, he went forth with four great ministers to search for them.
He saw the group of maidens sitting before the rishi and immediately asked:
"Have you fully attained the four dhyānas of emptiness?"
He replied, "I have not yet attained it.
He was asked again:
"Have you also attained the four immeasurable minds?
He replied, "I have not yet attained them."
The King asked again:
"Regarding the matters of the four dhyānas, have you attained them or not?
He replied as before:
"Not yet," [she] replied.
The King immediately said in anger:
"Regarding your spiritual merits, you say they are all not yet attained; you are but a commoner, staying alone with these women in this secluded place—how can you be trusted?"
He asked again:
"You have always been here; who are you, and what practice do you perform?"
The seer replied,
"I practice patience.
The king then drew his sword and said to him:
"If you are truly patient, I wish to test you to see whether you can endure it or not.
He then cut off both of his hands and questioned the seer, who still said, "I am patient."
He further severed both his feet and questioned him again, yet he still spoke of forbearance.
Next, he cut off his ears and nose, but his countenance remained unchanged as he continued to proclaim forbearance.
At that time, heaven and earth shook in six ways.
Then five hundred disciples of the rishi flew through the air and asked their teacher,
"Though you are subjected to such suffering, has your mind of patience not been lost?"
The teacher replied,
"My mind has not yet changed.
The king was then struck with astonishment and questioned him further:
"You claim to practice patience; what serves as proof?
The seer replied, "If my patience is genuine and my sincerity is not false, let my blood turn to milk and let my body be restored."
As soon as these words were finished, the blood turned instantly into milk, and his body was restored to its former state, whole and intact.
Seeing this proof of forbearance, the king’s terror redoubled, and he cried out, "Alas! How shameless I have been!"
"You have brought disgrace upon this great seer; I pray only that you will show compassion and accept my repentance.
The seer replied, "Because of your womanly beauty, you have used a blade to mutilate my body, yet I endure it as the earth does."
"When I later attain Buddhahood, I shall first use the sword of wisdom to sever your three poisons.

At that time, the various dragons and spirits within the mountain, seeing King Kali unjustly mistreat the Seer of Endurance, each harbored deep resentment; they raised great clouds and mists, with thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts, intending to harm the king and his retinue.
Then the seer looked up and said,
"If you would do me a favor, do not harm me so grievously.
Thereupon, after his repentance, King Kali frequently invited the seer to the palace to provide him with offerings.

At that time, there was a certain brahmin with a retinue of a thousand followers who, seeing the king’s great respect and hospitality toward Kṣāntivādin, became filled with intense jealousy. In a secluded spot, they sat upon him with dust, filth, and excrement, and smeared him with them.
At that time, seeing this, the rishi immediately made a vow:
"I shall now cultivate patience for the sake of all living beings; practicing without ceasing, I shall eventually attain Buddhahood."
"When I have attained the Way of the Buddha, I shall first use the water of the Dharma to wash away your dust and grime, remove the filth of your desires, and cause you to be forever pure.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who Kṣāntivādī was at that time, it was none other than myself."
The King Kāli and his four great ministers at that time were none other than the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, who are present now.
The thousand brahmins who then covered me with dust were none other than the thousand bhikṣus, including Upavīra, who are present now.
"At that time, because of that patience, I vowed that they should be delivered first; therefore, now that the Way is accomplished, this assembly has been the first to cross over from suffering.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and joyfully practiced it.
Chapter Thirteen: King Maitrībala’s Gift of Blood. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
At that time, after the midday meal, the Venerable Ānanda was sitting in meditation in the forest and reflected to himself:
"The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is truly extraordinary; all classes of sentient beings receive peace and happiness through him."
He further reflected:

"What roots of goodness have the five venerable bhikṣus, Kauṇḍinya and the others, planted? By what causes and conditions did they enter first when the Dharma-gate was first opened; hear alone first when the Dharma-drum began to vibrate; and receive the moisture first when the nectar-like Dharma descended?"
Having reflected on this matter, he rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, and reported everything he had been thinking to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha told him:
"Kauṇḍinya and the others truly have a karmic connection with me from previous lives."
In a past life, I satisfied his hunger and thirst with my own blood, enabling him to attain peace and security;
therefore, in this present life, he was the first to receive my Dharma and thereby achieve liberation.
The venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Regarding the past instance of saving those from hunger and exhaustion with his own blood—what were the circumstances?
We pray that you will fully reveal this, so that the entire assembly may understand it."
The Buddha told him:

"In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Mikhalavara—translated in the Jin language as 'Compassionate Power' (*Maitrabala*). He ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kings of Jambudvīpa and had twenty thousand consorts and ten thousand ministers."

The King possessed compassion and was endowed with the four immeasurable minds; he constantly took pity on all beings without ever becoming weary or indolent. He always instructed the common people through the ten virtuous actions, and thus those from the four quarters looked up to him with admiration.
Under the king's transformation and governance, the land was peaceful and happy; there were none who did not rejoice and rely upon him.
As for the various classes of pestilence spirits, they constantly consumed human blood and vital energy to sustain their own lives.
At that time, the people restrained their body, speech, and mind, and earnestly followed the ten wholesome paths;
various evil calamities and pestilences did not dare to approach them, nor were they afflicted by hunger, emaciation, exhaustion, or the debility of wasting away.
At that time, five yakṣas came to the king’s presence and said, "We and our kind depend upon the blood and vital energy of others to sustain our lives.
Because of your instruction, we have all observed the ten wholesome precepts; since then, we have had no food or drink and are utterly exhausted by hunger and thirst, with no way to survive."
"O Great King, have compassion!
Will you not take pity on us?
Upon hearing these words, the king was deeply moved by grief; he immediately opened his own veins and pierced five places upon his body.

At that time, the five yakṣas each took up their vessels and came forward to receive the blood for drinking; having drunk their fill of blood, they all relied upon the king’s grace and felt immeasurable joy.
The King spoke again, saying:
"If you are satisfied, then mindfully cultivate the ten wholesome deeds. I shall now provide for your hunger and thirst with the blood of my own body, bringing you peace and security;

when I later attain Buddhahood, I shall use the blood of the Dharma-body—its precepts, concentration, and wisdom—to eliminate your three poisons and the hunger and thirst of all desires, establishing you in the peaceful and secure state of Nirvana."
"Ānanda! If you wish to know who the King Maitrībala was at that time, it is my own self here now.
As for the five yakṣas, they are the five bhikṣus, Kauṇḍinya and the others, who are present now."
"In life after life, I have made a vow that you should be the first to be delivered; therefore, when I first preached the Dharma, you were liberated upon hearing it.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had said, all increased their reverence and respect, and joyfully put it into practice.
Chapter 14: Subduing the Six Teachers Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, having already attained the first fruit of the path, felt a faith and reverence that became even more profound and steadfast. He constantly provided the four supreme requisites for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, delighting in the shared virtue of others and dedicating his will to exhorting them toward goodness.

In the kingdom there were six teachers, such as Pūraṇa and others, who had previously appeared in the world; they preached with false views and inverted doctrines, deceiving and deluding the common people.
Those who were mired in ignorance believed in these heterodox teachings, and their followers spread widely until evil factions filled the land.

At that time, the king had a younger brother who venerated the six teachers; deluded by false views and inverted understanding, he believed they possessed the Way and exhausted his family’s wealth to provide for them.

The Buddha-sun has just risen, and the stream of wisdom has begun to moisten the earth; yet, though he was without need for extrication, he remained submerged within the dense net [of worldly existence]. His elder brother, King Bimbisāra, held him in great affection and esteem, and through diligent and skillful means, he sought to enlighten him to follow the Buddha. However, the younger brother clung to heterodox principles and did not comply with the king’s instructions; the king repeatedly commanded that the Buddha be invited to receive offerings.
The younger brother said to his elder brother, the king:
"I have my own teacher and cannot go again to serve Gautama.

However, since there is no reason to disobey Your Majesty’s command, I shall arrange a great assembly with no restriction on the number of those who come; if he comes of his own accord, I shall provide him with food."

After the king had granted permission, his attendants prepared the offerings and arranged many seats. When the preparations were complete, they held a gathering and sent messengers to summon the six heretical teachers; they all arrived and took their places at the head of the rows. Finding that the Buddha and the Saṃgha had not come of their own accord, they went to inform the king:
"Previously, Your Majesty repeatedly commanded us to invite Gautama. Now that the gathering has been prepared and the time for the meal is nearly upon us, why does he not come?"
The king said to his younger brother, "Although you cannot go in person to invite him, you may send someone to announce that the time has arrived.

Following these instructions, the king’s brother sent a messenger to announce the hour. The Buddha, together with the great assembly, arrived at the venue; there they saw the six heretical teachers already seated in the seats of honor, while the Buddha and the monks sat down in their proper order.

By means of his supernormal powers, the Buddha caused these six masters, together with their followers, to suddenly find themselves at the bottom of the procession. The six masters were filled with shame; each rose to move their seats, but once they had settled back down, they saw that they were still at the bottom.
Thus he moved his seat upward two or three times, yet he still saw himself remaining at the very bottom; lacking further strength, he sat there, looking up and down.
When the donor went forward to offer water at the head of the assembly before the Elder, the Buddha said to the patron:
"First give it to your teacher.
He took the water and went before his teacher; however, as soon as he lifted the jar, the mouth of the jar closed of its own accord, and the water would not flow out.
They returned before the Buddha and took their places in order according to the sequence established by the Buddha; only then did water emerge, so that everyone was able to wash their hands.
When the hand-washing was finished, it was time for the ritual of consecration (paritta). The donor held the food before the Elder of the Assembly, and the Buddha said to the donor:
"This was not originally intended for me; go before your teacher and have him perform the consecration himself."

Having received these instructions, he went at once to the abode of the six masters. The six masters were struck mute and unable to utter a word; they could only each raise their hands and point from afar toward the Buddha. The Buddha then offered a blessing, his Brahma-voice resonating clearly and expansively.
When the incantations and prayers were completed, it was time to distribute the food; wishing to follow the precedence of the senior monk, he intended to serve it in order.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"First give it to your teacher."

He immediately took the food and presented it to the six teachers; however, the food suddenly rose up and stayed suspended in mid-air, each portion remaining directly above its respective teacher, such that it could not be taken.
When the distribution of food to the Buddha and the assembly of monks was completed, the food then descended and settled before each person.
When the Buddha and the assembly of monks had finished eating all their food, and had rinsed their mouths and returned to their seats, it was time for the Dharma to be preached;
the Buddha said to the donor, "Let your teacher preach."
He then invited the six teachers, but the six teachers remained speechless; they could only simultaneously raise their fingers toward the Buddha.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, for the sake of the great assembly, produced a gentle and supple voice, eloquently expounding the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*), analyzing the principles and meanings, and responding appropriately to the dispositions of the multitude.

Upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, they all attained understanding and liberation. The younger brother of King Bimbisāra attained the pure Dharma-eye; the rest of the multitude attained various fruits, from the first fruit up to the third, while others left the household life to exhaust their outflows, resolved upon the unsurpassed mind, and dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression. Each obtained his wishes according to what his heart aspired to; they each came to recognize the truth, placed faith and reverence in the Triple Gem, and, regarding the six heretical teachers with contempt, abandoned them and ceased to offer them support.

Thereupon, the six teachers were filled with intense resentment and anger; each retired to a secluded place to seek out and learn extraordinary arts. The celestial Māra Pāpīyān, fearing that their resolve was weak and they would be unable to propagate the poison of evil and heterodoxy, immediately descended and manifested in the form of the six teachers. Before each one of them, he displayed the arts of the other five: flying through the air, emitting water and fire from his body, dividing his body and dispersing his limbs, manifesting a hundred kinds of transformations.
The foolish followers, relying upon one another, were incensed that their former leader had been humiliated and lost his offerings. The six teachers all assembled and deliberated together, saying:
"Our skills and talents are no less than those of Gautama; yet because of that previous humiliation, the hearts of the masses have become alienated."

"Recently, the various masters have displayed divine arts and miraculous transformations; now that we have examined these wonders, they are sufficient to subdue them. We should go to the King and request a contest to determine victory or defeat.

Once the deliberation was settled, they immediately went to the King’s presence and described their own intellectual capacities, spiritual transformations, and occult arts, expressing their desire to compete with the śramaṇas in a debate over marvelous manifestations, so that after the trial, right and wrong would become manifest of themselves.
The King laughed at them and said:
"How foolish you are!

The Buddha’s virtue is vast and great, and his supernormal powers are unimpeded. You wish to compare the light of a firefly to that of the sun, the water in a cow's footprint to the magnitude of the great ocean, a tiny jackal to contend with a lion for its ferocity, or an anthill to the height of Mount Sumeru!"
"The distinction between large and small forms is clearly evident; that you are so deluded as to hold such high opinions—how extreme is your folly!
The six teachers spoke again: "The verification of this shall come later.

Your Majesty has not yet witnessed our extraordinary transformations; it is for this reason that you harbor partiality and claim they are superior. Once we have put them to the test, the great and the small will be settled of their own accord."
The king spoke again, saying:

"If you wish to test [your powers], you may do so; however, I fear you will only bring upon yourselves disgrace. Even if you were to compete with the Buddha in the exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), you must allow us to witness the extraordinary transformations."
The six teachers said,
"Seven days from now, we pray that Your Majesty will prepare and level the site for our debate.
After the six teachers had departed, the king immediately prepared his carriage and went to where the Buddha was, reporting the matter to him:
"The six masters are in a state of great confusion, desiring to debate their doctrines; though we have rebuked them with reason, their intent does not cease.

We only pray that the World-Honored One will exert his supernatural power to transform and subdue these wicked ones, so that they may finally follow the good, and thereby allow us to witness such a miracle."
The Buddha told Bimbisāra,
“I myself know the proper time. Bimbisāra,

thinking that the Buddha consented to compete in supernatural powers with him, immediately commanded his ministers and officials to level a wide area, arrange seats, erect various banners and streamers, and adorn it with ornaments until it was most magnificent and exquisite.
On the day of the assembly, everyone looked forward to it with anticipation.
At that time, the Tathāgata and the community of monks departed from Rājagṛha and proceeded toward Vaiśālī.
Within Vaiśālī, the masters of the Vinaya and the common people all came forth to welcome them.
On a later day, when the people sought the Buddha and found him not, they asked for the truth and learned that he had gone to Vaiśālī.
The disciples of the six heretical teachers then raised a clamor, proclaiming:

"We have long known that Gautama’s wisdom and arts were shallow and limited. Yet the people remained hesitant and did not believe our words; now, having set a date to compete in arts, he has realized his own inferiority and fled in disarray to Vaiśālī."
The six heretical teachers became increasingly arrogant and, each leading their own followers, resolved that they must pursue and challenge him.

At that time, King Bimbisāra prepared provisions filling five hundred wagons; the king and his retinue of fourteen billion subjects each provided their own food and followed the Buddha, forming a continuous procession that eventually gathered at Vaiśālī. The six teachers then went to the masters of discipline and said:
"Allow us to compete with this Gautama in the display of supernatural powers and in discourse on the true nature of reality. If you grant us permission, we shall meet in seven days."
At that time, the masters of the Vinaya again went to inform the Buddha:

"The six teachers and their followers are deluded, yet they claim to possess the Way; they seek to compete with the Tathāgata in supernatural powers. We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant this!"
“Please deign to manifest your divine power and subdue them.
The Buddha replied again,
“The Buddha knows the proper time himself.”

The various masters of the Vinaya, together with their subjects and citizens, made elaborate preparations with great solemnity; like King Bimbisāra, they all looked forward to it with longing, awaiting the coming day.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks arrived at Kauśāmbī.
The king of Kauśāmbī, named Udayana, led his various ministers and came forth to welcome them.
The people of Vaiśālī asked the Buddha the following morning, only to be told that he had already departed for the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
Upon hearing this, the pride of the six heretical teachers flared up; they assembled their disciples and gathered a multitude, intending to corner and overwhelm him.

The various masters of the Vinaya prepared offerings on five hundred wagons to await the occasion for worship; leading a multitude of seventy million people from the kingdom, along with King Bimbisāra, they gathered at Kauśāmbī to witness the Buddha and the six heretical teachers compete in supernatural powers, filling the roads before and behind as they arrived in an unending stream.
When the six teachers arrived, they saw King Udayana recounting the circumstances as described above. The śramaṇas reflected within themselves: "We have no internal support or reliance;
we have fled in empty-handed retreat and cannot be coerced. We must wait for the king to reach a decision and command that we be given a trial."
King Udayana addressed the Buddha, recounting the words of the six heretical teachers:
"World-Honored One!
May we not rather compete with them?"
The Buddha spoke again, saying, "I myself know the proper time.
King Udayana, hoping that the Buddha would visit his kingdom, made elaborate preparations for the reception, just as King Bimbisāra had done; all were present at the appointed assembly.
The Buddha again departed with the community of bhikṣus and arrived at the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
King Candra of Vaiśālī, leading his people, came out to welcome the World-Honored One.
The people of Kauśāmbī did not inquire until the following day, by which time they were told that the Buddha had already departed for Vaiśālī.
The disciples of the six heretical teachers immediately followed in his wake.
At that time, King Udayana, together with eight hundred million followers, as well as the people of the various kingdoms such as Bimbisāra, all went forth and assembled in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
When the six teachers saw the king, they spoke at length, saying,
"We must have Gautama undergo a trial together with us.
Puṇṇa Taṇḍula went again and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha replied as before:
"The Buddha himself knows the proper time.
The king also made elaborate preparations.
As the day of the assembly drew near, the Buddha, together with the community of monks, proceeded toward Takṣaśilā.
In this country, there was a king named Indrabhūti, who, together with his ministers and subjects, also came to welcome him.
Cūḍapanthaka and five hundred million people, as well as King Bimbisāra and the other kings, ministers, and subjects, all followed the Buddha toward Takṣaśilā.
The six teachers having arrived, they addressed Indrabhūti, boasting and speaking with great arrogance:
"Grant us permission to compete with Gautama in a contest of supernatural powers."
Indrabhūti went again to inform the Buddha, but the Buddha replied as before:
"I myself know the proper time.
When the day for the preparations arrived, the Buddha departed once more along with the assembly of monks and went to Vārāṇasī.
The king of Vārāṇasī, named Brahmadatta, also came in person with his retinue to welcome the Buddha.
It was not until the following day that the people of Takṣaśilā learned that the Buddha had departed.
The six teachers pursued him, following his tracks in haste.
Indrabhūti, together with a multitude of six hundred million and King Bimbisāra, all followed after them.
Once the six teachers had arrived, they addressed the king as they had done before.
The King repeated his previous request and went to inform the Buddha; the Buddha likewise replied, "I myself know the proper time.
When the day for the grand preparations arrived, the Buddha again departed, accompanied by the community of bhikṣus, and proceeded toward the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
The Śākyas of Kapilavastu led a great multitude and all came out to welcome the Buddha;
the people of Vārāṇasī learned of this only the following day.
The disciples of the six heretical teachers continued to pursue him in turn.
King Brahmadatta with eight hundred million people, and King Bimbisāra along with the inhabitants of the six kingdoms, all followed behind the Buddha as he departed.
Once the Six Teachers arrived, they addressed the Śākya clans, clamoring and boasting of their own skills:
"We shall extensively demonstrate our arts and abilities; let it be heard that we shall compete in supernatural power with Gautama."
The Śākyas went again to inform the Buddha, reporting the matter in full detail. The Buddha spoke once more, saying:
"I myself know the proper time.
When the preparations were complete and the appointed day drew near, the Buddha, together with the community of monks, departed for Śrāvastī.
The King of Śrāvastī, named Prasenajit, together with his ministers and subjects, all came out to welcome the Buddha.
It was not until the following day that the Śākyas learned that the Buddha had departed.
The six heretical teachers led their disciples and pursued him from behind.

The Śākya general led a multitude of nine hundred million people, along with King Bimbisāra and the subjects of various nations, filling the rivers and overflowing the fields as they pursued Śrāvastī.
When the six masters arrived, they saw Prasenajit and fully recounted the circumstances from beginning to end:
"We wished to compete with Gautama in supernatural powers, but at the critical moment he fled; he cannot be constrained."
Now, together with this great assembly, we have pursued you all the way to your kingdom.
Great King!
You must grant us a decisive judgment.

King Prasenajit also laughed at this, saying, "The Buddha’s extraordinary transformations are inconceivable; how can you, with your lowly, vulgar, and ordinary nature, compete with the Great Dharma King in a test of power?"
The six teachers were arrogant and their speech grew increasingly haughty.
King Prasenajit went to see the Buddha and said:
"The six teachers are so persistent; I only pray, World-Honored One!"
"By manifesting his divine transformations, he causes all beings to submit, universally enabling them to distinguish the false from the true and recognize the authentic.
The Buddha said to the King:
"I myself know the proper time."

King Prasenajit immediately commanded his ministers and officials to level the ground, pile up abundant fragrant flowers, arrange seats, and erect various banners and streamers; when the preparations were complete, the great assembly gathered together.

On the first day of the twelfth month, the Buddha arrived at the examination grounds. On this day, King Prasenajit prepared a meal; at dawn, he personally offered a *yācī* twig to the Buddha with his own hands. After the Buddha accepted it and finished chewing, he cast the remains upon the ground. As soon as they touched the earth, they sprouted, growing lush and verdant; the roots and trunk surged upward to a height of five hundred *yojanas*, while the branches and leaves spread out like clouds in all directions.

Gradually flowers grew again, as large as chariot wheels; subsequently, fruits appeared, as large as five-peckle jars. The roots, stems, branches, and leaves were composed entirely of the seven treasures in various colors, shimmering with exquisite beauty; they emitted light according to their respective hues, eclipsing the sun and the moon.
Those who eat its fruit find it more delicious than ambrosia; its fragrance fills the four quarters, and all who smell it feel joy in their hearts.

When fragrant breezes blow and the branches and leaves brush against one another, they produce harmonious and elegant sounds that eloquently expound the essentials of the Dharma, such that those who hear them never grow weary.
When all the people beheld this transformation of the tree, their hearts of reverence and faith became doubly more sincere and profound.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma, adapting it to suit their inclinations; their minds were all opened and liberated. Those who aspired to Buddhahood attained the fruit [of enlightenment] or were reborn in the heavens, their number being exceedingly great.
On the following day, King Udayana invited the Buddha.

At that time, the Tathāgata transformed both sides [of the road] into two precious mountains, magnificent and beautiful to behold, composed of various jewels, radiant with five colors, and shimmering with brilliant flames. Various kinds of trees were lined up upon the mountains, their flowers and fruits flourishing and emitting a subtle and wondrous fragrance.

On one of its peaks, there is mature non-glutinous rice, smooth and delicious with a hundred flavors; its sweetness lingers upon the palate, and the various classes of people eat it to their heart's content.
On one of the mountains, there is soft grass, lush and sweet, provided for the sake of the animals; those who require it go there to eat it, and once satiated, their hearts are joyful.
The entire assembly, beholding the mountain manifest such wonders, felt joy after their meal, and their veneration grew ever deeper.

The Buddha, further responding to their needs, preached the sublime Dharma for them; each attained understanding and realization, resolved their minds upon the Unsurpassed Way, attained the fruits of the path, and were reborn in the heavens—those who did so were likewise numerous.
On the third day, the Cūḍa-antaras invited the Buddha for a meal offering. They presented him with pure water for his rinsing and cleansing.

When the Buddha spat out the water and discarded it, it transformed into a precious pond four hundred li in circumference on all four sides. It was composed entirely of the seven treasures interspersed together, their various colors reflecting one another with brilliant and shimmering radiance.

The water in that pond is endowed with the eight virtues; its bottom is entirely covered with sand of the seven treasures, and there are eight kinds of lotuses as large as chariot wheels—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, green, and purple—whose fragrant scents are rich and pervasive, wafting far and wide in the four directions.
Each lotus flower emitted light according to its color; this radiance shone forth, illuminating and dazzling heaven and earth.
Beholding this wondrous jewel pond, the great assembly rejoiced and praised the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues.

The Buddha, through observation, taught the Dharma with skillful means according to the inclinations of the people's minds, causing each to attain understanding and resolve for the Unsurpassed Way; they attained the fruits [of the path], were reborn in the heavens, and all increased their meritorious karma in numbers too vast to calculate.
On the fourth day, King Indrabhīmi invited the Buddha.
On that day, the Buddha caused the jewel pond to naturally develop eight channels on its four sides, which flowed into one another and revolved spontaneously.

The flowing water made a sound, a sound pure and wondrous, which expounded all dharmas: the five faculties and five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path, the three clarities and six supernormal powers, the six perfections and four immeasurables, and great kindness and great compassion. It exhorted, inspired, and guided, preaching various dharmas. All who heard or beheld it had their minds opened and understood; they resolved to seek Buddhahood, attained fruits, and were reborn in the heavens, increasing their merit and wisdom in numbers so vast as to be beyond counting.
On the fifth day thereafter, King Brahmadatta invited the Buddha for a meal offering.
On that day, the Buddha emitted light from his mouth, its golden brilliance shining resplendently throughout the great trichiliocosm.

Touched by this radiance, the three poisons and the five aggregates of all sentient beings are naturally stilled; their bodies and minds experience bliss, just like a bhikṣu who has attained the third dhyāna.
The assembly marveled at this with wonder and came to admire the Buddha’s virtue.

He then preached the Dharma for them; each attained understanding and enlightenment, resolved their minds upon the Great Way, and attained the fruits [of the path], being reborn in the heavens. As they advanced in merit and cultivated wisdom, those who did so were exceedingly numerous.
On the sixth day, the masters of the Vinaya in turn invited the Buddha.

On this day, the Buddha caused all sentient beings in the great assembly to know one another’s minds; each individual came to know the thoughts of all others—their good and evil intentions, their aspirations, and their karmic actions.
Everyone was filled with surprise and joy, admiring the Buddha’s virtue.

The Buddha then preached various sublime dharmas for them; all attained understanding and realization. Those who vowed to seek Buddhahood attained the fruit and were reborn in heaven, their number being exceedingly great.
On the seventh day, the Śākyas invited the Buddha.

On that day, the Buddha transformed all those gathered there, causing each to see themselves as a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), possessing the seven treasures and a thousand sons, with various kings, ministers, and subjects reverently honoring him and attending upon him without ceasing.
Each was struck with wonder and amazement, and their joy was immeasurable.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma for them, which suited their dispositions; they likewise resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and so many attained the fruits [of the path] and were reborn in the heavens that it is difficult to calculate their number.

Furthermore, on the eighth day, he accepted the invitation of Śakra, who prepared a lion throne for the Buddha. When the Tathāgata ascended the throne, Śakra attended to his left and Brahmā attended to his right; the entire assembly sat down in profound stillness.

The Buddha slowly extended his arm and caught the seat with his hand; suddenly there was a great sound like the trumpeting of elephants. At that very moment, five great spirits and ghosts appeared, crushing and dragging away the high seats of the six teachers. Vajrapāṇi, the Secret Keeper of the Vajra, brandished a vajra from which flames issued; he raised it to threaten the six teachers, who fled in terror. Humiliated by this profound disgrace, they threw themselves into a river and died.
The six teachers and their followers, a multitude of nine hundred million people, all came to take refuge in the Buddha and requested to become his disciples.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, bhikṣus!"
Their hair and beards fell away naturally, dharma robes appeared upon their bodies, and they all became śramaṇas.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, revealing the essentials of the teaching; their outflows were exhausted and their fetters severed, and they all attained arhatship.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted light from all eighty thousand pores, which filled the entirety of space. At the tip of each ray of light was a great lotus flower, and upon each flower sat an emanation Buddha surrounded by a great assembly, preaching the Dharma.
When the assembly beheld this unsurpassed transformation, their hearts of faith and reverence grew doubly more profound.

The Buddha then preached for them according to their respective capacities; some gave rise to the Great Mind (bodhicitta), some attained the fruits [of the path] and were reborn in the heavens, while others advanced in merit and increased in goodness—those who did so were exceedingly numerous.
On the ninth day, the Brahma King invited the Buddha.

The Buddha himself transformed his body so that it reached as high as the Brahma Heaven; his majestic and solemn presence was loftily manifest, so sublime as to be beyond measure, emitting a great radiance that brilliantly illuminated heaven and earth.

Everyone looked up in reverence and heard his words; the Buddha revealed various essential points of the Dharma for them, causing many in the great assembly to resolve their minds to seek Buddhahood, with those who attained the fruits of the path and were reborn in the heavens numbering beyond calculation.
On the tenth day, the Four Heavenly Kings invited the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One caused the entire great assembly to behold the Buddha’s physical body throughout all the heavens; from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, everyone saw the Buddha’s body emitting great radiance and preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of each respective assembly.
They all looked up from afar and saw him clearly; the entire assembly felt a profound increase in reverence and respect.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for them according to their individual dispositions, and they all resolved upon the Great Mind, abiding on the stage of non-retrogression. Those who attained the fruits [of the path] and were reborn in the heavens were beyond calculation.
On the eleventh day, Sudatta invited the Buddha.

On that day, while seated upon the high throne, the Buddha concealed his physical form, remaining in silent extinction and unmanifest; yet he emitted a radiant light and produced a gentle voice, analytically expounding the essentials of all dharmas.

Among those present at the assembly, many who heard the Dharma attained realization and enlightenment; some resolved their minds upon the Great Vehicle and dwelt in non-retrogression, while others attained the fruits of the path or were reborn in the heavens—indeed, such instances were exceedingly numerous.
On the twelfth day, the householder Citta invited the Buddha for a meal offering.
On this day, the Buddha entered the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), from which he emitted golden light that illuminated the great trichiliocosm.
When his light touches sentient beings, their minds of the three poisons are stilled, and compassion naturally arises;
he regards all beings equally, as a father or mother, as an elder brother or younger brother, with a heart of loving moisture that neither increases nor decreases.

Thereafter, he was taught various sublime Dharmas; he likewise gave rise to the Great Mind, dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, attained the fruit [of the path], and was reborn in heaven—achievements beyond measure.
On the thirteenth day, King Tuṇḍa-cela invited the Buddha in turn and prepared offerings.

On this day, the Buddha ascended the high seat and emitted light from his navel, which split into two extraordinary rays. They rose seven *zhang* above his body, each topped with a lotus flower, upon which sat a transformation Buddha no different from the Buddha himself. From the navel of each transformation Buddha, light again issued forth, likewise splitting into two extraordinary rays rising seven *zhang* above their bodies, each topped with a lotus flower and a transformation Buddha. In this manner, it spread throughout the entire Great Trichiliocosm.
All who beheld him were struck with amazement and filled with joyful surprise.

The Buddha, responding to the occasion, preached the Dharma according to their inclinations; many likewise gave rise to the Great Mind, attained the stage of non-retrogression, realized the fruits of the path, or were reborn in the heavens—their number being exceedingly vast.
On the fourteenth day, King Udayana invited the Buddha.
At that time, King Udayana scattered flowers over the Buddha.

The Buddha immediately, in response to the occasion, transformed the scattered flowers into one thousand two hundred and fifty-seven jeweled high chariots. They reached as high as the Brahma Heaven, outshining Mount Sumeru in brilliance; composed of various jewels and manifold colors, they shone with a radiant splendor. The golden light vibrated and gleamed in a wondrous and immeasurable manner, interspersed with divine pearls and necklaces.
Within each of the high chariots, there was a Buddha-body emitting great radiance that pervaded the three thousandfold world-system.
As the assembly beheld this transformation, joy and reverence welled up within their hearts.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma, dispensing medicine according to their ailments; all conceived the Great Resolve, some abiding in non-retrogression, while others attained the Way or were reborn in the heavens—the number being exceedingly great.
On the fifteenth day, King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha; the Buddha had previously instructed the king, saying, "You need only provide the food.
The king merely prepared the utensils, making them exceedingly abundant.

The time for the meal had arrived; all the vessels were filled with a hundred flavors of sweet delicacies, each of diverse and exquisite taste, providing more than enough to satisfy the entire assembly. Having eaten, their bodies and minds naturally became peaceful and joyful.

At that time, the World-Honored One pointed to the ground with his finger, and all eighteen hells appeared before them. Countless beings, as numerous as motes of dust, who were undergoing retribution for their sins, each spoke of themselves:
"In the past, I committed such evil deeds; now I undergo this suffering."
The entire assembly heard and saw this completely; they were moved by profound compassion, their hair standing on end with awe.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma for them, perfectly suiting their inclinations. There were those who gave rise to the Great Mind and attained the stage of non-retrogression, as well as those who realized the fruits [of the path] and were reborn in the heavens, beyond all reckoning.

The sentient beings in the hells, having encountered the Buddha and heard the Dharma, conceived a heart of reverence and respect; they all took refuge from afar, and in the end, all were reborn among devas and humans.
At that time, King Bimbisāra knelt on his right knee and addressed the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, your wondrous marks are thirty-two in number. Although I have previously beheld the various marks of your hands and body, I have not yet seen the wheel-mark beneath the soles of the Tathāgata’s feet. I pray that you will show it to the assembly, so that all may together gaze upon it with reverence."

The Buddha then extended his feet and showed them to the entire assembly; everyone beheld the wheel-mark on the soles of the Buddha’s feet, majestic and brilliant, its patterns and lines as clearly defined as a painting, distinct and vivid, such that one could never tire of gazing upon them.
The King was even more joyful and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I venture to ask, World-Honored One!
What merit did you originally cultivate that has resulted in such wondrous marks as these wheel-marks?"
The Buddha then told the king:
"It is because I cultivated the ten wholesome paths myself in the past and further taught them to others that I have attained these marks so clearly manifest as such."
The King again addressed the Buddha:
“I venture to ask, World-Honored One:
what is the manner in which one personally cultivates the ten wholesome actions and further teaches others to do so?”
"I pray that you will grant me an exposition.
The Buddha said to the king,
"Listen well and fix your mind."

In the past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Śrīdāman, who ruled over eighty-four thousand kingdoms, eight trillion villages, and ten thousand ministers.
The king had twenty thousand consorts, yet none of them bore a son.
The king was deeply distressed, fearing that the lineage of the state would be extinguished; he immediately performed extensive sacrifices and offered prayers to the various heavens.
The king’s first consort, named Sūryavarāmaṇī, after some time had passed, perceived that she was pregnant.

From the moment she conceived, her disposition became sharp and discerning; she was compassionate and merciful, exhorting others toward goodness. When the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son who was exceptionally handsome and extraordinary, his features radiant and beautiful, with light emanating from every pore of his body.
The king was filled with great joy and could never tire of gazing upon him.
He immediately summoned a physiognomist to determine whether his fortune was auspicious.
Upon examining him, the physiognomist sighed and said:
"How marvelous!
The marks of this child are preeminent and extraordinary; his virtue shall bring peace to the four quarters, and the whole world shall revere him.
The King was filled with even greater joy and commanded that a name be established for him.
The physiognomist said to the king,
"What extraordinary omen has occurred?
The king replied:

"Since this child was conceived, his mother has been wise, compassionate, and exhortative toward goodness; although there have been many other auspicious signs, we are greatly amazed by this particular wonder.
