The physiognomist, filled with joy and surprise, addressed the King, saying:

"The mother is already possessed of eloquence and wisdom, and her own body radiates light. We shall establish a name for him: Nāparama, which in the Jin language means 'Radiance of Wisdom' (Huìguāng)."

When the Prince grew up, his wisdom surpassed that of others. Upon the death of the Father King, after the funeral rites were completed, the kings and ministers assembled and exhorted him to succeed to the throne; however, the Prince firmly declined, saying he was incapable of the task.
The ministers each said, "The Great King has passed away, and there is only the Crown Prince; there are no other brothers.
Now that he says he is unwilling, to whom could he possibly defer the succession?"
The Prince replied:
"If the people practice evil and do not adhere to righteousness, and I were to impose punishments upon them, my guilt would be no small matter;
however, if I can lead the people to universally practice the ten wholesome deeds, I shall then be able to undertake the affairs of state."
The ministers said, "Excellent!
We only pray that you will ascend the throne; you should issue an edict for the practice of the Way of the Ten Virtues."

At that time, the Prince immediately ascended the throne and issued a proclamation to the people below, universally enjoining them to practice the ten wholesome deeds; all paid respectful obedience, reforming their hearts and changing their conduct.
The Demon King, filled with envy and desiring to subvert the king’s transformation of the realm, secretly composed a sealed letter and circulated it to all the kingdoms:
"The previous edict to practice virtue has yielded no beneficial results; you have merely exhausted yourselves in laboring at useless matters.
From this day forward, permit the people to act according to their own hearts and commit the ten evil deeds; do not hesitate to indulge your passions anymore."
When the various kings received the letter, they marveled at this extraordinary decree; for what reason would it transgress the principles of propriety by inciting people toward evil?
Each dispatched their own trusted confidants to inquire further regarding its origins.
Upon hearing these words, the king was struck with astonishment and said, "I have issued no such decree;
by what cause has this come to pass?

He immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared and traveled in person through the various kingdoms, where he personally met with his ministers and subjects to proclaim the reform of their divergent customs.

By the side of the road, Māra transformed himself into a man whose body was situated within a great fire, fiercely blazing and burning; therein he wailed and cried out, his voice pitiable and piercingly sorrowful.
The king immediately stepped forward and asked, "Why have you done this?
The man replied to the king:
"Before I sat here, I exhorted others to practice the ten wholesome deeds; now I undergo this suffering, its agonizing pain unbearable.
The King replied again, "How could such a thing be?"
‘I exhorted others to cultivate goodness, yet I have instead suffered this pain.
He asked again:
‘If I exhorted you to practice the ten wholesome deeds, why do you cause me to suffer?’
"Does the person who previously accepted the exhortation and practiced the ten wholesome deeds receive a wholesome retribution?
He replied, "That person receives only wholesome merit; however, because he taught others [to do evil], he alone undergoes this suffering."
Upon hearing this, the king replied with joy:
"Provided that the person before me attains wholesome merit, I am willing to undergo suffering and shall not harbor any resentment.
When Māra heard these words, he immediately vanished from sight and departed.

He traveled through all the lands, proclaiming the ten virtuous actions; the people submitted to his transformation, being careful in body, speech, and mind. His righteous teaching spread far and wide, and everyone revered him.

The King’s virtue was lofty and brilliant, so that auspicious omens descended; the Golden Wheel first manifested its response, and the seven treasures arrived in full. He traveled to transform the four quarters, making the guidance of others toward goodness his primary task.
Thus it is, Great King!
If you wish to know who that King Śuddhodana was at that time, he is none other than my father, King Śuddhodana, who is present now.
And she who was the mother at that time is none other than my mother, Mahāmāyā, who is present now.
That King Huiguang who transformed the people through the ten wholesome deeds was none other than my present self.
Because in that life I personally practiced the ten wholesome deeds and further exhorted the people to practice them, I have now attained this mark of a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of my feet.
Then King Bimbisāra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The six teachers, deluded and lacking self-awareness, are greedily attached to gain and offerings; they have given rise to a heart of jealousy and seek to compete with the World-Honored One regarding supernormal powers, saying: ‘If the Buddha performs one, I shall perform two.’”

The Buddha manifested supernatural transformations, wondrous and inconceivable; the six heretical teachers were utterly cowed and lacked even a single skill. Ashamed of their forms and their shadows, they threw themselves into the water and died; their followers dispersed and dissolved, leaving behind only calamity and suffering for themselves.
"Reflecting on their delusion, how extreme it is!
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Not only today; because the followers of the Six Teachers sought to settle a dispute with me for the sake of fame and profit, they lost their own assemblies."
"In a past life, they also contended with me; I likewise harmed them and seized their followers.
The king then knelt down on his knees and immediately addressed the Buddha, saying, "I do not understand, World-Honored One!"
"In a past life, you contended with the Six Heretics and seized their followers; what were the details of that event?
I pray you, explain it fully.
The Buddha told the King:
"Listen with focused attention.

In the past, incalculable, immeasurable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Mahāśaṃkuli who ruled over five hundred minor kings and had five hundred consorts, yet he had no crown prince to succeed him."
The King thought to himself:

"I have grown old, yet I have no son to succeed me to the throne. Should I one day pass away, the kings, ministers, and subjects will not be able to accept one another’s rule; they will surely raise armies and bring harm upon the lives of the people, and the kingdom will fall into chaos—what a terrible suffering this would be!"
Having reflected on these matters, his mind sank into an ocean of sorrow.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing the king’s grief from afar, immediately descended from heaven and transformed himself into a physician. He came to the king’s presence and asked about the cause of the king’s distress;
the king then explained the matter to the physician exactly as it was.
The physician who had manifested himself said to the king:
"Do not worry further!
I shall go for Your Majesty into the Snowy Mountains to gather and compound various medicines. When the Queen takes them, she and all the others shall become pregnant."
Upon hearing these words, the king’s sorrow was somewhat relieved; he spoke to the physician, saying, "If you can do so, it is well.

Thereupon, the transformed physician went to the Snowy Mountains, gathered various medicinal herbs, and carried them back to the royal palace, where he boiled them with milk and gave them to the chief consort.
The consort loathed the smell and, being suspicious in her heart, watched as the transformed physician returned to heaven; she subsequently refused to take the medicine.
The other minor consorts all shared it together, and before long after taking it, they each perceived that they were pregnant.
Each reported the circumstances to the Great Lady.
Upon hearing this, the lady was filled with grief and regret, and she immediately asked:
"Is there any remainder of what you have taken?"
He replied, "It has been exhausted.
He asked again:
"Is the previous draft still here?
He replied,
"It is still here."
He immediately ordered that milk be taken and boiled again over a high flame; he then presented it to the lady, who consumed it.
After taking it for several days, she too perceived that she was pregnant.
The various minor consorts each gave birth when their months were full; all were sons, exceptionally handsome and extraordinary.
When the king saw his sons, he leaped for joy, yet he remained anxious and longing as he thought of the chief consort.

When the lady’s month was full, she also gave birth to a son whose countenance was exceedingly ugly and whose form resembled a stump; when his parents saw him, they were not joyful at heart and thus collectively named him Tālaphuṣa—“Tālaphuṣa” meaning “stump” in the Jin language—and ordered that he be raised.
As he gradually grew up, his other brothers had all already married, yet they paid no heed to Zhuwu.

Later, a neighboring state raised an army and invaded their borders; the five hundred princes led troops to resist them, but when the battle first began, their army was defeated, and they retreated toward the city.
Prince Kūṭa asked his elder brothers,
"Why do you flee in retreat with such an appearance of terror?
His brothers replied:
"Going forth to battle was not advantageous; we were pursued by the enemy's army, which is why we retreated.
The stump said:
"If such bandits as these dare to invade and harass us, go and fetch the great bow and conch shell from the celestial temple of my ancestors, and I shall go to strike them down."
His ancestors had been wheel-turning kings, so he immediately dispatched many men to go and fetch it and carry it back to him.

When they took the bow and drew it, the sound of the bow was like thunder; the twang of the bowstring could be heard for forty *li*. Taking up the bow and grasping the conch shell, he then went alone to do battle.

Upon arriving, he first blew his conch shell; its sound was like a thunderclap. Hearing the sound, the enemy army was struck with terror and fled in disarray. Only after the foe had retreated did he return.
His father the King, having witnessed this extraordinary feat, treated him with affection and respect; he deeply contemplated a skillful means, desiring to arrange a marriage for him.

At that time, there was a king named Rājā Dharmapāla who heard that [the merchant] had a daughter whose beauty was peerless in the world. The king immediately dispatched an envoy to announce his request for her hand in marriage, pointing out one of her elder brothers by his physical appearance and saying, "For the sake of this son, I seek your daughter."
The envoy, having received these instructions, arrived and fully conveyed the King’s words; the Vinaya Master Batsa immediately consented to the marriage.
The envoy returned and informed the King, who was greatly delighted. He promptly dispatched carriages and horses to go and fetch her back, and personally instructed Zhuwu:
"Do not see your wife during the day; from this day forward, you shall meet and unite with her only at dusk."
At that time, the wives of the sons gathered together and conversed, each praising her husband’s various talents and virtues.
Then, the wife of the stump-bodied man also praised her husband, saying:
"My husband possesses the strength of a fierce and powerful wrestler, yet his body is also delicate and soft; he is truly worthy of respect and affection."
The other wives said to her, "You need not say such things;
your husband’s appearance is exactly like a tree stump. If you were to see him by day, it would surely cause you to be struck with terror."

When the stump-woman heard this, she took it to heart. She preemptively covered a lamp and hid it in a secluded spot; once her husband had fallen asleep, she lit the lamp to look at his body. Seeing his physical form, she was struck with great terror and that very night, having prepared her carriage, returned to her own country.
At dawn he awoke, feeling profound sorrow; grasping his bow and holding his conch, he followed the tracks and pursued them until he reached that kingdom, where he stayed with a certain minister.
"Later, when six kings heard that the Vinaya Master Batsa had a daughter of exquisite beauty, each coveted her and raised armies, gathering their hosts to compete for her hand."
At that time, the legal advisor Batsa was greatly distressed and troubled; he summoned his ministers to deliberate extensively on the matter:
"If we grant it to one, the others will harbor resentment.
What expedient means can be employed to repel this fierce enemy?"
A certain minister said:
"We should divide this woman into six portions and give one to each army; thus their intentions may be appeased.
Another minister said:

"Furthermore, issue a heavy recruitment notice: to whoever can repel the enemy army, I shall give my daughter as a wife, share the kingdom with them to rule it together, and grant them further rewards.
The king agreed to this and immediately went forth to proclaim the recruitment.

At that time, Tālāghuṣa took up his bow and conch shell and went out of the city toward the bandits. He blew the conch and struck the bow; the six armies were struck with terror and, paralyzed by fear, could not move. He then entered their midst, severed the heads of the six kings, seized their crowns and ornaments, and captured their followers.

The Venerable Batsa was filled with great joy; he offered his daughter to him as a gift, honoring him as the Great King. Taking charge of the seven kingdoms and all the military forces, and leading his host of officers, he returned to his own country with his wife.

When the father-king heard of his arrival, he went beyond the borders to welcome him. Seeing that the army led by his son was exceedingly vast, he offered the kingdom to his son and exhorted him to become the great king.
His son refused, saying, "As long as my father still lives, it is not right for this to be so."
Returning to the palace, he interrogated his wife thoroughly, saying:
"Why did you abandon me and flee in the middle of the night before?
His wife replied:
"Your body is extremely hideous; upon first seeing it, one is struck with terror and thinks it is not that of a human.

Tālahuṃśi took a mirror and looked at himself, only to see that his head and body closely resembled a tree stump. Loathing his own form and finding no pleasure in even looking at himself, he went into the forest, intending to commit suicide.
Śakra, knowing this from afar, immediately descended to his side and asked for the cause of his distress.
He consoled him and gave him a precious jewel, saying to him:
"Always wear this jewel upon the crown of your head, and you shall attain a beauty as extraordinary as my own."
He immediately joyfully accepted it and placed it upon his crown, feeling his body become twice as extraordinary.
Returning to the palace, he took up his bow and conch shell, intending to go out to play.
The wife saw him but did not recognize him, so she immediately said to him: "Who are you?
Do not touch these things; if my husband returns, he might perhaps harm you."
He then said to his wife,
"I am your husband.
The wife did not believe him at all, and she spoke to him, saying:
"My husband is extremely ugly, yet your form is upright and handsome.
Who are you that you claim this man as my husband?
The husband then withdrew the jewel, restoring his original appearance.
The wife was both surprised and delighted, asking, "How could this be?
Her husband then explained everything in detail, recounting how he had obtained the pearl.
From that time forward, she came to respect and love her husband; the name "Stump" (*zhū wù*) was eliminated from then on, and she instead addressed him by the name "Sudāsaṇa."
Later, he thought to himself:
"I shall lead my troops and rebuild the palace city.
He immediately went out to observe a level and open location and commanded his people:
"It can be built here.
Four dragon kings came in human form and asked,
"If you wish to build a city, what materials will you use?"
Sudārā replied, "It should be made of earth.
The nāga spoke again:
"Why do you not use jewels?
He replied, "The city is vast; how could one obtain so many jewels?"
The dragon spoke again, saying:
"I shall grant it to you.
He then transformed the four sides, creating four great springs, and said to him:
"If one uses the water from the eastern spring to form a moat, it will become lapis lazuli;
if one uses the water from the southern spring to form a moat, it will become gold;
if one uses the water from the western spring to form a moat, it will become silver."
"If one uses water from the northern spring to construct the moat, it will become crystal.
He immediately issued the command for its construction; as he had said, it became a precious gem, and he then ordered the building of a city four hundred li square.

He further commanded the construction of a palace, forty *li* square in extent; its city walls, streets, lanes, towers, pavilions, houses, groves, and bathing pools were all adorned with the four precious substances, pure, magnificent, and exquisite, much like those in the heavens.
When the palace was completed, the seven treasures appeared in response; he brought the four regions under his governance and transformed the people to cultivate goodness.
"In this way, Great King!
If you wish to know who that Mahāśakrāri was at that time, it is none other than my father, King Śuddhodana, who is present now."
The mother at that time is now my own mother, Mahāmāyā.
That Prince Dīrgharāva of ugly countenance is now myself.
She who was the wife at that time is now Gopī.
He who was her father-in-law is now Mahākāśyapa.
Those six kings who sought to seize the girl by force of arms are now the six heretical teachers.

In that past age, he vied with me for physical splendor; I harmed him and seized his host of followers. Even unto this day, out of envy for fame and profit, he sought to challenge me; finding no skill to satisfy his heart, he threw himself into the water and died. I have gathered his followers, a multitude of nine hundred million people, as my own disciples.
At that time, King Bimbisāra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What kind of practice did Tārākṣa originally perform such that his power of merit and virtue was so strong, yet his form is so ugly?"
The Buddha again addressed the king:
"All things have their causes and conditions.
In the distant past, immeasurable and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī. Within that kingdom was a mountain of seers called Ṛṣigiri."
At that time, in the mountain of the seers, there was a pratyekabuddha who suffered from a wind disorder and required the consumption of oil; he went to the house of an oil-maker and begged for it.
The oil-maker became enraged and rebuked him:

"Your head is like a stump and your hands and feet are like axles; you refuse to earn a living by waiting upon others' households, nor do you seek to buy with money, but only wish to obtain things for nothing."
Although he scolded and rebuked him in anger, he nevertheless gave him the oil dregs.
The Pratyekabuddha, with a heart of profound reverence and admiration, accepted them and immediately set off to carry them away.
The oil-maker’s wife came out from outside; seeing the Pratyekabuddha, her heart was filled with deep reverence and admiration, and she asked:
"O Noble One! From where have you come?
What will you do with this oil-cake that you carry?"
The Pratyekabuddha spoke to her according to the facts.
The wife was filled with resentment; she went back, summoned him, and immediately took his bowl and filled it with oil, reproaching her husband, saying:
"You are truly not right; why did you give him oil dregs?"
"I urge you to repent and remove the fault of your speech.
The oil-presser felt remorse in his heart and offered a sincere apology; husband and wife, with one mind, said to the Pratyekabuddha, "If you require oil, please come to take it every day."

Later, the Pratyekabuddha returned several times to take oil; moved by the master's kindness and diligence, he manifested his supernormal powers before him, soaring into the void, emitting water and fire from his body, and performing various transformations such as dividing and rejoining his limbs.
The oil merchant and his wife, witnessing such a divine manifestation, were redoubled in their joy and their reverence increased greatly. Having seen this, the husband said to his wife:
"When we receive the karmic fruit of the merit from the oil you offered, may we be husband and wife together."
The wife said to her husband:

"You have uttered evil words toward a noble being (kalyāṇamitra) while offering only oil-cake without a pure heart; the place where you shall be born will be utterly hideous. How could I be your wife?"
The husband replied again:
"I have constantly worked hard to accumulate these oil supplies; why do you wish to give them away alone without sharing with me?
I will never consent to your demand that we become husband and wife."
The wife spoke again, saying:
"If I am your wife, upon seeing your ugly form, I shall abandon you and flee at night.
Her husband replied to her, saying:
"Even if you were to die, we would pursue you until we had captured you.
When the husband and wife had finished speaking, they took refuge in the Pratyekabuddha with body and mind, sincerely repenting their transgressions.
Then the Pratyekabuddha said to the oil-maker and his wife:
"By virtue of your gift of oil, my illness has been cured.
Now, what wish do you, husband and wife, seek to fulfill?"
"I shall grant you whatever you seek; you shall obtain it all.
The husband and wife were filled with joy and knelt upright, making this vow:
"In every place where we are born, whether among gods or humans, may everything accord with our wishes."
"Thus it was, Great King!
If you wish to know who that oil-seller was at that time, he was Tāla-hu-shi (Tārāśrī).
The wife of that oil-maker at that time was Tāla-hu-shi’s wife."

At that time, because he saw a pratyekabuddha whose appearance was like a stump with limbs resembling axles, and who, despite being given oil-cake dregs, responded with an angry expression and speech, due to these causes and conditions, his physical form in every place where he was born was initially extremely ugly, just as his previous harsh words had described.
However, because he later repented and joyfully gave good oil, in the places where he was born, he subsequently attained a handsome and upright appearance.
By virtue of having offered oil as a gift, he constantly obtained great strength such that no one among the many tens of millions dared to oppose him.

Due to the retribution of his merit and virtue, he became a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), enjoying the blessings of the four quarters, with the five desires following his heart’s will. Thus, the retribution for the deeds of good and evil is imperishable.
"Therefore, all of you should keep the essentials of the Way in mind, be cautious in body, speech, and mind, and practice the path of cultivation.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, King Bimbisāra and the other kings, ministers, and commoners, the fourfold assembly, as well as devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, having heard what the Buddha taught, some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat; some planted the roots of goodness for Pratyekabuddhahood; some gave rise to the mind of the unsurpassed Great Way; and some were even advanced to the stage of non-retrogression. All were filled with joy, paid their respects, and vowed to practice accordingly.
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume II.
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume III.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Yuan Wei dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.
15. Chapter Fifteen: The Gift of the Body as a Sacrifice (Sūtaśarīradāna-parivarta).
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One suffered from a wind ailment;
the physician-king Jīvaka prepared a medicinal ghee by blending thirty-two kinds of herbs, instructing the Buddha to consume thirty-two *liang* daily.

At that time, Devadatta constantly harbored jealousy; his mind was haughty and he aspired to be equal to the Buddha. Hearing that the World-Honored One was taking medicinal ghee, he felt a greedy longing and desired to take it himself.
He then commanded Jīvaka: "You must prepare some for me."
At that time, Jīvaka again combined them and said to him,
"Take four liang every day.
Devadatta asked:
“How many *liang* does the Buddha’s robe weigh? Jīvaka replied,
“Thirty-two *liang* per day.”
Devadatta said,
"I too shall take thirty-two *liang*.
Jīvaka replied:
"The body of the Tathāgata is not the same as yours; if you consume it in large quantities, it will surely cause you further affliction.
Devadatta said, "If I were to consume it, I would certainly be able to digest it myself. What difference is there between my body and the Buddha’s body?"

"Simply give it to me to take. He then imitated the Buddha, taking thirty-two *liang* every day as well. The medicine circulated through his veins within his body; because his physical strength was so feeble, he could not digest or transform it. All the joints and limbs of his body were afflicted with extreme pain; he groaned and cried out, distressed and tossing about in agony.
The World-Honored One, out of compassion, reached out his hand from afar to stroke his head; immediately, the medicine was digested and the painful affliction was eliminated.
Once he had recovered, he recognized the Buddha’s hand and said:
"Siddhārtha’s other arts were not adopted by the world, yet he further studied the way of medicine and became skilled at its application."
At that time, Ānanda, hearing these words, was filled with sorrow and resentment; he knelt for a long time and addressed the Buddha:

"Devadatta does not recognize the kindness shown to him. Although the World-Honored One has compassionately pitied him and removed his afflictions for his sake, he now utters such unwholesome words; what manner of heart is this?"
"Able to give rise to such a mind, having long harbored thoughts of jealousy and directed them toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One," Ānanda, the Buddha told him:
"Devadatta has not only harbored unwholesome intentions to harm me today; in past lives as well, he constantly harbored evil intent to kill me."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "I do not understand the circumstances regarding the injury from the past; what were its causes and conditions?
The Buddha said:
“Listen well!
I shall speak for you.
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”
"Listen with a single-minded focus.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a great city in this Jambudvīpa named Vārāṇasī."

At that time, there was a king named Brahmadatta, who was fierce and cruel, devoid of compassion; he was dissolute, lustful, and fond of pleasure, constantly harboring malice and jealousy, and delighting in inflicting harm.

At that time, the king suddenly saw a beast in a dream; its body hair was golden in color, and from the tips of all its hairs issued forth golden light that illuminated everything to its left and right, making them all likewise golden.
Having awakened, he thought to himself:
"As it was in my dream, this must certainly exist in the world; I shall command the hunters to seek out its hide.
Having formed this thought, he summoned the hunters and addressed them, saying:
"I have dreamed of a beast whose body hair is golden; from the tips of each hair, light radiates, exquisite and brilliant.
I suspect that such a creature must surely exist within our kingdom's borders. I rely upon you all to travel far and wide to seek it out and capture it."
"If you obtain its skin, I shall grant you a heavy reward, so that your descendants may consume it for seven generations;
if you do not apply your minds and fail to find it, I shall utterly exterminate all of you and your clansmen."
At that time, having received the king’s command, the hunters were filled with grief and confusion; having no further plan, they gathered in one place and deliberated together on this matter:
"The beast dreamed of by the king is one never seen before in our lives; where should we seek it?"
"If we do not obtain it now, the royal law is difficult to violate, and we, our kindred, will forever have no way to survive.
Having discussed this matter, their distress increased all the more.
Furthermore, another said:

"In these mountain marshes, venomous insects and fierce beasts are also exceedingly numerous. To travel far in search [of him] will surely yield no result; instead, you will lose your life and perish, exhausted in the wilderness. For now, let us secretly hire one man and send him to seek him out."
The crowd said, "Excellent! and after selecting one among them, they exhorted him earnestly:
"You must exert all your strength to search far and wide. If you return safely, we shall combine our resources to reward you handsomely;
even if you should meet with misfortune in the mountains or marshes and fail to return, we shall still provide for your wife and children with these goods."
Upon hearing this, the man thought to himself:
"For the sake of these people, I shall sacrifice my life; having resolved this within myself, I may now proceed."

Having prepared his travel provisions, he set out across the perilous terrain. After traveling for a long time, his body was emaciated and his strength exhausted. Amidst the intense heat of the season, he reached a road of scorching sand; his lips were parched with thirst and he was so overcome by the stifling heat that he felt as if he were dying.
In extreme agony and bitter distress, he spoke in grief and exhaustion: "Who possesses compassion? Who will take pity on me?"
"Please grant me rescue and deliverance; save my life!

At that time, within the mountain wilderness, there was a wild beast named Śṛgāla, whose body hair was golden and whose tips of the hairs radiated light. Hearing his words from afar, it felt profound compassion for him.

He entered a cold spring and came to where [the man] was; he wrapped himself around and embraced him, and as his strength returned slightly, he led him to the water's edge to bathe him, gathered fruits and melons, and brought them for him to eat.
Once his body had recovered, he thought to himself:
"Beholding this extraordinary beast, its fur and color so radiant, it is exactly what my Great King requires;
yet I was on the verge of death and relied upon it to save my life. Grateful for its kindness, I have not yet been able to repay it—how could I now conceive the thought of harming it?"
"If I do not capture them, those hunters, along with their kinsmen and followers, shall be put to death.
Having thought this, he was overcome by grief beyond measure.
Gautama asked,
"Why are you unhappy?
She wept as she spoke of the matters harbored in her heart.
Gautama said: "Do not worry about this! My skin is easily obtained;
considering my past lives, I have sacrificed my body countless times, yet never for the sake of merit, so I can now sacrifice my life."
"Now, by using this skin of my body to save the lives of those many beings, my heart is filled with joy as if I have gained something of great value.
You may simply strip away the skin, but do not take my life; I have already given it to you, and I shall never feel regret."
At that time, the hunter slowly began to flay the skin. Then Jñāta immediately made this vow:

"Now, by giving this skin to this man, I save the lives dear to these many people. By the merit of this act, I dedicate it to all sentient beings, so that they may attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of Buddhahood, universally deliver all from the sufferings of birth and death, and be established securely in the place of eternal bliss, Nirvana."

Having made this vow, the three thousandfold world-system shook in six ways; the palaces of the various devas trembled and became restless, and being each struck with astonishment, they sought to discern its cause.
Seeing the Bodhisattva being flayed as an act of giving, he immediately descended from the heavens to where the Bodhisattva was, scattering flowers as an offering and shedding tears like rain.

After his skin had been stripped away, his body and flesh were laid bare; blood flowed and dripped, making him difficult to behold. Furthermore, eighty thousand flies and ants gathered upon his body and began devouring him all at once.
At that time, as he was about to enter the hole, he feared being harmed; enduring the pain and maintaining his composure, he kept his body from moving, offering himself as a gift and died therein.
At that time, the flies and ants that had crawled upon the Bodhisattva’s body all attained rebirth in the heavens after their lives ended.
Then the hunter, carrying the skin, arrived at the kingdom and presented it to the king.

The king saw it and was filled with joy; he marveled that such a thing had never been seen before. Finding its texture so fine and soft, he used it constantly for bedding and reclining; his mind thus became peaceful and secure, and his heart was filled with happiness.
Thus it was, Ānanda!
If you wish to know who that Śṛgāla was at that time, he is none other than my own self today.
That King Brahmadatta is none other than Devadatta today.
"The eighty thousand worms were those eighty thousand devas who attained the Way when I first became a Buddha and began to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
This Devadatta, during that past life, harmed me; even until today, he still lacks a virtuous heart, constantly thinking of how to harm me and seeking to bring me injury."

When the venerable Ānanda and all those gathered there heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were filled with both sorrow and longing; each was moved to self-exhortation and diligently sought the essentials of the Dharma. Some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat; some planted the causal conditions for Pratyekabuddhahood; some resolved upon the unsurpassed path of the Buddha; and some dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression. All were filled with joy, reverently upholding and practicing [the teaching].
Chapter Sixteen: The Chapter on the Bhikṣuṇī Subhadrā (16) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove Monastery.

After King Prasenajit passed away, his crown prince, Vidūḍabha, took charge of the government and acted as king; he was tyrannical and unrighteous, driving forth intoxicated elephants to trample and kill the people in numbers beyond reckoning.
At that time, the women of noble families, seeing him in such a state, felt their hearts break with grief; finding no joy in worldly life, they immediately went forth together to become bhikṣuṇīs.

The people of the kingdom, seeing these women—some of the Śākya clan and some of the royal lineage—who were noble, upright, and the most beautiful in the land, all renounced their desires to leave the home life for the path; there were five hundred such individuals, all of whom were praised with admiration and vied with one another to make offerings.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to one another:

"Although we have now left the household life in name, we have not yet taken the medicine of the Dharma to eliminate lust, anger, and ignorance. Why should we not go together to the bhikṣuṇī Sthūlanandā to inquire about and receive the teachings of the sūtras, hoping thereby to achieve our goal?"
They immediately went to where he was, paid their respects, and inquired after his well-being, each expressing their thoughts:
"Although we have set out on the path to the Way, we have not yet attained the Ambrosia; we pray that you will enlighten us."
At that time, Steunānanda thought to herself:
"I shall now instruct her so that she turns back from the precepts; would it not be a joy for me to take up my robes and bowl?"
He then said to them:
"You are of noble and distinguished lineage; your fields, seven treasures, elephants, horses, and servants are all provided for without lack. Why do you abandon these?"

"Maintaining the Buddha's prohibitions and precepts as a bhikṣuṇī involves such hardship; it would be better to return home, where husband, wife, sons, and daughters may enjoy one another’s company and practice generosity at will, bringing glory to this life."
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard these words, their hearts were filled with despondency; they immediately wept and departed from her.

They then went to the bhikṣuṇī Subhadrā, prostrated before her, and exchanged greetings according to the Dharma. Each of them addressed her, saying: "We lived as householders for a long time, long accustomed to worldly customs.

Although we have now left the home life, our minds remain dissolute and unruly; our passions burn fiercely and we cannot free ourselves. We pray that you will take pity on us, preach the Dharma for us, and open up and release the shroud of our transgressions."
At that time, Subhadrā immediately addressed them, saying:
"Regarding the three periods of time, what do you wish to ask?
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
“Setting aside the past and future for now, I pray you will explain the present so as to untie the knots of my doubt. Miaowu replied:

“As for lustful desire, it is like a raging fire burning through mountains and marshes; its spreading tendrils are most extensive, and the damage it inflicts is ever more widespread. Because people dwell in lustful desire, they harm one another; as days and months pass, this grows ever greater until they fall into the three miserable realms, with no time of escape in sight.”

Now, those who cherish their households are greedy for the union of kin, the causes and conditions of affection, honor, and pleasure. Yet they must endure separation through birth, old age, sickness, and death, as well as the afflictions of government officials. They weep and pine for one another in turn, their hearts and livers wounded and broken; they faint and then revive again. Their attachment to the household is deep and firm, binding their minds and wills more tightly than a prison.
I was originally born into a family of brahmins; my father was noble and foremost in the kingdom.

At that time, there was a son of a brahmin who was intelligent and wise; having heard that I was handsome and upright, he immediately sent a matchmaker to propose marriage, taking me as his wife. Thus we established a household, and later children were born to us.
The parents of my husband’s family subsequently passed away.
At that time, I was pregnant and said to my husband:
"I am now carrying a child; I am impure and unclean, and the months are nearly full. Should I fall into a state of grave distress, you must return to my home to see my parents."
The husband replied, "Very well.

He then sent her back; however, halfway on the road, her body pains intensified, so she stopped beneath a tree. At that time, the husband lay down separately, while I was giving birth in the night. A great amount of foul-smelling discharge flowed out, and a venomous snake, smelling the odor, came and killed the husband.

At that time, I called out to him several times during the night, but there was no sound. As dawn approached, I rose by my own strength and went to take my husband’s hand; I realized he had been poisoned by a snake, for his body was swollen and festering, and his limbs were falling apart.
When I saw this, I immediately fainted.
At that time, my eldest son, seeing his father’s body dead, wailed aloud with a broken voice.

Hearing my son's cry, I immediately regained consciousness; I then took my eldest son, placing him upon my shoulders, while my younger son embraced me from behind. We proceeded on our way weeping, though the road was vast and perilous, utterly devoid of any people.

Upon reaching the middle of the road, there was a great river, both deep and wide; he left the elder son behind on the bank, first carried the younger son across to the other side, and returned to fetch the elder.
When the child saw me from afar, he immediately came into the water, but the current swept him away;
I pursued him, yet my strength was insufficient to save him, and he drifted away, sinking and surfacing.
I then returned, intending to go to the boy, but the wolf had already devoured him; I saw only his blood flowing and scattered upon the ground.
I fainted again and remained unconscious for a long time before regaining consciousness.
Continuing on my path, I encountered a brahmin who was a close friend of my father;
he immediately asked me, "From where have you come, that you are so exhausted and emaciated?"
I then related to him in full detail all the bitter sufferings I had endured.
At that time, the brahmin, pitying my solitary suffering, wept aloud as he faced me.
I asked the brahmin:
"Are your parents and kinsmen all in peace?
The brahmin replied,
"In my family, recently a fire broke out, and my parents and all my relatives died at once."
When I heard this, I immediately fainted again; only after a long while did I regain consciousness.
The brahmin took pity on me and brought me home, providing for me without lack and caring for me as if I were his own son.
At that time, another brahmin, seeing that I was handsome, sought me as his wife; I immediately gave my consent, and we were soon joined in marriage.
I subsequently became pregnant, and the months of gestation were fulfilled.

At that time, my husband went outside to drink wine at another's house and returned at dusk. I was then in the throes of labor and was alone inside with the door closed. While the birth was not yet complete, the Brahmin knocked on the door and shouted loudly; as no one went to open it, the Brahmin grew enraged, broke down the door and entered, whereupon he immediately began to beat me. I explained the situation to him exactly as it was, but the Brahmin became even more furious and then seized the child and killed him.
They fried him in ghee and forced me to eat him.
I was deeply distressed and could not bear to eat it, yet I was beaten for my refusal.

After eating my son, my heart was bound with grief; I thought to myself that my merit had been exhausted that I had encountered such a man. I then fled and went to Vārāṇasī, where I sat down to rest beneath a tree outside the city.

At that time, there was a son of an elder in that country who had recently lost his wife; he buried her in a garden outside the city and, out of longing and affection for her, went out to the cemetery every day to weep and wail at her grave.
At that time, seeing me, he immediately asked me:
"Who are you? Why are you sitting alone by the side of the road?"
I spoke to him exactly as it was, and he said to me again:
"I now wish to enter that garden with you; would you be willing?
I agreed, and so we became husband and wife.
After several days had passed, the son of the elder fell ill and could not be cured; suddenly, his life came to an end.
At that time, according to the laws of that country, whatever one held dear during life was to be buried together with them in the tomb on the day of the funeral.
Although I was buried, my life had not yet ended; at that time, a band of thieves came and opened the tomb.
Then the leader of the thieves, seeing that I was beautiful, took me as his wife.

Within several weeks, he again committed robbery and was discovered by his master, who immediately cut off his head. The thief’s subordinate followers then took the corpse and brought it back to me; we buried it together according to the local customs of the country, burying me along with it.

At that time, having been inside the tomb for three days, various wolves, foxes, and dogs came again to open the tomb, wishing to devour the dead person; I was once more able to escape, and I reproached myself severely:
"What calamity did I commit in my past life that, within ten days, I have encountered such suffering and misery?"
"Having died and returned to life, whom should I rely upon to preserve my remaining life?
He then thought to himself:

"I have often heard that the son of the Śākya clan left his home to study the Way; having perfected the Way, he is called a Buddha. He thoroughly understands the past and the future; I should go to him and take refuge with my whole being."
He immediately set out on his way, hastening toward the Jetavana. From afar he beheld the Tathāgata, who was like a tree in full bloom or the moon among the stars.
At that time, the World-Honored One, through his untainted threefold knowledge, perceived that I was ready for deliverance and came forth to welcome me.
At that time, my body was exposed and I had nothing with which to cover myself; I immediately sat upon the ground and covered my breasts with my hands.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Take a robe and go to cover that woman."

At that time, having obtained the robe, I immediately prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and fully recounted my misfortunes and afflictions, praying that he would look upon me with compassion and grant me permission to enter the Path.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Take this woman and entrust her to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, so that she may be granted the precepts.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī immediately accepted me and ordained me as a bhikṣuṇī; she then taught me the essentials of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.

Having heard this Dharma, I applied my mind with diligent effort and attained the state of an Arhat, reaching a thorough understanding of the past and the future. The hardships I have undergone in this present life are difficult to describe in full; they correspond exactly, down to the smallest fraction, to what was created in former lives.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs addressed him again, saying:
"What fault was committed in a previous life that has resulted in this calamity?
We pray that you will explain it to us."
Subtle replied:
"Listen attentively.

In a past age, there was a householder of immeasurable wealth who had no children. He took a younger wife; though she was from a humble family, she was peerlessly beautiful. Her husband loved her dearly, and she subsequently became pregnant."
When the ten months were complete, a son was born; the husband and wife held him in high esteem, never tiring of gazing upon him.
The senior wife thought to herself:
"Though I am of noble lineage, I currently have no offspring to carry on the family line."
If this child grows up, he shall take charge of the household; all the fields, wealth, and possessions must be held by him.
My labors have been in vain, for though I accumulated property, I could not enjoy it freely.

Jealousy arose within her immediately, and she thought, "It would be better to kill him early. Having made up her mind, she took an iron needle and pierced it into the fontanelle of the child's head, driving it in until it was no longer visible.
The child gradually became emaciated and wasted away; within ten days, he passed away.
The junior wife was overcome with grief, fainting and then reviving; suspecting that the senior wife had killed her son out of jealousy, she immediately asked her:
"In your shameless cruelty, you have murdered my son out of resentment."
The senior wife immediately took an oath, saying:

"If you kill my son, may I, in every lifetime, have my husband killed by a venomous snake; may those who have sons see them swept away by water or devoured by wolves; may I be buried alive while still breathing; may I devour my own children; and may my parents and all my kin die in a fire."
"Why do you slander me?
Why do you slander me?

At that time, [the person] was told: "There is no such thing as the retribution for sin or merit; the curses and oaths previously uttered must now all be endured by you, and there is no one who can take their place."
"If you wish to know who the senior wife was at that time, it was I myself.
The bhikṣuṇīs asked again:
"What further merit did she possess that she was able to behold the Tathāgata and go out to welcome him?"
"Can one attain dwelling in the Hall of the Path and thus escape birth and death?
Miao-miao replied:

"In the past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a great mountain named Ṛṣigiri. Within it, there were always Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, non-Buddhist practitioners, and celestial immortals, with no vacancies."
At that time, a Pratyekabuddha entered the city to beg for alms.
A householder’s wife, seeing him, was filled with joy and immediately made offerings to him.
After the Pratyekabuddha had finished eating, he ascended into the void, emitting water and fire from his body, and sat and lay down amidst the air.
When the wife saw this at that time, she immediately made a vow, saying:
"May I attain the Way in a future life just as this.
The wife of that time was none other than myself.
"Because of this very reason, I was able to see the Tathāgata; my mind was opened and liberated, and I attained the path of an Arhat.

Today, although I have become an Arhat, I am constantly tormented by glowing iron needles that enter through the crown of my head and emerge from the soles of my feet. Day and night I suffer from this, with no end in sight."
"Calamity and fortune are thus; they never decay.

At that time, when the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs of noble lineage heard this teaching, their hearts were struck with awe. They contemplated the root of desire as being like a blazing fire, and the mind of greed never arose again. They perceived the suffering of household life to be worse than a prison; all defilements were extinguished, and they simultaneously entered meditative concentration, attaining the path of Arhatship.
Each with a unified mind, they addressed the Sublime One, saying:
"We were entangled and bound by lustful desires, unable to extricate ourselves; now, having received your compassionate guidance, we have attained deliverance from birth and death."
At that time, the Buddha praised them, saying:
"How wonderful and subtle!
Those who practice the Way and are able to instruct one another with the Dharma and admonish each other can truly be called sons of the Buddha."
Upon hearing these words, the entire assembly was filled with joy; they bowed their heads in prostration and reverently put them into practice.
Chapter Seventeen: Aśoka Gives Earth. (In the Danben [Dunhuang manuscript], this chapter is the twenty-second, located in the fourth fascicle. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with Ānanda, entered the city for alms in the morning.
He saw a group of young children playing in the road, each gathering earth to construct palaces and dwellings, as well as granaries and stores of wealth, treasures, and the five grains.

There was a young child who, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar and beholding the radiance of his physical marks, felt a sense of reverence arise within him. Overjoyed and leaping for joy, he conceived the thought of making an offering; he immediately took some of what was called "grain" from the granary and, cupping it in his hands, wished to give it to the Buddha.
Being small in stature and unable to reach it, he said to a young boy,
"I shall climb upon your back to offer this grain as a gift.
The boy was delighted and replied:
"Very well," he replied.
He immediately stepped onto the Buddha's shoulder and offered the earth to him.
The Buddha then lowered his bowl and bowed his head to receive the earth; having finished receiving it, he handed it to Ānanda and said:
"Take this and smear my room.
Having obtained the alms-food, he returned to the Jetavana; Ānanda used the earth to smear the floor of the Buddha’s room, smearing it evenly along one side until the earth was completely exhausted.
Having soiled [the floor], he adjusted his robes and reported everything in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The boy who just now joyfully offered soil—enough soil to smear one side of the Buddha’s chamber—by virtue of this merit, a hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, he shall become a king named Aśoka.”

The next youngest child shall serve as a great minister, together governing all the lands of Jambudvīpa; he shall cause the Three Jewels to flourish and manifest, provide extensive offerings, distribute the śarīra relics throughout Jambudvīpa, and for my sake, erect eighty-four thousand stūpas.
Ānanda was filled with joy and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"What merits did the Tathāgata cultivate in the past that he has now received this retribution of so many stūpas?"
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda, listen attentively.”
In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a great king named Prasenajit who ruled over eighty-four thousand kingdoms in Jambudvīpa.
At that time, there was a Buddha in the world named Puṣya.
King Prasenajit, together with his ministers and subjects, made offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus through the four types of requisites, their veneration being immeasurable.
At that time, the king thought to himself:

"In this great kingdom, the various classes of people constantly have the opportunity to see the Buddha, prostrate to him, and make offerings. However, as for the people in other small kingdoms located in remote and secluded regions, they have no means to cultivate merit. I shall therefore commission paintings of the Buddha’s image and distribute them to all nations, so that everyone may make offerings."
Having formed this thought, he immediately summoned a painter and commanded him to create a portrait.
When the painters arrived before the Buddha, they observed his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), desiring to paint them; yet, as soon as they painted one part, they forgot the rest.
They looked back again and began once more, but forgetting one thing after another, they were unable to bring it to completion.
At that time, Buddha Puṣya blended various colors and painted with his own hand to create a model, producing one standing image.

Thereupon, the painters were able to depict all eighty-four thousand images, making them exceedingly pure and wondrous, upright and just like the Buddha himself; he distributed them to various kingdoms, giving one to each country.
Furthermore, he issued a proclamation to the people below, commanding them to prepare flowers and incense for making offerings.
When the kings, ministers, and subjects obtained the image of the Tathāgata, they received it with joy and reverence, regarding it as if it were the Buddha’s own body.
Thus it was, Ānanda!
King Prasenajit is none other than my present self.

Because in that past life I had paintings of eighty-four thousand Tathāgatas made, distributed them to various kingdoms, and caused people to make offerings to them, by virtue of this merit I have received blessings in birth after birth. Whether among devas or humans, I have always been a sovereign king; in every place where I was born, I was handsome and extraordinary, possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
"By virtue of this merit, you shall personally attain Buddhahood; after your parinirvāṇa, you shall further obtain the karmic reward of these eighty-four thousand stūpas.
When the worthy Ānanda and all those in the assembly heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
18. Chapter Eighteen: The Gift of Seven Jars of Gold (In the Danben [Dharmaguptaka] recension, this is Chapter Twenty-three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus each dwelt in different countries, observing the rains retreat according to their preference;
when the ninety days had passed and the retreat was concluded, they each went to where the Buddha was to receive his holy teachings.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having been separated from the bhikṣus for a long duration, felt compassion and pity for them with a heart of loving-kindness. He immediately raised his divine hand, marked with the thousand-spoked wheel, to comfort them, and with humble intent he inquired after their welfare: "O you all!..."
"Living in such a remote place, do you have no lack of food, drink, or offerings?
The Tathāgata’s merit is peerless in the world; yet now he lowers his mind to look upon the bhikṣus, showing exceptional humility and respect.
When Ānanda saw this, he was greatly astonished by the reason for it and immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, your appearance in the world is most extraordinary; your merit and wisdom are rare in this world."
Now you have lowered your mind to comfort and inquire after the assembly of bhikṣus; how excellent this is!
We do not know, World-Honored One, whether these words of such humility were intended for those far away or for those nearby?
The World-Honored One said:
"Do you wish to know?
Listen attentively and reflect well!"
"I shall explain it for you.
"I shall listen well to your instructions," [replied Ānanda].
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, incalculable, immeasurable, inconceivable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī."

At that time, there was a man who took great pleasure in attending to his household affairs. His mind was particularly fond of gold; he labored diligently to accumulate wealth, subjecting his body to toil and engaging in business in all four directions. Whatever money and goods he obtained, he spent entirely on buying gold. Consequently, he acquired a jar, which he dug into the ground inside his house and buried there.

In this manner, through various means, he diligently subjected his body to hardship for many years, never consuming food or clothing. He gathered [the relics] without ceasing until he obtained seven jars, all of which he took and buried.
Later, that man fell ill and passed away; because of his attachment to gold, he was reborn as the body of a venomous snake and returned to his house to guard that golden jar.

After many years had passed, that house fell into ruin and was uninhabited; a snake guarded the golden jar, its lifespan nearly exhausted. After casting off its body, its craving did not cease, and it again assumed its original form, wrapping its own body around the various golden jars.

In this manner, passing through tens of thousands of years in successive rebirths, at his final incarnation, a sense of revulsion arose within him again. He reflected upon his past: "For the sake of this gold, I have endured these foul forms without end."
"Thinking, 'I shall now bestow this upon the field of merit that brings swift fruition, so that I may receive its blessed retribution in every lifetime,' he deliberated and decided.
He went to the side of the road, hid himself within the grass, and remained concealed to watch, thinking, 'Should anyone come here, I shall speak to them.'"
At that time, a venomous snake saw a man passing by along the road and called out to him.
Hearing the call, the man looked to his left and right; seeing no one else, he heard only the voice and continued on his way.
The snake manifested its form again and called out, saying:
"Ho, man! Come near me."
The man replied to the snake, "Your body is poisonous and evil; why do you call for me?
If I draw near to you, I might be harmed."
The snake replied to the man,
"If I harbor such evil intent, even if you had not come, I would have been able to cause you harm.
Terrified, the man went to where the snake was.
The snake spoke to the man, saying:
"In this place of mine, there is a jar of gold. I wish to entrust it to you for the purpose of making offerings and performing meritorious deeds; would you be able to do so?"
"If you do not do so, I shall kill you.
The man replied to the snake, "I can do it."
Then the snake led the man together to where the gold was, took out the gold and gave it to him, and further told him:
"Take this gold and offer it to the assembly of monks. On the day you provide the meal, remember me well and bring one *aśvattha* tree here; I shall take it upon myself and carry it away."

The man carried the gold to the saṃghārāma and entrusted it to the *karmadāna*, recounting all that had occurred to the Saṃgha. He said that a venomous snake had wished to provide an offering and had set a specific date for the meal.

The monks accepted the gold and prepared a fine meal for him. When the day arrived for the meal to be served, the man took a small *aśvattha* leaf and went to where the snake was. Upon seeing the man, the snake felt great joy; it greeted him with kind words and comforted him, then coiled its body and climbed onto the *aśvattha* leaf.
Thereupon, the man covered [the snake] with a cloth and carried it toward the Buddhist temple.
On the way, he met another person who asked the man carrying the snake,
"Where have you come from?"
"Is your health good?

The man remained silent and did not answer his question; though asked repeatedly, he uttered not a single word. The venomous snake he carried then became enraged, its poisonous heat blazing intensely as it sought to kill the man, yet it recoiled and struck itself.
He further reflected to himself:
"What kind of person is this?

Not knowing the propriety of timing, when others inquire with good intentions about his well-being and movements, asking three times with great earnestness, he offers not a single word in reply; how can he be so abrupt?"
Having had this thought, his poisonous intent arose once more; a fierce malice welled up within him, and he desired to harm him again.
Just as he was about to unleash his venom, he reflected further:
"This man has performed meritorious deeds for me, yet I have not yet repaid his kindness."
Thus he spoke a second and a third time, yet [the man] still remained prostrate.
"This person has already done me a great kindness; although he has committed a transgression, it is right that I endure it."
Having gone forward to an open space, the snake said to the man,
"Set me down upon the ground.
He then exhorted and instructed him most earnestly with the Dharma.
Thereupon, the man immediately reproached himself, gave rise to a humble mind, and began to show compassion toward all beings.
The snake admonished him once more, saying: "Do not do this again!"
The man, carrying the snake, arrived at the saṃghārāma and placed it before the assembly of monks.
At that time, the monks had reached the hour for their meal and stood in rows.
The serpent instructed the man to distribute the incense in succession, while he himself, with a mind of faith, gazed upon those receiving the incense.

When the incense was thus exhausted, he continued to look intently without wavering. As the assembly of monks led him forward to circumambulate the stupa, the man took water and washed the hands of the monks; the serpent, harboring a spirit of reverence, watched the man washing their hands without ever feeling weary.
When the assembly of monks had finished eating, [the layman] again preached the Dharma extensively for the sake of the snake.

The snake was doubly joyful and further increased its resolve to give; it took the *karmadāna* (monastic administrator) to the place where the original gold was kept, and offered all six remaining jars of gold to the Sangha.
Having completed his meritorious deed, he passed away; by virtue of that merit, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who that man carrying the snake was at that time, could it have been anyone else?"
I am that very person.
The venomous snake of that time is now Śāriputra.

When I was carrying the snake in days past, I was rebuked by it; filled with shame and remorse, I made a vow, cultivated a humble mind, and came to regard all beings with equanimity, never once wavering from that resolve until this very day.
At that time, the bhikṣus, including Ānanda and the others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter Nineteen: Kṣema’s Manifest Retribution (Kṣema-pratyakṣa-vipāka-parivarta). [In the Danben edition, this is Chapter Twenty-four. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, together with a vast assembly of his honored disciples.

At that time, there was a brahmin in the kingdom who lived in poverty and destitution, lacking both money and grain. Though he labored with tireless diligence, his misfortunes only grew more severe until his resources were utterly exhausted. With food and clothing no longer provided, he went to ask others:
"In this world, what practice can one perform so that a person may enjoy its blessings in their present life?"
Someone replied, "Do you not know?
Now a Buddha has appeared in the world, bringing blessings to deliver sentient beings and bestowing benefits upon all; there is none who does not attain liberation."

The Tathāgata further has four honored disciples—Mahākāśyapa, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and Aniruddha. These four worthy ones constantly take pity on those who are destitute and always practice acts of merit and benefit for sentient beings suffering in distress.
"If you can now, with a heart of faith and reverence, provide food and offerings to these worthy sages, then your wishes shall be fulfilled in this present life.

When the brahmin heard what the people had said, his heart was filled with joy. He went into the kingdom and traveled everywhere, advertising himself and performing manual labor to obtain a small amount of wealth. Carrying it to his home, he prepared food and drink, invited the worthy sages, and made offerings for one day, exerting himself with a focused mind in hopes of a reward in this present life.

The Brahmin woman, whose name was Kṣema (translated into Chinese as "Peaceful and Secure"), had finished serving the meal to the Saṃgha. Then the venerable disciples exhorted Kṣema to receive the eightfold fast; once she had received the fast, they each returned to their respective monasteries.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, while returning from a stroll in the forest groves toward the city, saw on the road a man who had committed a grave offense against the king; he was bound to the top of a stake and stood by the roadside. Seeing the king, the man felt sorrowful and begged for a little food.
The king’s heart was moved with compassion, and he intended to grant him the request, but just as he did so, they parted ways.
The king spent the entire day completely forgetting his previous promise; at night, he suddenly thought to himself:
"I previously promised that criminal a meal; how is it that I have suddenly forgotten?"
Immediately, he dispatched people to deliver food to him, but throughout the palace, both inside and out, there was no one willing to go. They all spoke thus:
"It is now midnight; we fear there may be fierce beasts, evil spirits, or rākṣasas on the road, and such calamities are many. We would rather die here than go."
At that time, the king, mindful of that man’s suffering and his afflictions of body and mind, felt profound compassion and immediately issued a decree throughout the kingdom:
"Whoever can deliver food to that man shall be rewarded with one thousand taels of gold."
Among the people of the kingdom, there was no one who accepted the recruitment.
At that time, Cāmā had often heard people say:

"If there are people in the world who observe the eight precepts of the fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), then all malevolent spirits, venomous beasts, and every kind of calamity will be unable to cause them harm."
Upon hearing this, Kṣema gave rise to this thought:
"My family is poor, and moreover, I am observing the fast; what the King is now recruiting for must surely be intended for me. I shall go now to receive the reward for this service."
Having thus resolved, he went to respond to the king's recruitment.
At that time, the king spoke again to Kṣema:
"Carry food for me to that person; if you reach him and return safely, I shall certainly give you one thousand pieces of gold."
Kṣema immediately carried [the food] as instructed; he maintained the fast with a sincere heart without any deficiency, proceeding along the road.
As he traveled further out of the city, he encountered a rākṣasa named Lambā.
At that time, the ghost gave birth to five hundred sons; as soon as they were born, they were overcome with extreme hunger and thirst, and seeing Cāma approaching, they hoped to have him for food.

However, as Khaṇḍadravya observed the fast without fail, the rākṣasa saw him and was struck with fear; yet, driven by hunger, he manifested his form and begged for the food she was carrying, saying, "Give me a small portion."
Kṣema did not resist and gave him a small portion; although what she bestowed was little, by the power of the spirits and deities, it served to satisfy them.
At that time, the rākṣasa asked Kṣema, "What is your name?"
The woman replied,
"My name is Kṣemā.
The rākṣasa was delighted and said to Kṣemā:

"Now that I have been restored to safety through my divided body, it is because of you that my life was saved; your benefit to me has been no small matter. Since I have received this life and furthermore heard such auspicious words, there is a cauldron of gold in the place where I dwell. Take this to repay you when you come; remember to take it."
Again he asked,
"Where do you wish to go? Kṣema replied:
"I wish to take this food and give it to that person.
Lambā spoke again:

"I have a younger sister who lives ahead of me; her name is Ālambā. If you see her, inquire after her for me, saying that I have divided my body and given birth to five hundred sons, and that my physical well-being is secure. Convey my feelings fully so that she may know of my news."
Kṣema followed these instructions and departed along the path.
Upon seeing Ālambā, he immediately went out to greet her and related the full details of his situation regarding Ālambā: that she had given birth to five hundred sons, all of whom were safe and well.
At that time, Ārāmā heard this and was filled with joy;
she asked the woman, "What is your name now? The woman replied:
“My name is Kṣamā.
When the rākṣasa heard this, he was also filled with joy, saying, “My sister has been restored to her former body and has attained peace; your name is also auspicious—how wonderful!”
"In this dwelling place there is a cauldron of gold; I shall give it to you, so remember to take it when you return.
He asked him again, "Where do you intend to go?"
Kṣema replied,
"I was carrying food for the king when I arrived at that person's place. Alambā said:
"I have a younger brother named Fen-na-qi who lives on the road ahead; please convey my greetings to him and deliver my sister's message.
Having said this, they took their leave and proceeded along the way.

Upon arriving before her as she wished, he saw that she was truly extraordinary; he explained the circumstances of his intention in detail to her two elder sisters, saying, "That elder sister has given birth to five hundred sons; her body is light and at ease, and there is nothing inauspicious."
At that time, Śrīnandā, having heard news that her two elder sisters were safe and well, was filled with joy and asked Kṣemā:
"What is your name?"
The woman replied,
"My name is Cāmā. The ghost answered:
“Your name is Peaceful (An-yin), and furthermore you bring news of my sister’s well-being; how much more joyful this is!
He then said to Kṣema:
“In this place where I dwell, there is a cauldron of gold which I shall leave for you; when you come back, remember to take it.”
Having finished their parting, he led the way and departed.

Recalling his former dwelling, he went to that man's place; after providing him with food, he returned to his own location, took three cauldrons of gold, and carried them to the man's house. Furthermore, at the royal court, he received a reward of one thousand *liǎng* of gold. Thereupon, the man’s family was pulled from poverty and immediately became wealthy.

The common people within the kingdom, seeing that his household abounded in wealth and treasures, each yearned for him and joyfully became his attendants; they came to his house to serve and carry out his commands.
When the king heard that this man’s merit was such as this, he immediately summoned him to the palace and appointed him as a high minister.

Having received the king’s stipend and his own household being wealthy, he became sincere and devout in his faith, extensively cultivating meritorious deeds; he invited the Buddha and the Sangha to perform a great act of giving.
The Buddha and his retinue all accepted their invitation.
When the meal was finished, the Buddha preached the Dharma for them; their minds were opened and liberated, and they attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
At that time, the members of the assembly, including Ānanda and the others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter 20: The Poor Woman Nandā (Twenty) [In the Danben edition, this chapter appears in the eleventh fascicle as the fifty-third. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, there was a woman in the kingdom named Nanda, who was poor and solitary, sustaining herself by begging.
Seeing the kings, ministers, and subjects—both great and small—each making offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks, she thought to herself:
"Due to my past misdeeds, I have been born into poverty and lowliness; though I have encountered this field of merit, I have no seeds."
Bitterly grieved and deeply remorseful, he went forth to beg for alms to provide a modest offering.
He did not cease his efforts until the day was spent, yet he obtained only a single coin; carrying it to an oil merchant’s house, he intended to buy oil with it.
The oil merchant asked, "I bought this oil for a single coin; it is too little to be of much use.
What shall I do with it? Nanda told him everything he was thinking.
The oil merchant, moved by compassion, gave him twice as much oil.

Having received it, he was filled with joy; the amount was sufficient to make a single lamp. He carried it toward the monastery and offered it to the World-Honored One, placing it among the many lamps before the Buddha, and made this vow:
"I am now poor, yet I have used this small lamp to make an offering to the Buddha."
"By this merit, may I attain the illumination of wisdom in future lives and extinguish all the defilements and darkness of sentient beings.
Having made this vow, he prostrated to the Buddha and departed.
When night had ended and all the lamps were extinguished, this one alone continued to burn.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana was on duty for his turn; observing that it was already dawn, he gathered up the lamps and tidied away the implements. Seeing this single lamp burning alone with a bright and fine light, its oil and wick undiminished as if it were a lamp newly lit, a thought arose in his mind:
"To burn a lamp during the day is of no practical use."
"If I wish to extinguish it, I shall plan to have it reignite by evening.
He immediately raised his hand and fanned the lamp out, yet the flame remained as before, without being diminished or extinguished;
he fanned it again with his robe, but the light of the lamp was not impaired.
The Buddha, seeing that Maudgalyāyana intended to extinguish this lamp, said to him:

"This lamp cannot be moved or extinguished by you, a śrāvaka. Even if you were to pour the waters of the four great oceans over it, it would still not be extinguished, for it is fanned by the wind of the *vairambha*."
"Why is this so? This is a gift bestowed by one who has developed the great resolve for universal salvation.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the woman Nanda came again to the Buddha and prostrated herself at his feet; thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately conferred upon her a prediction of enlightenment.
"In a future age, after two hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Dīpaprakāśa, fully endowed with the ten titles.
Thereupon, Nanda, having received this prediction, was filled with joy; he knelt upright and addressed the Buddha, requesting to leave the household life.
The Buddha immediately granted her permission, and she became a bhikṣuṇī.

When the venerable Ānanda and Maudgalyāyana saw that the poor woman had been delivered from her suffering and misfortune, had left the household life, and received her prediction of enlightenment, they knelt long upon their knees with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What past deeds did this woman Nandā perform such that for so long a time she lived in poverty, subsisting on alms?"
"Furthermore, by what practice did he encounter a Buddha and leave the household life, such that the fourfold assembly revered him and vied with one another to offer him support?
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"In the past, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa."

At that time, there was a householder’s wife in the world who went in person to invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; however, the Buddha had already accepted an invitation from a poor woman to receive her offerings, for that woman had already attained the stage of anāgāmin.

At that time, the householder’s wife, relying on her own wealth, looked down upon the poor; she resented that the World-Honored One had first accepted the invitation from the beggar and spoke again, saying:
"Why does the World-Honored One not accept my offering, but instead first respond to the invitation of that beggar?"
Because of those evil words, he treated the worthy and holy ones with contempt; from that time forward, for five hundred lifetimes, he was always born into poor, lowly, and beggarly families.

Because on that day he made offerings to the Tathāgata and the Saṅgha with a heart of reverence and joy, he has now encountered the age of a Buddha, left the household life, received his prediction of enlightenment, and is revered by the entire nation.
At that time, when the assembly had heard the Buddha speak these words, they were all filled with great joy.

When the king, his ministers, and the common people heard that this poor woman had been granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood for offering a single lamp, they all conceived feelings of deep reverence and respect; each of them bestowed upon her exquisite garments and robes, so that she lacked nothing among the four requisites of life.

The men and women of the entire kingdom, from the noblest to the humblest, from the eldest to the youngest, vied with one another to prepare various fragrant oil lamps. Carrying them to the Jetavana, they offered them to the Buddha.

The multitude was so vast that the lamps filled the Jetavana; throughout the groves of trees, extending for four sides, they were everywhere, like a multitude of stars arrayed in the sky. This continued day after day for seven nights.
