At that time, Ānanda was filled with great joy and, extolling the various virtues of the Tathāgata, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not understand, World-Honored One! [What is the meaning of this?]”
"What roots of goodness did he cultivate in past lives to bring about this fruit of retribution, the offering of these infinite lamps?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, two asaṃkhyeya kalpas and ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a great king in this Jambudvīpa named Po-se-chi (Vāsava), who ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kingdoms within this world."

The King’s principal consort gave birth to a crown prince whose body was the color of purple gold, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. Upon the crown of his head was a natural jewel; all his features were brilliantly radiant, its light dazzling the eyes of men.
He immediately summoned a physiognomist to examine his features for signs of good or ill fortune and to bestow upon him a name.
As the physiognomist examined him, he marveled at his extraordinary qualities and, raising his hands, proclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!

Now this Prince is without equal among all the world’s devas and humans; if he remains at home, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, and if he leaves the home life, he will become a self-enlightened Buddha.
The physiognomist addressed the king, saying:
"When the prince was born, what extraordinary events occurred?
The king replied to him:
"A jewel of supreme brilliance emerged spontaneously from his crown.
They then bestowed upon him the name Ratnaśikhin, which in the Jin language means "Jewel-Crested.
As he gradually grew up, he left the household life to study the Way, attained Buddhahood, and taught and transformed the people, delivering a great many.
At that time, the father-king invited the Buddha and the Sangha to provide them with offerings for three months.

There was a bhikṣu named Arimira—translated into Chinese as Shengyou (Holy Friend)—who pledged to serve as the donor of lamps for the three-month period. Day after day, he entered the city and went to various elders, lay devotees, and common people to solicit ghee, oil, and lamp-wicks.

At that time, the king had a daughter named Muni who, standing upon a high tower, saw this bhikṣu entering the city daily to procure his necessities. A feeling of deep respect arose within her, and she sent someone to inquire:
"Venerable sir, you are constantly undergoing such toil; what is it that you are managing?"

The bhikṣu replied, "For three months now, I have been acting as a donor of lamps for the Buddha and the Saṃgha; therefore, I entered the city to visit the worthy ones to seek the requisites for ghee, oil, and lamp wicks, so that I might return and report my success."
The princess was delighted and spoke again to the Noble Friend:
"From this day forward, do not go begging again; I shall provide you with the necessary materials to make lamps."
The bhikṣu agreed.
From that time forward, he regularly sent supplies of ghee, oil, and lamp wicks to the vihāra.
The noble friend, the bhikṣu, attended to these matters daily, lighting lamps as an offering; his resolve was to bring universal relief, and his sincere heart was deeply devoted.
The Buddha bestowed upon him this prediction:
"In a future age, after incalculable kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Dīpaṃkara, and you shall be fully endowed with the ten titles."
When the princess Muni heard that the bhikṣu Āryamitra had received the prediction of his future Buddhahood, she thought to herself:
"The offerings made to the Buddha-lamp were entirely mine; the bhikṣu managed them, and now he has received the prediction while I alone have not."
Having formed this thought, he went to where the Buddha was and personally expressed his inner aspirations.
The Buddha again bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment, addressing the Muni:
"In a future age, after two asaṃkhyeya kalpas and ninety-one kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood, named Śākyamuni, fully endowed with the ten titles."
Thereupon, having heard the Buddha’s prophecy, the princess was filled with joy in her heart; she transformed into a man, prostrated again at the Buddha’s feet, and requested to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha then granted his permission, and [the bhikṣu] practiced with diligent vigor, cultivating [the path] assiduously without ceasing.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Was that bhikṣu Ālimi at that time anyone else?"
In the distant past, it was the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
As for the princess Muni, could she have been anyone else?
It was I myself.

Because of his former practice of offering lamps, from that time onward throughout incalculable eons, he has naturally received blessings in both the heavens and the world; his physical form was extraordinary and far surpassed that of others, continuing until his attainment of Buddhahood, for which reason he now receives this retribution of various lamps.

At that time, when the great assembly heard what the Buddha had spoken, some attained the first fruit up to the fourth fruit; some planted the roots of goodness for the path of the pratyekabuddha, and some gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment.
The Venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly all received this with reverence upon their heads, leaping for joy as they put it into practice.

*The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Three (21), Chapter Sixteen: “The Circumstances of King Mahāprabha’s Initial Arising of the Bodhicitta. There are those who possess wisdom and skillful means; because of even a minor circumstance, they are able to give rise to the great mind and advance toward the Buddha-way.
Conversely, those who are indolent and lazy do not give rise to the intent to advance toward the Buddha-way, even when presented with great circumstances.
Therefore, a practitioner should fortify the mind, establish resolve, and apply themselves with courageous and skillful conditions. How is this known?

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, surrounded before and behind by the fourfold assembly, as well as kings, ministers, and commoners, who were making offerings and paying him respect.
Thereupon, many within the assembly were filled with doubt, asking:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions did you originally resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, thereby achieving buddhahood yourself and bringing benefit to so many?"
"We, too, shall resolve to attain the Way and bring benefit and peace to all sentient beings.
Venerable Ānanda, knowing the thoughts of the assembly, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and stepped forward to address the Buddha:
"Now this great assembly is filled with doubt: [what is the cause for these various transformations?]"
“World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions did you originally resolve to attain the Great Way?
We only pray that you will explain this, for the broad benefit of all.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Excellent, excellent!
That which you have asked will bring great benefit to many.
Listen attentively and reflect well!”
"I shall now speak for your sake.

At that time, the great assembly was silent and still; the winds, rivers, and mountain streams, as well as the hundred birds and running beasts, were all hushed and made no sound. Thereupon, the great multitude—including devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts—were struck with awe and delighted to hear [the teaching], focusing their single minds upon the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Mahāprabha. He possessed great merit and virtue, was intelligent and courageous, and was fully endowed with the marks of a king."
At that time, there was a king on the frontier who was a close friend of the Great King Mahāprabha.
Whatever that country lacked, King Mahāprabha sent as gifts at appropriate times;
likewise, whatever that country prized, they also presented as offerings to King Mahāprabha.

At that time, while King Mahāśaila was out hunting, he captured two elephant cubs. They were upright and exquisite, as white as mountains of crystal, with their seven limbs touching the ground; they were most worthy of affection, and the king thought with joy:
"I shall now bestow these upon King Prabhāsa."
Having reflected thus, he adorned it with gold, silver, and various jewels—the most precious treasures in the world—and dispatched a messenger to deliver it.
When King Prabhāsa saw this elephant, his heart was filled with great joy.
At that time, there was an elephant trainer named Sañjaya. The king immediately commanded him, saying, "Instruct this elephant;
provide it with care and training until it is well-disciplined.
Sañjaya followed these instructions, and before long the elephant became docile and obedient. Adorned with a network of various jewels, he went to inform the king, saying:
"The elephant I have been training is now well-disciplined; I pray that Your Majesty will observe its performance.
Upon hearing this, the king was delighted and, eager to see it, immediately struck the golden drum to assemble his ministers and subordinates, ordering them to witness the trial of the elephant.

When the great assembly had gathered, the king mounted the elephant; just as the radiance of the sun shines forth when it first rises over the mountains, so too was the king when he first mounted the elephant.
Accompanied by his ministers and subjects, he went out of the city for recreation and approached the place of trial.
At that time, the elephant was full of vigor; seeing a herd of elephants feeding on lotus roots in a lotus pond, he became desirous of charging after a female elephant and thus entered a deep forest.
At that moment, the king’s crown and robes fell away entirely; his clothes were torn and his body wounded, with blood flowing as he pulled at his hair.
The king then became dizzy and, realizing he would surely die, was seized by extreme terror and asked the elephant trainer:
"Will I have any life remaining?"

Sañjaya said to the king, "Among the trees in the forest, there are some that can be grasped; I pray that Your Majesty will seize one, for only then can you remain safe. The king grasped a tree branch;

the elephant departed while the king remained behind. He descended from the tree and sat upon the ground, seeing that he was no longer wearing his robes or crown and that his body was mangled and wounded. Overwhelmed by great suffering and distress, he emerged from the forest in a state of confusion, unaware of where his attendants were.

The elephant trainer moved slightly forward, seized the tree, and brought the elephant to a halt. He returned to seek an audience with the king, who sat alone in distress. The trainer prostrated himself before the king and said:

"May Your Majesty not be so deeply grieved. This elephant’s lustful mind shall soon cease; he will grow weary of the foul grass, find no pleasure in the turbid water, and long for the pure, rich, and delicious food of the palace. In this way, he will return of his own accord."
The king then declared:
"I no longer think of you or the elephant; because of this elephant, I nearly lost my life.
At that time, the ministers all conceived the thought that the king had already been killed by the mad elephant.

Searching for the way and investigating everywhere, he sometimes found celestial crowns and garments, and sometimes saw fallen blood; eventually, he beheld the king returning to the city, riding upon a remaining elephant.
The people within the city, seeing the Great King undergoing such suffering, were all filled with grief and distress.

At that time, the mad elephant, while in the wild marshes eating bitter weeds and drinking turbid, foul water, its lustful desires subsided; it immediately longed for the cool, sweet delicacies of the royal palace and, moving like a swift wind, returned to its original dwelling place.
Having seen this, the elephant trainer went to inform the king, saying:
"Great King, you should know that the elephant lost previously has now returned; I pray that Your Majesty will look upon it."
The king said,
"I have no need for you, nor do I have any need for the elephant.
Sañjaya addressed the king:
"If Your Majesty has no need for me or the elephant, I only pray that you will observe my method of training elephants.
The king then had a seat prepared upon level ground.
At that time, the people of the kingdom, hearing that the elephant trainer intended to demonstrate the method of taming elephants to the Great King, all gathered like clouds.

Then the King left the palace, followed by a great multitude, and sat upon his throne. The elephant trainer, Sañjaya, led the elephant to the assembly; he then ordered a craftsman to fashion seven iron balls, heating them until they were glowing red. Having finished, he thought to himself:
"If the elephant swallows these balls, it will certainly die."
"The King might later regret it.
He addressed the Great King, saying:
"This precious white elephant is obtained only by a Wheel-Turning King; since there is now but a minor transgression, it should not be lost."
The king said to him:
"If an elephant is not tamed, it should not be made to carry me;
yet if it were well-tamed, such a calamity as this would not occur."
"Now you are no longer needed, nor is the elephant needed," he said.
The elephant trainer spoke again:
"Even though you do not need me, the elephant is truly to be pitied!"
The King’s rage intensified, and he cried out, "Go far away!
When Sañjaya had risen, he spoke with tears:
"Your Majesty has no sense of kinship or distance; your heart is like poison, though you feign sweet words."
At that time, the assembly, both great and small, having heard this, shed tears and gazed intently at the elephant.
The elephant trainer then made a sign to the elephant, saying:
"Swallow this iron ball; if you do not swallow it, I shall split your brain with an iron hook."
The elephant, knowing his thoughts, reflected to himself:

"I would rather swallow these hot pellets and die than endure being killed by iron hooks; it is as if between two kinds of death, one would prefer the death by hanging rather than the pleasureless death by burning."
Bowing his knee toward the king, he shed tears, looking for salvation.
The king’s anger was intense; having looked at him, he cast his gaze elsewhere.
Sañjaya addressed the elephant:
"Why do you not swallow this pill now?

At that time, the elephant looked in all directions and thought, "In this assembly, there is no one who can save my life. He took the pill with his trunk, placed it in his mouth, and swallowed it. It entered his belly and scorched him until he was consumed, passing straight through so that he died; it was like a vajra striking a mountain of crystal, for when the iron ball fell to the ground, it remained hot and red as before.
When those assembled witnessed this, there was none who did not weep with grief.
Upon seeing this, the king was struck with terror and astonishment; he gave rise to a sense of remorse and immediately summoned Sañjaya, saying:
"Your elephant is so well-tamed; for what reason were you unable to control it while it was in the forest?"

At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, knowing that King Prabhāsa was about to resolve upon supreme bodhicitta, immediately exercised their supernormal powers to cause the elephant trainer to kneel and answer the king, saying:
"Great King!..."
"I am only able to train the bodies of elephants, but I cannot train their minds.
The king then asked,
"Is there anyone else who can both train the body and also train the mind?"
He addressed the Great King, saying:
"There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One!
He is able to discipline both body and mind."
At that time, King Prabhāsa, having heard the name of the Buddha, was struck with awe and his hair stood on end; he addressed Sañjaya, saying:
"Regarding this one called 'Buddha,' from what lineage or nature is he born?"
Sañjaya replied:
"The World-Honored Buddha is born of two natures: first, wisdom; second, great compassion.

He diligently practices the six matters, namely the six *pāramitās*. Having fully perfected both merit and wisdom, he is titled 'Buddha'; having already been able to discipline himself, he also disciplines all sentient beings."

Upon hearing this, the king was struck with awe and leaped for joy. He immediately rose and entered the palace, bathed in fragrant water, and changed into new garments. Ascending to a high pavilion, he prostrated himself toward the four quarters, gave rise to a heart of great compassion for all sentient beings, and burned incense while making this vow:
"May all my merits be dedicated to the Buddha-way; once I have attained Buddhahood, having first disciplined my own mind, I shall likewise subdue and transform all sentient beings."

If, for the sake of even a single sentient being, one must remain in the Avīci Hell for the duration of a kalpa, provided it would bring them benefit, one should enter that hell and never abandon the bodhicitta.

Having made this vow, the earth shook in six ways; the mountains and great oceans surged and subsided. From within the void, the sounds of music arose spontaneously, and immeasurable devas performed celestial music and sang praises of the Bodhisattva, saying:
"By what you have accomplished, you shall attain Buddhahood before long.
Once you have realized the Way of the Buddha, we pray that you deliver us; we too should have a share in this pure Dharma assembly."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who was the white elephant that swallowed the iron balls at that time, it was Nanda.
The elephant trainer at that time was Śāriputra."
The King of Radiance was none other than myself.
At that time, because I saw that this elephant had been tamed and brought under control, I first resolved my mind upon the Way and sought the path of Buddhahood.

At that time, the great assembly, hearing that the Buddha’s ascetic practices were such as these, had some who attained the fruits of the four paths, some who resolved upon the mind of the Great Way, and some who left the household life to practice the Way; there was none who did not rejoice, receiving and upholding [the teaching] with the highest reverence.
For this reason, because of their resolute will and courage, those who possess strong determination can accomplish great matters even through minor causes and conditions;
whereas those who are indolent and lazy are unable to achieve anything, even when encountering great opportunities.
Therefore, practitioners should apply themselves with diligent vigor toward the path of the Buddha.
*The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Four.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Northern Wei dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.
21. The Chapter on the Upāsikā Mahāśrī (22). The Chapter on the Upāsikā Mahāśrī, the Twenty-first. [This chapter is absent from the Danben edition.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove Monastery, surrounded and honored by a great assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, the Buddha praised the practitioner of wisdom, saying: "One who wishes to achieve the Way of the Buddha should delight in the sutras and dharmas, reciting and expounding them. Even if a layperson preaches the Dharma, all devas and spirits will come to listen and receive it; how much more so for one who has left the household life?"

For those who have left the household life, even while walking along a road, as they recite the sūtras and speak gāthās, various devas constantly follow them to listen and receive the teaching; therefore, one should diligently recite and expound the Dharma of the sūtras.
How is this known?
When the Buddha first arrived at the Jetavana Monastery, his meritorious virtues spread abroad, such that there were none who did not hear and know of them.
At that time, all virtuous people, hearing of the Buddha’s name and virtues, felt immeasurable joy and extolled him with praise.
Why is this so? Because wicked people of the world, upon hearing the name of a virtuous person, give rise to hatred and jealousy, while rejoicing when they hear of an evil one;

whereas a noble and good person suppresses evil and promotes goodness, desiring that it be widely known, and seeing someone commit an evil act, recognizes the underlying fetters and afflictions, responding with compassion and forgiveness.
When such virtuous people heard that the Buddha had appeared in the world, they praised and propagated the news, causing it to spread throughout all lands.
At that time, King Prasenajit had a small frontier kingdom named Vaiṇuka.
At that time, the people in this village were mostly of wrong views, and there was no Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha.
In that village, there was a woman named Mahā-upasikā, who, due to some business, traveled to Śrāvastī to the presence of King Prasenajit.

When his business was concluded, he heard of the Buddha’s virtues from among the faithful upāsakas and, desiring to see the Buddha, went immediately to the Jetavana. There he beheld the Buddha’s physical marks and signs, which were exceptionally magnificent and sublime; he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the Dharma of the five precepts for the great assembly: by not killing one obtains long life; by not stealing one obtains great wealth; by not engaging in sexual misconduct one obtains the respect and affection of others; by not speaking falsely one obtains words that are trusted and believed; and by not drinking intoxicants one obtains intelligence and clear understanding.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, Upasena was filled with great joy and came forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will grant me the five precepts;
I shall uphold them purely for as long as I live, and even at the cost of my body and life, I shall never violate them."
"Just as a hungry person cherishes food and a thirsty person loves water, and just as a sick person guards their health with mindfulness, so too do I guard the prohibitive precepts.
At that time, the Buddha immediately conferred the five precepts upon him.
Having received the five precepts, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
My dwelling place is remote and secluded; I shall now return to my residence. I pray that you will grant me a small portion [of your robes], which I shall reverently offer."

All the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have all expounded the *Dharmapada*; all the Buddhas of the future, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shall likewise expound this sutra.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave the *Dharmapada* to Upasena, instructing him to recite and practice it.
Having received it, he paid homage, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed. Returning to his native village, he contemplated and recollected the sutra bestowed by the Buddha.
At that time, during the middle watch of the night, atop a high building, he contemplated the virtues of the Buddha and recited the *Dharmapada*.

Then, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, wishing to go to the southern realm of Virūḍhaka, was passing above Upoṣadha with a thousand yakṣas. Hearing the sound of his recitation, they all immediately halted in mid-air to listen to what he was reciting, and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Sisters! You have well expounded the essential points of the Dharma.
Now, were I to bestow upon you celestial jewels, it would not be appropriate for you."

I now offer you this kind word as a gift: the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana have come from Śrāvastī and will stay in this forest; you should go tomorrow to invite them to a meal at our home.
"When he offers his benediction, he shall also invoke my name.
Having heard these words, Upasena looked up into the air; yet he saw no form, like a blind man who sees nothing at all in the pitch-black darkness of night.
He immediately asked, saying:
"Who are you? I do not see your form, yet there is only your voice."
From within the air, he replied, "I am the celestial king Vaiśravaṇa; I dwell here for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
The upāsikā said:
"The heavens do not speak falsely.
You gods and I, being human, have no cause whatsoever; for what reason, then, do you address me as 'sister'?
The Heavenly King replied:
“The Buddha is the King of Dharma and the Father of gods and humans. I am an upāsaka and you are an upāsikā; since we share the same flavor of the Dharma, I call you sister.”
At that time, the upāsikā felt great joy in her heart and asked, “O Heavenly King!
When I make offerings, I invoke your name; what benefit does this bring?”
The Heavenly King replied:
“As a Heavenly King, my divine ear hears from afar; when anyone calls my name, I hear it all. Because they call upon me, my power, majesty, and retinue increase.”

"I, too, shall employ my supernatural powers and command the spirits and deities to protect and mind this person, increase their fortune and merit, and cause them to be free from decline and affliction.
Having spoken these words, he immediately departed.
At that time, the upāsikā was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, thinking to herself:
"For a hundred kalpas, the Buddha practiced diligent and arduous austerities solely for my sake; by the grace of the Buddha, he has caused this king of ghosts to become my sister."
He did not sleep at all; as dawn was about to break, he finally managed to rest for a short while.
At that time, a servant from his household was regularly sent into the forest to gather firewood. On this occasion, the servant went into the forest early and climbed a tree to collect wood.

From afar, he saw five hundred bhikṣus, including the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, in this grove; among them, those who were diligent sat in meditation and recited the sūtras, while those who were indolent lay upon the sand and grass.
Then that messenger hurried after his master and arrived at the kingdom of Śrāvastī; thereupon, seeing the two venerable ones from afar and recognizing them, he thought to himself:
"Those whom our master honors and respects are now here in this grove."

"You do not know that if I were to gather the firewood slowly and then return to inform you, there might be another person who happens to arrive first and take it away; in that case, I would be at fault."
"By reducing the task at hand, one first accomplishes this essential point; only afterwards does one gather firewood, so that there is no hardship in the work.
He then descended from the tree, went to where the Venerable One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Venerable One's feet, and said:
"My master, Upasena, pays homage at your feet and inquires after your health."
The Venerable replied,
“May Upasena be at peace, enjoy happiness, and be liberated from birth and death.
He then addressed him, saying:
"Venerable sir!
My master, Upāsīna, invites you for a meal tomorrow; we pray that you will deign to accept.
The Venerable replied:
"Return home and tell Upāsikā Suppavāsā:
'Excellent, laywoman!
You know the proper time and what is appropriate.'"

The Buddha praised five kinds of giving that yield immeasurable merit: namely, giving to those who have come from afar, giving to those who are departing for afar, giving to those who are sick and emaciated, giving food and drink during times of famine, and giving to those who know the Dharma.
"These five kinds of giving bring merit in the present life.
Having received these instructions, the messenger took his leave and departed from the grove, returning home with great haste. Upon arrival, he asked the maidservant where the mistress was.
He replied, "On that high roof, he could not sleep during the first and middle watches of the night; it is only now that he has begun to sleep.
The messenger said, "I shall go to wake him," but the master said, "I dare not inform him."
"If you are unable to do so, I shall wake him myself.
They all said, "As you wish.
The messenger went up onto the roof, snapped his fingers to wake him, and once he had awakened, asked:
"What do you wish to report? He replied,
"O Great Lady!"
"The Venerable Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others are in that grove.
Upasena was filled with great joy and immediately took off his two golden earrings to give them as a reward.
He then spoke again, saying:
"Venerable Sir, you have sent excellent instructions to us.
He then said:
"What excellent teaching do you have? You may speak it now.
He then explained it to her in detail by means of the five kinds of giving.
At that time, the laywoman’s joy surpassed her former state; just as a lotus flower blossoms upon seeing the sun, so too was her understanding and liberation at that moment.
He immediately untied the many-jeweled necklace from his own neck and bestowed it upon him with great weight.
The messenger said, "My lord has risen at the proper time;

he has washed his hands and prepared food and drink for offerings. I have already conveyed your instructions to invite the two Venerable Ones and their five hundred disciples to come and eat today; please ensure the preparations are made in due time."
Having heard these words, he was even more elated and said:
"That which I desired to do has already been done for me; it is beyond words how delightful this is!
I now release you; you no longer belong to me. As you are so virtuous, whether living at home or as a renunciant, may you shine with splendor wherever you are—whether in villages or cities."
Then Upasena rose immediately, washed his hands, and addressed his family members and neighbors:
"You should prepare the food; you should kindle the fire; you should fetch water; you should spread the mats; you should gather flowers."
Having thus completed the various preparations and divisions, he personally took the medicine, pounded it into a powder, and mixed it.
When the offerings were ready, he sent this man back to announce that the time had come, saying, "The meal is prepared; we pray you know the time."
Then the two elders, together with the bhikṣus, donned their robes, took up their bowls, and went to that house, where they sat down upon the seats.

At that time, Upasena personally served water with his own hands and set out various foods, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor. All conditioned phenomena receive retribution according to karma: by giving food of beautiful color, one obtains a fine complexion; by giving food of excellent fragrance, one obtains a far-reaching reputation; by giving food complete in flavor, one obtains the retribution of eating according to one’s desires and attains great physical strength.
When the community of monks had finished eating, the Venerable Śāriputra offered them a blessing.
As he was offering the blessing, Upasena said to him:
"Venerable One!..."
"I pray that you shall invoke the name of that Vaiśravaṇa Deva.
When Śāriputra had finished his benediction, he immediately asked:
"What karmic connection do you have with the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, such that you invoke his name?"
He said: "Venerable Sir!
There is a rare and marvelous occurrence."
"Because I recited the *Dharmapada* last night, that Heavenly King remained in mid-air to listen to my recitation of the sutra, and praised me, saying:
'Excellent, excellent!'"
"Sisters!
You have well expounded the sublime Dharma.
I then looked up and asked:
"Who are you? I do not see your physical form; is there only sound?
He replied to me, saying:
"I am the celestial king Vaiśravaṇa; having heard you reciting the sutra, I have stayed here to listen.
I wish to bestow upon you heavenly jewels as a gift, yet they are not suitable for you."
"Now I shall present you with some virtuous words. I then asked:
"What do you wish to tell me?"
He then said:
"Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana will arrive at such-and-such a grove tomorrow; you may invite them to your home for offerings, and when reciting prayers of blessing, please mention my name."
I then asked him, "What benefit is there in reciting your name?
He replied to me, recounting all the aforementioned matters in detail.
"For these reasons, I now praise him. Śāriputra said,
"Truly it is extraordinary!"
“You humans and those devas are able to humble themselves to converse with you; who might you be, sister?
The upāsikā said, “I have yet another extraordinary matter.”
There is a deity dwelling in this house who is intimate with me, as if she were a woman with whom I frequently associate.
When I give alms, this deity says to me: "This one is an Arhat; this one is an Anāgāmin;

this one is a Sakṛdāgāmin; this one is a Srotāpanna; this one is an ordinary person; this one maintains the precepts; this one has broken the precepts; this one possesses wisdom; this one is foolish."
"Although I have heard this teaching, my mind remains equanimous and without duality; toward ordinary people who violate the precepts and the like, I am just as I am toward an Arhat.
Śāriputra said: "You are truly extraordinary!"
"One who is able to give rise to a mind of equanimity within this.
Mahāsena said: "I have another extraordinary and wonderful thing."
"I am a woman, moreover one living at home, yet I have been able to eliminate the twenty kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* and attain the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Śāriputra said, "Sister!"
"You are most extraordinary!
To be able to attain the stage of Srotāpanna while in a female body!
The upāsikā said:
"I have yet another wonder and marvel!
I have four sons, all of whom hold evil and heterodox views.
My husband is also evil and heterodox, and even more so; regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, he knows nothing of them and shows them no respect."
"If I were to make offerings to the Triple Gem or provide for the poor, they would immediately give rise to jealousy and anger, saying:
'We labor diligently at our household duties, yet you instead expend these resources on such useless pursuits.'"
"Although this may be said, regarding my resolve for the Way, I shall cultivate goodness and practice giving without ever retreating, nor shall I harbor resentment.

Śāriputra said, "It is the nature of women that at all times they are never independent: in childhood they are protected by their parents; in youth, they are protected by their husbands; and in old age, they are protected by their sons."
Yet you are not constrained by your teacher; you may cultivate goodness as you please. Sisters!
I now instruct you: you should apply your minds well.
"What is this good news?
It is that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will arrive at the Veṇugrāmaka forest this evening.
For this reason, I have sent word to inform you."
Having spoken thus, he took his leave and returned to his dwelling.
The upāsikā said:
"What the Venerable One has told me is truly most excellent!"
"After the Venerable One has departed, we shall prepare the offerings to await the World-Honored One.

Thus it was; when the World-Honored One arrived at this grove, Mahāsena was filled with great joy and immediately gathered the female lay disciples (*upāsikā*). That very evening, he went to where the Buddha was.

Seeing from afar the World-Honored One’s radiance and marks of excellence, his five senses were filled with joy and he leaped for immeasurable delight. Upon arriving, he prostrated himself; having completed offerings of various fragrant flowers to the Buddha, he withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha then preached for him the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven, the severing of desire, and nirvana.
Having heard the teaching of the Dharma and being about to return home, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha:

"The people of this village are all possessed of false views; they do not recognize the Buddha's Dharma, they do not know the Buddha's virtues, and they have no fondness for giving. This is why śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who enter this village to beg always come to my house."
"I only pray, World-Honored One!
May you and your disciples dwell in this village for as long as it pleases you, constantly accepting my invitations and receiving the fourfold offerings.

Having spoken thus, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet and withdrew. He then proceeded to observe the lodgings where the bhikṣus were staying, until finally he saw a sick bhikṣu lying within a grass hut. He immediately asked him:
“Venerable sir!
What ailment do you suffer from?
The bhikṣu replied:
"While traveling on the road, my four elements have become unbalanced; I am suffering and have little strength.
The upāsikā asked, "Venerable sir, regarding your ailment, what food would be most beneficial for you to eat?"
He replied,
"The physician prescribed that I should consume fresh, warm meat broth.
The upāsikā said:
"Do not seek anything further; I shall send it to you tomorrow.
He replied, "So be it."
The upāsikā prostrated at his feet and returned home, reflecting to herself:
"I have gained great benefit, having seen the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as well as Śāriputra and the other great elders."

He was deeply filled with joy and celebration; however, he did not recall that it was the fifteenth day of the month. Now, according to the laws of that country, on the fifteenth day no living being may be killed, and anyone who kills violates the royal decree.
At dawn the next morning, he commanded a messenger to take money and purchase fresh, warm meat.
Following these instructions, the messenger went to the market and searched everywhere, but returned empty-handed and said to his master:
"Today is the fifteenth day; there is no slaughtering in the market."
Then the upāsikā said to the messenger,
"Take these one thousand coins and buy a hundred coins' worth of meat.
There may be someone seeking profit who will give it to you."
The messenger was sent with money to search for him again; however, because the king’s penalty was so severe, no one dared to give him refuge.
The messenger returned and reported the matter exactly as it had occurred.
When the laywoman heard of this matter, her heart was filled with grief and she said, "Take these gold coins and purchase it at an equivalent weight.

At that time, although the messenger took the gold coins and searched for it as instructed, the butchers, though greedy for the profit, were afraid of the king’s severe laws and the loss of their own lives; thus, none dared to give it to him.
Thus they went back and forth, yet were utterly unable to obtain it.
At that time, the upāsikā’s distress increased manifold as she thought:
"The sick bhikṣu has already accepted my invitation; if I fail to provide his necessities, he may lose his life, which would be my own fault."
"What plan should I devise?
Having reflected on this matter, he pondered further:
"In the past, for the sake of a single pigeon, the Bodhisattva even cut his own flesh, not sparing the meat of his own body."
"How much more so for this bhikṣu who has been brought low by a pigeon; how could I not save him even at the cost of my own flesh?

Having formed this thought, he took a trustworthy man whom he usually employed, retired into his private chamber, purified himself by washing his body, and sat cross-legged upon his bed. He then commanded the man, saying:
"Now, cut the flesh from my thigh and take it."
At that time, the messenger acted according to his instructions and immediately cut the flesh with a sharp blade.
As he was cutting the flesh, the king was overcome by excruciating pain and fell to the ground in a swoon.
At that time, the maidservant immediately wrapped it in white flour.
Once the meat had been taken, she combined it with various medicinal herbs, boiled it into a broth, and sent it to the sick bhikṣu.
After the bhikṣu had accepted this food sent by the faithful donor, his illness was immediately cured.
At that time, the brahmin was not present; having gone out on a journey, he asked, "Where is Mahāsena?
He replied:
"In such-and-such a room.
Her husband went there to see her; her complexion was altered and unlike its usual state, so he immediately asked:
"For what reason are you now so withered and haggard?"
She replied,
"I am now afflicted by illness.
Her husband became sorrowful and immediately summoned various physicians to examine her ailment.
The physicians gathered together asked him:
"What ailment do you have?
How long has this illness been active?"
"Is there any interval of relief?
He replied, "I am in pain at all times; as it is now, my suffering knows no respite."
At that time, the physician examined her pulse but could not discern where she was in pain;
he departed in silence. Her husband, weeping, asked his wife, "What illness do you have?"
He spoke thus out of emotional attachment.
His wife replied to him,
"If even a skilled physician does not know it, how could I possibly know?"
Then the brahmin asked the members of his household:
"Do you know what illness Mahāsena is suffering from?
At that time, the attendants replied:
"Friends! We do not know;
we must ask those who are trustworthy and intimate.
Thereupon, the brahmin summoned the maidservant and questioned her in a secluded place, saying:
“How has my wife come to be ill?
The maidservant answered truthfully:
“My lady, you should know!”
"For the sake of a sick bhikṣu, he cut his own flesh to feed him.
Upon hearing this, the man conceived thoughts of malice and harm toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and immediately cried out at a loud voice in the streets:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat human flesh just like King Puṣpadanta!"

At that time, a devout upāsaka, hearing the brahmin revile the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, became sorrowful and unhappy; he went to where the World-Honored One was and prostrated himself at his feet.
The World-Honored One asked,
"For what reason are you so dejected and unhappy?
They replied:
“World-Honored One!

There was a brahmin who, in a place where many people were gathered, cried out in a loud voice, reviling the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha: ‘In the past, King Khaṇḍa used to eat human flesh; now these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do the same—they eat human flesh as well.’”
"I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
will command the bhikṣus not to eat human flesh.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and summoned the sick bhikṣu.
At that time, the sick bhikṣu, having heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, felt his heart leap with joy:
“The World-Honored One’s great compassion has even reached me!”
"Though your body is emaciated, you have come here by your own strength; having arrived, you prostrate at my feet and sit to one side.
The Buddha said, "Noble son!"
"What is your ailment?
The bhikṣu replied, "I am afflicted by illness;
now that I have seen the World-Honored One, I have recovered slightly."
The World-Honored One asked again:
"What did you eat today? He replied:
"Today I ate meat broth.
The Buddha asked,
"Was the meat you ate fresh?"
"Is it dried meat? He replied, "It is fresh meat;
in the land of India, it is so hot that meat does not last overnight."
"Is what you eat fresh or dried?
Good son! When you eat meat, do you ask whether it is pure or impure?"
He replied, "World-Honored One!
I have been afflicted by illness for a long time; I simply took it when I had the opportunity and truly did not ask."
The Buddha said,
"Bhikṣu! How is it that you have accepted impure food?"
According to the dharma of a bhikṣu, when a donor offers food, he should first ask:
"What kind of meat is this?
If the donor says:
"This is pure meat. One should examine it closely; if it is trustworthy, one may eat it;
if it is not trustworthy, one must not eat it.
At that time, the World-Honored One established this precept for the bhikṣus:
"None of the impure meats should be eaten;

furthermore, the three types of impure meat—those seen, heard, or suspected [to have been killed for one's sake]—should also not be eaten. In this manner, one should distinguish between what may and may not be eaten."

At that time, the upāsikā heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had specifically because of her prohibited the bhikṣus from eating meat; she felt great distress at this, for it was on account of her that he had caused the bhikṣus to never eat meat again. She then said to her husband:
"If you would please invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha to come here tomorrow and provide them with offerings for my sake, it would be most excellent!"
"If you cannot do so, I shall give up my life.
Since I have already offered my own flesh to others, what cause for regret do you have that you would even contemplate such a thing?

When this Brahmin, who had long lacked faith and reverence toward the Triple Gem, heard these words from his wife, he went into the forest to seek out the Buddha because of her. Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, he spoke thus:
“Śramaṇa Gautama!
Together with your disciples, please accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
At that time, the brahmin, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, returned home and said to his wife,
"The śramaṇa Gautama has already accepted your invitation. Thereupon,
the upāsikā immediately gave orders within the household to prepare various kinds of food, incense, flowers, and seating mats.
When the time arrived the following day, he sent a messenger into the forest to inform the World-Honored One:
"The meal is prepared; may the Holy One know the time.
The Buddha and the bhikṣus donned their robes, took up their bowls, and went to his house, where they took their seats.
Having sat down, he asked the brahmin,
"Where is Mahāsena now? He replied:
"A certain person is ill in such-and-such a room.
The Buddha said,
"Call him here!"
Then the brāhmaṇa went immediately to inform him, saying:
"Your teacher calls for you. He replied:
“I, Mahāsena, pay homage at the feet of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; I am suffering from illness and am unable to rise or move about.
Her husband went to inform the Buddha, saying:
“Upasena pays homage at the feet of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; he is suffering from illness and is unable to rise and come here.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go and tell Upavāna, 'Arise and see the Buddha.
Ānanda immediately went and told Upavāna:
“The World-Honored One calls for you; you should go to see him.
At that time, Upasena, while still upon his bed, joined his palms and said:

“I now pay homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, longing to see the World-Honored One. Just as one who is hungry requires food, one who is thirsty requires drink, one who is cold longs for warmth, one who is hot longs for coolness, and one who has lost their way longs to find the path—my longing to see the Buddha is exactly like this.”
"Though my mind wishes to go, my body refuses to follow.
Ānanda returned and reported to the Buddha exactly what Upasena had said.
The Buddha then commanded Ānanda:
"Bring him here on a bed carried by men.
Ānanda followed these instructions and had someone carry him there to the presence of the Buddha.

At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a great radiance; all those who encountered the Buddha’s light and its rays touched their bodies—those who were insane regained their composure, those who were distracted attained concentration, and the sick were healed.
At that time, once Upasena had encountered the Buddha’s light, his suffering and pain were immediately dispelled.
Then the deity of the house washed the wound with water, applied medicine to it, and restored it to its former state.

Then Upasena immediately rose from his seat, took a golden pitcher in his hand, personally provided water for washing, and served various kinds of food, complete with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.

After the Buddha had finished eating, he washed his hands and rinsed his bowl, and for Mahāsena he preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma—namely, the fruits of generosity and the observance of precepts, the rewards of humans and devas, the faults and afflictions of birth and death, the harm caused by craving and desire, the bliss of renunciation and cessation, and the ceaseless revolving of the twelve links of dependent origination.
At that time, Upasena, having heard what the Buddha taught, was able to sever stinginess and envy and attained the stage of Anāgāmin;
all the members of his household and kin received the five precepts;
and the Brahmin abandoned false views, came to have faith and reverence for the Triple Gem, and received the upāsaka precepts.

At that time, among the fourfold assembly gathered there, some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some attained the stages of Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat; others resolved their minds upon the Great Vehicle. All, both great and small, were filled with joy.
At that time, there were many people who feared birth and death, each of whom thought to themselves:
"How extraordinary it is that this woman is able to do such a thing as to cut her own flesh to provide for the śramaṇa!"
"If we were to abandon our villages, fields, and houses, would that be difficult?

They then each renounced their villages, families, and households, left the home life to seek the Way, and through diligent and arduous cultivation, severed all fetters and outflows, attaining the path of Arhatship.
At that time, in this village, faith in and practice of the Buddha-dharma were widely proclaimed and disseminated.

For this reason, even those with strong resolve—including women—recited the sutras and the Dharma; they did not spare their own flesh and blood to attain the various fruits of the Path. How much more so for men who apply themselves with diligence to the work of the Path—how could they fail to achieve success?
For this reason, sons of good family!

You should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas and stand in awe of birth and death. By doing so, you will cause your fetters and afflictions to become thin and weak, and you will leave behind birth and death. Although you may not attain liberation within this age of the Final Dharma, by virtue of these merits, you shall receive inexhaustible blessings among humans and devas.

In fifty-six billion ten-thousand-million years from now, the World-Honored One Maitreya will come here to attain Buddhahood and shall extensively expound the wondrous Dharma for you all. Within that teaching, you shall each fulfill your aspirations and attain the paths of the Three Vehicles, thereby achieving complete liberation. Receive this with reverence and practice it accordingly.
22. Chapter on the Merit of Leaving Home: Śrībhadrā (Twenty-second). [In the Danben edition, this chapter is in the seventh fascicle, thirty-third. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha, in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the merit and causal conditions of leaving home [to become a monastic], saying that its blessings are exceedingly great.
Whether one releases sons or daughters, or releases male or female servants, or permits members of the populace, or even one’s own self, to leave home and enter the Way, the merit is immeasurable.

The retribution for practicing generosity brings blessings for ten lifetimes; one may travel back and forth ten times among the six realms of gods and humans, yet this still does not equal the superior merit of releasing others to leave the household life or leaving the household life oneself.
Why is this? The reward for giving is finite;
the merit of leaving the household life is immeasurable and boundless.
Furthermore, the retribution for upholding the precepts includes becoming a divine seer with the five supernatural powers and receiving celestial blessings, reaching as far as the Brahma world;
yet within the Buddha-dharma, the fruit of renouncing the household life is inconceivable, such that its merit remains inexhaustible even until one reaches Nirvana.

Suppose there were someone who erected a stupa made of the seven treasures, reaching as high as the Heaven of the Thirty-three; the merit obtained from this would not equal that of leaving the household life. Why is this?
As for the stupa of the seven treasures, it can be destroyed by greedy and evil fools;
however, the dharma of renunciation cannot be ruined. For those who seek the wholesome dharma, there is nothing superior to the Buddha-dharma.
It is like a hundred blind people who have a skilled physician capable of treating their eyes so that they may suddenly see clearly.

Or it is like a hundred people whose punishment for their crimes should be the gouging out of their eyes, yet there is one person of great strength who can save them from that punishment so that they do not lose their sight.
Although the merit of these two persons is immeasurable, it is still not equal to the vast and great merit of one who listens to others going forth or goes forth themselves. Why is this?

Although one may bestow the eyes of two kinds of people upon others, these individuals will each obtain only the benefit of a single lifetime; moreover, the nature of the physical eye is subject to decay.

However, by permitting others to leave the household life, or by leaving the household life oneself, one successively guides sentient beings toward the unsurpassed wisdom-eye for eternal kalpas; the nature of this wisdom-eye remains indestructible throughout the passing of kalpas.

Why is this? Because within the realms of humans and devas, those who possess the retribution of merit enjoy pleasures at will, without end or exhaustion, until they ultimately achieve the Way of the Buddha. Why is this so?

Through the dharma of renunciation, one extinguishes the retinue of Māra, increases the lineage of the Buddhas, destroys unwholesome dharmas, nurtures wholesome dharmas, eradicates the defilement of sin, and gives rise to unsurpassed meritorious karma; therefore, the Buddha has said that the merit of renunciation is higher than Mount Sumeru, deeper than the great ocean, and vaster than empty space.

If one creates obstacles for those who have gone forth, preventing them from following their aspirations, the gravity of that offense is extreme; like the pitch-black night where nothing can be seen, the retribution for such a person’s sin is likewise: they shall enter the deep hells, shrouded in darkness and deprived of sight.
Just as the great ocean receives all the hundred rivers and streams that flow into it, so too is the retribution for this person's sins: all manner of evils gather within their very body.
Just as Mount Sumeru, when consumed by the fires at the end of an eon, leaves nothing behind, so it is with this person: burned by the fires of hell, there is no end to it.
For example, if the medicinal drug Kālakūṭa, which is extremely poisonous and bitter, were weighed in equal measure against rock honey, the retribution for good and evil would be just like that.

Whether one permits others to leave the household life or leaves it oneself, the merit is greatest. For those who have left the household life, they take the *Sūtras* as water to wash away the defilements of the fetters (*saṃyojana*); they can extinguish the suffering of birth and death and serve as the cause for *nirvāṇa*.

Taking the *Vinaya* as their feet, they tread upon the ground of pure precepts; taking the *Abhidharma* as their eyes, they discern the good and evil of the world. Thus, they wander at will along the path of the Eightfold Noble Way until they reach the wondrous city of *nirvāṇa*.
For this reason, whether one allows another to go forth or goes forth oneself—whether old or young—the merit is most supreme.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was an elder named Śrībhadra (translated into Chinese as Fuzeng, "Increase of Merit"), who was one hundred years old. Having heard that the merit of leaving the household life was thus immeasurable, he reflected to himself:
"Why should I not now leave the household life within the Buddha-dharma to practice the Way?"
He then took leave of his wife, children, male and female servants, and all his kin, saying, "I wish to leave the household life.

Because the man was aged and infirm, everyone in the household, both great and small, grew weary of him and held his words in contempt; none would follow his instructions. Yet, upon hearing that he wished to leave the household life, they all spoke with joy, saying:
"You should have left long ago; why do you come so late?
Now is precisely the right time.
Śrībhadrā immediately departed from her home and went toward the Bamboo Grove, desiring to see the World-Honored One and seek the way of renunciation.
Having arrived at the Bamboo Grove, he asked the bhikṣus:
"Where is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Great Sage, who with great compassion brings vast benefit to devas and humans, currently residing?"
The bhikṣu replied, “The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has other activities for teaching and transforming beings;
his benefit does not reside here. Śrībhadrā asked again:
"Next, who is the supreme disciple of wisdom among the Great Teacher, the Buddha?
The bhikṣu pointed toward the Venerable Śāriputra.
He then proceeded with his staff to where Śāriputra was, set aside his staff, prostrated, and said:
“Venerable One!
Please grant me permission to go forth.

At that time, Śāriputra, having observed this man, reflected that he was old and lacked the three requisites; being unable to engage in study, meditative concentration, or assist with the communal affairs of the Sangha, he said to him:
"Go away; you are too old, and it is not permitted for you to leave the household life.
Next he approached Mahākāśyapa, Upāli, Anuruddha, and so forth, and then the five hundred great arhats, all of whom asked him:
"Have you already approached others before?"
He replied,
"I first approached the World-Honored One, but as the World-Honored One was not present, I next approached the Venerable Śāriputra.
He asked again:
"What did he say? He replied, "He said this to me:"
"You are too old; you may not go forth.
The bhikṣus said, "Even Śāriputra, who is foremost in wisdom, did not grant you permission; we likewise do not grant you permission."

For example, if a skilled physician who is well-versed in diagnosing illnesses abandons the treatment of a patient, and other minor physicians likewise stand with their hands folded in impotence, one should know that this person possesses the signs of certain death.
Because Śāriputra, despite his great wisdom, did not grant permission, the other bhikṣus likewise refused him.
Śrībhadrī, unable to obtain ordination from the bhikṣus, returned to the Bamboo Grove and stood upon the threshold of the gate, weeping bitterly in distress and wailing aloud:
"Since my birth, I have committed no great transgression; for what reason, then, am I alone denied the opportunity to leave the household life?"
For example, Upāli was a lowly man who shaved hair;
Nanda was a base and filthy scavenger who removed excrement;
and Aṅgulimāla had killed countless people.

Even those such as Dāsaka and the great bandits and wicked men—people like these were still permitted to leave the household life; what crime have I committed that I am not allowed to leave the household life?

As he spoke these words, the World-Honored One immediately rose up before him, emitting a great radiance and adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, like Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, upon his high chariot of seven treasures.
The Buddha asked Puṇyavardhana, "For what reason are you weeping?

At that time, the elder, hearing the Buddha’s Brahma-voice, felt his heart leap with joy like a son who has seen his father. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he paid homage to the Buddha and, weeping, addressed him, saying:
"All sentient beings—even those who kill, steal, speak falsehoods, slander, or are of lowly birth—are permitted to leave the household life;
what crime have I alone committed that you specifically do not allow me to go forth in the Buddha-dharma?"
"Both the elders and the young of my household think that because I am old and decrepit, they no longer have need of me.
Now, within the Buddha-dharma, I cannot leave the household life;
and if I were to return home now, they would certainly not treat me with respect. Where, then, should I go?"
"I shall certainly pass away here now.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śrībhadrā:
"Who is able to raise their hand into the air and make a definitive declaration?"
"He ought to go forth into homelessness;
this person should not be old.
The elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Śāriputra, the foremost son of wisdom of the Dharma-Cakravartin King, who is next to the Buddha as the second Teacher of the World, has not been permitted by me to leave the household life and go forth in my Buddha-dharma.”
At that time, the World-Honored One,
out of great compassion, comforted Puṇyavardhana, just as a loving father comforts a filial son, and addressed him, saying:
"Do not be distressed!"
I shall now cause you to go forth into homelessness.
This is not due to Śāriputra’s diligent asceticism over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, nor his cultivation of merit for a hundred kalpas;

it is not because of Śāriputra’s difficult practices life after life—such as splitting his head, gouging out his eyes, or giving away his marrow, brain, blood, flesh, skin, bones, hands, feet, ears, and nose.
It was not Śāriputra who threw himself before a starving tigress, entered a pit of fire, had his body pierced by a thousand nails, or had a thousand lamps carved into his flesh;
it was not Śāriputra who gave away kingdoms, cities, wives, children, slaves, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures;

nor was it Śāriputra who, during the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, made offerings to eighty-eight thousand Buddhas, during the middle asaṃkhyeya kalpa, made offerings to ninety-nine thousand Buddhas, and during the final asaṃkhyeya kalpa, made offerings to one hundred thousand Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, leaving the household life, upholding the precepts, and fully perfecting the pāramitā of śīla.
"Śāriputra does not possess mastery over the Dharma;
how could he dare to dictate, saying, 'This one should leave the household life, but this person should not'?
Only I alone possess mastery over the Dharma."

I alone ride the precious chariot of the six perfections and don the armor of patience; beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon the diamond throne, I have subdued the enemy of the Māra king and attained the Buddha-way by myself, with none equal to me.
"Come, follow me; I shall grant you the going forth.

Thus, as the World-Honored One consoled him in various ways, Puṇyavardhana’s distress was immediately dispelled and his heart was filled with great joy. He then followed behind the Buddha into the Buddha’s vihāra, where [the Buddha] addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Let him go forth."

Why is this? Sentient beings attain liberation according to their conditions; some have a karmic affinity with the Buddha that others cannot provide for their deliverance, while others have an affinity with different beings that the Buddha cannot provide for their deliverance.
While Śāriputra has a karmic connection with me, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Aniruddha, Kumbhīra, and all the other disciples are not those whom I have delivered.
"In this manner, as they were passed along from one to another according to their respective connections, no other person was ordained.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana also thought:
"This man is advanced in years and senile; he lacks all three capacities—reciting the sūtras, practicing meditation, and assisting in the affairs of the community."
"However, since the Dharma-King has issued a decree for me to leave the household life, it is unreasonable to disobey.
He was immediately ordained and received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

This person had already planted the causes and conditions for liberation in previous lives; having swallowed the hook of the Dharma like a fish swallowing a hook, he would certainly emerge from the world without doubt. Having previously cultivated and accumulated various meritorious virtues, he practiced with diligence day and night, studying and reciting the *Sūtras*, the *Vinaya*, and the *Abhidharma*, until he was extensively proficient in the *Piṭaka* of the scriptures.

Because of his old age, he was unable to rise to greet, escort, or respectfully inquire after the senior monks as required by custom. Since those junior bhikṣus had been ordained earlier and were thus his seniors, they constantly spoke to him with harsh and cutting words:
"This decrepit old bhikṣu relies on his advanced age; though he recites the sūtras and studies the teachings, he is arrogant and conceited, showing us no respect or deference."
At that time, the elder bhikṣu reflected to himself:

"When I was at home, I was tormented by my family members, both great and small; now that I have come forth into the homeless life, I hoped to find rest, yet I am instead being provoked and pressed so harshly by these young men."
"What crime have I committed to be thus, only to increase my suffering and distress?
He further thought:
"I would rather die now."

At that time, by the side of the forest, there was a great river, both deep and swift. He immediately went to its bank, removed his *kāṣāya* robe, and placed it upon a tree branch. Kneeling long before the robe, he wept and shed tears, making this vow: "I do not now abandon the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; I only wish to give up my life.

As for this robe worn upon my body, may whatever merit results from my giving, my observance of precepts, my diligence, and my recitation of the sūtras, cause me—upon casting off this body—to be reborn into a wealthy and joyful family with harmonious and well-behaved relatives. May they create no obstacles to my wholesome dharmas, may I always encounter the Triple Gem, leave the household life to cultivate the Way, meet virtuous teachers, and be shown the realization of *nirvāṇa*."
Having made this vow, he intended to throw himself into a place in the river where the current was deep and swift and the waves surged and overturned.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, using his divine eye, observed what my aged disciple was about to do.
He soon saw his disciple cast himself into the water; before he had even reached the water, [the Buddha], by means of his supernormal powers, received him and placed him upon the bank, asking:
"O son of the Dharma!"
"What have you done? Śrībhadrā was deeply ashamed and immediately reflected to herself:
"How shall I answer?"
"I ought not now to deceive my teacher with false speech; for if I were to deceive him, I would incur sin in every lifetime and be deprived of the faculty of speech.
Furthermore, my Upādhyāya possesses supernatural powers and profound discernment; even if I were to speak falsely, he would surely know it."

If there is a person in the world whose wisdom is clear and penetrating, whose nature is substantial and upright, such a one should be revered by the devas. If there is one who possesses wisdom yet harbors flattery and deception, they may serve as a teacher for others, and people should respectfully honor and make offerings to them.
If one lacks wisdom but possesses integrity and straightforwardness, although they may not benefit others, their conduct is sufficient for their own salvation.

If a person is foolish and harbors deceit and flattery in their heart, they will be reviled as base and inferior among all the masses; whatever they say, everyone will recognize it, and all will declare:
"This person is hypocritical and deceptive; there is no truth in them."
"Even if I were to speak the truth, they would abandon me and not place their trust in my words.
Therefore, it would be improper for me to deceive my preceptor; I must speak according to reality."
He then said to his teacher, "I grew weary of the household life and left home seeking rest; yet now I find no joy in it, and thus I wish to take my own life.
Having heard this, Maudgalyāyana immediately thought to himself:
"If this person were not to be terrified by the fearsome matters of birth and death, they would find no benefit in leaving the household life and would depart empty-handed.
He then said to him:
"Now, with a sincere heart, grasp the corner of my robe and do not let go midway."

He immediately followed his teacher’s instruction; like the nature of the wind which, when it blows upon dust and grass, causes them to rise and strike against the void, he traveled through the air by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), as if grasping a single hair, reaching wherever he desired.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana was like a fierce hawk carrying a small bird as it soared through the void.
Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal power was likewise: his body ascended into the air, and in the mere twinkling of an arm being bent or extended, he reached the shore of the great ocean.

By the seashore there was a recently deceased woman, whose countenance was upright and whose physical form was exceptionally exquisite, endowed with all the marks of beauty. Maugalyāyana saw a worm emerge from her mouth and enter through her nose; it then emerged from her eye and entered through her ear. Having stood and observed this, he departed.
Śrībhadrā said, "Upādhyāya!
Who is this woman?"
"Is its appearance like this?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "The time has come; I shall explain it."

Proceeding a short distance further, he saw a woman carrying a copper cauldron upon her back. She set the cauldron in water, lit a fire beneath it, and blew on it until it boiled. Once it was boiling, she stripped off her clothes and threw herself into the cauldron. Her hair and nails fell away first; as her flesh cooked, it separated from the bone. As the boiling liquid blew the bones out onto the surface, the wind immediately restored them to human form. She then took the flesh for herself and ate it.
Upon seeing this, Pukkasāti was struck with terror and his hair stood on end; he addressed him, saying, "Upādhyāya!
Who is this person who eats his own flesh?"
Maudgalyāyana replied, “The time has come; I shall speak.

He then walked forward a short distance and saw a massive body covered with many insects that swarmed and bit it, even down to its joints, leaving not a single spot free as large as the point of a needle. A great sound of wailing and weeping arose, shaking everything near and far, like the cries from hell.
He addressed him, saying: "Preceptor!
As for this great and evil sound, who is it that makes it?"
Maudgalyāyana replied, "The time has come; I shall speak.

Next, he saw a great man surrounded by many malevolent spirits with animal heads and human bodies, who held bows, crossbows, tridents, and poisoned arrows with flaming tips, vying with one another to shoot him until his body was completely scorched and ablaze.
He addressed him, saying: "Upādhyāya!
Who is this person who endures such bitter suffering and has nowhere to flee?"
The teacher said:
"Wait! When the time comes, I shall speak."

After a long time had passed, he next saw a great mountain with swords and blades set upon its slopes. He saw a man who threw himself down from the top; as his body was pierced and mangled by the knives, spears, swords, and lances, they immediately withdrew and re-erected themselves in their original positions. The man then returned to the mountain top and continued as before without ceasing.
Having seen this, he said to his teacher,
"Who is this person who is undergoing such suffering?
The teacher replied:
"Cease for now!
When the time comes, I shall speak.
Next, he saw a great mountain of bones, seven hundred yojanas high, which was able to obscure the sun and cause the ocean to be shrouded in darkness.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana was walking back and forth in meditation upon a large rib of this mountain of bones, with his disciple following him. The disciple then reflected to himself:
"Since my preceptor has now reached the state of no-activity, why should I not inquire about what occurred previously?"
Having reflected thus, he said:
"I pray only that the Upādhyāya will explain for me the matter I have just seen."
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"Now is precisely the right time," and he immediately addressed his preceptor:
"Who was that woman you saw previously?

Maudgalyāyana replied, "If you wish to know, she is the wife of a great merchant (śreṣṭhin) from the city of Śrāvastī; she is of beautiful appearance and is dearly loved and respected by her husband."

At that time, the Sārthavāha wished to enter the great ocean; yet, out of greedy attachment to this woman, he was unable to part from her. He then took her with him to sea, boarding a ship with five hundred merchants and entering the ocean.

At that time, the wife would constantly hold up a mirror with the end of a three-jointed stick to look at her face; seeing her own beauty, she became arrogant and developed a deep attachment to herself.
Then a large turtle kicked the ship with its feet, causing it to break apart and sink into the sea. The caravan leader, his wife, and the five hundred merchants all perished.
The nature of the great ocean is that it does not tolerate corpses; when the waters swirl and turn back, yakṣas and rākṣasas cast them onto the shore.

When sentient beings reach the end of their lives, they are reborn within the midst of existence according to what they cherished and were attached to. Some may raise an objection, saying: "If one is reborn according to whatever one was attached to, who would love hell enough to enter hell? The assembly replied:

"If there are sentient beings who steal the property of the Triple Gem or the belongings of their parents, or even commit murder—committing such great sins for which they ought to fall into the Hell of Blazing Fire—and yet this person is oppressed by cold diseases and wind, they will then think of fire and desire to enter into it."
Having formed this thought, his life ended and he fell into this hell.

If a person steals the light or the value of a Buddha’s lamp, or steals the lamps, candles, firewood, or grass belonging to the Saṃgha; or if they demolish or ransack the dwellings or lecture halls belonging to the Saṃgha; or if, during the cold winter season, they strip people of their clothing; or if by force, during a freezing cold time, they pour water over slaves or other persons; or if, at the time of plundering, they strip people of their garments—for such karmic retribution, one should fall into the Hell of Cold Ice.
This person, oppressed by a feverish illness, constantly longs for a cool place; at the very moment he thinks of it, he falls into this hell.
It is the same for the Utpala, Padma, Kumuda, and Puṇḍarīka hells.

In the cold hells, those who undergo punishment find the flesh of their bodies parched by the ice like scattered scorched beans; their brains and marrow crack white with cold, their skulls shatter into hundreds of thousands of pieces, and their bones split apart like the notches of a bowstring.

If a person is stingy and greedy, depriving hungry sentient beings of food and drink at the proper time, they should fall into the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) and contract a disease of upward-moving qi, such that they cannot swallow their food.
When a caring friend or relative offers various kinds of food and earnestly urges them, saying:
"This is sweet, this is sour; this is delicious and easy to digest; you should force yourself to eat."
He then gave rise to a mind of resentment, thinking:
"When shall I never see food with my eyes?
At that moment his life ended, and he was reborn among the hungry ghosts.

If a person is foolish and does not believe in the Triple Gem, slandering and disparaging the Way, they should fall among the animals; being afflicted by illness, they can only lie prostrate and are unable to turn onto their side. They take no pleasure in virtuous words, and those around them know for certain that this person will surely die.

Thus, they urge them with pressing words: "You should listen to the Dharma, observe the fasts, and receive the precepts; you should behold the Buddha’s image and the community of bhikṣus; you should practice giving."
The person’s mind was entirely devoid of joy; though they were forcefully exhorted and instructed, their malevolent thoughts only increased:
"I wish I could find a place where I do not hear even the virtuous names of the Triple Gem—how indescribably pleasant that would be!"
At that time, his life ended and he was reborn among the animals.

However, if there were those who had cultivated roots of goodness and planted the causes for birth as humans or devas, such persons would not be afflicted by terminal illness; at the moment of death, their minds would not be confused. When those close to them and their attendants knew they were about to die, each would exhort them, saying:
"Would you like to hear the Dharma?"
"Do you wish to see the image?
Do you wish to see the bhikṣus and hear the verses of the sutras?
Do you take pleasure in receiving the upavāsa precepts?"
"Would you like to obtain wealth by making offerings to the Buddha image?
They all replied,
"Excellent."
He further spoke to them, saying:
"By making offerings to the images of the Buddha, one attains the Way of the Buddha;
by making offerings to the Dharma, wherever one is born, one shall attain profound wisdom and penetrate the characteristics of all phenomena."
"If one gives to the Sangha, in whatever place one is born, one will obtain great treasures and lack for nothing according to one's wishes.
Having heard this, the sick person rejoices and makes this vow:
"May I always encounter the Triple Gem in whatever place I am born, and may I hear the Dharma to attain awakening."
At that time, when their life comes to an end, they will be reborn among human beings.

If a person extensively plants the wholesome causes for rebirth in heaven—practicing pure giving and precepts, delighting in hearing the Dharma, and cultivating the ten wholesome paths of action—then as that person approaches death, they will lie peacefully on their back. They will behold the image of the Buddha, celestial palaces, and heavenly maidens, and hear celestial music. With a serene and joyful countenance, they will raise their hands upward; at that moment, when their life ends, they will immediately be reborn in the heavens.

This wife of the Sārthavāha, out of self-attachment to her own body, was reborn after death as an insect within that very same body; having cast off this insect body, she fell into the great hells, where she suffered immeasurable pain.
Śrībhadrā said: "Upādhyāya!
Who was that woman who ate her own flesh?"
Maudgalyāyana replied:

"This is the maidservant of a female lay devotee (upāsikā) in Śrāvastī. That lay devotee invited a pure monk who maintains the precepts to spend the ninety-day summer retreat, providing him with offerings and support. She built a dwelling for him at her own gate and prepared various kinds of fragrant and delicious food and drink."
