When the time arrived, she sent a maidservant to deliver food as an offering.
Upon reaching a secluded spot, the maidservant selected the finest and most delicious portions for herself to eat, giving the remainder to the bhikṣu.
The mistress of the house noticed that the maidservant’s complexion was radiant and healthy, bearing the signs of having eaten well, and asked her:
"You have not defiled the food of the bhikṣus," he replied,
"O Great Lady!"
"I too have faith and am not a person of wrong views; for what reason would I eat first?
After the bhikṣu has eaten, give me the remains, and only then shall I eat them."
‘If I eat first, may I, in every successive life, eat my own flesh.

Because of this causal condition, he first undergoes the light retribution of being bound and imprisoned; at the end of his life, he shall fall into the great hell to undergo the full karmic fruit, suffering immeasurable agony and bitterness.
Puṇyavardhana said:
"Who is this being with such a massive body that various insects devour it as it emits a great, horrific sound?
He replied to Puṇyavardhana:

"This *naiṛta* steward-monk, having acted with self-will, used the flowers, fruits, food, and drink belonging to the Saṃgha to send them to laypeople; as a result of this karmic retribution of flowers, he will, at the end of his life here, fall into the great hells.
Those who devour various insects are precisely the people who received those goods at that time."
Puṇyavardhana said: “Upādhyāya!
That person who raises his voice in wailing, upon whom arrows rain down in competition, whose body is pierced through and ablaze with fire—who is he?”
Maudgalyāyana replied:

"In a previous life, this person was a great hunter who killed many birds and beasts. Because of these sins, he has undergone such bitter suffering; now that his life here has ended, he has fallen into the Great Hell, where he will remain for a long time before he can escape."
He asked again: "Upādhyāya!
Who is this person who throws himself down from that great mountain, where swords, blades, spears, and lances pierce and cut his body, yet having thrown himself, he climbs back up again?"
Maudgalyāyana replied:

"This was a great and powerful general of the King of Rājagṛha. Because of his fierce valor, he stood at the vanguard; having wounded and killed living beings with swords, blades, spears, and lances, he now undergoes this retribution."
"Having died thereupon, one falls into the Great Hell and undergoes suffering for a long time.
Puṇyavardhana asked again,
"And as for this mountain of bones now, whose is it?"
Maudgalyāyana said to him, "If you wish to know, these are the bones of your own former body.
Upon hearing these words, Śrībhūti was struck with terror; his hair stood on end, and he broke into a cold sweat from fear. He addressed him, saying:
"Upādhyāya! While my heart has not yet burst asunder, please tell me the full account of the causes and conditions from beginning to end.
Maudgalyāyana replied:

“The cycle of birth and death revolves without end; yet wholesome and unwholesome karma never decays, and one must inevitably experience its retribution. Having performed various karmas, one receives their retribution according to one’s conduct.”
Maudgalyāyana spoke again:

"In a past age, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Dharmavardhana (translated in the Qin language as 'Dharma-Increase'). He delighted in practicing giving, observing the precepts, and hearing the Dharma; he possessed a heart of compassion and was by nature neither violent nor cruel. He did not harm the lives of living beings, was endowed with the marks of a king, and ruled the country according to the True Dharma for a full twenty years."
While affairs were few and he was at leisure, he engaged in board games with others.
At that time, there was a man who had committed a crime by killing someone. The ministers addressed the king, saying:
"There is a man outside who has violated the laws of the realm; how shall his punishment be determined?"
At that time, the king was in a playful mood and replied to him:
"I shall deal with this according to the laws of the land.
He then applied the penal code; since the man had committed murder, he deserved death, and the king promptly executed him.
After the king had finished gambling, he asked his ministers,
"Where is that criminal who was here just now?
I wish to pass judgment upon him."
The minister addressed the king, saying, "In accordance with the laws of the land, he has now been executed.

Upon hearing these words, the king fainted and fell to the ground. His ministers stood around him and sprinkled cold water on his face; after a long while, he regained consciousness and spoke while shedding tears:
"Where are my palace attendants and courtesans, my elephants, horses, and the seven treasures?
Now I am here alone, by myself in hell, enduring all manner of suffering."
"Even before I became king, there was royal governance within this palace; I shall not die for long, and here too there shall continue to be royal governance."
"I am called a king, yet I take the lives of others; you should know that I am thus a *caṇḍāla* king. I do not know where I shall go in future lives.
I have now resolved that I must no longer be a king."
He immediately renounced the throne and entered the mountains to dwell in seclusion.
When the king passed away, he was reborn in the great ocean as a makara fish, his body reaching a length of seven hundred yojanas.

Kings and great ministers, relying on their own power and influence, oppress and exploit the common people, alienate the populace, and strip the living beings of their resources; at the end of their lives, they mostly become *makara* sea-monsters, upon whose bodies many insects swarm and devour them, just as when one is seized by lice and nits, so too are the insects that infest their bodies.
Because his body was itchy, he rubbed against the crystal mountain, crushing and killing many insects; the flowing blood defiled the sea, turning it crimson for a hundred li.
Due to these karmic conditions, his life came to an end there, and he fell into the great hell.

At that time, the makara fish sleeps for a hundred years; having awakened, it becomes hungry and thirsty and immediately opens its mouth, so that the seawater flows in like a great river pouring forth.

At that time, there happened to be five hundred merchants who had entered the sea to gather treasures. They encountered a fish with its mouth wide open; as their ship was sailing swiftly, it headed straight for the fish's maw. The merchants were struck with terror and raised their voices in loud lamentation, each saying:
"Today we are certain to die."

Each paid homage according to their own devotion; some invoked the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, while others invoked the various devas, mountains, rivers, ghosts, and spirits, as well as their parents, wives, children, brothers, and kinsmen, all saying:
"Today is the last time we shall see Jambudvīpa; henceforth, we shall never see it again."
At that time, as they were about to enter the mouth of the makara fish, they all simultaneously raised their voices in unison and cried out, "Namo Buddha.
Upon hearing the cry of "Namo Buddha," the fish immediately closed its mouth, the ocean waters stilled, and the merchants were restored from death to life.
Driven by hunger, this fish died and was reborn within the city of Rājagṛha.

The yakṣas and rākṣasas then took its body out and placed it on this seashore; exposed to the sun and drenched by the rain, its flesh decayed until only the bones remained—this mountain of bones is that very place.
"Puṇyavardhana, you should know this!
That King Dharmavardhana at that time was none other than yourself.
Because of the karmic condition of killing a human being, you fell into the great ocean and became a makara fish."
"Now that you have regained a human body, yet you do not weary of birth and death—if you die here, you shall fall into hell, and it will be extremely difficult to escape.

When Śrībhadrā saw her former body and heard these words, she became terrified of birth and death. She recollected the Dharma she had practiced in successive order, binding her mind and fixing her attention. Observing her former body, she understood the impermanence of all phenomena, grew weary of and detached from birth and death, exhausted all fetters and outflows, and attained the path of Arhatship.
Maudgalyāyana was filled with joy and said,
"O son of the Dharma!
That which you ought to have done has now all been completed."
"Come here; you have come by my power, but now you may depart by your own supernatural power.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana ascended into the air, and Śrībhadrā followed after her preceptor like a fledgling following its mother, returning to the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the youths, not yet having realized the Path, continued to provoke him as before;
but Śrībhūti’s mind was already disciplined and compliant, his deportment serene and composed, and he remained silent without uttering a word.

Knowing this matter and wishing to protect the bhikṣus from giving rise to unwholesome karma, and also wishing to manifest the virtue of this elderly bhikṣu, the Buddha addressed Puṇyavardhana in the midst of the great assembly, saying:
"Come here, Puṇyavardhana!"
“Did you go to the shore of the great ocean today?
Puṇyavardhana replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
“Tell me now what you have seen. The bhikṣu Puṇyavardhana reported to the Blessed One in detail everything exactly as he had seen it.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Bhikṣu Puṇyavardhana!
It is exactly as you have seen; the facts are indeed so.”

You have now departed from the suffering of birth and death and attained the bliss of nirvana; you deserve to receive the offerings of all humans and devas, and you have fully accomplished all that a bhikṣu ought to do.
When the young bhikṣus heard these words of the Buddha, they felt deep sorrow and remorse, thinking:
"How is it that we, who are ignorant, have with evil intent pierced and gored such a person of wisdom, virtue, and goodness? How shall we endure this retribution for our sins?"
Then the bhikṣus rose from their seats, went to where Puṇyavardhana was, prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, and spoke these words:
"When virtuous people are born, they are born together with compassion; since you, O Virtuous One, have now been born, you too should be born together with great compassion."
"I only pray that you will give rise to a heart of compassion for me and accept my confession of transgression.
Puṇyavardhana replied, "I harbor no ill will toward these people; you may indeed confess your transgression."
When Śrībhadrā saw that the youths were filled with fear, she immediately preached the Dharma for them.

Upon hearing it, the bhikṣus grew weary of the phenomena of birth and death; through diligent cultivation and practice, they severed their fetters, exhausted their outflows, and attained the path of Arhatship.
The causes and conditions for Puṇyavardhana’s increase in merit spread as a virtuous reputation throughout the city of Rājagṛha, and all the people said:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!
This elder, who was aged and infirm and received no alms in this city, has now gone forth in the Buddha-dharma, realized the Way, and clearly proclaims such rare and wondrous Dharma."

At that time, many people within the city conceived pure faith; some permitted their male and female slaves and subjects to leave the household life, while others left the household life themselves. There was no one who did not rejoice and encourage others to do the same.
For these reasons, the merit of leaving the household life is immeasurable and boundless.

Even one who waits until the age of a hundred to leave the household life and thereby accomplishes such great merits as these—how much more so for those in the prime of their youth who seek the wondrous, supreme, and great fruits of retribution? They should diligently practice the Dharma, leave the household life to study the Path, and joyfully put this into practice.
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume Four;
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume Five.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Huìjué and others of Liangzhou during the Northern Wei Dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.

Chapter 23: The Śrāmaṇera Who Commits Suicide While Observing the Precepts (24). Chapter Twenty-three: The Śrāmaṇera Who Commits Suicide While Observing the Precepts. In the Dan-ben (Dunhuang manuscript), this chapter is in the seventh fascicle as the thirty-fourth.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Andhra.

At that time, the World-Honored One earnestly praised those who uphold the precepts, who guard and maintain the prohibitions, and who would rather sacrifice their own bodies and lives than ever violate them. Why is this?
Precepts are the primary foundation for entering the Path, the subtle essence for exhausting all outflows, and the level highway to the peace and bliss of Nirvana.
If one maintains pure precepts, the merit thereof is immeasurable and boundless.
For example, the great ocean is immeasurable and boundless;
the precepts are likewise.
Just as the great ocean is the dwelling place of many great beings, such as asuras, turtles, aquatic creatures, and makaras; so it is with the precepts.
The ocean of precepts is likewise; it is inhabited by many great beings of the three vehicles.

Just as the great ocean abounds with various treasures such as gold, silver, and lapis lazuli, so too does the ocean of precepts produce many wholesome dharmas, including the four truths of impermanence, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the various dhyānas, samādhis, and other such jewels.
It is like the great ocean, which has a bed of diamond and is surrounded by diamond mountains; though the four great rivers flow into it, they neither increase nor decrease its volume.

The ocean of precepts is likewise: with the *vinaya* as its bed and the mountain of *abhidharma* surrounding it, the rivers of the four *āgamas* flow into it, remaining serene and constant, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Why is it that the water poured in neither increases nor decreases?
The fire from the Avīci Hell below surges upward to strike the great ocean; because the seawater is thus evaporated, it does not increase.
Because [the water] constantly flows in, it does not decrease.
In the ocean of the Buddha’s Dharma and precepts, there is no increase because of non-negligence, and no decrease because of the possession of merit.
Therefore, one should know that those who are able to uphold the precepts possess exceedingly great virtue.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the land of Andhra, there was at that time a bhikṣu who lived on alms and delighted in solitary, quiet places, fully endowed with dignified deportment.
This bhikṣu who lived on alms was one praised by the Buddha, not one who dwelt among the crowds.

Why is this? Because a bhikṣu who begs for alms has few desires and is content; he does not store or accumulate possessions, practices sequential begging, dwells wherever a seat is laid out, eats but one meal a day, and maintains only three robes—such matters as these are worthy of honor and esteem.

Among the monks, there are those who have many desires and no contentment; they hoard and accumulate, greedily seeking and stingily grasping, being envious and attached. For this reason, they cannot attain great renown.

That bhikṣu who lives on alms was pure and complete in virtuous conduct, possessed the fruits of the śramaṇa, had attained the six supernormal powers and the three types of clear knowledge, dwelt in the eight liberations, and was renowned for his dignified and orderly deportment. His fame spread far and wide.

At that time, in the country of Andha, there was an upāsaka who revered and had faith in the Triple Gem and observed the five precepts: he did not kill, did not steal, did not engage in sexual misconduct, did not speak falsely, and did not drink intoxicants. Devoted to giving and cultivating virtue, his fame spread throughout the kingdom and its towns; he invited this mendicant bhikṣu and provided him with sustenance for the rest of his life.
The merit of making offerings is received as retribution in accordance with its cause.
If one invites the Saṃgha to one’s own home for offerings, it hinders and interrupts their practice of the Path, subjecting them to the hardships of travel through cold and heat;
when the time comes to receive the retribution, one must exert mental effort and go out to seek after it before finally being able to obtain it.
If one goes there to offer worship and support, then when receiving the resulting merit and retribution, one will sit and enjoy it spontaneously.
This upāsaka’s faith was pure and profound; he prepared various foods of diverse colors and fragrances and sent people to deliver them, doing so every day in this manner.
There are four kinds of śramaṇas, whose goodness or evil is difficult to discern, just as it is hard to know whether the mango fruit is ripe or unripe.

There may be a bhikṣu whose deportment is dignified and orderly, who walks slowly and looks attentively, yet within him are fully present greed, hatred, and delusion, along with broken precepts and unrighteousness—like a mango fruit that is ripe on the outside but unripe within.

There may be a bhikṣu whose external conduct is coarse and neglects proper decorum, yet who internally possesses the full virtues of a śramaṇa, including meditative concentration and wisdom—like an amra fruit that is ripe within but unripe without.

There may be a bhikṣu whose deportment is coarse and unruly, who violates the precepts and commits evil deeds; within him are also present greed, hatred, delusion, avarice, and envy, just as both the interior and exterior of an amra fruit are produced together.

There may be a bhikṣu whose deportment is dignified and composed, who maintains the precepts and guards himself, and who is inwardly endowed with the śramaṇa’s virtues of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, and liberation—like an amra fruit that is ripe both inside and out.
That mendicant bhikṣu was likewise fully endowed with both internal and external qualities; because his virtuous conduct was complete, he was revered by all people.
At that time, there was an elder in the country who had faith and respect for the Triple Gem. He had a son who thought to himself:
"I wish to have him renounce the world; I must seek out a good teacher to entrust him to."
Why is this so? By associating with virtuous friends, one increases wholesome dharmas; by associating with evil friends, unwholesome dharmas arise.
It is like the nature of wind, which is empty, yet when it blows from a sandalwood grove or a campaka grove, the wind carries a wondrous fragrance.
If that wind passes by excrement, filth, or a stinking corpse, the wind itself becomes foul-smelling.
It is like a clean garment placed in a casket of incense: when the garment is removed, it retains the fragrance of the incense;
yet if it is placed in a foul location, the garment likewise takes on that foul odor.

By associating with virtuous friends, goodness flourishes daily; by attaching oneself to evil friends, evil increases. Therefore, I shall now give this child to this venerable one so that he may renounce the household life.
Having thought thus, he went at once and said to the bhikṣu:
"I have this one son whom I now wish to ordain; I only pray, O Venerable One, that you will compassionately accept him and deliver him."
"If you cannot accept it, you shall take it back home.

At that time, the bhikṣu observed with his divine eye that this person, upon leaving the household life, would be able to maintain the pure precepts and cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish; he immediately accepted him and ordained him as a śrāmaṇera.
At that time, an upāsaka had a close friend, a householder, who invited the upāsaka, along with his wife, children, and all the household servants, for a guest-gathering the following day.
In the early morning, the upāsaka thought to himself:
"I am now to attend this gathering; who shall stay behind to guard the house?"

If I were to use force and compel one person to remain, I would be failing him in his rightful share; however, if there is anyone who can voluntarily open their mind and stay, I shall offer a separate reward upon my return from the assembly.
The female lay disciple then said to her parents:
"I pray only that you, my parents, go with the servants and attendants to fulfill the invitation; I am capable of guarding the house from behind."
His father said with joy:
"Excellent, excellent!
Now that you remain here to guard the household, your mother and I are exactly the same; regarding the welfare of the family, my mind has no further anxiety."
Thereupon, the entire family went to accept the invitation, while the girl remained alone inside the house, firmly closing the doors and windows.
On that day, the lay devotee was in such a great hurry that he forgot to send the food.
At that time, the Venerable One thought to himself:
"The sun is setting and worldly people have many affairs; perhaps they have forgotten and will not send the food. Should I now send someone to fetch it?"
He then addressed the śrāmaṇera: "Go and fetch food;

maintain your dignified deportment as the Buddha has taught. When entering a village to beg for alms, do not give rise to greedy attachment. Be like a bee gathering from flowers: take only its nectar without damaging its color or fragrance."

You are now in the same situation: having gone home to fetch food, you must restrain the gates of your senses and not crave forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tactile objects; if you maintain the prohibitive precepts, you will surely attain the Way.
For example, Devadatta, though he recited many sūtras, fell into the Avīci Hell because he committed evil deeds and violated the precepts;
likewise, Kokālika entered hell for slandering those who had broken the precepts;
yet Cūḍapanthaka, though he could only recite a single verse, attained arhatship because he maintained the precepts.

Furthermore, the precepts are themselves the gateway to entering nirvana and the cause for experiencing happiness. For example, according to the Brahminical tradition, if one observes a long fast for three or four months, one invites various eminent Brahmins who maintain the precepts and practice pure conduct; because these are invited through careful selection rather than universally, those left behind feel resentment, as if they were sealed out by an official seal.

There was a certain brāhmaṇa who, though highly learned in the scriptures, was by nature lacking in integrity; because he craved the sweetness of the honey, he licked the seal clean until it was gone. When he arrived at the assembly place the following day, he presented the seal, which had now been opened.
Next, there was a brahmin who wished to enter without a seal.
The official in charge said to him,
"Do you have a seal?"
He replied, "I had some,
but because it was sweet, I licked it all up.
The other said:
"You have already had enough," he said;

thus, [the monk] was unable to proceed further. Yet, out of greed for a small bit of sweetness, he lost the sweet and fragrant delicacies of the four-month period, as well as the various precious treasures of the concluding *dakṣiṇā*.

You must not now, out of such greed for trivial matters, break the seal of the pure precepts, thereby losing the exquisite flavors of the five desires among humans and devas, as well as the immeasurable Dharma-treasures of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the peace and bliss of nirvana that are free from outflows.
"Do not violate the precepts of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, nor defile the Triple Gem, your parents, or your teachers.
Having received these instructions, the śrāmaṇera prostrated at his feet and departed.
He went to her house, knocked on the door making a sound, and the woman asked:
"Who is this? He replied,
"It is a śrāmaṇera, coming to receive food for his preceptor."
The woman’s heart was filled with joy, thinking, "My wish is fulfilled.
She immediately opened the door for him.

This woman was upright and her features were exceptionally beautiful; she was sixteen years of age and consumed by the fire of lustful desire. Before the śrāmaṇera, she displayed all manner of seductive charms, shaking her shoulders and casting glances at her own reflection, manifesting the signs of passion most deeply.
Having seen her, the śrāmaṇera thought to himself:
"Does this woman suffer from a wind-disorder, epilepsy, or a seizure?
Or is she perhaps driven by the fetter of desire, wishing to corrupt my pure conduct?"
He maintained his dignified demeanor with unwavering composure.
Thereupon, the woman prostrated herself on the ground and addressed the śrāmaṇera, saying:
"That which I have long desired has now reached its time; I have always wished to speak to you, but until now I have found no opportunity for peace."
I believe that you also always have a heart for me, and you shall grant me my wish.

Within this house of mine, there are many treasures, gold, silver, and storehouses, like the precious treasuries of the palace of King Vaiśravaṇa, yet they have no owner. You may deign to accept the role of master of this house; I shall become your wife, providing for all your needs and serving you at your command. Please do not refuse me, but fulfill my wish.
The śrāmaṇera thought to himself:
"What transgression have I committed to encounter such an evil circumstance?
I would rather give up this life than violate the prohibitions and precepts established by the Buddhas of the three periods of time."
In the past, a bhikṣu went to the house of a courtesan; he would rather have thrown himself into a pit of fire than commit an act of sexual misconduct.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who were plundered by bandits and bound with grass; though the wind blew upon them and the sun scorched them, and various insects bit and ate them, they did not cut the grass away for the sake of guarding their precepts.
Like a swan swallowing a pearl, a bhikṣu, though seeing it, did not speak of his extreme suffering because he was upholding the precepts.
Like a sea vessel that has wrecked, a junior bhikṣu, because he guarded the precepts, gave his wooden board to the senior bhikṣu and drowned in the sea.
If these people alone are disciples of the Buddha and are able to uphold the prohibitive precepts, while I am not a disciple and cannot uphold them;
and if the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is their teacher alone and not my teacher?
Just as when *campaka* flowers and sesame seeds are pressed together, the oil has the fragrance of *campaka*;
yet if foul-smelling flowers are mixed in, the oil will likewise smell foul.
Now that I have encountered a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), how could I today create unwholesome dharmas?
"I would rather sacrifice my body and life than ever break the precepts or defile the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, my parents, or my teachers.
He further reflected:

"If I were to flee, the woman’s lustful desire would be so intense that she would cast aside all shame and modesty; she would pursue me outside and seize me, and people on the streets would see it, leading to nothing but defamation and disgrace."
"I shall certainly pass away here this very day.
He spoke these words by way of a skillful means:
"Close the doors and windows securely; I shall enter a room and perform what needs to be done, and only then will I come to you."

The woman immediately closed the door. The śrāmaṇera entered the room, bolted the door, and found a razor; his heart was filled with great joy. He stripped off his clothes and placed them on a rack, then joined his palms, knelt toward the place in Kuśinagara where the Buddha had entered nirvāṇa, and made this vow:

"I shall not forsake the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha; I shall not forsake my preceptors or teachers, nor shall I forsake the precepts. It is precisely for the sake of upholding the precepts that I renounce this body and life.
May I be reborn so that I may leave the household life to study the Way, purely cultivate the Brahma-faring, exhaust all outflows, and attain the Path."
She immediately cut her own throat and died; the blood flowed profusely, staining her body.

At that time, the woman, wondering why he was so late, went to the door to look and saw that it was not open. She called out but received no answer; she tried various means to open the door and found him already dead. Her natural complexion vanished and her lustful desire instantly subsided. Overcome with shame and anguish, she tore out her hair, clawed at her face and eyes, and rolled about in the dust and ashes, wailing piteously with tears until she fainted and lost consciousness.
When her father returned home, he knocked on the door and called for his daughter, but she remained silent and did not respond.

Her father, finding it strange that she was so quiet, sent someone to climb over the wall; upon opening the door and looking inside, he saw his daughter in such a state and asked her: "Why have you done this?"
"Has anyone encroached upon you or insulted you?
The woman remained silent and did not answer, reflecting to herself:
"If I were to speak the truth now, it would be deeply shameful."
"If you say that the śrāmaṇera has insulted me, you will be slandering the virtuous and shall fall into hell to undergo infinite suffering.
You must not deceive.
He then answered with the truth:
"While I was guarding this place alone, a śrāmaṇera arrived to seek food for his teacher; my lustful mind became intense, and I sought to harass the śrāmaṇera, hoping he would comply with my wishes."
Yet that one who guards the precepts, with an unchanging mind, employs skillful means to enter the chamber and sacrifice his own life.
Because I, with my defiled body, would seek to destroy such a pure vessel, my transgression is as grave as this; therefore, I find no joy in it.
Upon hearing his daughter’s words, the father felt no alarm or fear.
Why was this? Because he understood that such is the nature of the fetters (*saṃyojana*). He then said to his daughter:
"All phenomena are entirely impermanent; do not grieve or fear!
He then entered the room and saw the body of the śrāmaṇera, its blood smeared crimson like a sandalwood stand. He immediately prostrated before it and praised him, saying:
"Excellent! "
"I shall uphold the Buddha's precepts even at the cost of my own body and life.
At that time, according to the laws of that country, if a śramaṇa died in a layperson's house, a fine of one thousand gold coins was to be imposed upon them and paid to the government.
At that time, the upāsaka placed one thousand gold coins upon a copper tray, carried it to the royal palace, and said:
"Great King!
I have incurred a fine which ought to be paid to Your Majesty; I pray that you will accept it."
The king replied to him, saying:

"In my kingdom, you revere and have faith in the Triple Gem; you are loyal and upright, guarding the Way, and your words and deeds are never at variance. You alone—what transgression could you possibly have committed that you should be required to pay a fine?"
At that time, the lay devotee recounted the preceding circumstances in detail, disparaging his own daughter while praising the merit of the śrāmaṇera’s observance of the precepts.
Upon hearing the facts of the matter, the king was struck with alarm and awe; his profound faith increased greatly, and he addressed him, saying:
"The śrāmaṇera protected the precepts even at the cost of his own life. You are innocent and blameless; how could there be any punishment for you?"
"Simply take this back to your home; I now wish to go to your house in person to make offerings to the śrāmaṇera.
He then struck the golden drum and issued a proclamation to the people of the country, leading the way with a retinue of attendants before and behind as he proceeded to the man's house.

The king entered the inner quarters himself and saw the body of the śrāmaṇera, as red as sandalwood. He prostrated before him and praised his meritorious virtues. He then adorned a high carriage with various precious gems, placed the deceased śrāmaṇera upon it, and traveled to a level piece of ground where he piled up various fragrant woods and performed the cremation as an act of offering.

He adorned this woman with the most exquisite ornaments in the world and placed her in a high and prominent position so that everyone in the assembly could see her. He addressed the multitude, saying:
"This woman is so exceptionally beautiful and her radiant countenance is such as this; among those who have not yet abandoned desire, who would not feel a mind of attachment?"
"Yet this śrāmaṇera, having not yet attained the Way, has offered up his life while still possessing a body subject to birth and death; this is most marvelous and rare!
The king immediately dispatched messengers to invite his teacher to extensively preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.

At that time, everyone in the assembly who saw or heard these matters was filled with joy; some sought to leave the household life to uphold the pure precepts, while others resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, all of whom received [the teaching] upon the crowns of their heads and practiced it accordingly.
24. Chapter on the Elder Lacking Ears, Eyes, and Tongue (25). Chapter Twenty-Four: The Elder Lacking Ears, Eyes, and Tongue. [In the Danben edition, this is Chapter Thirty-Five. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove Monastery, preaching the Dharma to a great assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, within the kingdom, there was a great elder whose wealth was immeasurable. Possessing gold, silver, and the seven treasures; elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; male and female slaves and subjects; his granaries and treasuries were overflowing. Yet he had no sons, only five daughters, who were upright, intelligent, and discerning.
While his wife was pregnant, the elder passed away.
At that time, the law of that country stipulated that if one died leaving no male heir, all of their property and wealth should revert to the state.
The king dispatched a high minister to seize her property, which was on the verge of being confiscated by the state.
The girl thought to herself:
"My mother is pregnant; it is not yet known whether she will bear a son or a daughter. If it continues to be a daughter, this wealth should belong to the government."
"If it be a male, he shall be the master of the wealth.
Having thought this, she went to inform the king, saying:
"My father has passed away; since there is no son, the property should rightfully pass to the King."

However, my mother is currently pregnant and must wait until she has given birth; if it should be a girl, there will be no delay in bringing in the dowry, but if it should be a boy, he shall be the master of the wealth.
At that time, King Prasenajit, abiding in the integrity of the Dharma, approved what had been reported and granted his consent as requested.

Before long, the mother’s term was fulfilled and she gave birth to a son. His body was muddled and indistinct; he lacked both ears and eyes, had a mouth but no tongue, and possessed neither hands nor feet, yet he did have male organs. They immediately gave him a name, calling him Mañcibhāri.
At that time, this woman went to question the king, reporting these matters in full.
Having heard this, the king reflected upon its meaning:
"One does not become a master of wealth by means of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, feet, and so forth."
"Because he is male, he shall become the master of the wealth.
Since the boy possesses the male organ, he ought to receive his father's property.
He then addressed the daughters:
"The wealth belongs to your younger brother; I shall not take it.

At that time, the eldest daughter went to marry into another family. She served her husband with humility and reverence, sweeping and dusting his bedding, providing food and drink, seeing him off and welcoming him home, and rising to bow and inquire after his well-being, just as a maidservant serves her mistress.

Recently, when an elder observed her acting in this manner, he was astonished and asked, "The way of husband and wife is common to every household; why have you alone changed your conduct in such a way?"
The girl replied, "My father has passed away, leaving behind immeasurable wealth. Although I have five sisters, I was still destined to become the king's consort;
however, my mother conceived another child who became my younger brother. He lacks eyes, ears, tongue, hands, and feet, possessing only male organs, yet he shall be the master of the estate."
"For this reason, although there may be many daughters, they are not equal to a single son;
it is for this very cause.
Having heard this, the elder was astonished by such words and immediately took his daughter to the Buddha's dwelling, where he addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions was that son of a householder born into a wealthy family and become its master, despite being without eyes, ears, tongue, hands, or feet?”
The Buddha said to the householder:
"Excellent is your question!
Listen attentively and reflect well!"
"I shall speak for you.
"Indeed, we would delight to hear it.
The Buddha addressed the householder:

"In the distant past, there were two brothers who were great elders. The elder was named Dānaśreṣṭhin and the younger was named Śīlaśreṣṭhin. From his youth, the elder brother was loyal, trustworthy, and sincere;

he always delighted in practicing generosity and relieving the poor and destitute. Because of his faith and goodness, the entire nation praised him, and the King appointed him to handle the affairs of state, such that all matters of litigation and disputes were decided by him."

At that time, according to the laws of the land, when lending or borrowing money, no written contracts were required; everyone would go to the arbitrator Tan-yue Shi-zhi to serve as a guarantor for their integrity.
At that time, there was a merchant who intended to go out to sea; he borrowed a great deal of money from his younger brother, Shi-luo Shi-zhi, to provide for his needs.

At that time, the younger brother, who was a householder, had only one son; as the boy was still young, the brother took him along with the money he had withdrawn and went to the office of the judges, where he said:
"Elder brother!..."
"This merchant's son borrowed money from me to go to sea and has now returned; he ought to receive this much.
You, brother, are a man of integrity; should I pass away, you must bear witness so that he may obtain it."
The elder brother, the householder Śāṇakavāsin, spoke thus.
Before long, his younger brother, the elder, passed away.

At that time, the merchant’s son boarded a ship and entered the sea; when a wind arose and the waves surged, the ship was wrecked and he lost everything. The merchant’s son seized a plank and survived, returning to his native country.
At that time, when the merchant’s son heard that the ship had been wrecked and they were returning empty-handed, and saw only this man, he thought to himself:
"Although this man owes me a debt, how can it be recovered now that he is destitute and penniless?"
"One must have debts to repay.
At that time, he saw this merchant elder once again join with other traders to enter the sea, where they obtained great treasures and returned safely and auspiciously.
He thought to himself:
"Although that son of a householder saw me before, he did not repay my debt.
When I lent him the money, this man was still a child; perhaps he does not remember?"
"Perhaps he does not demand payment because I was previously impoverished?
Now I shall test him.
He then prepared a fine horse adorned with various jewels and dressed in precious garments, and mounted the horse to enter the marketplace.

Seeing that the man’s clothing and carriage were such as these, the son of the elder thought to himself, "This person seems to still possess wealth; I shall try to collect a debt from him. He immediately sent a messenger to say:
"You owe me money; you should repay it now."
He replied, "So be it.
I shall consider what is appropriate and bring it to completion."
The merchant thought to himself:
"The undertaking is too vast; it will weigh heavily upon my life and there is no way to complete it. I must devise a single stratagem to bring it to an end."
He immediately took a precious gem and went to the wife of the official, saying: "Madam!

I originally borrowed a small amount of money from Śīlavat as collateral. His son has come to collect the debt from me; I now offer this one gem, worth one hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. If he demands his debt from me, you should instruct the official not to act as a witness for him."
His wife replied,
"The elder is sincere and faithful; he certainly would not do such a thing,
yet we should speak to him as a test."
He immediately accepted the pearl.
When the steward returned home in the evening, he reported the matter in full.
The elder replied:
"How could such a thing be?
Because I am loyal and trustworthy and do not speak falsely, the King appointed me to the office of state arbitrator; were I to utter even a single falsehood, this would be impossible."
Then the merchant arrived and related the circumstances in detail, whereupon [the judge] immediately returned the pearl to him.
The merchant’s son then offered another pearl worth two hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and went again to say:

“I pray you, may you grant me this request: since this is but a minor matter, were you to utter but a single word, I would obtain three hundred thousand [pieces]. Even if he should prevail, though he be my nephew, I would not have a single coin’s share; this principle is sound.”
At that time, the woman, coveting the precious jewel, accepted it immediately.
That evening she spoke again to her husband:
"The matter I mentioned yesterday can indeed be managed; I pray you will certainly keep this in mind."
The elder replied:
"This is utterly impossible.

Because I am trustworthy, I have been able to serve as a mediator; were I to speak a single falsehood, I would become untrustworthy in this present life and must undergo immeasurable suffering for countless kalpas in future lives."
At that time, the elder had a son who was not yet able to walk. His wife wept and said:
"I am now your wife; even in the face of death, I hoped you would not go against my wishes. If you cannot grant me this small request with a single word, what is the use of my living?"
"If you do not comply, I shall first kill my son and then take my own life.
Upon hearing this, the elder was like a man choking, unable to swallow and unable to spit out; he thought to himself, "I have only this one son;
if he dies, there will be no one to whom I can entrust my wealth."
"If I follow these words, I shall no longer be trusted by others now, and in the future I will surely undergo immeasurable suffering.
Despite being pressured and urged repeatedly, he finally consented.
His wife was delighted and said to the merchant, "The elder has already given his consent.

Upon hearing this, the merchant returned home in high spirits; he adorned a magnificent elephant with various jewels, dressed it in a great precious robe, and mounted the elephant to enter the marketplace.
When the son of the elder saw him, his heart was filled with joy and he thought to himself:
"This man must be wealthy, for his clothing and carriage are such as these; I shall obtain riches.
He immediately went to him and said:
"Sārthavāha, you should know!
The money previously owed must now be repaid.
The merchant was startled and said:
"I do not recall ever having wronged you at any time.
If I have indeed wronged you, who is this person that speaks so clearly?
The son of the elder said:
"For so many months and days, my father and I entrusted this money to your hands; you were our honest man for the management of these affairs.
For what reason do you say you have not [received it]?
The merchant's son said:
"I do not think so now; if there is indeed a factual basis for this, I shall repay you accordingly.
He then led the man with him to the place where the judge was.
The elder’s son said:
"In the past, this man personally borrowed a certain sum of money from my father. You, uncle, are a discerning person, and I too witnessed it at that time.
Is the matter not so?"
He replied, "I do not know.
His nephew said in astonishment:
"Uncle, if at that time you truly neither saw nor heard this, and did not speak such words, then this matter might be so;
yet did you not point with your hand and foot to this wealth?"
He replied, "No. The nephew said in anger:

"Because Bo was loyal and virtuous, the King entrusted him with affairs of state; the people of the realm trusted and relied upon him, and I myself am his close disciple. If such injustice occurred even toward him, how much more so toward outsiders? How many who have been wronged could there not be?"
"Whether this was true or false, future generations shall know for themselves.
The Buddha told the elder:
"If you wish to know who that elder Pingshi was at that time, he is none other than this present-day Māṃciviri, who is blind and deaf, lacking both ears and eyes."
Because of that single instance of lying at that time, he fell into the great hells and suffered manifold poisons;
upon emerging from hell, for five hundred lifetimes, he constantly assumed a formless, chaotic body.

Because you practiced giving generously at that time, you have always been born into wealthy families and attained the status of a master of riches; for the retribution of good and evil, though long deferred, never fails. Therefore, you all!
"You should be diligent and energetic, restraining your body, speech, and mind, and never recklessly committing evil.

At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, attained the first fruit up to the fourth fruit of the path; some gave rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta. All were filled with joy, receiving and upholding the teaching with the highest reverence.

Chapter 25: The Poor Couple Who Attained Immediate Retribution through Combined Almsgiving (26). Chapter Twenty-Five: The Poor Couple Who Attained Immediate Retribution through Combined Almsgiving. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the Jetavana Monastery, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus, preaching the Dharma.
At that time, there was an elder in the kingdom whose wife became pregnant; when the months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter who was upright and exquisite, her beauty having few equals.
At the time of his birth, he was born wrapped in fine, soft white cloth.
His parents, finding this strange, summoned a master to examine his physiognomy.
The master said, "Most auspicious!"
She possessed great merit and virtue.
Consequently, he gave her a name; in the Qin language, it means "white. As Śuklā grew up, her skin became increasingly fair.
This girl was so exquisite and beautiful that people from near and far throughout the kingdom vied with one another to seek her hand in marriage.
The parents thought to themselves, "Our daughter has reached marriageable age; she ought to be given in marriage.
They immediately had a craftsman fashion a necklace for her.
Śūli asked his father,
"What is this metal used for?
His father replied to him:
"You are now of marriageable age; I wish to give you in marriage, which is why I have made these bracelets for you.
The daughter said to her father, "I wish to leave the household life; I do not delight in being married away."
The parents, out of love and affection, did not oppose her wishes; they immediately brought out the cloth to make five robes for her.
When the girl saw this, she asked again:
"What do you intend to make?"
He said, "I shall make a robe for you," and spoke thus to his parents.
"I have now fully completed all that I was to wear; there is nothing further to be made. I only pray that you will permit me to go at once to the place where the Buddha resides.
His parents then immediately led him to the Buddha's presence, where he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and requested ordination.
The Buddha said, "Welcome!

Her hair fell off of its own accord, and the white cotton cloth she was wearing immediately became the five robes. She was entrusted to Mahāprajāpatī and ordained as a bhikṣuṇī; through diligent practice, before long, she attained the path of Arhatship.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What roots of merit did the bhikṣuṇī Śuklā originally plant, that she was born into a family of great wealth, emerged from her mother's womb wrapped in fine cloth, and after a short time since her renunciation, attained the path of Arhatship?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Listen attentively and reflect well!
I shall now speak of it.”
Ānanda replied, “Indeed.
The Buddha said:

"In the distant past, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin. Together with his disciples, he extensively delivered all beings; at that time, the king, ministers, and common people made many offerings and performed the Pañcavārṣika festival."
There was a bhikṣu who constantly traveled about exhorting others to go to the Buddha’s presence to listen to the Dharma and practice giving.

At that time, there was a woman named Dhanika who was extremely poor; husband and wife shared but a single piece of cloth. When the husband went out, he would wrap himself in it and depart, leaving his wife sitting naked upon a grass mat;
when the wife wrapped herself in the cloth and went outside to seek alms, the husband would sit naked upon the straw bedding.
The monk who was traveling for the purpose of exhortation arrived at her house next; seeing this woman, he exhorted her, saying:
"It is rare to encounter the appearance of a Buddha, rare to hear the sutras and the Dharma, and rare to obtain a human body. You should listen to the Dharma; you should practice giving."
He spoke at length on the retribution for stinginess and greed, as well as for the practice of giving.
The woman said,
"Venerable sir, please wait a moment."
Returning to her house, she said to her husband:

"Outside there was a śramaṇa who urged me to see the Buddha, listen to the Dharma, and practice giving. Because we failed to practice giving in our previous lives, we have fallen into this poverty; what should we now do to provide for ourselves in future lives?"
The husband replied to her, saying,
"My family is so impoverished that although I have the intention, with what could I possibly give?
The wife said:
"In my past lives I did not practice giving, and thus I have met with this present distress;
if I do not sow the seeds of merit now, where shall I go in the future?
You need only listen to me, for I am determined to give."
The husband thought to himself, "This woman may perhaps have some private property; I shall allow her to keep it.
He then spoke these words to her:
"Give it away as you wish to give," she replied. He then said,
"My intention is to offer this cloth as a gift."
The husband said:

"This single layer of cloth belongs to both you and me; we have relied upon it for our daily needs and survival. Now, if you give it away as an offering, we shall both face death. What plan do you wish to make?"
The wife said, "Human life ends in death; if you do not practice giving now, you will inevitably return to death anyway.
It would be better to die after having practiced giving, for there is hope for the future life."
"To die without having given is to face even greater suffering hereafter.
Thereupon, Huānxǐ said,
"I shall divide my death to give as alms."
The wife immediately went back out and said to the bhikṣu, "Venerable One!
You may stay under the eaves of my house; I shall provide you with alms."
The bhikṣu replied,
“If you wish to give, you should give in my presence so that I may offer prayers for your blessing.
Śūli addressed him, saying:
"This is my only shawl; there is no other garment within. A woman's body is foul and impure; it is not fitting for this to be removed.
She then re-entered the inner quarters, reached down from above, removed the shawl from her body, and presented it to the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu offered a blessing and carried it to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
"Bring this cloth here."
The bhikṣu offered it to the Buddha, and the Buddha received this soiled cloth with his own hands.
At that time, the king and the assembled multitude felt a slight sense of resentment in their hearts toward the Buddha for accepting such a dirty cloth.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts of the assembly, addressed them, saying:
"I observe that among the pure and great acts of giving in this assembly, none surpasses this gift of fine cotton cloth.
Upon hearing this, the great multitude was not without trepidation.
The lady was filled with joy and immediately removed the ornaments, necklaces, and precious robes she was wearing, presenting them to Dhanika;
the king was likewise delighted and removed his own garments, giving them to her husband and ordering him to go to the assembly.
Vipaśyin Buddha extensively expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly; at that time, many among the gathered multitude attained liberation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who that poor woman, Dhaniyā, was at that time, she is now the Bhikṣuṇī Cūḍā."

Because he offered cotton cloth with a pure mind at that time, for ninety-one kalpas, in every place where he was born, he was always provided with cotton cloth; he lacked nothing and obtained it all according to his wishes.
Because they encountered that Buddha, heard the profound and wondrous Dharma, and aspired for liberation, they have now met me and attained arhatship. Therefore, you all!
"You should diligently apply yourself with vigor to hearing the Dharma and practicing giving.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, many attained the Way; all were filled with joy and received the teaching upon their heads to practice accordingly.

26. Kātyāyana Teaches the Old Woman Who Sells Poverty (27). Chapter Twenty-Six: Kātyāyana Teaches the Old Woman Who Sells Poverty. (In the Danben [Dharmaguptaka] edition, this is Chapter Thirty-Seven. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Ālavi.
At that time, in that country, there was an elder who possessed great wealth and abundant treasures, yet he was miserly, greedy, violent, and cruel, lacking any heart of compassion.

He had a maidservant who was sent running about morning and night, finding no moment of peace; for even the slightest lapse or error, she would be subjected to flogging and beating. Her clothes did not cover her body and her food did not sustain her; aged, exhausted, and haggard, she longed for death but could not obtain it.
At that time, she happened to be carrying a jar and went to the river to fetch water; reflecting upon this suffering, she raised her voice and wept aloud.
Then Kātyāyana came to her place and asked, "Old mother! Why do you weep?"
"Why are you weeping and so distressed?
He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"

"I am already advanced in years and have constantly performed arduous labor; moreover, I am impoverished and lack sufficient food and clothing. I long for death but cannot attain it; for this reason, I weep."
Kātyāyana said,
"If you are poor, why do you not sell your poverty?
His mother replied:
"How can poverty be sold?
Who would buy poverty?
Kātyāyana said:
"If you are truly poor, you may indeed be sold.
This was said three times, whereupon the woman replied:
"If I am so poor that I may be sold, I ought to ask for instructions on how to proceed."
He immediately said,
"Venerable sir!
How can a poor man like me sell it?"
Kātyāyana said:
"If you truly wish to sell it, follow my words exactly and answer 'yes, sir'.
He then instructed him:
"First, you must bathe.
After he had bathed, [the teacher] said to him:
"You should practice generosity."
He said, "Venerable Sir! I am extremely impoverished.
As for my person now, I have not so much as a hand to offer in payment. Although I have this jar, it belongs to another; with what, then, shall I give?"
He immediately gave him the bowl, saying, "Take this bowl and fetch a small amount of pure water.
Following these instructions, he fetched it and presented it to Kātyāyana.
Kātyāyana accepted it and immediately offered a prayer of blessing.
Next, he instructed him in receiving the precepts, and afterwards taught him the various merits of mindfulness of the Buddha.
He then asked:
"Do you have a place where you reside?"
He replied, “There is none.

When it is time to grind, I lie down beneath the grinding stone; when it is time for pounding rice or cooking, I lie down amidst the work; and sometimes, when there is no work to do, I stay overnight on a heap of dung.”
Kātyāyana said: "Maintain your composure well;

serve with diligence and respect, harboring no resentment. Wait until the master of the house has finally fallen asleep, then quietly open his door. Inside the doorway, spread a seat of clean grass and contemplate the Buddha, ensuring that no evil thoughts arise."
At that time, the old woman followed the instructions and returned; acting according to the command, she passed away during the latter part of the night and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
When everyone rose early in the morning, they saw that the maidservant had died;
filled with resentment, they said, "This maidservant was constantly forbidden from entering the house; why then did she die here this evening?"
He immediately dispatched men who bound his feet with grass ropes and dragged him away to the Cold Forest (*śītavana*).
At that time, there was a certain son of heaven (*devaputra*) in the celestial realm, who had five hundred sons of heaven as his retinue and possessed a magnificent and beautiful palace.
At that time, the deva-son’s merit was exhausted and his life ended; this old woman immediately took his place.
According to the laws of rebirth in heaven, those with sharp faculties know their own future causes, while those born with dull faculties know only how to experience pleasure.
At that time, having been born among the devas, this woman enjoyed herself and experienced pleasure with five hundred sons of gods, unaware of the causes and conditions for her birth.
Then Śāriputra, while in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, knowing the karmic causes and conditions for this son of a god’s birth in heaven, asked him:
“Son of a god!
"By what merit were you born into this heavenly realm?
He replied, "I do not know."
At that time, Śāriputra, employing his divine eye, beheld the causes and conditions by which his former body had been reborn in heaven due to Kātyāyana;
he then led five hundred devaputras to the Śītavana forest, where they scattered flowers and burned incense as an offering to the corpse.

The radiance of the devas illuminated the village and the forest; seeing this transformation, the head of the household marveled at its cause and issued a proclamation to those far and near to come to the forest and observe.
Seeing the sons of the gods making offerings to this corpse, he immediately asked the devas:
"This maidservant was ugly and filthy; even while she was alive, people found her loathsome to behold, how much more so now that she is dead."
"Why do the devas bestow such offerings?
At that time, the devaputra explained in detail the causes and conditions for his birth among the devas from beginning to end, and they all immediately proceeded together to where Kātyāyana was.

At that time, Kātyāyana extensively expounded the various teachings for the devas and humans, namely: the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven; he spoke of how sensual desires are impure and that renunciation is bliss.

At that time, those devas and five hundred sons of gods, having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and flew back to their celestial palaces.

When the assembly had heard this Dharma, each attained the fruits of the Path, up to the fourth fruit; there was none who did not rejoice, receiving it upon their heads and practicing it accordingly, as they paid homage and departed.
Chapter 27: On Kimnara (28). Chapter Twenty-Seven on Kimnara. In the Dan edition, this chapter is in the fifth fascicle as the twenty-fifth. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in this land, there was an elder whose family was immensely wealthy with countless treasures; he begot a son whose body was golden in color.
The elder was filled with joy and celebration; he immediately established a sacrificial assembly and invited various physiognomists to divine his fortune.

At that time, the physiognomists took the child in their arms and examined him; seeing his extraordinary marks, they were overcome with joy beyond measure. They then conferred a name upon him, naming him Śuddhodana-deva (in the Jin language, Jintian).

This child’s merit and virtue are exceedingly pure and profound. On the day of his birth, a well spontaneously appeared within the house, eight feet in length and breadth, and likewise in depth. The water drawn from it could satisfy every human desire: if one required clothing, clothing emerged; if one required food, food emerged; and for gold, silver, precious jewels, or anything else needed, by making a wish to take them, they were obtained immediately according to one's heart's desire.
As the boy grew older, his talents and arts became widely renowned; the elders cherished him and did not dare to oppose his wishes, yet they thought to themselves:

"Our son is handsome and his appearance is peerless. We must seek out and select a famous maiden whose form and features are extraordinary and surpass all others, one with a golden countenance and a wondrous body who resembles our son; we shall go to seek her."
He immediately recruited various merchants and searched for her everywhere.

At that time, in the kingdom of Yamunā, there was a great elder who had a daughter named Śubhavarṇā (in the language of Jin, "Golden Radiance"). She was exceptionally beautiful and extraordinary; her body was golden in color, shining so brightly that it outshone others, and her skin was fine, smooth, and lustrous.

On the day of his birth, there was also a natural well of eight-foot-deep water; this well could likewise produce various kinds of rare treasures, as well as clothing, food, and drink, all provided in accordance with human needs.
However, that elder also thought to himself:

"My daughter is upright and beautiful, the most exquisite among people; I must find a worthy man whose appearance and radiance are comparable to my daughter's before I can give her in marriage and form an alliance."
At that time, the maiden named Yuanbu (Far-Reaching Fame) lived in Śrāvastī, and the reputation of the Golden Heaven (Suvarṇadeva) had also reached her family.
Then the two elders, each harboring great joy, went to one another’s homes and sought to form a marriage alliance; having finished taking the bride, they returned to Śrāvastī.
At that time, the household of Suvarṇadeva prepared superior offerings and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to provide sustenance for one day.

The Buddha accepted their invitation and went to their residence for a meal. Having finished eating and set aside his bowl, he extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for the elder Suvarṇadeva and his wife, opening and liberating their minds.

The King of Golden Heaven, his wife, and their parents immediately destroyed twenty billion eons of dark and evil karma; their minds were opened and liberated, and they attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
At that time, the World-Honored One returned to the vihāra.
Thereupon, Suvarṇadeva and Suvarṇaprabhāsa together addressed their parents, requesting permission to leave the household life.
Their parents immediately granted them leave; they both went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, performed circumambulations, and requested to enter the Path.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent and praised him,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he instantly became a śramaṇa.

Thereupon, the bhikṣu Jintian remained among the assembly of monks, while the bhikṣuṇī Jinguangming was entrusted to Mahāprajāpatī; through gradual instruction, they both became arhats, fully endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, possessing every merit in its entirety.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not understand, World-Honored One!

What deeds did the husband and wife Suvarṇadeva originally perform, such that from birth they have possessed abundant wealth and jewels, their bodies are golden in color, they are foremost in physical beauty, and they have obtained this single well capable of producing everything?"
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will fully proclaim and reveal it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in the world named Vipaśyin. After that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, his bequeathed Dharma remained in the world."
Later, there were certain bhikṣus who, traveling about to teach and transform others, arrived at a village.

There were many people there—noble and eminent elders—who, seeing the assembly of monks arrive, vied with one another to provide them with robes, bedding, food, and drink, so that nothing was lacking.
At that time, there was a husband and wife who were impoverished, hungry, and exhausted. They often thought to themselves:
"When my father was alive, his wealth and treasures were accumulated in full measure, overflowing beyond reckoning;

yet now I am so extremely poor and destitute, sleeping and sitting upon straw mats, with clothing that does not cover my body and no grain in the house even by the measure of a *sheng* or a *dou*—how bitter this is!"
"At that time, although I was wealthy and possessed immeasurable treasures, I did not encounter such a Sangha of noble ones;
now that I have met them, I have no money to offer.
Having reflected thus, he wept piteously; overcome with grief, his tears fell upon the arm of his wife.
When the wife saw her husband weeping, she asked him,
"What is it that does not suit you, that you are so distressed?
Her husband replied to his wife:
"Do you not know?
Just now a community of monks passed through this village, and the noble and virtuous lay devotees all rose to provide offerings.
My family is poor and destitute; we alone have not even a single *sheng* or *dou* to offer. Thus, regarding these monks, we have failed to plant seeds of wholesome conditions."
"Now we are impoverished in this life, and it will be even more severe in the next.
Having reflected on this, I weep for this reason.
The wife replied to her husband:
"Now what shall we do?
We wish to make an offering, yet we possess no wealth or jewels; though our intention remains, our vow cannot be fulfilled.
The wife spoke thus to her husband:
"Now you may go to your former home and search for wealth and treasures within the old storehouse; if you should find any, you must use it to make offerings.
Then the husband, following these words, went to the old storehouse and searched everywhere until he found a single gold coin, which he brought back to his wife.

At that time, his wife possessed a bright mirror; they reached a mutual agreement that it should be used for almsgiving. She prepared a new jar, filled it with pure water, placed these gold coins into the water within the jar, set the mirror on top, and carried it to the place where the Sangha was. Having arrived, she offered it to the Sangha with a sincere heart.
At that time, the community of monks accepted the offerings; each took water and used it to wash their alms bowls, while others took water and drank it.
Then the husband and wife, filled with joy and gladness, completed their meritorious deed. When they fell ill and passed away, they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The poor man who at that time gave a single jar of water as an offering to the Saṃgha was none other than this present-day couple, Suvarṇadeva."

Because in a previous life he offered this single coin, a vessel of water, and this bright mirror to the community of monks, he has been handsome in every lifetime, with a golden body and a radiance so exceptionally wondrous that it is beyond compare; for ninety-one kalpas, he has always remained thus.
Because at that time he possessed faith and reverence, he was able to leave behind birth and death and attain the state of an Arhat.
Ānanda, you should know that no merit should ever fail to be performed; as that poor man did through a small gift, he thereby obtained such immeasurable retribution of blessings.

At that time, Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, all gave rise to the mind of giving, diligently cultivated meritorious deeds, and joyfully put them into practice.
Chapter 28: On Repeated Lineages (29). Chapter Twenty-Eight on Repeated Lineages. According to the Danben (Dunhuang manuscript), this is Chapter Twenty-Six. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in the kingdom, there was a wealthy elder of noble standing whose riches were immeasurable; yet, as he had no offspring, he was constantly filled with melancholy and anxiety, offering prayers and sacrifices to the gods and spirits in his quest for a son.

Through their sincere and devoted devotion, the woman became pregnant; when the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son. The child was so handsome that he was rarely seen in the world. On an auspicious occasion, his parents and kinsmen gathered together and went to the banks of a great river to drink wine and enjoy themselves.

The parents took their child and went to the assembly hall; out of love for this child, the father carried him on his shoulders while sitting and dancing. When the father had finished dancing, the mother took him up again, carrying him through the rows of seated guests, lifting and tossing him about, enjoying themselves in joyful amusement.

Upon reaching the riverbank, his mind suddenly became distracted and his grip was not firm; he lost the child, who fell into the water. He immediately searched for and grasped at him, but in the end, he could not find him.
At that time, the parents, out of pity for their child and with hearts pained by their deep attachment, fainted and then revived.
By virtue of the child's merit, he did not die after all; he went into the river water and floated and sank along with the current.

At that time, there was a fish that swallowed this boy; although he was within the belly of the fish, he still did not die. At that time, there was a small village downstream where a wealthy family lived who also had no offspring; they sought after one in every possible way, yet were exhausted and unable to obtain one.
In that wealthy household, there was a servant constantly ordered to catch fish for sale and deliver the proceeds to his master.

This servant made a daily profession of fishing; one day, he caught a "child-swallowing" fish (*kumārabhakṣaka*). Upon cutting open its belly to examine it, he found a small boy inside with handsome features. Greatly delighted, he took the child and presented him to his master.
Everyone looked on and congratulated themselves, saying:
"Our family has long prayed to the gods and spirits in search of offspring; through the response of our sincere devotion, Heaven has granted us this child."
He immediately rubbed and cleaned him, nursing and raising him as his own child.

At that time, the parents from the upper village, having heard that the elder of the lower village had found a boy in the belly of a fish, went at once to his place to search for and demand him back, saying to him:
"This is our son; we lost this child in that river, and now you have found him. We pray that you will return him to us."
Then that elder replied to him, saying, "In my family, we have long offered prayers and sacrifices seeking a son; now the deity has granted a response, bestowing upon me a son."
"Where has your deceased son ended up?
As the dispute remained unresolved, they went to the King to seek a judgment.
Thereupon, both families cited their respective principles; the parents of the boy said:
"This is my son; at such-and-such a time, I lost him in the river.
Then that elder further said of himself, "I found him in the belly of a fish in the river; this is truly my son, not one born of you."
When the king heard their words, he did not know what course to take, so he immediately consulted with the two families regarding this matter:

"O two elders, each of you claims this child. Now, if I were to give him to only one, it would be contrary to principle. Therefore, let us raise him together in mutual cooperation until he reaches adulthood; then, each shall marry him off and establish a household for him, so that they may live separately in two different places."
"The child born of this wife shall belong to this family; the child born of that wife shall belong to that family.
At that time, the two elders each followed the King's instruction.
When the sons had grown up, their parents married them off and provided for all their needs so that they lacked nothing.
At that time, the sons said to their two parents:

"Since our birth, we have encountered the hardships of the net; we were swallowed by fish after falling into the water and were nearly dead before being rescued. Now, with sincere intent, we wish to leave the household life. We only pray that our parents will grant us permission."
At that time, his two parents, out of love for their son, could not refuse him and immediately gave their consent.
The boy then took his leave and went to where the Buddha was; prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he requested to enter the Path. The Buddha granted his request and praised him, saying:
“Welcome, Bhikṣu!”

His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and he immediately became a śramaṇa named Chongxing (Rebirth). The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the exhaustion of all suffering; thereupon, while still on his seat, he became an arhat.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“I do not understand, World-Honored One!

What deeds did this Bhikṣu of the Ghoṣila clan perform in the past, and what roots of goodness did he plant, that in his present life he fell into the water and was swallowed by a fish, yet did not die?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen for a moment!
I shall explain it for you."
In the distant past, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Vipaśyin, who gathered a great assembly and preached the sublime Dharma for them.

At that time, there was an elder who came to the assembly; hearing the Tathāgata extensively expound the Great Dharma on the merit of giving and the merit of observing the precepts, he rejoiced upon hearing it. With fierce faith, he immediately received the three refuges and the precept against killing from that Buddha, and further offered a single coin as an offering to him.
"For this reason, he has received blessings in life after life, possessing wealth and treasures at his disposal without ever lacking anything.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who that son of a householder was at that time, it is the bhikṣu Ghoṣila here now."

Because he gave a single coin to the Buddha at that time, for ninety-one kalpas he was constantly wealthy in money and goods; even unto this present life, his parents from both families have supplied all his needs.
Because he received the precept against killing, he fell into a great body of water as a fish, yet was not swallowed by death.
Because he received the Three Refuges, he has now encountered my world, bathed in pure transformation, and attained the path of Arhatship.

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, cultivated virtuous conduct and revered the Buddha's teachings; with joy and faith they accepted them, and wearing them upon their heads, they put them into practice.
Chapter 29: Sāndhāna (30). Chapter Twenty-Nine: Sāndhāna. According to the Dan-ben (Dunhuang manuscript), this is Chapter Twenty-Seven. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was together with his disciples, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.
At that time, there were five hundred beggars in the country who constantly relied upon the Tathāgata and followed the assembly of monks, seeking alms to sustain their lives.
As the years passed, a sense of weariness arose within them, and they spoke these words:
"We people here! Although we have been granted the remaining span of our lives through the merit of the Saṃgha, our hardships remain many."
They all thought to themselves:
"We should now seek ordination from the Buddha.
Together they went to where the Buddha was, and there the multitude addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely rare to encounter. We, all of us, were born into lowly circumstances; yet, having received the grace left by the Honored One, our lives have been sustained. Having already received such extraordinary nourishment, we long to leave the household life. We do not know, World-Honored One!”
"Can you not obtain it?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the beggars:

"My Dharma is pure; it makes no distinction between noble and base. It is like pure water that washes away all impurities: whether noble or base, beautiful or ugly, male or female—whatever the water washes, there is nothing that is not purified."

Furthermore, it is like fire: wherever it reaches, whether mountains, rivers, rocky cliffs, or all that exists between heaven and earth—be they great or small—all things that are touched by it will be scorched and consumed without exception.
Furthermore, my Dharma is like empty space; whether male or female, great or small, poor or rich, noble or humble—whosoever enters within it may act according to their own will and pleasure.

At that time, when the beggars heard what the Buddha had said, they were all filled with joy; their faith doubled in intensity, and they turned toward the Buddha with sincere devotion, seeking to enter the Path.
The World-Honored One said,
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
Whereupon his beard and hair fell away naturally, the Dharma robes were upon his body, and the appearance of a śramaṇa was thus fully perfected.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them; their minds were opened and their understanding was resolved, whereby they immediately exhausted all outflows and attained the state of Arhat.
