At that time, the various eminent elders and commoners within the kingdom, hearing that the beggars had been permitted by the Buddha to enter the Path, all gave rise to arrogance and spoke thus:
"How can the Tathāgata permit these lowly, wretched beggars to take their place among the ranks of the Saṅgha?"

"If we, as members of this assembly, were to cultivate meritorious deeds by inviting the Buddha and the Sangha to partake of a meal, how could we allow these lowly and base individuals to sit upon our couches and mats and take hold of our eating vessels?"
At that time, the prince named Jeta prepared various offerings and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, sending a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One, together with the community of bhikṣus, will graciously accept my invitation for tomorrow."
He then sent word to the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding those beggars who have been ordained as bhikṣus, I do not invite them; please be careful not to bring them along.
The Buddha accepted the invitation.
On the day after tomorrow at mealtime, when it is time for the Buddha and the assembly of monks to accept an invitation, he addressed the bhikṣus who were beggars:

"We shall accept the invitation, but you do not fall under this category. You may now go to Uttarakuru, take naturally ripened non-glutinous rice, and return to that house to eat the non-glutinous rice at your own leisure according to your rank."

Then the bhikṣus, acting according to their instructions, went to that world by means of the supernatural power of an arhat. Each took [food] until his bowl was full and returned; maintaining their dignified deportment, they followed one another in order, traveling through the air like the flight of a king of geese, until they arrived at the house of Jeta, where they sat down in succession and each ate his fill.

At that time, the Prince beheld the bhikṣus’ dignified deportment, their supernatural powers, and their merit; with a heart of reverence and joy, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not understand, World-Honored One! [What is this?]”
This assembly of noble and virtuous sages possesses towering majestic power and is endowed with all the marks of excellence; from what direction have they come to this place?
They are truly worthy of veneration. We pray that the Tathāgata will [reveal this to us].
"Now, please explain to me the origins and circumstances regarding his followers.
The Buddha told Jeta:
"If you wish to know, listen well and reflect upon it!"
I shall explain this for you.
These bhikṣus are precisely those whom I did not invite yesterday.

When I and the assembly of monks were about to go to accept the Prince’s invitation, these bhikṣus, because they had not been invited, went to Uttarakuru to gather naturally grown non-glutinous rice and ate it themselves.
At that time, when Jeta heard these words, he was filled with extreme shame and remorse, reproaching himself:
"How foolish and obscured I am, failing to distinguish between light and darkness!"
He further said:
"The merit of the World-Honored One is inconceivable!

These beggars, who were the most lowly and base in this land, have today received your pure transformation and are most deeply favored by your vast bounty. Having attained the bodily blessings of peace and happiness in this present life, they shall further obtain the bliss of non-action for all eternity."
The reason the Tathāgata has appeared in the world today is solely for the sake of these people; there is no other purpose remaining.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, we do not know what wholesome deeds these followers planted in past ages, nor what merits they cultivated, that they have now encountered the World-Honored One and received such extraordinary grace.
"What further transgression have I committed that, from birth until now, I must live by begging and endure such hardship?
O World-Honored One, in your compassionate pity,
please grant me an explanation!"
The Buddha told him:
"If you wish to know, you should listen attentively!
I shall explain this matter to you in its entirety, from beginning to end; listen well!"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Jeta:
"In the distant past, immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī."
In the kingdom there is a mountain named Lishi—which in the Jin language means "Immortal Mountain"—where many Buddhas of antiquity resided.
When there were no Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas would dwell there;

and even when there were no Pratyekabuddhas, various practitioners of the five supernatural powers who studied the arts of immortality would take up residence there, so that it was never left empty or abandoned.
At that time, there were more than two thousand pratyekabuddhas dwelling constantly within the mountain.
At that moment, a fire-star appeared in that country; it was a sign of an impending calamity.
This star has already appeared; for twelve years, the kingdom shall suffer from drought with no rain from heaven, making cultivation impossible, and the state will surely perish.

At that time, there was a householder within the country named Sandhāna, whose family was immensely wealthy with immeasurable wealth and grain, and who constantly provided offerings and provisions to various practitioners.
At that time, a thousand sages went to his house seeking alms and made this request:
"We, all of us, dwell upon that mountain; having encountered a drought in the land, we have been unable to obtain food through begging. Elder, if you can provide us with food, we shall remain here;
if you do not grant it to us, we shall go to other regions."
At that time, the elder immediately asked the storekeeper:
"Is all the grain and rice currently in my storehouse sufficient to provide food for these great beings?"
"I wish to invite him.
The storekeeper replied, "I only pray that you will invite him at your convenience; the grain and food we have are abundant and sufficient to provide for him."
The elder immediately invited the thousand pratyekabuddhas and provided them with food and offerings.
Those remaining thousand people also went to his house and likewise requested offerings.
The elder again asked his storekeeper:
"How much grain do you have stored?
There are another thousand people who also wish to provide offerings; will you be able to manage it?"
The storekeeper said, "The grain and provisions under my charge are surely sufficient; if you wish to provide an offering, you may invite them at your convenience.
Thereupon, the elder immediately extended the invitation.
Five hundred attendants were dispatched to provide and prepare food.
As time passed and many years went by, these attendants, while handling the cooking utensils, grew weary and spoke thus to one another:
"The reason all of us have undergone such hardship is entirely due to these beggars."
At that time, the elder always ordered one person to inform him when the time had come.
This messenger kept a puppy, which would follow him whenever he went to announce the time; this was so every day.
At that time, the messenger happened to forget one day and did not go to announce the hour; when the time arrived, the dog went alone to its usual place and barked loudly toward the great beings.
When the pratyekabuddhas heard the dog barking, they immediately knew that he was inviting them; they went to his house and received food according to the Dharma.
Thereupon, they said to the elder:
"It shall rain today; you should plant your crops."

The elder followed these instructions and immediately ordered his laborers to take their tools and work with diligence to cultivate the land; he sowed all types of edible grains, including both large and small barley.
After several hours, the things they had planted all transformed into gourds.
When the elder saw this, he was astonished and questioned them.
The great beings said:
"This matter requires no suffering; simply apply diligent effort and irrigate it according to the season.
Just as he said, through diligent irrigation, they later reached maturity; all the gourds became large and grew exceedingly abundant.
He immediately split it open and saw that, according to the seeds sown within, it had become well-cultivated, pure, and excellent, filled to the brim with barley.

The elder was filled with joy; the entire family stored it away until their house overflowed. He then shared it with his kinsmen and all throughout the kingdom, so that everyone received its beneficial grace.
At that time, the five hundred food-preparers thought to themselves:
"The karmic reward of these fruits they have obtained must surely be due to the grace of these Great Beings."
"How could we have spoken such evil words toward him?
They immediately went to his location and requested that he accept their repentance.
The Great Being listened to them; once they had finished repenting their transgressions, they further made this vow:
"May we, in future lives, encounter the worthy and the noble, and be granted liberation.
Because of this, for five hundred lifetimes he was always a beggar;
however, because he repented and made a renewed vow, he has now encountered my era and attained transcendence.
"O Crown Prince, you should know this!
As for that wealthy man Sandhana at that time, could he have been anyone else?
It was I myself."
The minister in charge of the treasury at that time was none other than Sudatta today.
The person who went daily to announce the arrival of the hour was King Udayana.
As for the puppy of that time, because of its barking, he has had beautiful voices in every lifetime; he is the Elder Meghadatta (Beautiful Voice).
"The five hundred people who were preparing food at that time are these very five hundred Arhats here now.

At that moment, Jeta and the members of the assembly, beholding this supernatural transformation and moved by the Buddha’s merit, applied themselves with diligent resolve. Some attained the first fruit [of the path] and others the fourth fruit; some became practitioners of the *kṣānti* (patient endurance) of the Noble Ones; and others gave rise to the aspiration to seek the Buddha-way. Each applied themselves with diligence to fulfill their original intent, leaping for joy as they received and practiced the teaching with the highest reverence.
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume Five;
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume Six.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Northern Wei Dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.
Chapter 31: King Candraprabha’s Gift of His Head (30). Chapter Thirty: King Candraprabha’s Gift of His Head. [In the Danben edition, this chapter appears in Volume Five as the twenty-eighth.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in the Āmra Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

"One who has attained the four bases of psychic power can remain for an eon. I have cultivated the four bases of psychic power to the utmost perfection; how long, then, shall the Tathāgata's life now endure?"
Thus it was repeated a second and a third time;
at that moment, Ānanda, being deluded by Māra, heard the World-Honored One’s instruction but remained silent and did not respond.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda again:
“You should rise and go to a secluded place for reflection.
The Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat and went into the forest.
After Ānanda had departed, the Māra Pāpīyas approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying:

“The World-Honored One has dwelt in the world teaching and transforming for a long time; his work of delivering sentient beings is complete, and those who have attained liberation from birth and death are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Now that he is advanced in years, it is fitting that he enter parinirvāṇa.”
At that time, the World-Honored One took a small amount of earth from the ground, placed it upon his fingernail, and addressed Māra, saying:
"Which is more: the earth on the ground, or that upon my fingernail?"
Māra replied to the Buddha, “The soil of the earth is exceedingly vast; it is not like the soil upon my fingernail.
The Buddha spoke again:
"The sentient beings already delivered are like the soil upon a fingernail; those remaining yet to be delivered are like the soil of the great earth.
He further addressed Māra, saying:
"Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
At that time, Pāpīyas, having heard these words, departed with joy.

Then Ānanda was sitting in the forest when he suddenly fell asleep and dreamed of a great tree that completely covered the void; its branches and leaves were lush and verdant, and its flowers and fruits were abundant. All living beings depended upon it for their sustenance, and the various wonders of that tree’s merit were beyond measure.

A whirlwind suddenly arose, blowing violently against the tree; its branches and leaves were shattered like fine dust and vanished at the place where the Malla was staying. All living beings were moved by grief and lamentation.
Ānanda was startled awake; filled with fear and unable to find peace, he further reflected:
"The tree I dreamed of was exceptionally wondrous and beyond measure; all under heaven relied upon its grace. For what reason has it been shattered and destroyed by the wind in such a manner?"
"Now the World-Honored One nurtures and protects all beings like a great tree; could it be that the World-Honored One intends to enter parinirvāṇa?
Having had this thought, he was overcome with great trepidation. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated before him, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the matters I dreamed of just now, could it be that the World-Honored One intends to enter parinirvāṇa?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“As you have said, three months from now I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Just now I asked you:”

"If one who has attained the four bases of psychic power can remain for a kalpa, and I have cultivated these four bases of psychic power to the utmost perfection, how long could the Tathāgata live today?"
"Thus, although I repeated this three times, you did not respond.
After you had departed, Māra came and urged me to enter parinirvāṇa, and I have already granted him my consent.

Upon hearing this, Ānanda was overcome with grief and bewilderment; he was so distressed and overwhelmed that he could not compose himself. His disciples, one after another, spoke to one another, and each harboring deep sorrow, they came to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda and his disciples:
"All things are impermanent; who can remain forever?
For you all, what was to be done has been done, and what was to be taught has been taught. You should simply apply yourselves with diligence to cultivation and practice; why do you grieve?"
"Without benefit and without practice.
At that time, Śāriputra, hearing that the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, felt deep sorrow and lamentation, and thereupon said:
"How swift is the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa!"
"The Eye of the World has been extinguished; we have forever lost our reliance and protection.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I cannot bear to see the World-Honored One pass into parinirvāṇa; I now wish to enter nirvana before him."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave.
Thus he requested three times.
The World-Honored One said: “Know that this is the time; all worthy sages are eternally in cessation.

At that time, having received the Buddha’s approval, Śāriputra adjusted his robes, knelt with his knees on the ground, and circumambulated the Buddha one hundred times. Coming before the Buddha, he praised him with various verses. Having done so, he grasped the Buddha’s two feet, reverently placing them upon the crown of his head; doing this three times, he stood with palms joined in attendance upon the Buddha and spoke as follows:
"This is the last time I shall behold the World-Honored One," he said,
and with palms joined in solemn reverence, he withdrew and departed.
Taking the novice Cunda with him, he went to Rājagṛha and arrived at his native land.
Having arrived, he immediately commanded the śrāmaṇera Cunda:
"Go into the city and throughout the villages, and inform the kings, ministers, old friends, and all the donors that they should come together to take their leave."
At that time, after Cunda had prostrated at his teacher’s feet, he went everywhere to proclaim:
“My upādhyāya Śāriputra has now arrived here and intends to enter parinirvāṇa; those who wish to see him should go there at once.”

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, along with the country’s eminent and noble donors—the fourfold assembly—having heard the words of Jvālita, were all filled with grief and lamentation; with one voice and in unison, they spoke these words:
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
"The Great General of the Dharma, whom all classes of sentient beings revere and look up to—
how can his parinirvāṇa now be so swift?
Each of them rushed to the place where he was, prostrated themselves before him, and after their inquiries were concluded, they spoke together, saying:
“We have heard that the Venerable One intends to relinquish his life and enter nirvana; we, of our kind, shall lose our reliance.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the assembly, saying:
“All things are impermanent; all who are born must come to an end. All within the three realms are suffering—who can find peace?”

You all possess the merit of past lives, having been born to encounter the age of a Buddha; the sutras and Dharma are difficult to hear, and a human body is difficult to obtain. Therefore, be mindful and diligent in performing meritorious deeds, seeking deliverance from birth and death.
In this manner, through various and manifold skillful means, he extensively administered medicine according to the specific ailments of all people.

At that time, the assembly, having heard what was taught, attained the first fruit up to the third fruit of the path; some left the household life to become arhats, while others vowed their hearts to seek the Buddha-way. Having heard the Dharma, they paid homage and departed.

Then, during the latter part of the night, Śāriputra straightened his body and composed his mind; fixing his attention before him, he entered the first dhyāna. Rising from the first dhyāna, he entered the second dhyāna; rising from the second dhyāna, he entered the third dhyāna; and rising from the third dhyāna, he entered the fourth dhyāna.

Emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the concentration of the sphere of infinite space; emerging from the sphere of infinite space, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness; emerging from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the sphere of nothingness; emerging from the sphere of nothingness, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of cessation; emerging from the attainment of cessation, he attains parinirvāṇa.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that Śāriputra had already entered parinirvāṇa, came to his location accompanied by hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts as his retinue. Each carried flowers, incense, and various articles of worship, filling the void of space. They all wailed in grief, their tears falling like heavy rain, scattering flowers everywhere until they reached the height of the knees.

They further said to one another: "The Venerable One’s wisdom was as deep as the great ocean; his swift eloquence responded to the needs of the occasion, his voice like a gushing spring. Endowed with the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, he was a great general of the Dharma who would have followed the Tathāgata in widely turning the wheel of the Dharma. That he has entered nirvāṇa—how sudden it is!"

When those both inside and outside the city and its precincts heard that Śāriputra had already entered parinirvāṇa, they all brought ghee, oil, incense, flowers, and various offerings, rushing together in haste. Overwhelmed by grief and longing, they could not restrain themselves; each holding incense and flowers, they used them to make offerings.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, commanded Viśvakarman to gather various jewels and adorn a lofty carriage; he placed Śāriputra upon the carriage, while the devas, nāgas, ghosts, kings, ministers, and commoners escorted him with wailing cries until they reached a level and broad expanse of ground.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, commanded the yakṣas:
"Go to the shore of the great ocean and fetch gośīrṣa-candana.

Having received these instructions, the yakṣas immediately went, retrieved the wood, and returned. They piled it into a great pyre, placed his body upon it, poured ghee over it, set fire to it for cremation, paid homage as an offering, and then each departed.

After the fire was extinguished, the novice Cunda collected his teacher’s relics, placed them in a bowl, gathered his three robes, and carried them to where the Buddha was. He prostrated before the Buddha, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha:
“My preceptor Śāriputra has already entered parinirvāṇa; these are his relics, and these are his robes and bowl.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard these words, was overcome with grief and distress; his sorrow deepened all the more, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now that this Honored One, the Great General of the Dharma, has entered parinirvāṇa, upon whom shall I rely?"
The Buddha told him:
"Śāriputra, although he has entered parinirvāṇa, his morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—such a Dharma-body as this—is likewise not extinguished."
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
it is not only today that you cannot bear to see me enter parinirvāṇa and pass away before me;
in past lives as well, you were unable to endure seeing my death and passed away prior to me.
The venerable Ānanda joined his palms and addressed the Buddha:
"I venture to ask, World-Honored One:
what were the circumstances regarding his previous death in the past?"
"I pray that you will explain this for me.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and asāṃkhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Candraprabha (in the Jin language, 'Moonlight'), who governed eighty-four thousand kingdoms, sixty thousand mountains and rivers, and eight billion villages throughout Jambudvīpa."

The king had twenty thousand ladies and court attendants; his principal consort was named Sumāndā (translated into Chinese as Huashi), and he had ten thousand ministers, the chief of whom was named Mahācandra (translated into Chinese as Dayue).
The king had five hundred princes, the eldest of whom was named Śīlabhadra, which in the language of Jin means "Virtuous in Precepts.

The city where the king resided was named Bhadra-jīva, which in the language of Jin means "Worthy Longevity. This city measured four hundred yojanas in length and breadth; it was composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, and possessed one hundred and twenty gates on its four sides, with streets, lanes, and alleys laid out in perfect symmetry.

Furthermore, within that land, there are four rows of trees, likewise composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; some have golden branches and silver leaves, some have silver branches and golden leaves, some have lapis lazuli branches and crystal leaves, and some have crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves.
There are various jeweled ponds, likewise composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; the sands at the bottom of these ponds are also made of these four treasures.
The king’s inner palace is forty li in circumference and is entirely constructed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
That land was fertile and lush, its people lived in happiness, and its rare and wondrous treasures were beyond counting.
At that time, as the king sat in his main hall, this thought suddenly arose in him:

"When a person dwells in this world with honor, glory, and noble status, being venerated by all under heaven, their words never being disobeyed, and the five exquisite sensual pleasures arriving at will—such karmic fruits are all brought about by the accumulation of virtue and the cultivation of merit."

It is like a farmer who, having sown extensively in spring, reaps an abundant harvest in autumn and summer; yet when spring arrives again, if he does not diligently sow, what can he hope for in autumn and summer?
Just so, I have now obtained this wondrous fruit through the merit previously cultivated; if I do not sow again now, there will likewise be no hope for the future.
Having formed this thought, he addressed his ministers:

"I now wish to bring forth my treasury of rare jewels and place them at the city gates and in the marketplace, and establish a great act of giving, providing everything that sentient beings may require, granting it all to them."
He further commanded the eighty-four thousand minor kingdoms below:
"Open all treasuries and bestow their contents as gifts upon everyone.
The ministers said:
"Excellent! We shall respectfully follow the King's instructions.
They immediately erected golden banners and struck golden drums, widely proclaiming the royal edict so that everyone far and near, both within and without, might hear and know it.

At that time, within the kingdom, śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, the elderly, and those who were destitute, supported one another—both strong and weak alike—and gathered like clouds and rain. To those who needed clothing they gave clothing; to those who needed food they gave food; and gold, silver, precious objects, and medicines according to their ailments—all things required, they gave them as desired.

All the ministers and subjects within Jambudvīpa, having received the King’s bounty and grace, experienced boundless happiness. Songs of praise and hymns of eulogy filled the thoroughfares; his virtuous reputation spread far and wide, reaching the four quarters, such that there were none who did not revere him and yearn for the transformative influence of his benevolence.
"At that time, on the borderlands, there was a small kingdom whose king was named Vimalasena.
Hearing of King Candraprabha’s great and lofty reputation, he harbored feelings of jealousy; unable to find peace even upon his bed, he reflected to himself:
'As long as Candraprabha is not eliminated, my own fame shall not emerge.'"
"I shall employ skillful means to invite various practitioners and seek out those who aspire to this path, so that we may accomplish this matter.

Having reflected thus, he immediately issued orders to summon the brahmins within the kingdom, providing them with a hundred-flavored feast of delicacies and serving them with the utmost reverence, never failing to honor their wishes.
After three months had passed, he addressed the brahmins:
"I now have a sorrow that entangles my heart; day and night I toss and turn, unable to find relief. How can it be dispelled?"
"You practitioners of the Way, you are those whom I honor; you should devise skillful means to assist me in clearing away this calamity.
The brahmins together addressed the king, saying:
"What is the cause of Your Majesty's anxiety?"
"Please show me the words.

The king then said, "That King Candraprabha’s name and virtue are far-reaching and renowned; his reputation is heard throughout the four quarters. I alone am lowly and vulgar, possessing no such beautiful renown."
"Our hearts and minds have a desire that we wish to eliminate.
What skillful means can be employed to accomplish this?
When the brahmins heard these words, they each said to one another:
"King Candraprabha’s compassionate kindness and benevolent grace moisten all beings; his sorrowful rescue of the destitute and distressed is like that of parents to their children.
With what heart could we proceed with this evil plot?"
"I would rather kill myself than do this.
Thereupon, they each dispersed, paying no heed to the offerings.
At that time, Vimalasena’s distress and confusion increased even further; he immediately went out and issued a wide recruitment, proclaiming his command everywhere:
"Who can obtain the head of King Candraprabha for me? I shall share half the kingdom with him and give my daughter to him as a wife.
At that time, there was a Brahmin on the mountain slope named Raudrākṣa, who, having heard the king’s proclamation, came to respond to the king's recruitment.
The king was greatly delighted and spoke to him again:
"If you can indeed accomplish this, I shall not violate my solemn oath.
If you are able to depart, on what day shall it be?"
The brāhmaṇa said, “Prepare the provisions required for my journey; in seven days from now, I shall set forth.

At that time, the brāhmaṇa performed incantations to protect himself. When the seven days had passed, he came to take leave of the king. The king provided him with his necessities, and he set out on his way.

At that time, various portents and anomalies appeared throughout King Candraprabha’s kingdom: the earth split open in every place, meteors and stars fell like flashes of lightning, and the sky was shrouded in gloomy mist and darkness even by day, with thunder and peals of lightning. Flocks of birds in the void cried out with piteous and piercing sounds, plucking at their own feathers; while tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, and other beasts of prey threw themselves down, leaped about, and howled.
The eighty-four thousand minor kings all dreamed that the golden banner of the Great King suddenly snapped and his golden drum suddenly burst.
The Grand Minister of Mahācīna dreamed that a ghost snatched away the King’s golden crown. Each harbored deep sorrow and could not find peace of mind.
At that time, the deity of the city gate, knowing that the brahmin wished to beg for the king’s head, likewise became bewildered and blocked him, refusing to let him enter.

The brahmin circled the city gate several times but was unable to proceed. The devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, knowing that King Candraprabha was about to give his head as an offering and thereby fulfill his perfection in *dāna*, spoke to the king in a dream, saying:

"You have vowed to practice giving and do not oppose the wishes of the multitude; yet the beggar stands at the gate with no means of proceeding. To be a donor while such circumstances prevail is contrary to what is required."
The king awoke in astonishment and immediately commanded the Great Month Minister:
"Go to all the gates and order that no one be turned away.
When the Great Month Minister arrived at the city gate, the deity of the gate immediately manifested his form and said to the Great Month:
"A brahmin has come from another country harboring evil intent, wishing to beg for the king's head; for this reason, I did not grant his request.
The minister replied, "If such a thing were to happen, it would be a great calamity."
"However, there is a royal decree which we must not violate; what shall we do?
At that time, the deity of the city gate ceased obstructing him.
Then, the Great Minister of Candra reflected to himself:
"If this brahmin should insist on begging for the king's head, we shall have five hundred heads made of the seven precious gems and use them to trade for it.
He then issued the command to have them made.
At that time, the brahmin went straight to the front of the palace and cried out in a loud voice:
"I am from a distant land; having heard of the King's merit—how you give all things away and never refuse anyone's request—I have traveled from afar wishing to obtain something."
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy; he went out to meet him, paid his respects, and inquired:
"Are you not exhausted from traveling?

Whatever you desire—be it the kingdom, cities, wife, children, precious jewels, carriages, palanquins, elephants, horses, the seven treasures, or male and female slaves and servants—I shall grant you all that you wish to have."
The Brahmin said:
"Although all external objects may be used for giving, the retribution of such merit is not vast;
the merit of giving one's own flesh is truly sublime."
"I have come from afar for this very purpose: I wish to obtain the king's head.
If you do not refuse me out of malice, it should be granted to me.
Upon hearing these words, the king leaped for joy beyond measure.
The brāhmaṇa said,
"If you will give me your head, when shall it be given?
The king replied, "Seven days from now, I shall give you my head."
At that time, the Great Moon Minister, carrying the seven-jeweled head, came to apologize and offer it; he prostrated himself before him and said to the Brahmin:
"This king's head is a combination of bone, flesh, and blood—an impure thing. Why do you seek this?"
"I now offer these heads made of the seven precious gems as a trade for yours. You may take them;
by exchanging them, you will surely obtain enough wealth to sustain you for the rest of your life.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I have no need for this; I desire the king's head to fulfill my own purpose.
At that time, the Great Minister Yue admonished him in various ways, yet he never turned back. Immediately, overcome with indignation, his heart split into seven pieces, and he died before the king.
At that time, the king issued a command to his ministers: "Mount the eight-thousand-li elephant and proclaim throughout all the kingdoms:
'Seven days from now, King Candraprabha shall offer his head as alms to a brahmin.'"
"If you wish to come, proceed there with all speed.

At that time, eighty-four thousand kings arrived in an unending stream; they all beheld the Great King, prostrated themselves before him, and said: "The people of Jambudvīpa rely upon Your Majesty’s grace and benevolence; each has attained abundance and joy, living in merriment free from affliction."
Why would you suddenly, for the sake of a single person, forever abandon the multitude and no longer feel compassion for them?
We only pray that you will show us mercy!
Do not give away your head.

The ten thousand ministers all threw themselves to the ground, pressing their bellies against the king’s feet, and said: "We pray only that you will look upon us with compassion and pity; do not give away your head, lest we be forever abandoned."
The twenty thousand ladies also cast their bodies to the ground and looked up, addressing the King:
"Do not forget us and abandon us; please grant us your protection.
If you give away your head, what shall we rely upon?"
The five hundred princes wept before the king and said:
"We are orphaned and young; to whom shall we turn for refuge?
We pray that you will have compassion for us and not give away your head."
"You have nurtured us and enabled us to attain our place among human beings.
Then the Great King addressed his ministers, subjects, ladies, and crown prince:

"Consider that since I first received this body, I have traversed the cycle of birth and death for a vast duration. Whether in the hells, I was born and died repeatedly within a single day, casting off my body countless times as I passed through the Ash River, the Iron Bed, the Boiling Excrement, the Fire Chariots, the Charcoal Pit, and other such hells."
In such bodies as these, they are burned, pierced, boiled, and roasted; cast away again and again, they never attain any karmic reward.

If born among animals, they prey upon one another or are killed by humans; their bodies are offered for the mouths of many, being destroyed and consumed in countless instances. Thus they waste this body in vain, likewise receiving no karmic reward.

Some fall among the hungry ghosts, with fire issuing from their bodies; others become flying wheels that come to sever their heads. Though severed, they are born again, undergoing such deaths countless times. Yet even through such self-sacrifice, there is no karmic reward of merit.

If born among humans, they contend over wealth and beauty; with eyes blazing and fury intense, they kill one another, or raise armies to face in battle, hacking and severing each other—such deaths as these are likewise beyond counting.
Driven by greed, hatred, and delusion, one has constantly killed many bodies throughout time, yet never performed a single act of merit before casting off this life.
Now, this body of mine is composed of various impurities; it must inevitably be abandoned and cannot endure for long.
"Since I am trading this head—perishable, fragile, foul, and evil—for a great benefit, how could I not give it?
I shall offer this head to the Brahmin; by means of this merit, I vow to seek the path of Buddhahood."
If I attain the Way of the Buddha and my merits are fully perfected, I shall deliver you from suffering through skillful means.
Now that my resolve to give has reached the point of fulfillment, take care not to obstruct my aspiration for the unsurpassed path.
When all the kings, ministers, subjects, ladies, and crown princes heard the king’s words, they remained silent and spoke no further.
At that time, the great king said to the brahmin:
"If you wish to take my head, now is precisely the right time."
The brāhmaṇa said:

"Now the king is surrounded by a great multitude of ministers and subjects; I am but a single person, weak in strength and power, and cannot strike off the king's head here. If you wish to give it to me, you should go to the rear garden."
At that time, the Great King addressed the minor kings, princes, ministers, and subjects:
"If you truly love and respect me, take care not to harm this Brahmin."
Having spoken these words, he entered the rear garden together with the brahmin.
At that time, the brahmin spoke again to the king, saying:
"Your body is in its prime with the strength of a mighty athlete; if you were to suffer the pain of being cut, you might perhaps later come to regret it."
"Take your hair and tie it firmly to a tree; only then will you be able to cut it off.

At that time, the king followed these words and sought out a sturdy tree with lush foliage and firm branches upon which to tie himself. He knelt before the tree, tied his hair to it, and said to the Brahmin:
"Cut off my head and let it fall into my hands; only then may you take it from my hands."

Now I give my head to you; by means of this merit, I do not seek the pleasures of Māra, Brahmā, Śakra, or the Wheel-Turning Sage King within the three realms, but rather seek the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path, vowing to deliver all sentient beings to the bliss of Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the brahmin raised his hand, intending to strike; seeing this, the tree deity was deeply distressed, thinking, "How can such a person wish to kill?"
He immediately seized the Brahmin by the ear with his hand; the man’s neck twisted backward, his limbs became convulsed, he dropped his knife to the ground, and was unable to move.
At that time, the Great King spoke to the tree deity:
"Since my past lives, I have already used nine hundred and ninety-nine heads as offerings here beneath this tree."
"Now, by giving this head, my count will reach one thousand; once I have sacrificed this head, my practice of *dāna* will be fully perfected.
Do not obstruct my resolve for the unsurpassed path.
When the tree deity heard these words from the king, he restored the Brahmin to his former state.
At that moment, the brahmin rose from the ground, took up his sword once more, and struck off the king’s head; the head fell into his hands.
At that time, heaven and earth shook in six ways, and the palaces of the devas trembled and became unsteady; each was filled with terror, wondering at the cause of such a marvel.

They soon saw the Bodhisattva, who, for the sake of all beings, had given away his head as alms. All descended [from the sky], moved by his extraordinary deed, and with tears falling like rain, they praised him together, saying:
"The Great King Candraprabha has given his head in charity; thus, he has now fulfilled the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)."
At that time, this sound spread throughout the world.
When King Vimalaśrī heard these words, he was filled with joy and leaped for joy, yet he was so struck with astonishment that his heart burst asunder and he died.
At that time, the brahmin took the king’s head and departed. When the various kings, ministers, subjects, consorts, and crown princes saw the king’s head cast upon the ground, they wailed in unison;

some fainted and then revived, while others were so overcome with grief that they bled from their mouths and died. Some stood stunned, unable to recognize anything; some tore out their own hair, while others rent their garments. Some used both hands to tear at their faces as they wept uncontrollably, rolling about upon the ground.
At that time, the brahmin, loathing the stench of the king’s head, immediately threw it to the ground, trampled it with his feet, and departed.
Or perhaps someone else said to the brahmin:
"Your cruelty is truly extreme; since this is of no use at all, why did you seek it out?"

At that time, the brahmin proceeded on his way and departed; those who saw him rebuked him, and as no one provided him with food, he became emaciated by hunger and reached the very limit of suffering and distress.

While on the road, he encountered someone and inquired after news; learning that King Vimala had already passed away, he lost all hope and was overcome with such agonizing distress that his heart split into seven pieces, and he died from vomiting blood.
King Vemacitrin and Raudrākṣa, upon the end of their lives, both fell into the Avīci hell.
As for the other subjects and citizens, those who died out of deep, sorrowful longing for the king’s benevolence were all reborn in the heavens.
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
You should know that the King Candraprabha of that time was none other than my own self.
King Vimalaśrī was none other than Pāpīyān."
The Brahmin Raudrakṣa at that time was the present Devadatta;
the tree deity at that time was the present Maudgalyāyana;
and the great minister Mahācandra at that time was the present Śāriputra.
At that time, being unable to bear seeing my death, they died before me;
even until today, being unable to bear seeing me enter nirvana, they have entered extinction first.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the venerable Ānanda and all the disciples, having heard what the Buddha taught, were filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy. With one voice and in unison, they all together praised the Tathāgata’s marvelous and extraordinary virtues.

They all practiced with single-minded devotion; some attained the fruits of the four stages of the path, while others resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. All were filled with great joy, reverently upholding and practicing [the teaching].
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume Six (32). Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Circumstances of King Kṣema’s Gift of His Eyes. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma; the people of the city who delighted in hearing the Dharma went to the Buddha’s location, following one after another in succession.
At that time, there was a blind brahmin sitting by the side of a street who, hearing a great multitude of people walking with rapid strides, immediately asked a passerby:
"Where is this great multitude of people going?"
The practitioner replied, "Do you not know?
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter; he is currently in this country, expounding the transformative teachings of the Way."
"We wish to go and listen to his preaching of the Dharma.
This brahmin possessed a certain art: among all living beings, there are eight kinds of voices, which he could distinguish and identify all, knowing their characteristics and fortunes.
What are the eight kinds? First is the voice of a crow;

second is the voice of a three-footed crow; third is the broken voice; fourth is the voice of a wild goose; fifth is the voice of a drum; sixth is the voice of thunder; seventh is the voice of a golden bell; eighth is the Brahma-voice.
As for those with the voice of a crow, their innate nature is such that they do not recognize kindness or nurturance, and their will is neither modest nor pure.
Those with the "three-footed crow" voice are by nature fierce and violent; they delight in inflicting injury and lack compassion and obedience.
As for those with broken voices, if a man makes a woman’s voice or a woman makes a man’s voice, such persons will be of meager merit, impoverished, and lowly.
As for those with the voice of a wild goose, their intellects and natures are sharp and discerning; they have many friends and associates, and they welcome guests from all quarters.
He with the sound of a drum will possess eloquent and swift speech, explaining principles with clarity, and shall certainly become a National Preceptor.
He with the sound of thunder possesses profound and far-reaching wisdom; he analyzes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and is capable of transforming the world through his teachings.
As for those with voices like the sound of a golden bell, they will possess immense wealth and riches; such a person will surely accumulate ten billion taels of gold.

As for those with voices like the Brahma-sound, their merit and virtue are exceedingly high; if they remain at home, they will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, and if they leave the household to study the Way, they will certainly attain Buddhahood.
At that time, the brahmin said to the passersby:

"I am able to distinguish the voices of men. If this is truly the Buddha, he must possess the Brahma-voice. You may take me to his location so that I may test and hear it, to verify whether he is indeed the Buddha."
At that time, a traveler was led along by force until he gradually drew near the Buddha’s dwelling.

Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma—his Brahma-voice complete, profound, far-reaching, and flowing—he leaped for joy with exultation. His two eyes were opened, and he beheld the Buddha, whose purple-golden body possessed the thirty-two marks, as radiant and brilliant as the sun. He immediately prostrated before the Buddha, filled with immeasurable joy and celebration.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for him; with a sincere mind, he listened and received it, immediately destroying twenty billion evils and attaining the stage of Srotāpanna. Having already obtained the eye of wisdom, he then sought to leave the household life.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome! and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
The Buddha, employing skillful means once more, extensively expounded the Dharma for them, whereupon they immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Among the entire assembly, there was none who did not marvel at this.
The Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The appearance of the World-Honored One in the world truly brings immense benefit; he rescues those who are blind and ignorant, and his kindness is beyond measure.
This brahmin, in a single moment, has had his physical eyes opened and his eye of wisdom purified.”
"How profound and generous is the Buddha's kindness toward this person?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I gave him his eyes not only today; in past lives as well, I likewise gave him his eyes."
Ānanda spoke again:
"I do not understand, World-Honored One!
What was the matter regarding the giving of the eyes in the past?"
“I only pray that you will show compassion and explain this in detail for me.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“In the distant past, immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great city named Pukaravati.”

At that time there was a king named Sūdira, which means "Quick-Eyed" (Kātyāyana). He was so named because his eyes were clear and pure, exquisite beyond compare; he could see through walls and behold things for forty *li*. For this reason, he was given the title Kātyāyana.
He ruled over eighty-four thousand kingdoms, sixty thousand mountains and rivers, and eight billion villages in Jambudvīpa.
The king had twenty thousand queens and court ladies, ten thousand ministers, and five hundred princes; his eldest prince was named Śīlabhadra, which means "Virtuous in Morality."

The king possesses compassion and takes pity on all beings; he nurtures the people and creatures like a loving father. He transforms and guides them with goodness, and the people follow his regulations. The winds and rains are timely and harmonious, the four seasons are temperate and appropriate, and the kingdom is prosperous and joyful, so that all living beings receive his bounty and reliance.
At that time, the king withdrew to reflect within himself:

"By virtue of my past merit, I am now the sovereign of men; with wealth, treasures, and the five desires, I possess the four seas. When I speak, those below are transformed by me, like grass bending before the wind."
The resources used in this life will not have a successor; I fear that in future lives, poverty and suffering will be my lot.

It is like a farmer who sows extensively in the spring and harvests in the autumn and summer, thereby surely gaining much; yet when spring arrives again, if he should be lazy, what can he hope for regarding the grain in the coming autumn?
"Therefore, I must now sow extensively within the fields of merit while the time is right; it is not fitting to be indolent.
He then addressed his ministers:

"Bring forth from my treasuries the gold, silver, precious gems, clothing, food, drink, and all necessary articles, and place them at the city gates and pile them up in the marketplace. Proclaim this everywhere: 'All you people, whatever you may lack, come and take it.'"
Furthermore, he issued a proclamation to the eighty-four thousand subordinate kingdoms, ordering them likewise to open their treasuries and bestow their wealth upon all.
Thereupon, the ministers received the King’s decree; they immediately erected golden banners, beat great golden drums, and circulated the King’s compassionate edict throughout Jambudvīpa.
To the people of Jambudvīpa—whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the solitary, the poor, those in distress, the elderly, or the sick—he shall give whatever they desire, according to their wishes.
All people, relying on the King’s compassionate grace, dwell in peace and joy, free from further anxiety; they sing praises and offer hymns of laudation, all extolling the King’s virtue.

"At that time, in a remote borderland, there was a small kingdom whose king was named Prasenajit. Relying on his distance [from the central court], he was arrogant and did not submit to the King’s transformation through教化 (teaching and transformation). Furthermore, in his administration, five matters lacked moderation: by nature he was impulsive and lacked reflection; he was addicted to sensual desires and neglected the affairs of state; though the country had loyal and worthy men, he would not go to consult them; the lands on the borders were subjected to double the usual labor services; and when merchants arrived in the country, they were taxed and plundered beyond the norm."

That king had a minister named Raudrākṣa, who was wise and possessed of strategic insight, clearly understanding the principles of statecraft. Observing that the king’s conduct violated the laws of propriety, he stepped forward and admonished him, saying:
"Your Majesty, there are five matters by which a kingdom cannot be pacified; they will surely invite calamity and disaster, and I fear the dynasty will not endure long.
If Your Majesty has no objection, please allow me to speak of them."
The King said,
"Speak then. Thereupon,
he knelt for a long time and addressed the King.
"Your Majesty’s nature is impulsive and lacks deliberation; when matters are handled improperly on such a grand scale, regret will inevitably follow.
You are so addicted to sensual desires that you neglect the affairs of state; consequently, there are injustices and delays abroad, and those seeking redress have nowhere to turn."
If a state possesses loyal and wise men yet does not consult them, it will fail to anticipate and guard against future events.
If the people of the borderlands are burdened by excessive labor and taxation, they will think of defying their allegiance and joining another state.
Merchants' taxes have been plundered, exceeding the normal regulations; people dread traveling to and fro, and precious goods have become exceedingly expensive.
These five matters are omens of the ruin of a state; I pray that Your Majesty will change your ways and begin anew with the people.
"King Suddhodana’s benevolence is vast and universal; all people of Jambudvīpa receive his wise grace.
Yet our own country alone does not show obedience, and its remote and secluded inhabitants do not receive his nourishing moisture."
"I pray that Your Majesty will soften your mind and return to accept our service; thus you may ensure that your descendants enjoy their stipends for a long time.
When Prasenajit heard these words from his minister, his heart was filled with resentment and his countenance darkened, and he did not follow his advice.
I, the minister Raudrāśva, grew increasingly resentful and agitated, yet I thought to myself:

"I observe that while Your Majesty governs, your transformative influence is not all-pervasive; I have presented my loyalty and hope to provide mutual support, yet you respond with even greater fury and do not follow my words."
"Since my words were not heeded, should I be killed, I shall instead proceed to eliminate him and remove this scourge for the sake of the people.
Before his plan could be carried out, the matter was already exposed; the King assembled his troops and intended to go and execute him.
At that time, Raudrākṣa, knowing the king intended to capture him, immediately mounted a swift horse and fled. His troops pursued him in hot pursuit.

Raudrākṣa was naturally skilled in archery and knew that there were eighteen vital points on a human body where a shot would cause death. Although his pursuers caught up with him, they did not dare draw near; thus he proceeded directly until he reached the kingdom of Puṣkarāvatī.

Having seen King Kaimu, they paid their respects and exchanged greetings; as they conversed with the king, every point of discussion was reasoned and sound. The king immediately approved of them and appointed them as his ministers.
Gradually gaining access, he related all that had occurred and reported it to the King.
Having heard this, the King asked his ministers:
"Does that kingdom not belong to me?"
The ministers replied, "They all belong to Your Majesty;
it is only because they rely on their great distance that they have not come to pay homage and submit. Raudrākṣa said:

"That Paudālavatsa is obstinate, foolish, wicked, and ignorant; he is licentious and deluded, lacking knowledge of ritual propriety. Relying on his distance and persisting in his errors, he does not obey the royal command.
His subjects detest him and regard him as an enemy; therefore, take your ministers and troops and go yourself to subdue him."
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately granted his consent.
He issued proclamations to the various kingdoms to select their troops, and set a date for them to assemble en masse and march toward the kingdom of King Pradyota Bimbisāra.
At that time, the King of the country of Pāṭaliputra sent a messenger to say to him:
"Throughout Jambudvīpa, a general order has been issued to mobilize the troops; they shall assemble at your kingdom.
Are you sitting so complacently and at ease?"
When Prasenajit heard this news, he was overcome with grief and confusion, not knowing what to do; he donned soiled black robes and sat in a place of darkness.
A brahmin counselor came to where he was and asked him the reason for his state of mind:
"What is the cause of Your Majesty's sorrow?
We pray that you will reveal it to us."
King Pradyota Bimbisāra said, "Have you not heard?

Previously, Raudrākṣa fled to the side of King Kṣemadarsin; because of this provocation, he caused King Kṣemadarsin to mobilize the military forces of eighty-four thousand kingdoms, intending to come and attack me."
"If he should come in the future, he will surely destroy my kingdom.
The prime minister said,
"We should have the various ministers try to deliberate upon this together."
They immediately consulted together, each proposing a different plan, and spoke to one another:
"I have heard that King Kṣemadarsin has made a vow to practice giving, with the sole exception that he does not give his parents; for all other things, he does not refuse those who come to him."
"In this kingdom, there is a blind brāhmaṇa; you should urge him to go and beg for the king's eyes. If he can obtain them, our army will be sufficient to repel [the enemy]."
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately agreed and promptly dispatched his chief minister to go and request his assistance.
The minister at once sent a messenger to summon him, and as soon as he arrived, he addressed him, saying:
"I now have affairs of state that require your labor; I pray you will deign to attend to them and assist me in their execution."
The brāhmaṇa said, "I am now blind and ignorant; what am I capable of doing to assist you?
The minister spoke again:

"King Sūtila intends to assemble his troops to invade our country. If he comes, even though we who are strong and capable might be able to escape, we still fear being slaughtered; how much more so for you, who are blind—how could you possibly escape?"
That king had made a vow:
"I shall give all things as alms according to whatever each person requires, never refusing anyone's wishes.
He went there to beg for his eyes, hoping he would surely obtain them.
"If you can obtain those eyes, the hostilities may be brought to an end.
Once this matter is accomplished, I shall reward you handsomely.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"Now that I have no one to see [to], how can this be?
The king urged him earnestly:
"I shall dispatch people to escort and protect you on your way."
He immediately provided him with provisions for the journey and the necessities required for traveling, and led the way as they departed.
At that time, all manner of calamities and portents appeared throughout the kingdom of King Kṣemadatta.

In the sky, there was the sound of crumbling, trailing lightning and falling stars; dark mists and thunder clapped as the earth split apart in every direction. Flocks of birds wailed with piercing grief, writhing their bodies and tearing out their own feathers. Tigers, wolves, lions, and other wild beasts roared among the people, rolling upon the ground.
The king and his subjects wondered at the reason for this.
At that time, the brahmin gradually reached the great city and went straight before the palace, crying out in a loud voice:
"While I was in another land, I heard of the King’s fame and virtue; you give all things in charity and never refuse anyone's request. Therefore, I have traveled from afar, desiring only to beg."
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately descended from his seat to inquire after him:
"Having traveled such a long distance on foot, are you not weary?

Whatever you may desire, whatever you require—be it the treasures of the kingdom, chariots, horses, palanquins, clothing, bedding, food, drink, or medicine according to your ailment—all that you need shall be provided to you."
The brahmin said:
"The giving of external objects yields meager merit; the giving of one's own body brings forth a vast reward.
Having long been deprived of my sight and dwelling in darkness through the long night, I have come here upon hearing of Your Majesty, desiring to beg for the King's eyes."
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and said to the brahmin,
"If you wish to obtain eyes, I shall give them to you.
The brahmin replied:
"Whoever wishes to give to me, when will they be able to give?
The king said to him,
"Seven days from now, I shall give it to you."
The king immediately issued a proclamation throughout the eighty-four thousand minor kingdoms:
"Seven days from now, King Sūtila shall gouge out his own eyes to give them as alms to a brāhmaṇa."
"Let all who wish to come assemble here at once.
When the kings and the people heard this command, they all rushed to the presence of the Great King.

Eighty-four thousand kings, ministers, and subjects threw themselves upon the ground, striking their bellies against the king's feet; with tears streaming down their faces, they addressed the king, saying:
"We, the people of Jambudvīpa, rely upon Your Majesty for protection and shelter.
If you were to gouge out your eyes to give them to a brāhmaṇa, what would all the people have left to depend upon?"
"We only pray that you will change your mind; do not, for the sake of one person, abandon all of us.
Ten thousand ministers also prostrated themselves upon the ground and looked up, addressing the king:
"Why do you not show us compassion and pity?"
"For the sake of one person's whim, you have abandoned us.
We only pray that you will change your mind and not give him your eyes.
Twenty thousand ladies struck their heads against the ground and beat their breasts before the King, all of them likewise entreating him:
“Only we pray, Great King!
Turn back your mind and change your resolve; do not give away your eyes, but comfort us.
Thus did the five hundred princes weep and wail before the King.
"O Heavenly Father!
We pray that you will show us compassion and not give away your eyes; please continue to nourish and protect us.
Then, Prince Śīlabhadra addressed the king once more, saying:
"I pray that you pluck out my eyes to take their place for my father, the King. Why is this?
Though my body may perish, it will cause the kingdom neither loss nor gain."
"Great King, you are without eyes; within the four seas, there is no one left to rely upon.
At that time, King Kāśyapa addressed his ministers, queens, and crown prince:
"Since I first received this body, my cycle of birth and death has been long. Were I to pile up my bones, they would exceed Mount Sumeru in height;"
The blood from being cut and stabbed exceeds the waters of the four seas;
the milk drunk from a mother's breast surpasses the volume of the four great rivers;
and the tears of sorrowful parting are more numerous than the waters of the four seas.
Within the hells, their bodies are shattered; they are burned, boiled, hacked, and pierced, and their eyes are lost in countless numbers.
Among the hungry ghosts, they assume various forms; fire issues from their bodies and consumes them from within, and thus destroyed, their eyes are likewise lost in countless numbers.
Among the animals, they devour one another; their various deaths and injuries are likewise beyond reckoning.

When receiving bodies in the human realm, many die prematurely; some contend over beauty and desire, plotting against one another and killing each other, such that their deaths are not limited to a single cause.
Thus they were shattered and dispersed; though they possessed countless eyes and even attained birth in the heavens, their lifespans were likewise short.

Calculating from the beginningless past, they have assumed many forms within these three realms, circling through the five destinies like rolling waves. For the sake of greed, anger, and delusion, their bodies have been crushed as many times as there are motes of dust, yet they never gave anything in alms to seek the path of the Buddha.
Such a foul eye, a fragile thing, will before long naturally rot and decay;
since you have now obtained it for the purpose of giving, you should not refuse to give it.
Now, holding these eyes, I offer them as a gift in order to seek the unsurpassed eye of all-knowledge of a Buddha.
If my vow is fulfilled, I shall grant you, too, the pure eye of wisdom.
"Do not obstruct my aspiration for the unsurpassed path.
Those present in the assembly remained silent and spoke no word.
He then addressed those around him:
"Pluck out my eyes.
The ministers on his left and right all said in unison:
"We would rather have our bodies shattered like mustard seeds than raise our hands against the Great King’s eyes."
The king said to his ministers, "Among you, seek out one whose complexion is perfectly black and who looks downward with a steady gaze; once found, summon him here.
The ministers sought him out, brought him before the king, and presented him to him.
The king immediately handed over the knife and commanded him to gouge it out.
Once one eye had been gouged out, he placed it in the king's palm, and the king then made this vow:
"I have used this eye as an act of giving; I vow to seek the path of the Buddha."
"If it is certain that I shall attain the Way of the Buddha, let this Brahmin take one of my eyes and use it to see.

Having made this vow, the king immediately placed his eye into the socket of the Brahmin’s eye; the Brahmin was able to see at once, beholding the king’s body and the rest of the assembly. Overjoyed and leaping for joy beyond measure, he addressed the king, saying:
"Having obtained one of Your Majesty’s eyes, it is sufficient for me to see. I pray that you keep one eye so that Your Majesty may use it to look upon the world yourself."
The king replied again, "I have already made my decision and promised to give you both eyes; I ought not to go back on my word.
He then gouged out another eye, placed it in his palm, and swore a solemn oath once more:
"I offer my eyes as a gift, seeking the path to Buddhahood.
If it is certain that I shall attain Buddhahood and my sincerity is not in vain, then may this Brahmin, having received my eyes, immediately use them to see."
He then placed in one eye, which he was immediately able to use for seeing.

At that moment, heaven and earth shook, and the palaces of the various devas also trembled. The devas and humans of the time were struck with awe and fear; they soon saw the Bodhisattva gouging out his eyes as an act of giving, and they all flew there, filling the void, scattering various flowers and incense as offerings, and praising him, saying:
"Excellent!"
"What Your Majesty has performed is most marvelous and extraordinary!
The Heavenly Emperor stepped forward and asked,
"It truly is extraordinary!"
“Since you are able to perform such deeds, what recompense do you seek?

The King replied, “I do not seek the pleasures of Māra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, or the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings within the three realms. By means of this merit, I vow to seek the Way of the Buddha, to deliver all sentient beings, and to lead them to the bliss of Nirvāṇa.”
The Lord of Devas asked again:
"Now that you have gouged out your eyes and suffer such agony, do you feel any regret, withdrawal, or anger?
The King replied: "I have no regret, nor do I harbor any resentment."
The Lord of Devas spoke again:
"I now observe you; with blood flowing and your body trembling, yet you speak without regret—this is difficult to believe."
The king then made this vow:
"I have gouged out my eyes as an act of giving, without any thought of regret, seeking thereby the path of the Buddha; I shall surely attain its fulfillment.
If this is truly not false, let both my eyes be restored to their former state."
Once the King had finished his vow, both eyes were restored to their original state, clear, bright, and seeing with penetrating clarity, surpassing his former vision by many times over.
All the devas, the people, and the entire great assembly celebrated with joy and leaped for happiness, unable to contain themselves.
The King said to the brahmin:
"I now give you my eyes so that you may see; later, when I attain Buddhahood, I shall further cause you to obtain the wisdom-eye to see."
He took the Brahmin into the treasury and allowed him to take as much as he wished in one load, then sent him on his way.
Upon returning to his own country, Pradyota Bimbisāra went out himself to meet him; having seen him, he asked first:
"Did you obtain the eyes?"
He replied, "I have regained my sight; I am now using it to see.
He asked again:
"Is that king now alive or dead?
He replied, "The devas descended, and immediately he made a vow; his eyes were restored to their former state, and they are even better than before."
When Pradyota Bimbisāra heard these words, he was overcome with distress and indignation; his heart burst and he died.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "If you wish to know who King Sūtila was at that time, it is I myself."
Prādurvarman is now Devadatta.
The Brahmin who at that time begged for my eyes is this blind Brahmin in the assembly here who has attained the Way.
In previous lifetimes, I gave them my eyes, and even unto this day, because they have seen me, they have obtained both the physical eye and the wisdom-eye.
"For your sakes, I have practiced asceticism through life after life, accumulating merit and virtue until I attained Buddhahood today; you all should diligently seek the essential way of deliverance.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, those present in the assembly were moved by the Buddha’s grace; they exerted themselves within their own bodies, and among them there were those who attained the stages of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat, as well as those who resolved to attain the unsurpassed path.
The worthy Ānanda and all those present in the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(33) Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Story of the Five Hundred Blind Boys Who Followed the Buddha on His Journey. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, there were five hundred blind men who sustained themselves by begging.

They heard people say: "The Tathāgata has appeared in the world; he is most marvelous and extraordinary. Any sentient beings who behold him shall have all their ailments, deformities, and infirmities healed. The blind shall see, the deaf shall hear, the mute shall speak, and those with hunched backs shall straighten. Those with crippled hands or feet shall regain their limbs, the deranged shall attain sanity, and the poor shall receive food and clothing. All sorrow, anxiety, suffering, and calamity can be completely dispelled."
When the blind men heard these words, they again deliberated together, saying:
"Our sins have accumulated, and our bitter suffering is especially great; if we were to encounter the Buddha, we would surely be saved."
He then asked the people,
"In which country is the World-Honored One currently residing?
The people replied to him:
“In Śrāvastī. Having heard these words, they stood by the roadside together and entreated him with humble speech:
“Who has compassion and pities us?”
"We pray that you will guide us to the kingdom of Śrāvastī, to where the Buddha resides!
They called out for companions for some time, but there was no one who responded.
Then the five hundred men deliberated together, saying:

"Previously, when I tried to hire someone with my empty hands, no one would respond; now that we are traveling together to beg for alms, each of us can provide a single gold coin to hire a guide, which will be sufficient to reach our destination."
Each of them went out to beg for several hours; each person obtained one coin, totaling five hundred. Once they had gathered the money, they called out to those around them:
"Whoever will take us to Śrāvastī, we shall pay five hundred gold coins as wages for your labor."
At that time, there was a man who came and agreed with him; once their agreement was settled, he gave him money.
He then commanded the blind men to lead one another by the hand, guiding them at will until they reached the kingdom of Magadha. There, he abandoned the blind men, leaving them in a marshy wasteland.
At that time, the blind men, not knowing where they were or what country it was,
took each other by the hand and walked across another's field, damaging and destroying the seedlings and grain.

At that time, there was an elder who happened to come out to inspect his fields; seeing five hundred men trampling the crops and destroying them in great numbers, he was filled with intense anger and rage, and commanded that they be severely punished.
The beggar, seeking compassion, recounted the aforementioned events in detail. The elder took pity on him and ordered an attendant to escort him to Śrāvastī.
Upon arriving in that country, he heard further that the World-Honored One had already returned toward the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, the messenger returned and brought them back toward the kingdom of Magadha.

Then those blind men, filled with deep reverence for the Buddha, fixed their minds on the desire to see him; though their physical eyes were closed, their mental eyes had already beheld him. With joy arising from within, they were unaware of their exhaustion.
Having already arrived in Magadha, they heard that the World-Honored One had returned to Śrāvastī.
Thus they pursued him, traveling back and forth seven times in total.
At that time, the Tathāgata observed that the roots of goodness of the blind men were already matured and their reverent faith was pure and firm; he therefore remained in Śrāvastī to await them.
He was led by a guide and gradually arrived at the place where the Buddha was.

When the Buddha’s light touched his body, he was filled with immeasurable joy and wonder; immediately, both his eyes were opened and cleared, and he beheld the Tathāgata surrounded by the fourfold assembly. The Buddha’s body was radiant and brilliant, like a mountain of purple gold. Grateful for this extraordinary grace, he could not contain his joy.

They proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves on the ground with their five limbs touching it, and paid homage to the Buddha. Having completed their prostrations, they spoke to the Buddha with one voice in unison:
"We only pray that you will look upon us with compassion and grant us permission to enter the ranks of the Path."
Then the Buddha addressed him, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and the Dharma robes appeared upon his body. The Buddha preached the Dharma to him again, and he attained Arhatship.

At that time, Ānanda saw that the blind men’s physical eyes had become clear and pure, and furthermore, they had exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and attained arhatship. He knelt down with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The appearance of the World-Honored One in this world is truly extraordinary; the virtuous deeds he performs are inconceivable.”

Furthermore, these blind people have received a particularly sublime grace; their physical eyes having been cleared, they have further attained the eye of wisdom. It is precisely for the sake of those such as these that the World-Honored One has appeared in the world.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is not only today that I have dispelled their darkness; in the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago, I likewise dispelled this great, profound darkness for these very beings."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"I do not understand, World-Honored One!
Regarding this dispelling of darkness in past lives, what were the circumstances?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, five hundred merchants of this Jambudvīpa were traveling together through a vast wilderness. They passed along a perilous road through a great mountain valley that was exceedingly dark."

At that time, the merchants were bewildered and distressed with grief, fearing they would lose their wealth; as this place was full of bandits, they were filled with terror. With one mind, they turned toward Heaven and Earth, the sun, moon, mountains, seas, and all the deities, weeping and entreating them for mercy.
At that time, the caravan leader, out of compassion for the merchants' suffering from confusion and distress, addressed them, saying:
"Do not be afraid!
Each of you should settle your minds; I shall act as a great illumination for you."

At that time, Sāthava immediately wrapped his two arms with white cotton cloth, doused them with ghee, and used them as torches; leading the merchants, he traversed this darkness for seven days before finally emerging from it.
At that time, the merchants were deeply moved by his kindness; their reverence was immeasurable, and having each attained peace and security, they could not contain their joy.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Was the caravan leader at that time anyone other than myself?"
I am that very person.

Since ancient times, I have constantly bestowed my kingdoms, cities, wives, children, as well as my own flesh and blood upon sentient beings; for this reason, I have now attained this preeminent honor.
As for those five hundred merchants at that time, could they have been anyone else?
They are these very five hundred bhikṣus now.
In past lives, by the power of saṃsāra, they bestowed light upon him; now that they have attained Buddhahood, they likewise bestow the eye of untainted wisdom.

At that time, the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, attained the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*; some planted the roots of goodness for *pratyekabuddhahood*, while many others generated the aspiration for the unsurpassed path and were delivered.
The venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(34) Chapter Twenty-nine: The因缘 of Pūrṇa Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, there was an elder named Dharmasena—this name meaning "Dharma Army"—who was the foremost in great wealth within that country.
At that time, the elder’s wife gave birth to a son. As it happened that troops were being dispatched to campaign against a foreign land, she named her son Śeṇa, which means "army.
Later, she gave birth to another son; as it happened that the king had gone out on a military expedition and achieved victory, she again named her son Vijayaśeṇa, which means "Victorious Army."
When the two sons had grown up, he married each of them off.

At that time, the elder suffered from a grave and critical illness; he repeatedly summoned various physicians to attend to his ailment, overseeing the doctors and providing them with every kind of delicious food.
The physician, greedy for gain and desiring to rid himself of the lingering illness, harbored deceitful intentions and instead administered other medicines so that the disease would not be cured.
At that time, there was a maidservant who attended to the elder with food, drink, and medicinal decoctions, always knowing the proper timing; she said to the elder:
"From this day forward, these physicians need not be called again; they have misled you with evil intent, and the illness will not be cured further."
"Now I shall attend to myself according to the prescribed methods, providing whatever is required for my illness; there is no need to call a physician again.
