The maidservant then looked after him, and the elder recovered.
Thereupon, the maidservant said to the elder:
"O Master! I have attended to you and provided for your needs, and your illness has been cured; I only pray that you will take pity on me and grant me one wish."
The householder asked, "What do you seek?
Then the maidservant spoke.
"I wish to share my household with you; if you do not oppose me, I shall follow my own desire.
The elder did not refuse him, and thus his wish was fulfilled.
When the journey had concluded, he suddenly felt that he possessed a body.

At that time, the maidservant’s pregnancy reached its full term of ten months, and she gave birth to a son. Because his wish had been fulfilled, the boy was named Pūrṇaka, which means "Fulfillment of Wishes."

Handsome and possessed of merit, he is well-suited for wealth; skilled at commerce and trade, he prospers manifold in his various means of livelihood, obtaining double the profit. Wherever he goes, there is nothing inauspicious.

Although he has inherited the physical form of the elder and his talents, arts, wisdom, and capacity surpass those of ordinary men, he was born of a lowly slave woman; thus he does not rank among the sons, and his name is included among the ranks of slaves.

At that time, the elder again became afflicted with a chronic illness; he was so gravely ill that he lay upon his bed, and death would soon be near. He left behind earnest instructions, telling his two sons:
"After I have passed away, you must take care not to divide our property."
The elder was stricken with illness; although he took medicine, it could not save him, and he suddenly reached the end of his life.
At that time, the two sons, following their father’s instructions, lived together in one place for many years.

At that time, having encountered the right conditions, they wished to go to another country to engage in trade for their livelihood. Each entrusted their wives and children at home to Pūrṇaka, saying:
"Please look after these people, both young and old, as well as all other household affairs on our behalf."
"I entrust all matters to you; I shall now depart.
At that time, Purnaika accepted his instructions and took charge of the household affairs.

The two elder brothers' sons frequently went to him to request food, drink, and other necessities. Purnaika provided for their needs according to their wishes, purchasing whatever they requested and giving it to them.
One day, having run out of money for his expenses, the boy Jayasena said to Pūrṇaka, "I am now hungry and thirsty; give me food and drink.
Having no money in his hand, he sought food but could not obtain any.
The young boy, filled with resentment, went to his mother and said, "Now, Pūrṇaka harbors partiality in his heart;
when he sees my paternal uncle’s son, he provides him with whatever he desires, yet when I ask for food, he alone refuses me."
Upon hearing her son’s words, the mother felt resentment and thought, "This servant-girl dares to harbor such partiality.
When Vijaya returned home, his wife and son, their anger still unabated, recounted all that had occurred to him in detail.
Upon hearing this, Jayasena’s anger redoubled:
“This slave-born wretch dares to disobey my command and treat my son with such contempt; I shall kill him!”
Having fixed his resolve, he requested that his elder brother divide the household.
The elder brother, out of respect for his father’s command, could not grant this immediately.
Vijaya was distressed and continued to request it repeatedly without ceasing.
Seeing that his younger brother’s intentions were fervent and observing the plan he devised, the elder brother realized his brother harbored resentment;

having no choice, he accepted his words: "I permit you to live separately. Take all the family wealth and property—the means for livelihood, gardens, and houses—and use one portion for yourself; take another portion for Fuṇāka; from these two portions, you may take whichever you prefer."
This means that when the elder brother took the wealth, he intended for himself to become wealthy while wishing to kill Pūrṇaka.

Knowing that Jayasena’s heart harbored malice toward Pūrṇaka, [the younger brother], out of a compassionate mind of pity, took Pūrṇaka and, leaving his wife and children behind, came out alone and empty-handed to live with other households.
At that time, Pūrṇaka asked his brother-in-law, saying, "Give me a little money; I wish to buy firewood.
His brother-in-law replied:
"There are only five coins," he said, and immediately untied them to give.

Then, Puṇyaka took these five coins and went to the market to buy firewood; seeing a bundle of firewood being sold for five coins, Puṇyaka immediately purchased that firewood for the price of five coins.

He soon saw a piece of gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood within the bundle of firewood; his heart was filled with great joy, so he carried the wood home, took this fragrant timber, and divided it into ten pieces.

It happened that the King’s consort was suffering from a severe fever, for which it was necessary to grind *gośīrṣa-candana* sandalwood and apply it to her body to cure the illness. The entire kingdom searched for it, but could not find any. The King then issued a decree throughout the land:
"Whoever possesses even one *liang* of this fragrant wood shall be granted one thousand *liang* of gold."
At that time, Pūrṇaka went to respond to the king’s recruitment; carrying a small piece [of the hair], he presented it to the royal household.
In accordance with his original command, the king rewarded him with a thousand taels of gold.
In this manner, through successive transactions, ten loads of fragrant wood were all sold out, yielding ten thousand taels of gold.

He used this wealth to acquire residences, gardens, fields, houses, elephants, horses, carriages, servants, and livestock; thus his household affairs became abundant and complete, surpassing his former state by several times over.
At that time, there were also five hundred merchants who had made a pact together to enter the great ocean; they called for Pūrṇaka to be their companion.
Pūrṇaka said to his elder brother, "I seek to go with you to gather treasures."
The elder brother immediately granted his permission and provided whatever was required.
When the companions reached the great ocean, they obtained jewels as they desired, loaded them upon themselves, and returned.
Upon reaching a perilous place halfway home, everyone saw three suns appearing within Jambudvīpa; marveling at this, they questioned their guide:
"Now that three suns have appeared, what omen does this portend?
The guide replied,
"You should know this!"
"The first is the 'Correct Day,' and the second is the 'Fish Eye.
That which is white between them is the 'Fish's Tooth. Where the water is now cast into the dark and murky place, that is the 'Fish's Mouth,' which is the most terrifying of all."
"We now have no way to return to life; having come before the mouths of the fish, we are certain to die.
There was a wise man who revered and believed in the Buddha’s Way, who addressed the merchants:
"You must simply call out 'Namo Buddha' with a devout heart."

In the three realms, none possesses greater virtue than the Buddha; he rescues those in distress and hastens to the aid of the urgent, compassionately saving all beings, and is most capable of providing protection for sentient beings suffering in calamity.
O, only the Buddha is divine and holy!
"I pray that you will save us from this peril and deliver these people, even those with but a hair’s breadth of life remaining.

At that time, upon hearing the name of the Buddha invoked, the makara fish immediately closed its mouth and sank away into the depths of the ocean. Thereupon, the merchants returned safely to their own country.

At that time, Pūrṇika took a large golden table and filled it to overflowing with various exquisite jewels, mani-gems, and other treasures. He presented these to his elder brother, Kṣema, and kneeling for a long time while gazing up at him, he addressed his elder brother, saying:

"I have already accumulated wealth and treasures for you, brother; all the property of our house is now complete, enough to sustain seven generations of descendants without exhaustion. I only pray, O elder brother!"
"Listen to me regarding my renunciation.
Xian-na replied, "I shall not oppose you;

however, you are still young and have not yet mastered the ways of human relations. The Buddha-dharma is of vital importance and is extremely difficult to uphold. Wait for several more years, and then you may fulfill your wish."
Punna said: "Elder brother, you should know that human life is impermanent; it cannot be preserved for even a moment."
Previously, while at sea, we encountered a makara fish that sucked our ship toward its mouth;
our lives were in peril as we stood on the verge of death, but by the divine grace of the Buddha, we were able to save our remaining lives.
"I only pray that you will grant me permission to be admitted into the ranks of the Path.
His elder brother immediately granted his consent.

At that time, Pūrṇika and his five hundred followers who had been gathering treasures all arrived at the kingdom of Śrāvastī with faith. Reaching the place where the Buddha was, they paid their respects, inquired after his well-being, and then addressed the Buddha in detail, requesting ordination.
The Buddha immediately granted his permission and allowed them to enter the Path,
saying in praise: "Welcome!"
He immediately became a śramaṇa.

The Buddha preached the Dharma to him with various kinds of urgent and piercing exhortations; the minds of the five hundred bhikṣus were opened and liberated, they reached the end of all suffering, and became arhats.

Only Pūrṇika’s fetters and afflictions were deep and heavy; although the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, he was unable to fully comprehend it. Yet, with sincere and earnest devotion, he first entered the first fruit of the path, practicing with diligent application without ceasing or slackening.
At that time, as the days for the summer retreat drew near, the Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to enter retreat according to their own inclinations.
Then Puṇyaka went to the Buddha and said, "I, your disciple, wish to go to the country of Kalandaka to observe the three-month retreat; I only pray that you will grant me leave."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇika:

"The people of that country are wicked, believing in heterodoxy and holding perverted views. You have only recently begun your studies; within the Buddha-dharma, you have not yet fully perfected the noble practices of the Buddhas. If you were to be insulted and humiliated by those people, what would you do?"
Punna said, "Even if I am subjected to the most extreme insults and humiliation by others, I only pray that I may not be harmed.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"That man is extremely wicked; should he come to harm you, what would you do then?
Pūrṇika said, "World-Honored One, you should know!"
"Even if that person were to insult and harm you, do not take his life; rather, cherish his kindness.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"If you go there and suddenly encounter an evil person who takes your life, it will be of no benefit to you; what then shall you do?"
Punna said: "World-Honored One, you should know that all things,
having form, return to non-existence."
"If they were to kill me, I would share in their death.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Pūrṇika:
"If those wicked people were to insult, humiliate, and harm you, yet had not yet taken your life, would you feel anger?"
Punna-kumāra said:
"No, World-Honored One."

Even if that person were to slander him with groundless charges, subjecting him to insults and disgrace beyond the bounds of worldly propriety; or even if they were to strike him with knives and staves, beat and harm him, or proceed to kill him—yet before his life was utterly destroyed and at the very moment his breath was about to cease, he would never give rise to a single thought of malice.
The Buddha then praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
That which a disciple practices is indeed most joyful."
At that time, Pūrṇika took up his robes and bowl, paid homage to the Buddha, took his leave, and traveled to the country of Kalandaka.
At dawn the following morning, he entered the city to beg for alms and arrived at the house of a very wealthy Brahmin.
At that time, seeing this bhikṣu, the brahmin immediately conceived an evil intent and came to revile and drive him away; the bhikṣu then went to another house to beg for food.
From the following day onward, he continued to beg for food at that man's house.
At that time, the brahmin struck the bhikṣu again with extreme force, yet the bhikṣu remained joyful, his countenance unchanged.

Seeing this bhikṣu—harmed and beaten, suffering and on the verge of death, yet without a trace of resentment and harboring no anger—the brahmin immediately reproached himself, repented, and apologized for his transgression.

At that time, Pūrṇika, practicing diligently and without slackening within that kingdom, exhausted all fetters and afflictions; his mind suddenly opened to understanding, and he attained the realization of the outflow-free state.
When the *varṣā* retreat had concluded, he took his leave of the donor and entrusted him with this instruction for his elder brother:
"Be careful not to go out to sea; the perils within the great ocean are many and beyond counting. Your wealth and treasures are sufficient to sustain you for seven generations."
Having finished his instructions, he returned to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated himself, and exchanged greetings; having completed his greetings, he stayed there as he pleased.

At that time, his elder brother, Śreṇika, did not heed his advice. A group of merchants came to Śreṇika and repeatedly entreated him, saying they would go together into the great ocean. Śreṇika did not refuse them, and so they departed together.
Upon reaching a coastal island, they took as much as they desired for themselves; however, Xuan-na alone took a great quantity of ox-head sandalwood, filling his boat before returning.

The dragon was by nature stingy and cherished the fragrant wood; thus, midway along the route, he seized the vessel, hoisted the sails to catch the wind, and prevented them from passing. All the passengers were certain that they would die.
Xian-na, who was in distress, invoked the name of Pūrṇaka, saying, "I have now encountered this bitter calamity; I pray that you will deliver me.

At that time, Pūrṇaka was at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, sitting in meditation and contemplation. From afar, he heard with his divine ear that his brother Xian-na was in peril and was sincerely confessing his plight with a sorrowful and single-minded heart, invoking the name of Pūrṇaka.

Pūrṇika, by means of the supernatural power of an arhat, transformed his body into that of a golden-winged garuḍa king in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, and went to the great ocean, intending to terrify the nāgas.
The dragon, seeing the bird’s form, was terrified and entered the bottom of the sea; thus, the merchants returned home in safety.
At that time, Pūrṇika exhorted his elder brother to erect a small hall for the World-Honored One, covering it with wood from the village and using sandalwood exclusively for its construction.
When the hall was completed, he exhorted his elder brother to invite the Buddha.
Yan-na replied,
"Regarding the propriety of inviting the Buddha, with what kind of offerings can we truly humble the World-Honored One?"

At that time, Pūrṇaka, together with his elder brother, prepared the offerings; each holding an incense burner, they ascended a high tower and, facing toward Jetavana from afar, burned incense and took refuge in the Buddha and the noble Saṅgha, saying:
"We only pray that tomorrow you will deign to visit our humble kingdom and awaken these ignorant, deluded, and blind sentient beings."

Having finished making her vow, the incense smoke, as she had willed, rose into the air and traveled to the top of the World-Honored One’s head, where it merged and gathered together to form a single canopy of smoke.
Afterwards, she used water from afar to wash the World-Honored One’s feet; the water likewise rose through the air like a hairpin-stalk, reaching the World-Honored One’s feet as she had willed.
At that time, Ānanda, seeing this occurrence, marveled and asked the Buddha,
"Who has released this smoke and water?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Arhat Bhikṣu Pūrṇika, in the country of Kapitha, exhorted his elder brother Kṣemaka to invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha; therefore, he released smoke and water as a token of his invitation."
Thereupon, he commanded Ānanda:

"Go to the midst of the Saṃgha, distribute voting sticks, and announce to the bhikṣus endowed with supernatural powers: 'Tomorrow all must come to attend the invitation of Śreṇya; there, we shall manifest transformations to travel through that country.'"
Ānanda, having received the command, convened the Saṃgha to distribute voting sticks (*śalākā*). Those possessing supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) were to receive the invitation on the following day.
At that time, the bhikṣus each received a voting stick.

At dawn on the following day, there was a monk preparing food named Qiqian-zhi (this means "Continued Birth"). This man had already attained the stage of Anāgāmin and constantly provided for all the monks. Seated in the full lotus posture, his body emitted light that radiated in the four directions. He led the cooking utensils—the ladles, spoons, *jianzhi* (fire-stirring tools), and a great cauldron capable of holding a hundred *hu*—following behind him as he traveled through the air by supernatural power toward that kingdom.
Xian-na asked,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:
"No, it is not so. These bhikṣus are cooks who have come specifically to assist us in preparing the food and drink.
Thereupon, Yaśas immediately made offerings of flowers, incense, and music; having finished his offerings, he then departed.

Subsequently, there were sixteen more śrāmaṇeras, including Cunda and others, each using their supernormal powers to transform themselves into groves of trees; they gathered flowers and fruits, manifesting various transformations and radiating bodily light that illuminated heaven and earth, as they traveled through the void in continuous succession until they arrived.
Xenana asked again,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:

"No. These people who came before us are disciples of our same teacher; they are seven years of age, have attained the path of Arhatship, with all outflows forever exhausted and their supernormal powers fully perfected. They have come first for this reason: to gather flowers and fruits."
They immediately presented flowers and incense as a complete offering; having finished their worship, they each departed.

Next, an elder Great Arhat manifested a thousand dragons, joining their bodies together to form a seat. Their heads all protruded in four directions, and their thunderous roars shook the heavens. From the mouths of all these dragons, there rained down the seven treasures. Furthermore, he established a great jeweled throne upon them, ascended into the void, and emitted radiance from his body that illuminated the world, as he arrived at the kingdom.
Xenana asked again,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:

"No. This is the teacher's disciple named Kauṇḍinya. When the Buddha first attained the Way and was at the Deer Park, turning the Wheel of Dharma for the first time to extensively deliver sentient beings, these five people were the very first to receive his transformation. Among all disciples, he is the foremost leader; he is fully endowed with supernatural powers and is free from all obstructions."
Upon hearing these words, Kṣemaka redoubled his reverence; he offered incense, flowers, and music as acts of worship. Having completed his offerings, he then departed.

Thereafter, Mahākāśyapa again manifested a lecture hall made of the seven treasures, adorned with the seven treasures; his body emitted a brilliant light that shone forth in all four directions as he traveled to that land.
Xianna saw him and asked Funanqi,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:

"No. This is the teacher's disciple, Mahākāśyapa. He is pure, frugal, and contented; he constantly practices the dhūta austerities and takes pity on the lowly and humble, providing relief to the poor and destitute."
Xian-na immediately completed his offerings with incense, flowers, and music, and then departed at once.

Following him, Śāriputra mounted a thousand lions, coiling their bodies together as a seat; their heads all faced outward, their mouths rained down the seven treasures, and they roared like thunder, shaking heaven and earth. Upon them he spread a great jeweled couch, magnificently adorned and decorated, and sat upon it. His body emitted radiance that illuminated the four quarters, and he soared through the void, flying majestically until he arrived.
Xian-na asked,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:
"No. The one who has come here on horseback is the Great Disciple of the Teacher, of vast and expansive great wisdom, named Śāriputra.
Having heard this, Kṣemana’s joy redoubled; he immediately made offerings of flowers, incense, and music. Once the offerings were completed, he departed at once.

Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana set out following after him. He manifested himself as a thousand elephants with their heads arrayed in four directions; each of these elephants had six tusks, and at the tip of every tusk were seven bathing pools. Within each pool were seven lotus flowers, and upon each flower were seven jade maidens. Through such various transformations, their number was immeasurable. They emitted a great radiance that moved those in the surrounding regions, and having further established a precious throne above them, he sat upon it and traveled directly through the void.
Xenana asked, "Is this your teacher?
He replied:
"No. This is the teacher's disciple named Mahāmaudgalyāyana, foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), whose virtuous conduct is perfectly complete.
When Yaśas heard this, he was filled with joy and reverence; he made offerings of incense, flowers, and music, and having completed his offerings, he departed.

Subsequently, there was again Aniruddha, who manifested by his own power a bathing pool made of the seven treasures. Within this pool grew golden lotuses, the stalks of which were all composed of the seven treasures. Standing upon one of these flowers, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), with the radiance of the sun encircling his neck, illuminating the world. Wherever his light shone, everything became golden; then, traveling through the void, he arrived at the kingdom.
Xenana asked again:
"Is this your teacher? He replied:
"No. This is the teacher’s disciple, Aniruddha, who, among this great assembly, is foremost in the divine eye.
When Kṣemaka heard this, he was filled with joy and reverence; he made offerings of flowers and incense, and then departed.

Subsequently, there was again a younger brother of the Buddha named Nanda, who manifested a thousand horses yoked to a chariot made of the seven treasures. Upon the chariot was a great canopy of the seven treasures, which emitted radiant light that shone forth in the four directions. He traveled through the air at great speed until he arrived at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
Xian-na saw him and asked Fu-na-qi,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:
"No, it was not he. This was the World-Honored One’s younger brother, named Nanda, who was endowed with all the marks of excellence and possessed of pure and complete virtue.
Having thus made offerings of incense, flowers, and music, Kṣemana departed.

Then Subhūti came again shortly thereafter, creating a mountain of the seven treasures and sitting within a cave of lapis lazuli; his body emitted various mixed-colored radiances that illuminated heaven and earth as he arrived in that land.
Xenana asked, "Is this your teacher?
He replied:
"No. This is the teacher's disciple named Subhūti; he possesses vast wisdom and extensive learning, and is foremost in the understanding of emptiness.
Having finished making offerings of flowers and incense, [the deity] immediately departed.

Next, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra manifested one thousand garuḍa kings, joining their bodies together to form a seat. Their heads were turned toward the four directions, and they held various jewels in their mouths, emitting a harmonious and mournful melody. Furthermore, he established a great precious throne upon them and sat thereon, arriving by traveling through the void.
Xenana asked, "Is this your teacher?
He replied:
"No, it was my fellow disciple named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; his eloquence was most excellent and peerless.
Having thus offered flowers and incense, he then departed.

Next, the disciple named Upāli manifested himself as a flock of a thousand geese with their bodies joined together. Their heads and mouths emitted sounds, wailing in harmonious unison; they held various jewels in their beaks and soared through the void. Upon their bodies, he arranged many jeweled thrones that radiated great light, illuminating the four quarters and the distance. Seated upon them, he galloped forward until he arrived.
Xian-na asked,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:
"No. This is the teacher's disciple named Upāli; among the bhikṣus, he is foremost in upholding the Vinaya.
Having heard this, Kṣemana immediately took flowers and incense, completed his offerings, and then departed.

Thereafter, there was another śramaṇa named Śāriputra, who manifested walking trees in the air and created a path for walking with deep blue lapis lazuli. He further adorned both sides of the trees with the seven treasures and demarcated the edges of the path with various exquisite gems; walking along this path, he gradually reached that country.
Xian-na asked,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:
"No. This is a disciple of the Buddha named Śramaṇa Viśvabhū, who is foremost among the bhikṣus in diligence.
Having completed his offerings of flowers, incense, and music, he then departed.

Thereafter, there was again a great kalpa named Piṇi, who manifested seven-jeweled trees; upon these trees were various flowers and fruits, and beneath each tree was a high seat made of the seven treasures. Seated upon these thrones, they emitted great radiance and arrived by traveling through the void.
Xian-na asked,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:
"No, it was not he. This is a disciple of the Buddha named Kapphiṇa, who is preeminent and courageous, and foremost in his physical beauty.
Having heard this, Śreṇika joyfully made offerings of flowers, incense, and music; once the offerings were complete, he immediately departed.

Next, there was a disciple named Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja, who sat upon a precious lotus flower, with the radiance of the sun encircling his neck; emitting a thousand rays of light that brilliantly illuminated heaven and earth, he ascended into the void and came to that land.
Xian-na asked,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:
"No. This is the teacher's disciple named Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja; he is skilled at entering meditative concentration and is foremost among those who practice seated meditation.
Having finished making offerings of incense and flowers, he immediately departed.

Next, Rāhula followed behind to lead the way; he transformed his own body into that of a Wheel-Turning King, fully endowed with a thousand sons and the seven treasures, and accompanied by a retinue before and behind, arrived at that kingdom.
Xian-na asked,
"Is this your teacher? He replied:

"No. This is the son of the Buddha, named Rāhula. Had he remained at home, he would have ruled over the four continents, with the seven treasures coming to him spontaneously; weapons would not have been required, as all would have submitted naturally. Now, having renounced this position to leave the household life and study the Way, he has attained arhatship. His six supernormal powers are pure and penetrating, free from all hindrance; it is for this reason that he has now transformed his body into this form and station."
Having heard this, Śreṇika made offerings of incense and flowers and immediately departed.
Each of his five hundred disciples possessing supernatural powers manifested transformations beyond measure.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that all his disciples had departed for that country, emitted a great radiance that illuminated heaven and earth, making them entirely golden in color.
Then Pūrṇika said to his elder brother:
"The World-Honored One has now first resolved to come here; therefore, he has first emitted this light as an auspicious omen."
At that time, as the World-Honored One first lowered his feet from the seat to tread upon the ground, the heavens and earth immediately shook in six ways.
Then Pūrṇika said to his elder brother,
"Now that the World-Honored One has first lowered his feet from the seat to tread upon the ground, for this reason the heavens and earth have shaken greatly."
At that time, the World-Honored One had just emerged from the vihāra and was staying outside; eight Vajra-devas resided at the eight sides.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings led the way in front;
and Śakra, Lord of Devas, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of devaputras from the desire realm, attended upon him on the left side.
Mahābrahmā, together with an immeasurable multitude of devas from the realm of form, took his place on the right side;
the disciple Ānanda stood behind the Buddha.
Surrounded by the great assembly, he emitted and spread forth radiance that illuminated heaven and earth, then ascended into the void and proceeded toward the country of Paṅkadhātu.

Along that path, he encountered five hundred laborers who were tilling the fields with a thousand oxen. When the oxen saw the Buddha passing through the air, their bodies radiating a golden light that illuminated the entire world, they gazed up at the World-Honored One with sincere hearts and profound reverence; they remained standing in the furrows and did not move.
The laborers saw the oxen looking up and gazing intently; wondering at the cause of this marvel, they also beheld the Buddha and immediately knelt down, saying:
"We all arise with sincere devotion; we pray only that the Tathāgata [will grant us his grace]!"
"Please look upon us with compassion and deign to descend and deliver us, so that we may leave behind birth and death.

Out of his heart of pity, the Buddha knew they were ready for deliverance; he immediately descended and preached various sublime Dharmas for them. The five hundred laborers had their minds awakened and enlightened; they severed twenty billion deep-seated evils and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
At that time, the ox passed away and was reborn entirely in the heavens, where all were filled with universal joy.

Then the Tathāgata set out once more; not long after he had departed, five hundred young maidens were wandering together in a vast wilderness. Seeing the ground turn golden in color, they looked up at the transformation and beheld him traveling through the void. All harbored great joy and, joining their palms, addressed him, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One [will accept us]!"
"May you look upon us with compassion and grant us temporary deliverance.

The Buddha, knowing that their past conduct made them ready for conversion, immediately fulfilled their wish; he went to their location and, according to their capacities, expounded the various Dharmas.
Having received it with faith and attained understanding, they became *srotāpannas*.
Having completed his miraculous transformations, he proceeded on foot.

Furthermore, there were five hundred sages dwelling in the forests and marshes who saw the light shining everywhere until the ground was entirely golden. Looking up, they beheld the Tathāgata traveling through the air with the great assembly; their hearts leaped with joy and their reverence redoubled as they looked up and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the Great Sage [will descend]."
"Endure this temporary hardship of body and spirit; by doing so, you shall attain transcendence and be permitted to join the ranks of those on the Path.
The Buddha, perceiving their past causes and conditions and knowing they were ready for deliverance, immediately descended and stood before them.
Seeking to become a śramaṇa, the Buddha immediately granted him permission, saying:
"Welcome, bhikṣu!
He then became a śramaṇa; the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and his mind was purified and awakened. All outflows were forever exhausted, and he attained arhatship.
Following behind the Buddha, they arrived traveling through the air.
At that time, Pūrṇika saw the Buddha approaching from afar; his radiance illuminated heaven and earth, and the great assembly moved through the void. He said to his elder brother, Kṣema:
"The World-Honored One and the multitude have now finally arrived."

When the Buddha arrived in that country, Kṣemaṇda was filled with joy; he immediately presented incense, flowers, and various musical performances as offerings, and once the rites were completed, they proceeded together to the assembly hall.

When the Buddha arrived at his house, he took his seat according to the Dharma. Kṣemaṇa and his entire family prepared a sumptuous meal; he personally provided water for washing and respectfully offered the food. The Buddha gave a discourse on the merits of giving (*dakṣiṇā*). After the meal, having rinsed and purified himself, he expounded the sublime Dharma for the sake of the entire household, including all members of the nation, great and small. Consequently, everyone in the family attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.

There were those who possessed both paths and the fruits of the third and fourth stages; furthermore, there were those who resolved their minds to enter the Mahāyāna, and others who firmly abided in the stage of non-retrogression.
When the Buddha finished preaching the Dharma, the men and women of the entire nation who attained deliverance were so numerous as to be beyond calculation.
Ānanda knelt down with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms together, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"I venture to ask, World-Honored One:
what evil deeds did this Pūrṇika commit in past lives such that he was born into a lowly station and became a slave belonging to another?"
"Furthermore, what merit did he possess to encounter the Buddha and attain deliverance?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know this, listen attentively and reflect well!"
"I shall explain it for you. He replied,
"Indeed, I pray that you will reveal it fully."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was an elder of immeasurable wealth who established a saṃghārāma for the Buddha and the community of monks. He provided the four requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for the sick—preparing them all so that nothing was lacking for anyone."

At that time, the elder fell ill and passed away. Subsequently, one of his sons left the household life to study the Way. After his father’s death, the offerings for the Buddhist monastery all diminished; the assembly of monks dispersed, and the temple fell into ruin with no one remaining to dwell there.

That son, the bhikṣu, diligently exerted himself to gather together donors and acquaintances, accumulated wealth, repaired what was dilapidated, and once again assembled the community of monks to resume their offerings.

At that time, a great multitude resided in that monastery, diligently and single-mindedly practicing and perfecting all the paths; among them, a certain practitioner of the Way served as the presiding leader of the Sangha.

At that time, there was an arhat practitioner who, in turn, was on duty for the day. He swept away the grass and soil and piled it up in the central courtyard, but did not discard it at the proper time.
Then a bhikṣu, with a malicious mind, rebuked him:
"This bhikṣu is no different from a slave; though he knows how to sweep the ground, he cannot discard the refuse."
"Ānanda, you should know!
That bhikṣu who was the Great Sovereign at that time is none other than the present bhikṣu Pūrṇaka.
Because he harbored an evil heart and reviled those who had attained the Way, comparing them to slaves, due to these words, for five hundred lifetimes he has constantly been born as a slave."

Furthermore, because they established offerings and encouraged the masses to provide for the Saṃgha, their retribution for past offenses was fully expiated; subsequently encountering my world, they were graced with liberation.
Those among the people of this land who have received transformation through my teaching are all those who assisted in the past; by virtue of this karmic fruit, they have all attained deliverance.
Ānanda and the rest of the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(35) Chapter Thirty: The Story of the Ordination of Niti. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the city of Śrāvastī was densely populated; as dwellings were cramped and toilets were scarce, many people had to go outside the city to relieve themselves.
There was a person of noble rank who, being unable to go out himself, would relieve himself into a vessel and hire someone to remove it.
At that time, there was a man named Niti, who was extremely poor and lowly, having no other means of livelihood; he supported himself by working as a hired laborer to clear away excrement.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that he was ready for deliverance, took Ānanda alone and entered the city, wishing to rescue him.
Having traveled one *li*, they encountered Niti, who was carrying an earthenware vessel filled with impurities, intending to go and discard them.
Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, he was filled with extreme shame and humiliation; he retreated onto a side path, seeking a secluded spot to depart.

Just as he was about to leave the village, he saw the World-Honored One again, and his sense of shame and disgrace redoubled. Turning toward another road, he sought once more to avoid him; in his frantic agitation, he struck a wall with his water jar, which immediately shattered, and excrement and urine drenched his body. Deeply ashamed and remorseful, he could not bear to look upon the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where he was and said to Niti,
"Do you wish to leave the household life? Niti replied:
“The Tathāgata honors those of the lineage of the Golden Wheel-turning Kings; his attendant disciples are all of noble birth.
I am lowly, base, and utterly wretched—how could I go forth as a renunciant together with them?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"My Dharma is pure and subtle, like clear water that can completely wash away all defilements;
it is also like a great fire that can burn all things, whether large or small, good or bad, and consume them all."
My Dharma is likewise: vast and boundless. Whether poor or wealthy, noble or humble, male or female—whosoever is able to cultivate it shall exhaust all desires.
At that time, Niti, having heard what the Buddha had said, conceived faith in his heart and desired to leave the household life.

The Buddha sent Ānanda to take him outside the city to the banks of the great river to bathe his body; once he was purified, they returned to the Jetavana. There, the Buddha preached the Dharma to him concerning the principle of urgent suffering, the terrors of birth and death, and the eternal peace of Nirvāṇa.
His mind was suddenly awakened and he attained the realization of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he requested to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!

His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and the Dharma robes appeared upon his body. The Buddha further explained for him the essential Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; he attained the exhaustion of all outflows and became an Arhat, fully endowed with the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers.
At that time, when the people of the country heard that Nandika had left the household life, they all harbored resentment and spoke thus:
"How can the World-Honored One permit such a lowly person to leave the household life and study the Path?"
"How shall we pay him homage?
Even if we were to prepare offerings and invite the Buddha and the Sangha, should this man come, he would defile our beds and mats."
As they passed the news from one to another, it eventually reached the King.

Upon hearing it, the King was also filled with resentment; his mind became restless and uneasy, so he immediately mounted a carriage adorned with feathered ornaments and, accompanied by his attendants, went to the Jetavana to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding his doubts.
Having arrived before the gate, he paused for a moment.

Outside the gate of the Jetavana, there was a large rock where the bhikṣu Niti sat upon the rocky crag mending old robes. Seven hundred devas and humans, each holding flowers and incense, made offerings to him, circumambulating him to the right in reverent salutation.
When the king saw this, he was deeply moved with joy; he went to where the bhikṣu was and said to him, "I wish to see the Buddha;
I pray that you will announce my request for me."
At that moment, the bhikṣu vanished from within the rock and emerged from inside it, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"King Prasenajit is currently outside; he wishes to enter to pay his respects and seek your counsel."
The Buddha told Niti:
"Go back by your original path and tell him to come forward.
At that moment, Niti emerged from the rock as if rising from water, without any obstruction, and spoke to the king, saying:
"Having finished reporting to the Buddha, Your Majesty may proceed forward.
The king thought to himself:
"Let me set aside for now the matters I previously doubted; first I shall inquire: what meritorious deeds does this bhikṣu possess that his supernormal power is such as this?"
The king entered and beheld the Buddha; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Just now, that bhikṣu’s supernormal powers were beyond compare; he entered the stone as if it were water, yet emerged from the stone without leaving a hole. What is his clan and name?”
"I pray that you will grant me an explanation.

The World-Honored One replied, "In this kingdom, there was a person of the lowest station whom I have already transformed and delivered, causing him to attain Arhatship. It is for this reason, Great King, that you have come to inquire about this matter."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the king’s arrogance was immediately dispelled, and he felt immeasurable joy. Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the king, saying:

“When ordinary people dwell in this world, whether they are noble or humble, high-born or lowly, rich or poor, and whether they experience suffering or pleasure—all these result from their past actions (*pūrvakarma*). Those who are benevolent, compassionate, modest, and compliant; who respect their elders and love the young, shall become persons of honor.
Those who are cruel, violent, arrogant, and self-important shall become persons of low station.”
King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The Great Sage has appeared in the world to bring benefit and salvation to many; even for a person as vulgar, lowly, and base as this, he has extracted their bitter suffering and caused them to dwell in constant peace and happiness.”
For what causes and conditions was this Niti born into such a lowly station?
Furthermore, what merit did he plant that he was able to encounter the Holy Honored One, receive the transformation of the Rishi’s teaching, and immediately become an Arhat?
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and analyze this for me.
The Buddha told the king:
"Listen attentively and hold this well!
I shall explain it so that you may attain awakening.
In the distant past, after the Tathāgata Kāśyapa appeared in the world and entered parinirvāṇa, there were one hundred thousand bhikṣu-saṃghas."

Among them was a śramaṇa who held authority over the saṃgha; though his body was afflicted by illness and he took medicine to purge himself, he was arrogant and relied upon his power, refusing to go out to relieve himself. Instead, he used a gold or silver basin to collect his urine within it and ordered a disciple to carry it away and discard it.
However, his disciple was a *srotāpanna*.

Because he had been arrogant and disobedient during his previous life, relying on his great wealth to take charge of monastic affairs, he suffered a slight ailment for a time; yet out of laziness he would not rise himself, instead driving the noble ones to clear away filth.

Due to these causes and conditions, he wandered through birth and death, constantly remaining lowly and base; for five hundred lifetimes, he served as a scavenger of excrement, continuing even until the present.
"By virtue of his renunciation and the merit of upholding the precepts, he has now encountered my era, heard the Dharma, and attained the Way.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"If you wish to know who that monk Svayambhu was at that time, it is the bhikṣu Niti here before you."
King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is truly extraordinary; he brings benefit to immeasurable sentient beings suffering in affliction.”
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said."
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"In the cycle of the three realms, there is no fixed status. By accumulating goodness and practicing benevolence and harmony, one is born into a noble and honorable family;
by habituating oneself to evil and indulging in license, one is born into a lowly and humble state."

The king was greatly delighted and free from any sense of pride; he immediately rose to his knees, grasped Niti’s feet, and prostrated himself before him, repenting and apologizing while vowing to expiate his transgressions.

At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded for him the subtle and profound meaning of the Dharma, namely: discourse on generosity, discourse on ethical discipline, and discourse on rebirth in the heavens; [he spoke of] the perception of impurity regarding sensual desires, and how renunciation is bliss.
At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, each attained realization of the Way and received it with faith, practicing accordingly.
*The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Seven,
translated by the Śramaṇa Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Yuan Wei dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.
31. Chapter on Mahākaśyapa (36). Chapter Thirty-one on Mahākaśyapa. In the Danben (Dunhuang) edition, this chapter originally appeared in the fourth fascicle as the eighteenth.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a king named Prasenajit. At that time, to the south there was a kingdom called Suvarṇabhūmi;

its king was named Kapphiṇa. The king had a crown prince named Mahākapphiṇa. When his father passed away, the prince succeeded to the throne. By nature he was intelligent, possessed great strength and valor, and governed thirty-six thousand kingdoms. His military forces were vast and flourishing, such that none could oppose him. His majestic prestige resounded afar, and all were subdued by him.
However, they did not maintain communication with China.
Later, there was a merchant who traveled to the Kingdom of Gold and presented four bolts of fine silk to its king.
Having accepted them, the king asked the merchants, "These goods are excellent; from where do they originate?
The merchants replied:
"He comes from the Middle Kingdom.
The King asked again:
"What is the name of that Middle Kingdom?"
The merchant replied, "Its name is Rājagṛha, and it is also called Śrāvastī; its population is so vast that I cannot describe it in full.
The king asked again:
"The kings of the various Chinese states—for what reason do they not come to present offerings to me?
The merchant replied, "Each rules over his own territory, and their prestige and fame rival one another; for this reason, they do not come to pay their respects."
The king thought to himself:
"Now, by my power and influence, I am able to command and awe the entire world; for what reason do these kings not come to pay me tribute?"
"I shall now exert my power to cause them to submit.
He then asked the merchants,
"Among the kings of the Middle Kingdoms, which one is the greatest?"
The merchant leader replied,
"The King of Śrāvastī is the foremost. Thereupon,

King Suvarṇabhūmi immediately dispatched an envoy to the kingdom of Śrāvastī, carrying a letter with detailed instructions and instructions on the proper course of action, addressing King Prasenajit as follows:
"My majesty pervades all of Jambudvīpa; yet you, relying upon that power, have severed the flow of official communications. Therefore, I now dispatch this envoy to communicate with you."
If you are lying down and hear my voice, you should immediately rise and sit up;
if you hear it while sitting, you should immediately stand;
if you hear it while eating, you should immediately spit out what you have taken into your mouth.
"If you hear my voice while bathing, you must immediately grasp your hair;
if you hear it while standing, you must immediately approach me.
Seven days hence, come to meet me. If you do not act thus, I shall raise an army to destroy your kingdom."
Upon hearing this, King Prasenajit was deeply alarmed and immediately went to the Buddha to report the matter in detail.
The Buddha said to the king:
"The King should return and tell the messenger:..."
"I am not great; there is a Great King even greater than I.
The king, honoring the Buddha's teaching, said to the messenger:
"There is a Holy King in this world, residing nearby in these very parts."
"You may go to the border and convey your king's command.
The messenger immediately went to the Jetavana.

At that time, the World-Honored One transformed his own body into that of a Wheel-Turning King and caused Maudgalyāyana to become the Minister of the Army, with all seven treasures and attendants fully provided.

Furthermore, he transformed the Jeta Grove into a jeweled city. Surrounding the city on all four sides were seven tiers of moats, within which there were rows of trees made of the seven treasures and lotus flowers of various colors, beyond measure or calculation, their radiance shimmering and shining forth with brilliant splendor.
The palaces within the city were likewise composed of various precious gems; the king sat upon his throne, majestic and awe-inspiring.

Thereupon, the envoy entered the illusory city, and upon beholding the great king, he was struck with profound alarm and trepidation. He thought to himself, "My sovereign has brought this calamity through his own misconduct";
yet, having no other choice, he presented the letter to him.
When the Transformation King received the letter, he stepped upon it with his foot and addressed the envoy, saying:
"I am the Great King who presides over the four quarters; your king is obstinate and deluded, daring to defy and obstruct me."
"Return quickly to your kingdom and proclaim my instructions.

On the day the letter arrives, you must hasten to come and pay your respects: if you hear of me while lying down, you shall rise; if you hear me while sitting, you shall stand; and if you hear my command while standing, you shall immediately set out upon the road."
"A period of seven days has been fixed; there must be no delay. Should anyone dare violate this decree, their punishment shall not be subject to appeal.
Having received these instructions, the envoy returned to his own country and reported all that he had heard and seen in detail to King Bhūmipati.

Upon receiving this inquiry, the king deeply reproached himself; he assembled the various minor kings under his command, prepared his chariots and horses, and intended to pay court to the Great King. However, harboring certain doubts, he did not yet set out on the journey.
He first dispatched a messenger to say to the Great King:
"Of the thirty-six thousand whom I command, shall Your Majesty take all of them, or take half?"
The Great King replied:
"I permit half of you to remain; bring only half with you.
Then King Suvarṇa, leading eighteen thousand minor kings, arrived at the same time. Having seen the Transformation King (Nirmāṇarāja) and completed his salutations, he thought to himself:
"Although the Great King's physical appearance surpasses mine, his strength must surely be inferior.
At that time, the transformed king commanded his minister in charge of the military to give him a bow;
however, the King of Kinnapatha was unable to lift it with his own hands.
The Transformation King took it back, drew the bow with his finger, and held it out to him again, commanding him to pull it;
however, the King of the Golden Land was utterly unable to draw it.
The Transformation King took it once more and plucked its string, causing the three thousandfold world system to tremble and shake.

Next, he again took up an arrow and drew his bow to shoot; once it left his hand, it transformed into five arrows. From each of those arrowheads issued forth countless rays of light, and upon each tip of the light there was a lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel. Upon each flower sat a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), fully endowed with the seven treasures, who radiated brilliant light that universally illuminated the trichiliocosm. Among the sentient beings of the five realms of existence, there were none who did not receive its benefit. Within the realms of the various devas, upon seeing this light and hearing the preaching of the Dharma, their bodies and minds became pure. Some attained the second or third fruits of the Path; some resolved to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi); and others reached the stage of non-retrogression.

Among the beings of the human realm, those who saw the Buddha’s radiance and heard his teaching felt their hearts leap with joy; among them, some attained the first, second, or third fruits of the path, while others left the household life to enter the essential state and attain arhatship. Furthermore, there were countless others who resolved to attain supreme, perfect enlightenment and reached the stage of non-retrogression.

Those among the hungry ghosts who see the Buddha’s radiance and hear what he teaches all attain full satisfaction; their bodies and minds become pure, free from all burning afflictions, and they give rise to a heart of loving-kindness. They revere the Buddha and immediately attain liberation, being reborn among humans and devas.

Those among the animals who behold the Buddha’s radiance find that the poisons of greed and hatred are all eliminated; their deluded and obscured minds immediately attain awakening. All become filled with joy, develop faith and reverence for the Buddha, and thereby attain liberation, being reborn among humans or devas.

Those within the hells, upon seeing the Buddha’s radiance, find warmth when it is cold and coolness when it is hot; in places of suffering, they immediately find rest. Their bodies and minds leap with joy as they cultivate loving-kindness and reverence for the Buddha, whereby they immediately attain liberation and are reborn among humans and devas.

At that time, King Mahākapphiṇa and the various kings of Suvarṇabhūmi, having witnessed this transformation, their minds were filled with faith and submission; they became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye, as did all eighteen thousand kings simultaneously.
In a brief moment, the Buddha withdrew his supernormal power and returned to his original form, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus.

King Suvarṇabhūmi and his followers sought ordination, and the Buddha immediately granted his permission; their hair and beards fell away naturally, the saṃghāṭī robes appeared upon their bodies, and as they contemplated the sublime Dharma, they all attained the fruit of arhatship.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:

"What virtues did this King Kanakavarṇa plant in his past lives that he was born into such noble and honored status, with such towering merit, encountered the age of a Buddha, and attained the state of outflowlessness?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Sentient beings receive their retributive fruits through their actions.
Long ago in the past, after the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was an elder who built for him a stūpa and temple, constructed halls and pavilions, and provided the four articles of offering.”
As time passed, the stupa collapsed and the bedding, clothing, and food supplies were also cut off.

The elder who was its patron had a son who was a bhikṣu; he then went forth to exhort the people, urging each of them to contribute a portion of their resources to repair the stupa, and provided food, drink, and bedding.
All the people were of one mind, and together they made offerings and service, thereby making this vow:

"In a future age, may we be wealthy, noble, and long-lived; may we encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world, hear the Dharma and attain realization; and may our past actions and their retributions be fully accounted for, so that all may bring their fruits to fruition."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The son of the elder who was a bhikṣu at that time is now King Mahā-Kapphiṇa of Suvarṇabhūmi.
Those among the people who received his guidance and transformation are now these eighteen thousand kings."

When the Buddha had spoken this Dharma, those in the assembly who heard it attained realization of the Path; they resolved their minds with non-retrogression, received and upheld the supreme teaching, and joyfully practiced it.
32. Chapter on the Seven Sons of Licchavi (37). Chapter Thirty-Two: The Seven Sons of Licchavi. [In the Danben edition, this chapter is in the fourth fascicle as the twentieth. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit had a high minister named Liqimī. His family was immensely wealthy, and he had fathered seven sons. He had already married off six of them; with the seventh son remaining, he was about to seek a wife for him.
He thought to himself:
"I am advanced in years and have but one son; when I take a wife for him, she must be most excellent.
At that time, this elder had a close and intimate Brahmin friend who came to visit him, and in the course of their conversation, they discussed the matter, saying:
"Now I wish to seek a marriage for my young son, but I do not yet know where to find such a place.

Since you have traveled through various kingdoms from long ago, I now wish to trouble you to search on my behalf. If you see a girl who is upright, virtuous, and wise, whose nature is compatible with his, and who suits my son's wishes, then you should seek her out."
At that time, the brahmin immediately agreed.
He traveled everywhere searching until he reached the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, where he saw five hundred young maidens playing together in a group, gathering beautiful flowers to use as decorative fans.
This brahmin followed along, observing her.

As they proceeded further and were about to cross a shallow stream, all the young women took off their leather sandals; yet one girl alone did not remove hers, and entered the water together with them.
Proceeding further, they encountered another river; while the other women bared their garments before entering the water, this one woman alone entered with her clothes on.

Moving forward into a forest, the women each climbed trees to gather flowers, but this one woman did not climb the tree herself; instead, she requested them from others, obtaining a great many flowers.
At that time, the brahmin asked the girl,
"I have a slight doubt and wish to question you.
The girl replied:
"If you have a doubt, ask.
The Brahmin said, "Just now, when those women were about to enter the water, they all removed their leather sandals, yet you alone did not remove yours; what was your intention?"
Then the woman replied:
"How extreme is your folly?

The purpose for which these sandals were made is simply to protect the feet; as for matters on dry land, when there is something visible to the eyes—such as thorns, shards, or stones—one can avoid them."
"Hidden at the bottom of the water and invisible to the eye, there may be thorns or various venomous insects that could injure one's feet;
for this reason, I did not take them off. Then the brahmin asked again:
"For what reason did you enter the water together with your clothes?"

Then the woman replied, “A woman’s body has both beautiful and unattractive features. If one were to lift one's garment and enter the water, and be seen by others, it would be acceptable if the features were beautiful; if they were not, one would be ridiculed. For this reason, I do not lift my garment.”
Then the brahmin asked again,
"For what reason do you alone not climb the tree?
The girl replied:
"If I were to climb the tree, its branches might perhaps break, endangering my life; for this reason, I shall not ascend.
This woman was the daughter of Dhammāhāsena, the younger brother of King Prasenajit.
I envy those who, having fled to that country due to their crimes in the past, established a home and married therein, giving birth to this daughter named Viśākhā.
When the Brahmin heard what the girl said, he knew she must be wise and capable, and he asked her:
"Are your parents still living?"
The woman replied, "I am here.
She then followed him to the gate and requested an audience.
The daughter went in and informed her father, "There is a brahmin outside who wishes to see you, sir.
Thereupon, Dharmaghoṣa came out to meet him; after the greetings were concluded, he spoke to him, saying:
"Was that woman just now your daughter?
He replied, "She was."
"Is it owned by anyone? He replied, "No."
The brāhmaṇa said, "In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there is a high minister named Liqimi; do you know him?
He replied:
"An old acquaintance," the brahmin said. "This is Liqimi;
his youngest son is upright and intelligent. He wishes to seek your daughter for marriage. May this be granted?"
Dharmaghaṣa said, "He is of noble lineage and was originally my match; if he truly desires this, there should be no obstacle to our feelings.
Having received permission, they set a date together and, accompanied by a companion, departed for Śrāvastī.
At that time, the brahmin immediately wrote a letter to Liqimi, detailing the circumstances of the matter.

Upon hearing this, the elder prepared wedding gifts, including carriages, horses, and mounts, and set out for the kingdom of Takṣaśilā. As he drew near his destination, he first dispatched a messenger ahead.
At that time, Dharmaghaśena treated him with great respect and hospitality; he immediately prepared a banquet and gave his daughter in marriage to him.
Once all matters were concluded, he was about to return to Śrāvastī.
Then the girl’s mother, before the assembly, entrusted her daughter with these words:
“From this day forward, always wear fine clothes, constantly eat delicious food, and every day look into a mirror; do not let these things cease.”
The woman immediately knelt down and respectfully accepted his instructions.
When Liqimi heard this, he harbored a secret resentment, thinking:
"In a single lifetime, suffering and joy are not fixed; how can fine clothing and delicious food be obtained forever?"
"Constantly illuminating a mirror—this too is unreasonable.
Although he harbored this thought, he found it difficult to ask about it.
After the guest and host had exchanged their farewells, they parted ways; the master and his disciples, both great and small, set out on the road to return to their own country.

Along the way, there was an inn with eaves extending on all four sides, which was extremely cool and refreshing. Those who arrived first rested beneath it; when the daughter-in-law arrived later, she addressed her mother-in-law, saying, "This place is not fit to stay in;
let us quickly go outside."
The husband did not go against her wishes and went out toward an open space; however, several people on his left and right were unwilling to leave.
At that time, there were elephants and horses that, feeling itchy, rubbed their bodies against the pillars, causing the house to collapse and burying those who were beneath it.
At that time, Ligimi thought to himself:
"It is because of this daughter-in-law that I have now escaped death.
His heart of reverence and esteem for her became doubly profound and generous.

Even as they traveled in their carriage back toward their destination, they came upon a large stream where the grass was lush and the water fine; there, the company halted their carriage and stayed by the side of the stream.
When the daughter-in-law arrived later, he said to her, "It is unpleasant staying here;
come quickly out onto the bank.
She followed his words and rested far away by a mountain stream.
In an instant, clouds arose, thunder shook the earth, and rain poured down in torrents, overflowing the mountain streams.
At that time, the householder Likhita thought again:
"Today we have escaped death for a second time; it is because of this daughter-in-law that our lives have been saved."
He again ordered his carriage to be prepared and proceeded forward on the road.

Upon reaching his native country, his kinsmen and relatives from both sides of his family all came to offer congratulations and inquiries after his welfare. The elder was filled with joy and immediately prepared offerings; they enjoyed themselves together until the end of the day, when the guests finally departed.
At that time, the elder summoned his sons' wives and addressed them, saying:
"I am now advanced in years and weary of manifold affairs; I wish to entrust the household goods and utensils to someone."
"Among you all, who is able to serve as my treasurer and hold the key?
The six wives of the elder sons all declined, saying they were unable to do so; only the seventh spoke up, saying she was capable of taking on the task.
At that time, the elder entrusted all the keys to his treasuries to him.

Having received these instructions, he was diligent and conscientious without negligence; every morning he rose early to sweep and clean the halls and rooms. Once the cooking and steaming were finished, he first fed his mother-in-law and father-in-law, as well as their sons and daughters, and afterwards fed the slaves and servants. He then directed each person to their respective stations to attend to their tasks, and only after that did he eat himself; this became his constant practice.
Seeing that his loyalty and devotion were unlike those of ordinary men, and finding it strange that he had not followed the instructions left by his stepmother, the husband asked him:
"When you came here previously, your mother instructed you:
'Wear fine clothes, eat delicious food, and use bright mirrors every day.'"
"What were the circumstances?
You may explain them.
The daughter-in-law knelt upright and answered in full detail regarding the facts of the matter:

"My mother’s instructions were as follows: regarding the fine garments she provided, she taught me to cherish them, keeping them always clean so that they might appear fresh and exquisite during occasional gatherings.

As for the fine food she commanded, it was not for its sweetness or richness; she taught me that when hungry at the evening meal, one should eat so that even the coarsest and finest portions are all delicious.

And as for that bright mirror, it was not made of copper or iron; she taught me to rise early to sprinkle and sweep both inside and out, to arrange the bedding and mats, and to ensure everything was kept pure and clean."
"Such were the instructions given by my mother.

When her mother-in-law heard this, she recognized that she possessed marvelous talent; her feelings toward her treatment of her grew twice as warm as before. She entrusted all the household goods to her, and she remained joyful and composed, free from any further anxiety.

At that time, there was a flock of geese flying into a coastal islet to feed on non-glutinous rice; having eaten their fill, they flew back with grains in their beaks and, passing over the royal palace, dropped them before the hall.
When the people saw it, they took some to present to the king.

The king, seeing that it was extraordinary and beautiful, knew it would certainly be suitable for medicinal use; he issued a decree to preserve the seeds so they would not be discarded or scattered, and distributed them among his various ministers, ordering each to plant them.
At that time, Vimalakīrti also obtained a small amount [of seeds] and brought them home, instructing his family to plant them.
His daughter-in-law took charge, directing the servants to prepare the garden beds and sow the seeds therein; they grew lushly and yielded a great harvest of fruit.
As for those others who had planted them, because they failed to manage the cultivation according to the proper measure, none of their crops grew at all.
At that time, the king’s consort suddenly fell gravely ill. He summoned various physicians to inquire about the origins of their treatments for the disease.
Among them, one physician said:
"One must prepare food with non-glutinous rice from a sea islet; only by eating it can she be cured."
The king recalled his own thoughts:
"In the past, I obtained its seeds and assigned them to people for cultivation; now I should investigate whether they still exist or not.
He immediately summoned his ministers and questioned them, saying:
"Did the rice previously ordered to be sown ripen?
Today we have an urgent need for it to treat a debilitating illness.
The ministers each recounted the details of the matter; some said it had not grown, while others said it had been eaten by rats.
Then, upon returning home, Vimalakīrti asked:
"Did the rice planted previously bear fruit?
I wish to obtain it to cure the illness of the King’s consort."
The daughter-in-law replied, "The household has an abundance;
this would suffice as medicine for an entire kingdom, not just for one person.
Thereupon, Liqimi sent it to the king, who immediately used it to prepare food and gave it to his consort.
After the lady had eaten, her illness was completely cured.
The king was greatly pleased and bestowed upon her a magnificent reward.
At that time, the two kingdoms of Takṣaśilā and Śrāvastī were at odds with one another and remained constantly discordant.
At that time, King Takṣaśilā wished to test whether Śrāvastī possessed holy wisdom.

He dispatched a messenger to the kingdom of Śrāvastī with two mares, mother and child; their forms and coat colors were identical and indistinguishable. "He who can correctly identify them shall be truly most excellent," he declared.
The king and his ministers were unable to distinguish between them.
At that time, Viśākhā returned home from the palace, and her daughter-in-law asked,
"What news do you have?"
The mother-in-law replied, "It is exactly as you have just seen.
The daughter-in-law said, "This matter is easy to understand; why should it be a cause for concern?"
He simply took some fine grass and gave it to them with their heads together;
the one that was the mother pushed the grass toward her calf, while the one that was the calf pulled at and ate the clumps of grass.

Then, Liqimi immediately went to inform the king; the king followed his words and tested them with grass, and indeed, according to his stratagem, the mother and child were distinguished from one another.
He then said to the messenger:
"This is the mother of the horse; that is her foal.
At that time, the messenger replied:
"It is exactly as the Tathāgata has spoken; there is no error whatsoever.
The king was greatly delighted and doubled his rewards and honors.
Then the envoy returned to his own country and reported all these matters in detail.

At that time, King Takṣaśilā sent another messenger, delivering two snakes whose thickness, fineness, length, and shortness were identical to one another, saying: "If you can distinguish the male from the female, that would be most excellent."
King Prasenajit and his various ministers were unable to identify her.
At that time, Viśākhā returned home and asked her daughter-in-law, "What is this?"
The daughter-in-law replied:

"Spread out a single piece of fine woolen cloth upon the ground, take these two snakes and place them upon the cloth; if it is the female, she will remain still and motionless, whereas if it is the male, he will be restless and agitated."
How is this known?
By nature, women are attached to smoothness and softness; they become impassioned upon encountering what is tender and do not wish to move.
Men are by nature rigid; they feel restless when turning or shifting their positions.
"By inferring from this, one can fully understand [the matter].
Having heard this, the elder immediately went to inform the king.
The king followed his plan and tested him at once; indeed, it was just as he had said, and [the boy] distinguished them with perfect clarity.
He said to that messenger,
"Is it male or female?
The messenger immediately replied:
"It is indeed so, and not false," the king said,
greatly rejoicing and bestowing upon him a great quantity of wealth and treasures.

At that time, the king of that country further sent a piece of wood one zhang in length, with its root and tip perfectly equal and free from any knots or marks made by knives or axes, and spoke to him, saying:
"If one could distinguish the top from the bottom of this tree, it would be most excellent and beyond measure.
Neither the king nor his ministers were able to identify them.
Then Ligīmi again questioned his daughter-in-law, and she replied:
"This matter is easy; simply take that wood and place it in the water, and its root will naturally sink while its top floats above."
Having heard this, the elder went back again to inform the king.
The king followed his advice and tested it; indeed, it was just as he had planned: they floated and sank according to their respective differences.
He said to the messenger, "That which floats is the head; that which sinks is the root.
Then the messenger replied:
"It is as you have described," the king said,
his joy increasing all the more, and he bestowed further rewards upon him.
That messenger returned to his own country and related the circumstances in full detail.
Upon hearing this, the king’s heart was moved to faith and submission; he dispatched an envoy once more, presenting rare treasures along with a message that said:
"In Your Majesty's kingdom there truly are men of wisdom and virtue; from this day forward, we shall cultivate friendly relations."
King Prasenajit, his heart leaping with even greater joy, summoned Riṣi-mi and asked him:
"Regarding all these recent events, by what means did you come to know them?"
Liqimi replied, "This is beyond my own understanding;
it is the wisdom and eloquence of my daughter-in-law.
Upon hearing this, the king was deeply moved with joy and respect; he honored his daughter-in-law and appointed her as his royal sister.

After a short time had passed, the son’s wife became pregnant; when the months were complete, she gave birth to thirty-two eggs. From within one of these eggs, a male child emerged, whose physical form and countenance were exceptionally handsome and distinguished.
As he grew up, he became peerless in valor and strength; the power of a single man was equal to that of a thousand men. His parents cherished him dearly, and the entire nation revered him.
Later, he took wives, all of whom were daughters of the country’s most eminent and virtuous families.
At that time, the people of Vaiśālī, their faith awakened and their minds liberated, invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to receive offerings at their homes.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and the entire family and their kinsmen attained the stage of Srotāpanna; only the youngest child had not yet realized the traces of the Path.

At that time, he was riding a white elephant, intending to go out for recreation. Outside the gate was a moat, both deep and wide, over which stood a large wooden bridge. Just as the youth arrived at the bridge, a son of a high minister was coming out from the opposite direction in a carriage; they met in the middle of the bridge, and each, relying on their noble lineage, neither yielded nor avoided the other.

The son of Vaiśālī, filled with rage, climbed onto the elephant, lowered his body toward the ground, seized the son of the prime minister along with his carriage, and hurled them into the moat. His body was mangled and all his joints were in agony;
weeping as he returned home, he said to his father, "The son of Vaiśālī has unjustly insulted me and wounded my body; my pain is such as this."
When his father heard this, he was deeply distressed and spoke to comfort his son:
"That man is powerful and is also a relative of the state; it will be difficult to overcome him in combat. You must devise a secret plan to avenge this grievance."
He then fashioned thirty-two horse-whips from the seven precious gems, using fine, tempered steel to create blades set within them. He gave one whip to each of the thirty-two men and said to them:
"You are young and by nature fond of play; I have therefore made these whips as a gift for you. I hope you will accept them and always carry them in your hands."
The people rejoiced and accepted it.
At that time, according to the laws of the kingdom, it was improper to carry a sword when appearing before the king.
Consequently, the prime minister, having seen that [the sword] had been accepted yet continued to hold it constantly, proceeded to slander the king deeply, saying:
"The thirty-two sons of Vaiśālī are in the prime of their youth and possess great strength; each man could match a thousand. Now they harbor a sinister scheme, plotting to harm the King.
Although the King heard this, he was still not convinced in his heart.
He further addressed the king:

"The matter is indeed true and not false; there is present evidence to prove it. Each of us has fashioned a sharp blade and placed it within our horse-whips; by this means, the truth of the matter will be made manifest."
The king immediately summoned them to inspect them; indeed, they were exactly as had been said. The king’s mind was thus convinced, and he believed it must certainly be so.
He selected powerful men and stationed them within the palace, summoning [the victims] one by one to have them killed inside.
He placed thirty-two heads inside a single casket, bound it securely, sealed it, and sent it to his sister.
