On that very day, the people of Vaiśālī invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha to their homes for a meal offering; seeing the king sending the casket, they thought he was bringing provisions to assist them in preparing the offerings, and so they wished to open it and look inside.
The World-Honored One said, "Stop for now and do not untie it; you must wait until the meal is finished.
When they had finished eating and were satiated, he ordered them to sit and preached the Dharma for them.

"This body is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; it gives rise to much peril and fear, cannot endure for long, and is entangled by manifold afflictions. Its bitterness and pain are beyond reckoning; through the separation from those one loves, we grieve and long for one another, needlessly exhausting the consciousness of the body without benefit for the Path."
"Only the wise are able to understand this evil.
At that time, Viśālī was suddenly awakened in mind and attained the stage of Anāgāmin. With joy, he joined his palms and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Please deign to show us compassion!"
I request that you grant me four vows:
first, that sick bhikṣus be provided with sufficient medicinal decoctions and food and drink according to their ailments;
second, that those bhikṣus who attend to the sick also be provided with food.
Third, one should first provide offerings to bhikṣus who have come from afar.
Fourth, one should provide and prepare provisions for bhikṣus traveling on a journey. Why is this so?
Because sick bhikṣus lack medicinal decoctions and wholesome food, their illnesses are difficult to cure, and some may even lose their lives.

Furthermore, because nursing bhikṣus lack food, they must abandon their alms-round; if they fail to attend to the needs of the patient at the proper times—morning or evening—the patient’s condition may worsen, leading to frustration and anger, which makes recovery difficult. For these reasons, one should provide them with food.

When there are bhikṣus coming from afar in other regions who have newly arrived in a foreign land and have no acquaintances, if they go out to beg for food, they might encounter vicious dogs or meet with wicked people who, perhaps out of anger, might injure, harm, or insult them; for this reason, one should first give them food.

"O bhikṣu traveling afar, you must have a companion; for if you lack provisions, or fail to keep pace with a companion, the road will be remote and perilous, filled with many venomous beasts, and should you attempt to traverse it alone, you may encounter danger."
"For this reason, I shall provide for them.
At that time, having heard that Vaiśālī requested these four vows, the World-Honored One praised them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"As you have wished, your virtue is vast and great; your offering to the Buddha is no different from others.
He then returned with the assembly of monks to the Jetavana.

After the World-Honored One had departed, he opened the casket and looked inside; there were thirty-two heads, all within the casket. Because he had severed his attachment, no resentment arose, and he spoke these words:
"How tragic! How sorrowful!
Human life is subject to death and cannot endure for long; driven through the five realms of existence, why must we suffer so?
When the thirty-two sons and their wives' relatives heard this principle, they were filled with extreme indignation and cried out in unison:
“The Great King has acted without righteousness, unjustly slaying a virtuous man; we have assembled our troops and intend to take revenge.
The multitude of soldiers gathered like clouds, surrounding the royal palace.
At that time, the king was terrified and retreated toward the Buddha’s location.
Hearing this, the people immediately led their troops and horses to surround the Jetavana.

Then Ānanda, hearing that King Prasenajit had killed the thirty-two sons of Vaiśālī and that the wife’s family and kinsmen intended to take revenge, knelt long upon his knees with palms joined and addressed the World-Honored One:
“For what cause and condition were the thirty-two sons killed by the king?
The World-Honored One replied, “These thirty-two sons of Vaiśālī were not only killed by the king today; thirty-two people died all at once in the past as well.”
"Listen well now!
Keep this in mind, and I shall speak for you. Ānanda said:
"Yes," Ānanda replied. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, long ago, these thirty-two people were close friends. They consulted one another and together stole a cow belonging to another."
At that time, there was an old woman in the country who had no children and was destitute and in dire straits.
Then, some thieves went to her house, intending to slaughter an ox together;
the old woman rejoiced and prepared for them firewood, water, and the cooking utensils.
As the butcher was about to apply the blade, the ox knelt down and begged for its life. The men were filled with indignation and were determined to kill it. The ox then made a solemn vow:
"If you kill me now, in a future life I shall not let you go; even if you attain the Way, I will still not release you."
Having finished making this vow, she was immediately killed.
The people roasted and boiled her, vying with one another to devour her; the old mother, in turn, also obtained her fill and spoke with joy:
"I have provided for guests since long ago, but today has been the most auspicious."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The ox at that time was none other than King Prasenajit here now.
The man who stole the ox at that time were these thirty-two sons of Vaiśālī here now."
The old woman of that time is now Vaiśālī.
Due to this karmic retribution, she has been constantly subjected to being killed for five hundred lifetimes, continuing even until the present day.

At that time, because of her sympathetic joy, for five hundred lifetimes she was always my mother; though she suffered extreme distress, it was only now, upon meeting me, that she finally attained the realization of the Path.
Ānanda joined his palms and addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"By cultivating what further merit does one become wealthy, noble,
and powerful? The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was an old woman who had faith and reverence for the Triple Gem. Her family was very wealthy; she gathered various kinds of incense, blended them with oil, and intended to go and anoint the stupa."
On the way, he encountered thirty-two people and exhorted them, saying:
"I wish to smear oil upon the stupa; you may assist me, and you shall thereby obtain merit and virtue, such that in every life you are born into, you will be handsome and possess great strength."
Then the thirty-two people departed together with joy.
Having finished anointing the stupa, they each spoke these words:

"Because of this old mother, we have been able to plant seeds of meritorious karma. We pray that in every place where we are born, may she be our mother—noble, honorable, and wealthy—and may we be her sons; may we never be separated from one another, and may we see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and swiftly attain the fruit of the Path."
The old woman was delighted and granted her permission.
From that time forward, for five hundred lifetimes, she was always born into a noble and honorable family.
The old woman of that time is none other than this present Vaiśālī.
"The thirty-two men at that time are now these thirty-two sons.
When the military host heard what the Buddha said, their anger subsided, and they spoke thus:

"The execution carried out by the Great King was not done arbitrarily; this man sowed the seeds himself and now receives the retribution. Because he killed a single ox, the consequence was already such as this."
"King Prasenajit is our lord; why would we harbor malice and seek to harm him?
They immediately cast aside their weapons, threw themselves before the king, and pleaded for mercy and forgiveness.
The king, too, was relieved and did not question them regarding their offense.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the fourfold assembly, extensively expounded all dharmas: that wholesome karma should be cultivated and evil conduct should be abandoned; he further elaborated and analyzed the wondrous Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
All those in the assembly who heard this attained realization of the Way, received and upheld the Buddha’s teachings, and joyfully practiced them.
Chapter 33: Śatruñjaya (In the Dan edition, Chapter 21) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:

“What auspicious merit did the five companions, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, possess in their past lives? By what causes and conditions did they alone first hear the Dharma drum vibrate when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, and why were they the first to taste the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma?”
"I only pray that you will show compassion and explain this in full detail for me.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"These five people, in a previous life, first ate my flesh and thereby attained peace and security; for this reason, today they were the first to receive the food of the Dharma and thereby attain liberation."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"What were the causes and conditions for eating meat in previous lives?
I pray that you will fully explain this to me."
The Buddha told him:

"In the distant past, immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Śatruñjaya. He ruled over eighty-four thousand kingdoms, sixty thousand mountains and rivers, eight billion villages, and twenty thousand queens and court ladies."
The King possessed great compassion and took pity on all classes of people; there was no one who did not rely upon his grace.
At that time, a comet appeared in the land. An astrologer observed it and addressed the King, saying:
"If such a comet appears, there shall be a drought lasting twelve years without rain."
"Now that this calamity has occurred, what should be done?
Upon hearing these words, the king was deeply distressed and sorrowful, thinking:
"If such a disaster occurs, what will become of the people and their possessions?"
"If the lives of the people cannot be saved, there will be no kingdom remaining.
He then assembled his ministers and deliberated with them together.
All the ministers said:

"Record the current population and households of all the nations, and further have them calculate the number of granaries and baskets and the amount of grain currently present, so that the exact measure in *hu* and *dou* may be known; then determine how much each person shall receive over the course of twelve years."
The king followed this proposal and immediately issued a proclamation, urgently ordering that the population be counted.

When the total count was completed, it was found that even if every person received one *sheng* per day, there would still not be enough; from that time forward, the people suffered from famine, and those who died were numerous.
The king thought to himself,
"What plan should I devise to save and sustain my people? Thereupon,
accompanied by his queen and court ladies, he went out to tour the gardens and pavilions, where they each took their rest.
While the assembly was fast asleep, the king rose from his seat, prostrated toward the four directions, and made this vow:

"Now the people of this land are emaciated by hunger and have no food; I shall sacrifice this body and vow to become a great fish, so that with the flesh of my own body, I may provide sustenance for all."

He immediately climbed to the top of the tree and threw himself to the ground; his life ended instantly, and he was reborn as a miraculously born fish in the great river, his body reaching a length of five hundred yojanas.
"At that time, there were five carpenters in the country who, each carrying an axe, went to the riverbank intending to cut timber.
When those fish saw them, they immediately spoke in human speech and addressed them, saying:
'If you are hungry and desire food, come and take my flesh.'"
"If you have eaten your fill, you may take it with you.
You shall first satisfy your hunger by eating my flesh; later, when you have attained Buddhahood, I shall deliver and liberate you all through the food of the Dharma."
"You may announce to the people of the kingdom, both great and small: 'Whoever requires food, let them all come and take it.

" The five men were filled with joy; they immediately went and cut [the fruit] for themselves, ate their fill, and carried the remainder back home, subsequently relating the matter in detail to the people of the kingdom.

Thereupon, the people told one another, and the news spread throughout Jambudvīpa until everyone had gathered there to devour his flesh. When the flesh of one flank was exhausted, he immediately turned his body over; they then took the other flank and devoured that as well until it was gone. Where the flesh had been consumed, it grew back again, and he turned his body once more to give them more.
In this manner, he repeatedly offered his own flesh to provide for all beings for twelve years.
All those sentient beings who ate his flesh gave rise to a heart of compassion, and after their lives ended, they were reborn in the heavens.
“Ānanda! If you wish to know who that King Śatānīka was at that time, it was none other than myself.
As for those five carpenters who previously ate my flesh, they are now the five bhikṣus, Kāuṇḍinya and the others.”
Those people among the populace who later ate meat are now these eighty thousand devas and those disciples who have attained liberation.

At that time, I first used my own flesh to sustain those five men, enabling them to survive; therefore, today I preached the Dharma for the first time to deliver those five, using a small portion of the flesh of my Dharma-body to eliminate their suffering from the hunger of the three poisons.
The venerable Ānanda and all those present, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were both moved by sorrow and joy; they received it upon their heads and practiced it accordingly.

Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
The venerable Ānanda sat within the Bamboo Grove and thought to himself:
"The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is truly marvelous and extraordinary!"
Now these disciples, having received the Buddha’s grace and benevolence, lack nothing in the four types of offerings; each has attained peace and security, reaching the end of suffering.

All the kings, ministers, and subjects of the world have likewise obtained great benefit, encountering the Triple Gem; that the people enjoy such peace and happiness is entirely due to the majestic power of the World-Honored One.
Having formed this thought, he rose from his seat and went to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One was extensively expounding the sublime Dharma for the fourfold assembly.

The Venerable Ānanda adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, recounting what he had contemplated while in the forest.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As you have said, the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is truly extraordinary!
He causes all sentient beings to obtain benefit."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment has not only benefited and brought benefit to sentient beings today; it has likewise done so in past ages.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“I do not understand, World-Honored One!
Regarding the past lives, how did you benefit sentient beings?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there were four rivers in this Jambudvīpa and two great kings. One king was named Bharadvāja—translated into Chinese as 'Brahmadeva' (梵天)—who alone possessed three rivers; his people were numerous and flourishing, yet they were weak and feeble.
The other king was named Vajrasena—translated into Chinese as 'Vajraskandha' (金剛聚)—who possessed only one river; his people were few, yet all the inhabitants of that land were brave and robust."
At that time, Vajrasena was seated alone in the main hall, reflecting:

"Although my troops are fierce and valiant, the water we have obtained is meager. That kingdom is weak and fragile, yet it holds sole dominion over the three rivers; I shall now dispatch an envoy to seek peace and request one river."

If you give it to me, we shall become close friends; when the country has fine things, we shall present them as gifts to one another, and if there be any hardship or calamity, we shall come to each other's rescue.
If you do not grant it, I shall simply use force to compel you to take it by seizure.
Having formed this thought, he summoned his ministers to deliberate upon this matter.
The ministers all said, "Now is precisely the right time.
He immediately dispatched a messenger on horseback to the kingdom of Brahmā, to announce the King's intention in full to the Brahmā King.
Upon hearing this, the Brahmā King reflected again to himself:

"My kingdom is prosperous and abundant, and its population is vast. Furthermore, this realm belonged to my father-king, who transferred it to me; as for engaging in a contest of strength, I am not inferior to him."
Having thought this, he replied to the messenger, saying:
"This kingdom is not something I have acquired for myself; rather, it was bestowed upon me by my father, the King."
"As for me now, my strength is no less than yours; if you wish to decide by means of strength, I do not fear you.
The messenger returned to his own country and reported this in full to the king.

The king immediately assembled his armies and attacked the kingdom of Brahmadatta. After one engagement, the army of Brahmadatta was defeated; [the king] pursued them on horseback until he reached the outskirts of the city. The people were terrified and cowered, no longer daring to come out. The ministers gathered together and went to the place where King Brahmadatta was; with one mind, they addressed the Great King, saying:
"The troops of the foreign nation are powerful, while our own country is weak and feeble. Out of惜 (regard/attachment) for a single river, we have now suffered this defeat."
In this way, before long, he will fear losing his kingdom.
I only pray that you will open your mind and grant him a single river; by establishing friendly relations with him, it will be sufficient to ensure our safety.
The king’s mind was immediately opened, and he agreed with the counsel of his ministers.
He dispatched a messenger at once to that army, who addressed their king, saying:
"Why do we neighboring states continue to commit such evil?"

"The river water you requested is now granted to you; I shall take your daughter as my queen. Whatever rare treasures our kingdoms possess, we shall exchange as gifts; and in times of urgent distress or peril, we shall come to each other's rescue."
At that time, Vajrasamudgata, following his wife's intention, immediately welcomed the woman and honored her as his consort; they each reached a reconciliation and returned home with their army.
After some time had passed, the king’s consort became aware that she was pregnant.

Once she had conceived, there was always a great canopy made of the seven precious jewels that appeared spontaneously above her; whether sitting, lying down, walking, or standing, it never left her side.

When the ten months were complete, he gave birth to a son whose body was the color of purple-gold, with hair as deep blue-black as sapphire; his radiant marks were so brilliant that they had few equals in the world, and even as the child emerged from the womb, a canopy appeared above him.
He summoned various physiognomists and ordered them to examine this child.
The physiognomists opened and inspected him, then raised their hands and proclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!"
With one voice and in unison, they addressed the Great King, saying:
"Beholding the Crown Prince now, his virtuous power is peerless; his physical marks are complete, and he is a rarity in this world."
The king and his ministers, overjoyed beyond measure, immediately informed the physiognomist to establish a name for him.
At that time, according to the laws of the kingdom, names were given based on two factors:
first, auspicious omens; second, the positions of the stars.
The physiognomist addressed the king, saying:
"Since this crown prince entered the womb, what auspicious omens have there been?
The king replied to him:
"There was a canopy made of the seven treasures that was always over his head.
They then gave him the name Kṣatragupta, which in the Jin language means "Protected by a Canopy," and they served him with various exquisite offerings at all times.
When he reached adulthood, his father passed away.
Once the funeral rites were completed, the various minor kings and ministers collectively installed Ghasuri as the Great King.
"After ruling for several years, he went abroad on an excursion and saw the various people laboring at their plowing and sowing.
He asked his attendants, 'Why do the many people of my kingdom perform these various kinds of service?'"
The minister replied to the king, saying:
"A state takes its people as its foundation, and the people take grain as their life-force.
If it were otherwise, the lives of the people would not be sustained."
"If the lives of the people are not preserved, the state will perish.
The King then said:
"If my merit corresponds to that of one who should be king, let my people obtain grain spontaneously and no longer perform such labor."
When he had finished speaking, all the people’s granaries and baskets became spontaneously full; various kinds of mixed grains were available to them all according to their wishes.

After several more periods of time, he went out again to travel abroad and saw the people of that country gathering firewood, drawing water, and performing labor such as pounding grain and grinding it. He asked his ministers:
"Why are these masses of people still toiling so hard?"
"Why is this so? The minister replied to the king:

"By the grace of Your Majesty’s benevolence, we have obtained natural grain; yet as this grain cannot be eaten raw, it must be processed for ripening. For this reason, the common people prepare various kinds of cooked food."
The king spoke again, saying:
"If my merit is such that I ought to be a king, let all the people within my realm have food appear spontaneously before them whenever they wish to eat."
As soon as these words were spoken, the entire realm obtained food that appeared spontaneously.

After some time had passed, the king went out again for an excursion and observed that the multitude were busily engaged in their respective tasks, spinning, weaving, and tailoring, preparing garments and provisions.
The king asked his ministers,
"For what reason do these people labor so hard at their tasks?"
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"By the grace of Your Majesty, we have obtained food that appeared spontaneously; now, while performing our labor, we have prepared these garments.
The king spoke again, saying:
"If my merit is such that I am destined to be a king, let all the trees within my realm produce garments of their own accord.

As soon as these words were spoken, the various trees throughout the kingdom all produced exquisite garments—extremely fine and soft, in blue, yellow, red, and white, according to whatever each person desired.
After some more time had passed, the king went out on a tour again and saw the people each vying with one another to manufacture various musical instruments. The king again asked his ministers:
"For what reason are the people of my kingdom thus laboring and toiling at their crafts?"
The minister addressed the king, saying:

"These people, having received the grace of Your Majesty, have their food and clothing provided spontaneously and each has attained peace and security. As they require music and performance for their own amusement, they are now preparing musical instruments."
The king then said:

"If I possess merit and am destined to be a sovereign, let there appear upon every tree within my kingdom all manner of musical instruments—drums, lutes, harps, biwas, and kōhōs—as well as everything else required, all appearing according to my heart's desire."
After several more intervals had passed, all the kings, ministers, and subjects came to offer their congratulations;
it happened to be the time for the king’s meal, so the king immediately invited them to stay and provided them with food and drink.
At that time, when the ministers received the king’s meal, which was complete with a hundred flavors, they all said together:
"The food in our own homes is meager in flavor; now that we have obtained the king’s food, its delicious taste is extraordinary."
The King said to them:
"O you ministers and subjects, if you wish to always obtain food such as mine, then at the time I eat, all who eat shall likewise obtain such food."
He immediately commanded his officials:

"When the time for my meal arrives, always beat the great drum so that all the people may hear and know of it; by providing me with a meal at the proper time, they shall receive the most excellent offerings of a hundred flavors."

From that time forward, whenever it was time to eat, drums would be struck; all the people, upon hearing the sound, would think of food, and a hundred flavors of exquisite delicacies would naturally appear before them. The people lived in such abundance and joy that it cannot be fully described.
At that time, King Brahmā sent an envoy to the kingdom of Kapphiṇa and said to him:
"When your father was alive, I gave you this river water; now that your father has passed away, you ought to return it to me."
At that time, King Chatri replied to the messenger, saying:
"The territories and the rivers within my domain were not obtained by my own power, but were acquired from you through force; nevertheless, as a king, I do not exhaust the people or their resources."
"This is but a minor matter; it should be set aside for later. Only when I have met your king face-to-face shall I fully explain the essentials regarding our kingdom.
The envoy returned to his country and reported everything to the king one by one. The king agreed with his intention and fixed a date for their meeting.

When the appointed time had elapsed, the two kings advanced together, surrounded by a vast and countless multitude of troops. Each established a great camp on one side of the river, and the two kings met upon their boats in the middle of the stream.

At that time, King Brahmā first beheld the sight of the canopy; his body was radiant and resplendent like a mountain of purple gold, his hair shone brilliantly like deep blue lapis lazuli, and his eyes were wide and long, such as are rarely found among men. A sense of reverence arose within him, and he thought, "This must be Brahmā."
Upon arriving, they exchanged greetings and sat together; there they conversed about their two lands and discussed the matter of seeking water.
Gai replied, saying:
"The people of my country have whatever they desire appear naturally before them, and they are free from the toil of taxes, corvée labor, or military service."
Before he had finished speaking, the time for the meal had arrived; as they were serving King Muṇḍa’s army, the drums were beaten to signal the meal.

At that moment, Brahmā Sahāmpati became extremely terrified, thinking that [the king] intended to seize and kill him. In his fear, unable to remain at ease, he rose to apologize for his own transgression, spreading his hands and feet out like a spider and slapping his belly against the ground before him.
As the matter arose spontaneously, he informed him and ordered him to sit down again,
saying further: "Great King!..."
Why is there such terror?
When my army eats, the drums always sound of their own accord. Why is this so?
"When it is my time to eat, by using my timely food, all shall receive offerings of the finest delicacies of a hundred flavors.
Then King Brahmā rose again, joined his palms, and said to the Lord of the Canopy:
"I only pray, Great King!"
"May you look upon me and my people with universal compassion; may they all submit to your grace, and may all the common folk receive your benevolent favor.
Thereupon, he presided over Jambudvīpa, and all the people attained complete peace and happiness.

"After ascending the throne, while he was situated in the main hall with his various ministers and officials standing in attendance as guards, at the moment the sun first rose, a precious golden wheel (cakraratna) appeared from the east.

When the King saw it from afar, he immediately descended from his throne, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and faced the direction of the wheel, beckoning it three times with his hand. The wheel then arrived, complete with its thousand spokes, its radiant color brilliantly manifest."
The king said to him,
"If I am destined to be a Wheel-Turning King, then abide within this place according to the Dharma.
Thereupon, the wheel-treasure remained suspended in the air before the king, seven *tāla* trees above the ground.
The elephant-treasure, the divine pearl, the jade woman, the minister of war, and the minister of treasury arrived in succession.

At that time, King Kapphiṇa possessed these seven treasures and ruled over the four continents; all sentient beings received the king’s benevolence and virtue, and could enjoy all their desires at will. The king instructed them all to practice the ten wholesome deeds, so that after their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As for King Kṣāntigarbha at that time, was he anyone else?
It was I myself."
At that time, King Śuddhodana, who punished Jaṭila, was my father, King Śuddhodana, as he appears today.
At that time, the mother was my mother, Mahāmāyā, as she appears today.

Because in the past I took pity on sentient beings and constantly gathered them in through both material gifts and the Dharma, by virtue of these causes and conditions, I have personally attained Buddhahood, becoming the sole Honored One of the three realms, with no one equal to me.
"For this reason, all sentient beings should cultivate great compassion to provide nourishment and benefit.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not fully understand, World-Honored One!"

In a past life, for what causes and conditions did the Cakravartin King Kṣemankara obtain such immeasurable merits as these, such that from the very moment he first entered his mother’s womb, a precious canopy followed and covered him?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Furthermore, in the distant past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, in the country of Vārāṇasī, within the mountains of the Rishis, there was a Pratyekabuddha who constantly dwelt therein."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha suffered from an imbalance of his physical elements and went to consult a physician.
The physician said to him, "You have a wind disorder; you must consume milk."
At that time, in that country, there was a caravan leader named Ariyamitra, which in the Jin language means "Noble Friend.
The Pratyekabuddha went to his house, explained the cause of his illness, and begged him for milk.
The Sārthavāha was filled with joy and invited him to receive offerings, providing him with milk daily for three months.

When the three months had passed, his physical illness was cured. Grateful for the merchant’s kindness and wishing to bring great benefit to his host, he leaped into the air and manifested eighteen transformations: sitting, reclining, walking, and standing; emitting water and fire from his body; manifesting a massive body that filled the void of space, and again manifesting a minute form that entered within the eye of a falling hair. He displayed such various wonders.
Thereupon, the Holy Friend was filled with supreme joy.
He descended once more from the sky, accepted their offerings again, and after a period of time had passed, entered nirvana.

The Sārthavāha was filled with grief and sorrow; he recollected his past deeds for immeasurable eons. He cremated the body, collected the relics, and placed them within a precious vase. He then erected a stūpa and offered worship with incense, flowers, music, and various exquisite objects.
He took the large parasol he was holding and placed it atop the stupa, making offerings to it for the remainder of his life.

Because he had made these fourfold offerings to a single pratyekabuddha, by virtue of this meritorious retribution, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he was either born in the heavens or dwelt among humans, distinguished by his noble and eminent status, with few equals in the world.
He further addressed Ānanda:
"All sentient beings, whether lay or ordained, should all cultivate merit; in every successive birth, they shall obtain such benefits as these."
At that time, Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Chapter 35: The Great Almsgiving and the Emptying of the Ocean (40). Chapter Thirty-Five: The Great Almsgiving and the Emptying of the Ocean. (In the Danben [Dunhuang manuscript], this is Chapter Thirty-Nine. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty venerable disciples.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought of needing an attendant. His various venerable disciples, including Kauṇḍinya and others, each observed one another and knew what the Buddha was thinking.
Then Kauṇḍinya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha:
"I long to serve you closely, to hold your robes and carry your alms bowl; I only pray that you will show me compassion!"
"I beg you to grant me your instruction and permission.
The Buddha told him, "You are advanced in years and must have someone to attend to you yourself; how could I bear to have you serve me in return?"
At that time, Kauṇḍinya, knowing that the Buddha would not permit it, paid homage and returned to his seat.
Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and five hundred other disciples followed in succession, each petitioning the Buddha to serve him as an attendant, but the Buddha refused them all.

At that time, Aniruddha examined the Buddha’s mind and perceived his intention: the World-Honored One’s heart was set upon Ānanda, just as when the sun rises in the east and illuminates a house, its light passing through the eastern window and reaching directly to the western wall;
such was the World-Honored One’s intent, and all the great disciples likewise observed and understood it.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana rose from their seats, went before Ānanda, and said to him:
"The World-Honored One’s intention is that he wishes to have you, O virtuous one, as his attendant."
"You, O Benevolent One, possess virtuous merit and have alone been granted this commendation; you should go at once to inform [the Buddha] and request to become an attendant to the Buddha.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, seeing the elder monks arrive before him and hearing their words, immediately rose with palms joined and addressed the elders, saying:

"The World-Honored One’s virtue is profound and his wisdom is deep and far-reaching. Because I have always attended upon him in close proximity, I fear I may incur blame and bring upon myself calamity and suffering."
Śāriputra and the others spoke to him again, saying:

"Behold now how the World-Honored One focuses his attention with single-minded intent, desiring to have you as his attendant. It is like the rising sun illuminating a house; its light passes through the eastern window and shines directly upon the western wall. The World-Honored One’s concentration of mind is just like this."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, you thoroughly understand human nature and know who is capable and fit; therefore, you have taken this to heart. It would be appropriate for you to inform him at once and request that he become your attendant.
Having received these words again, the Venerable Ānanda reflected on the matter, not knowing what to do. He joined his palms once more and addressed the senior elders:
"If the World-Honored One now grants me three wishes, I shall be able to serve as the Buddha’s attendant."
"What are these three?
May the World-Honored One not give me his old robes to wear;
may the World-Honored One not let me eat his leftover food."
"The time has arrived; let it be according to my discretion.
Only by being granted these three vows can I attend upon the Buddha.
Having heard these words, Śāriputra and the others went to inform the World-Honored One of the matter in its entirety.
Having heard this, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "O disciples!

The reason Ānanda seeks not to wear my old robe is that Ānanda has long reflected on the possibility that some disciples might harbor feelings of jealousy, and thus he conceived this thought: [fearing they would think, 'The World-Honored One has bestowed his old robe upon Śāriputra, yet he does not bestow it upon us; surely the World-Honored One holds Śāriputra in higher regard than us. We too should strive to attain such a state as Śāriputra’s, so that the World-Honored One will likewise bestow his old robe upon us. If we do not practice diligently, we shall never attain such a state.']"
"The king, his ministers, and the subjects, as well as various donors, have offered the Buddha robes of high value, fine and soft;
Ānanda, out of greed for these, requested to serve as an attendant."
Furthermore, when he again sought someone who would not eat his leftovers, he did so out of concern that his disciples might again give rise to this thought:
"The remnants of what the Tathāgata has eaten from his bowl consist of a hundred flavors, sweet and delicious; there is no such food in the world.
It is because Ānanda craves them that he comes to stay near him."

The reason Ānanda sought to personally determine the proper timing for bringing forth [the teachings] was that he feared disciples and followers of external paths might come seeking instruction; if they were to pose difficult questions without knowing the proper time, they might inadvertently cause offense or disturbance. Furthermore, as his attendant, he was responsible for observing the seasons to provide appropriate food and drink that would be conducive to their comfort and benefit their bodies, ensuring that every regulation was established with consideration for avoiding any faults or excesses.
For this reason, he first requested these three wishes in advance.
Furthermore, Ānanda, it is not only today that he has requested to know the proper time; in past lives as well, while serving me, he was well-acquainted with what was appropriate for the occasion.
Then Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I do not yet understand how, in the past, he served the Buddha and skillfully knew the proper timing—what were those matters?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If you wish to hear it, listen attentively and take it to heart;
I shall speak for you."
“Yes, World-Honored One!
We shall listen attentively.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"In the distant past, incalculable, immeasurable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, there was a great king who ruled over eighty-four thousand small kingdoms and eight billion villages throughout Jambudvīpa. The city where the king resided was named Bharuśeṣa."

Now, within the city, there was a brahmin named Nyagrodha, who was intelligent and widely learned, possessing a transcendent natural genius. The King held him in the highest esteem, honoring and serving him as his teacher;

eighty-four thousand minor kings all looked upon him with distant reverence and admiration, gazing toward his location, sending tributes from afar and dispatching envoys to seek his counsel, treating him in brief as they would a great sovereign.

Now this brahmin was as wealthy as a royal house, yet he had no son to carry on his lineage; whether entering or leaving, sitting or reclining, he was constantly burdened by this sorrow, not knowing by what means he might obtain a son.

He immediately offered prayers and sacrifices to Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, Maheśvara, as well as all other deities—the sun, moon, and stars, and the spirits of mountains, rivers, and trees—performing every kind of ritual offering without exception.

After twelve years of sincere devotion and the accumulation of merit, the chief lady perceived that she had conceived. Being a woman of great intelligence, she was able to discern this; knowing for herself that what she bore would surely be a son, she informed the Brahmin of these circumstances.

The Brahmin was filled with joy and his delight redoubled; he immediately commanded the ladies and maids of his household to come and attend to the Queen’s every movement, ensuring her food, drink, bedding, and seating were of the finest quality, provided in perfect harmony and abundance, never failing to accord with her wishes.
When the ten months were complete, a son was born; his body was the color of purple gold, his hair was deep blue-black, and he was so exceptionally handsome that such human features are rarely found.
When the Brahmin saw this, he was overcome with joy and immediately summoned a physiognomist to examine the child together.

As the physiognomist inspected him, he marveled at such an unprecedented sight, saying: "The marks and features of this child are of vast merit and virtue; he shall be looked up to by all under heaven, just as a son relies upon his mother."
His father was filled with joy and commanded that a name be established for him.
In India, names are formed according to two principles:
either based on the lunar mansions or based on significant transformations.
The physiognomist then asked:
"Since you have been pregnant, what extraordinary changes have occurred?
His father replied:
"The mother of this child was formerly ill-tempered and harbored aversion; she lacked compassion and obedience, and did not cultivate loving-kindness or wisdom.

Since becoming pregnant, however, her disposition has been transformed: she now feels pity for those in distress and hardship, loves them as a mother loves her own child, delights in the practice of giving, and is free from greed or stinginess."
Upon hearing this, the physiognomist spoke with joy:
"It is because of this child's aspiration that it has become so.
You should establish a name for him, Mahātyāgakaṇḍa; in the Jin language, this means 'Great Giver'."

"As the boy gradually grew up, his father loved him dearly. He built a separate palace for him and established a three-season hall: warm in winter, cool in summer, and situated in the middle for spring and autumn. He settled various entertainers and attendants there to provide him with amusement."

The boy was intelligent and fond of learning; he recited and maintained the eighteen secular scriptures. Having mastered their texts with fluency, he was also well-versed in their meanings. He studied various arts and crafts, there being nothing he did not understand.
Thereafter, Mahātyāga said to his father,
"Having long remained within the deep palace, I desire to go out for a stroll.
Upon hearing these words, the father immediately issued an edict to his ministers and officials:

"My son Mahādāna wishes to go out for a stroll; therefore, sweep and sprinkle the streets, remove all impurities, erect banners and pennants, scatter flowers and burn incense, and adorn the roads so that they are utterly pure."

Having completed the preparations for the great offering, he mounted a magnificent white elephant adorned with the seven treasures. With bells and drums being struck and various musical performances being rendered, a procession of thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of horsemen escorted him from the front and rear as he proceeded along the royal highway toward the city gate.
At that time, the people of the kingdom, atop their pavilions and along both sides of the road, vied with one another to gaze upon him, never tiring of the sight; they all said to one another:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
Beholding his majestic appearance, it was as if he were Brahmā.
Continuing further on his way, he saw various beggars wearing tattered rags and holding broken vessels, speaking with humble words and seeking pity:
"Give us a little."
When Mahādāna saw them, he asked them,
"Why are you all so weary and distressed?
Some answered him, saying:
"I have no father, mother, brothers, wife, or children; I am poor, orphaned, and solitary, with nothing to rely upon.
Or someone might answer:
"I suffer from a chronic illness and cannot perform labor; I have no way to support myself."
Some might answer, saying:

"I am unfortunate, having repeatedly suffered ruin and loss; debts have accumulated until they overwhelm me, and my body and mouth are so pressed by necessity that I have no means to sustain myself. It is for this reason that I beg for alms to preserve my remaining life."
Having heard this, Mahādāna sighed with sorrow and departed.
Continuing further on his journey, he saw several butchers flaying and skinning livestock, carving and slicing them into portions for sale.
Mahātyāga saw them and asked, "Ho! What are you doing?
Each of them replied:
"Since my grandfather's time, our family has made its living through slaughter; if I were to abandon this work, there would be no means by which I could support myself.
Great Giver sighed and departed, leaving it behind.

Next, he saw a plowman tilling the earth with a plow; worms emerged from the soil and were swallowed by a frog. A snake then came and devoured the frog, whereupon a peacock flew down and pecked at and ate the snake.
Mahātyāga asked him:
"What is this being done? He replied:
"By tilling the soil and sowing seeds therein, one shall later obtain grain to provide for oneself, as well as to pay tribute to the royal house.
Having heard this, Mahādāna sighed deeply and departed.
Proceeding further, he saw hunters spreading nets and setting snares to capture various birds and beasts;
he saw the birds and beasts fallen into the snares and nets, pulling and thrashing themselves, unable to escape, crying out piteously to one another, each filled with terror.
Mahātyāga saw them and asked, "Why are you doing this?
They each replied together, "We rely solely on hunting and killing for our livelihood; if we do not do this, there is no way for us to survive."
Having heard these words, he departed in sorrowful distress.
Continuing further on his way, he saw a fisherman who had spread out his nets and caught a great many fish, which were piled upon the land and still writhing.
He asked them again for the reason:
"Alas! Why have you done this?
Each stepped forward and replied:
"Since my grandfather's time, we have had no other means of livelihood; we rely solely on fishing, selling our catch to provide for our food and clothing.
Upon seeing this, Mahādāna was filled with deep pity and reflected to himself:
"All these sentient beings, because they lack food and clothing due to poverty, commit such evil deeds as killing living beings, taking pleasure in them to the utmost."
"After my life comes to an end, I shall surely fall into the three miserable realms, passing from darkness into darkness; how strange and grievous this is!
Having had this thought, he turned his carriage back toward the palace, brooding over these matters with sorrow and distress, finding no joy.
He went to see his father and requested a single boon.
The father said to Mahātyāga,
"I shall never go against whatever you request."
He then spoke of himself, saying:

"Yesterday morning I went out for a stroll and observed those people seeking clothing and food; they exhaust their bodies and labor their minds, committing acts of killing, harming, and deception, and are fully possessed of all manner of evil karma. My heart felt deep compassion for them, and I thought of providing for their relief."
"I only pray that you will bestow your grace upon me and grant me this great treasury, allowing me to give freely to relieve the deficiencies of the multitude.
His father said to him, "I have accumulated these wealth and treasures solely for your sake; since this is your wish, how could I possibly go against it?"
"Having received his father's instruction, the son immediately issued a proclamation to all the people:
'Mahādeva wishes to perform a great act of giving; whoever has any need, let them all come and take what they require.'"

Once the proclamation had been made, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, the poor, those burdened by debt, the orphaned and the afflicted with illness, departed from all the cities and along the roads, one after another.

Among the multitudes of people, there were those who came from distances of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, five hundred, or one thousand li, as well as those who came from three thousand, five thousand, or ten thousand li; they all gathered from the four quarters like clouds, supporting one another according to their strength and weakness, and everything was provided for them to fulfill their every wish.

If they require clothing, he gives them clothing; if they require food, he provides them with food; gold, silver, and the seven treasures; carriages, horses, and palanquins; gardens, fields, and domestic animals—he gives these according to their wishes.
As he continued to give alms in this manner for some time, two-thirds of the goods in the treasuries had already been given away. Then the treasury official went to inform his father:
"Mahāśakrāditya, since you began giving alms, two-thirds of the goods in the storehouses have already been bestowed."
"The envoys of various kings will surely come and go; I pray you reflect deeply on this, lest you later be held accountable.
Upon hearing the official's words, the father reflected to himself:
"I love this son and cannot reject his wishes. Rather than leaving my treasury empty, how could I possibly interrupt such an act of giving?"
After another period of time had passed, he used two-thirds of the remaining stored goods.
The official reported once more:
"Of the remaining goods from before, two-thirds have already been consumed."
"The envoys of various kings must be informed of these matters; now that the treasure is about to vanish into thin air, I pray you will reconsider this once more.
Then the Brahmin spoke to the official, saying:
"I love this son with such profound affection that I have never before failed him or contradicted his wishes face-to-face."
"You should employ skillful means and fabricate some pretext; when he comes seeking goods, first claim that you are not at home, so as to delay him for some days and months.
Having received these instructions, the official immediately closed the storehouse door and went elsewhere for a short while.

The beggars gathered and arrived at the place of the Great Benefactor; the Great Benefactor went to the official to request goods, but the official was not there. He searched for him over a period of time until, exhausted, he finally found him. Although he obtained the goods, they did not meet the urgent requirements of the moment.
Mahātyāga thought to himself:
"How could this minor official dare not comply with my will by his own power?
It must be because of his father's intention that he acts thus."
"Furthermore, according to the way of a son, it is not fitting to exhaust the treasury of one's parents until nothing remains.
Now, what little is left in this treasury—how may I obtain much wealth and treasure to fulfill my purpose and provide for all living beings?
Having had this thought, he reflected: "How can I acquire great riches to satisfy my intent and relieve the multitude of beings?"
He then asked the people:
"In this world today, what occupation can one pursue to acquire such vast wealth that it is difficult to exhaust?
Some people replied:
"One may cultivate various kinds of the five grains and tend gardens and orchards to acquire much wealth.
Or someone might say:
"One may raise many domestic animals, allowing them to multiply according to the seasons, to acquire much wealth."
Or someone might say:
"One who does not avoid great hardships and travels far away to trade will obtain the greatest amount of wealth.
Or someone else might say:
"Only by entering the sea to gather precious jewels can one obtain the greatest amount of wealth.
Upon hearing this, Mahādāna said to himself:
"Plowing fields, raising livestock, and traveling far abroad to trade are not suitable for me; they yield but little profit."
"Only by entering the sea can this plan be followed.
I shall exert myself with all my might to accomplish this matter.
Having formed this thought, he went to inform his parents:

"I now wish to enter the sea to seek many precious treasures, so that upon my return I may bestow them as gifts to relieve the deficiencies of the people. I only pray that you will grant me leave to fulfill this aspiration."
Upon hearing these words, the parents were startled and asked:
"When people of the world enter the sea, being destitute and having no other recourse, they cast away their lives and bodies without any lingering attachment."
"What business do you have that you wish to practice this again?
If you wish to give in charity, let all the property I possess, as well as the remnants in my storehouses, be yours to use entirely; do not enter the great ocean."

Furthermore, within the ocean there are many great perils: surging waves and eddying currents, the makara fish, malevolent nāgas and rākṣasas, and mountains of aquatic hue; such manifold dangers make it difficult to traverse.
"What urgent matter do you have that you cast yourself into this peril?
As long as our lives remain, we shall never grant your request.
You should cease your intent and not cause further commotion."
Upon hearing this, Mahātyāga’s wish was not fulfilled; he felt profound dejection and thought to himself:
"The great task I now desire to accomplish—how can it be achieved if I am still attached to my own body?"
He spread his body upon the ground and prostrated before his parents, saying:
"If you must insist on keeping me here and thus contravene my own aspirations, I shall lie here upon this earth and never rise again."
Upon hearing this, their parents were filled with burning anxiety; together with the palace attendants, they went before him and exhorted him, saying:
"The sea route is vast and distant, fraught with many perils and hardships. Of those who go forth, very few return."

I recall that in my quest for a son, I prayed to the various heavens with such sincerity and earnest devotion that there was no deity to whom I did not turn; after twelve years had passed, I was finally exhausted by my efforts when my wish was granted.
"Now that you have grown up, do you wish to abandon me?
Renounce this intention and return to take food and drink.
For one day, two days, and up to six days, he admonished and exhorted him in these various ways, seeking to bring him to understanding.
His words remained as they were at first, and his resolve did not waver.
His parents became fearful and deliberated among themselves, saying:

"In all that this child has done before and since, whatever he intended to do, he has always brought it to completion without ever withdrawing midway. Even if we send him into the sea, we still hope for the time of his return; yet now, if we certainly block and forbid him, on the seventh day disaster will surely manifest—what shall we do?"
"You should be allowed to go; otherwise, we shall only grow more anxious for you hereafter.
Once their deliberation was concluded, they both went to the child's side, each grasping one of his hands, and said to him:
"We grant you your wish; rise and return to eat."
Upon hearing this, Mahādatta immediately rose and went to the meal.
When he had finished eating, he rose and went outside to issue a proclamation widely, addressing the multitude:
"I now wish to enter the sea in person to gather treasures; who among you wishes to go?"
"We may proceed together.
I shall act as the caravan leader and provide all the necessary provisions for the journey.
At that time, there were five hundred people in the kingdom who, having heard this command, unanimously accepted the call.
He immediately prepared what was required and fixed the date for his departure.

When the day arrived, he readied his carriage and took his leave to set out on the road. The king, along with his ministers, his parents, various princes, and the multitude of subjects—numbering several million—accompanied him as far as the roadside. Each presented him with exquisite jewels and provisions necessary for the journey; they wept until their voices were choked with grief, and then they parted.
After traveling for several days, he halted for the night in a desolate wilderness. There he encountered a band of robbers who came intending to lie in wait and plunder him;
out of compassion, the Bodhisattva took what he had brought with him and gave it all away as alms.
Continuing on his way, he arrived at a city named Pātra-pratigrahaṇa. In that city lived a brahmin named Kapila.
At that time, the Great Giver went to his residence, intending to borrow three thousand ounces of gold from him.

At that time, the Brahmin had a wonderful daughter whose body was the color of purple gold and whose hair was deep blue-black; she was of such peerless beauty that there was no one her equal in the world. Eighty-four thousand minor kings, all acting as suitors for the prince, sought her hand, but he refused them all.
At that time, Mahātyāga arrived at his gate and asked Kāpila, "I wish to see you.
His daughter, who was inside, heard the voice from outside; filled with joy and starting up in surprise, she said to her parents:
"The one who is outside is my son-in-law.
At that time, Kapila came out to meet him; observing his appearance and countenance, he knew he was certainly no ordinary man. Hearing that he required gold, he granted it all to him.
Furthermore, with his left hand he grasped a golden water-pitcher and with his right hand he took hold of the girl, saying to Mahādāna:
"This daughter of mine possesses extraordinary beauty; kings have sent messengers from all quarters seeking her for their sons.
Now that I behold you, O Sārthavāha, who are so remarkably handsome and well-proportioned, I pray that you accept this girl to serve you."
Mahādatta replied, "I am now about to embark on a perilous journey across the sea; how can I know whether I shall return in safety?
To accept your daughter in advance is not appropriate."
Kāpilī said, "If you can ensure that he returns safely, I shall accept him for myself.
At that time, Mahādāna immediately gave his consent.
At that time, Kapila was filled with joy and gave him three thousand *tolas* of gold, as well as whatever else he required.

Thereupon they took their leave of one another and proceeded further until they reached the sea. He commanded the merchants to have their ship reinforced until it had seven layers of planking. When the favorable wind arrived, they pushed the ship out into the open sea and moored it to the shore with seven large cables. Then, shaking a bell, he proclaimed to the assembly of merchants: "Listen all of you! There are many perils within the ocean:
the black winds, the *rākṣasas*, the swirling eddies, the poisonous breath of evil dragons, the mountains of colored waters, and the great *makara* fish; these and many other hardships abound."
"A hundred companions enter the sea; at that time, only one returns safely.
Whoever wishes to retreat may stay here;
once the rope is severed, there will be no time for regret."

If one can be firm of mind, disregarding even body and life, and by parting from one's parents, brothers, wife, and children, encounters safety and returns with the seven treasures, then for seven generations of descendants, their provisions will never be exhausted.
Having issued this command, he then cut one rope; he did so day after day.

On the seventh day, after the proclamation had been made again, he cut the seventh rope. Raising the sails in accordance with the wind, the ship sped like an arrow, and together with the entire company of merchants, they reached the place of treasures.

The Great Donor, being widely learned and possessing clear discernment regarding all treasures—distinguishing their weight, value, quality, and appearance—showed them to the merchants, saying: "Such a treasure of this color and appearance is not heavy in weight, yet it is of high value and may be taken."
"Such treasures as these are of high value but appear cheap; none of you should take them.

Furthermore, I strictly command that you take a moderate amount of treasure; if you take too much, the ship will become heavy, and being heavy, it will sink. If you take too little, although the ship will be light, it will not compensate for your labor."
When the instructions were finished, everyone diligently gathered the treasures, piled them onto the ship, and adorned themselves with jewels, intending to return.
At that time, Mahādāna did not wish to board the ship. When all the people assembled and asked him the reason for his intent, Mahādāna replied:
"I wish to advance further to the palace of the Naga King to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi); even at the cost of my very life, I must not fail to return."
Upon hearing this, the merchants were filled with grief and despondency;

they spoke together, saying, "We have relied upon the Sārthavāha, forsaking what we hold dear and braving these perils to reach this place, hoping that through his grace we might all be saved and return home."
"Why is it that you now wish to abandon us? Mahādāna replied,
"I shall make a vow on your behalf to seek [your welfare], so that all of you may return to your country in safety."
Upon hearing this, the merchants' hearts were relieved from their fear.
The Great Giver, the Guide, took a censer in his hand and, facing the four directions, made this vow:

"I do not shrink from toil as I traverse the seas to seek treasures, so that I may relieve the distress of hunger and poverty among all living beings; having accumulated this merit, I shall seek the Way of the Buddha."
"If my sincerity is such that my vow shall be fulfilled, let these merchants and the treasures on this ship meet no misfortune, but return safely to their own country.
Having finished making this oath, the merchants went forward and embraced the guide’s hands and feet; weeping and lamenting with deep sorrow, they took their leave and returned to their country.
Having cut their mooring ropes and raised their sails, they returned to Jambudvīpa, all receiving peace and security as they emerged from the great ocean.
At that time, after parting from the multitude, Mahādāna proceeded forward into the water; the water reached his knees, and he traveled for seven days.
Continuing further on, the water gradually deepened until it reached his armpits, and he traveled for another seven days.

Advancing in this manner for seven days, he reached the waist-deep water; for another seven days, he reached the neck-deep water; and for seven more days, he floated on the surface. Upon reaching the edge of a mountain, he grasped a tree with both hands and climbed up by piercing his way through the rock. After seven days had passed, he finally reached the mountain summit.
On that mountain, he traveled level for seven days, then descended the slope for another seven days until he reached the edge of the water.
Within the water were golden lotuses, and there were various venomous snakes whose poison was extremely potent; they all coiled their bodies around the roots of the lotuses.

Upon seeing this, the Bodhisattva immediately sat upright, focused his mind, and gathered his thoughts, entering the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). He reflected that when these venomous snakes were first born, it was because their anger and jealousy were excessively intense that they were born therein and received such evil forms. With the utmost heart of loving-kindness, he felt compassion and pity for them. Once his loving-kindness was perfected, the venom of those snakes was entirely extinguished of its own accord.
Mahādāna immediately arose and proceeded by treading upon the flowers; after another seven days had passed, he was finally able to pass beyond the snakes.
Continuing further on his way, he encountered various rākṣasas who, having smelled the human scent, all came forward seeking him.

Having witnessed this great act of giving, the rākṣasas focused their minds on compassionate contemplation; a spirit of reverence arose within them naturally, and they approached with gentle words to ask:
"Where do you wish to go?"
The Great Giver replied,
"I wish to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel.
The rākṣasa was delighted and thought to himself:
"This person of merit is still far from the Dragon Palace; how can we cause him to undergo such hardship?
I shall escort him past all the treacherous difficulties."
Immediately, he took him away and traveled four hundred yojanas before setting him down upon the ground.
Thereupon, Mahātyāga continued forward on his own and saw a silver city, pure white and radiant; knowing it to be a city of nāgas, he approached it with joy.
He saw that outside the city there were seven layers of moats, all of which were filled with venomous snakes; their poison was so fierce and potent that they were loathsome to behold.

The Great Giver, the Guide, contemplated those venomous snakes; because they had all accumulated intense anger and malice in previous lives, they had received such loathsome forms. He regarded them with compassionate pity as if they were his own infants; once his heart of loving-kindness was fulfilled, the snake venom was entirely eliminated.
He immediately rose and stepped upon it, proceeding toward the Dragon City.
He saw two dragons coiling their bodies around the city wall, with their heads intertwined at the threshold of the gate; seeing Mahātyāgavat, they raised their heads and gazed at him in astonishment.
At that moment, Mahādatta again entered a state of loving-kindness; the dragon’s venom was immediately dispelled, and it lowered its head and did not look up.
Mahādatta then stepped forward, treading upon it and passing by.
Within the city there was a dragon who sat in a palace made of the seven treasures. Seeing the Bodhisattva from afar, he sprang up in alarm and thought to himself:
"Now, outside my city, within the sevenfold moats, there are venomous snakes, other dragons, and yakṣas; none dare to cross them recklessly."
"Who is this person who has been able to come here?

He immediately went forward to meet him, inquired after his well-being, paid homage with reverence, and invited him to take a seat. He seated him upon a bed of the seven precious gems and provided him with various kinds of exquisite delicacies as offerings.
After he had finished eating, they conversed, and [the king] asked him the purpose of his visit. The Bodhisattva replied:

"The people of Jambudvīpa are impoverished and suffer; in their quest for wealth and treasures to provide food and clothing, they commit murder, deception, and all manner of evils. After their lives end, they fall into the three evil realms."

With profound compassion and a desire to rescue and deliver others, I have traveled through perilous distances to see Your Majesty and seek the Cāndana-maṇi jewel to go and provide salvation. By accumulating this merit, I vow to seek the path of Buddhahood.
"If you do not reject or oppose me, I shall simply grant it to you.
The Dragon King replied, "The Cāndamaṇi is a rare treasure; you have traveled through distant and perilous places specifically for this purpose."
"If you can open your mind and stay for one month to receive a small offering, and thereby allow me to preach the Dharma for you,
then, Candramaṇi, you shall be able to obtain it."
The Bodhisattva consented.

Day after day, the Dragon King provided a hundred flavors of food and performed various musical performances to make offerings to the Bodhisattva, while the Bodhisattva, in turn, fully and analytically expounded the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness.
When the month had ended, he took his leave to return.
The Dragon King was filled with joy; he untied the precious jewel from his topknot and presented it as an offering, saying:

"The Great Being’s compassionate heart provides universal succor beyond compare. This resolve of yours is powerful and fierce; you will surely attain the Way of the Buddha. I vow to become your disciple of wisdom."
The Bodhisattva agreed with him and asked,
"Now, what power does this pearl of yours possess?
He immediately replied:
"This jewel can rain down all that is required within two thousand yojanas.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"Although this jewel is excellent, it still does not suffice for my great task of universal salvation."
The dragons, both great and small, escorted him to the gate and repeatedly took their leave with expressions of gratitude.
Thereupon, they departed, and he continued forward until he saw from afar a city made entirely of blue lapis lazuli, its color pure and pristine; he then proceeded toward it.
Outside the city walls, there were likewise seven layers of moats, all of which were filled with venomous snakes.

Having seen this, the Bodhisattva reflected that these snakes had come here because of their anger and jealousy, and thus had received such poisonous forms. He sat upright and entered the state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), contemplating them with the utmost compassion. Once his heart of loving-kindness was fully matured, the poison was entirely eliminated.
He stepped upon them and proceeded toward the city gate.
There he saw two nāgas coiling their bodies around the city wall with their heads joined at the threshold; having seen the Bodhisattva, they raised their heads and glared at him in anger.
The Bodhisattva immediately contemplated a mind of loving-kindness; once his loving-kindness was perfected, the poison was eliminated, and the snake bowed its head as the Bodhisattva stepped over it.
At that time, there was a dragon king within the city who sat in a palace made of the seven treasures. Seeing the Bodhisattva from afar, he rose in alarm and thought to himself:
"I have seven layers of moats filled with serpents outside my city; not even the various dragons or yakṣas are able to cross them."
"Who is this person who has been able to come here?

He immediately descended to welcome him, inquiring after him with reverence and prostrating himself. He invited him to the palace hall to sit upon a throne of the seven precious gems, prepared a variety of hundred-flavored delicacies and sumptuous meals. When the meal was finished, they conversed slowly about the circumstances of his arrival.
The Bodhisattva’s reason for coming in response to the answer was:
"I wish only to beg for the Candra-maṇi.
The Dragon King said:
"The Candra-maṇi is exceedingly difficult to obtain!
If you truly desire to acquire it, I pray that you will accept my invitation to stay here for two months and graciously reveal to me the practices of a bodhisattva."

The Dragon King prepared various kinds of food and drink and performed diverse musical performances as offerings; when the Bodhisattva had fully received them, he explained for him the matters concerning the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
After two months had passed, he was about to take his leave and return home.
The Dragon King then drew forth a precious jewel from within his topknot and presented it as an offering, making this solemn vow:

"Great Being, you have applied yourself with diligence to compassionately rescue all living beings; your mind is vast and expansive, and you will surely attain the Way of the Buddha. I wish to become your disciple endowed with divine power."
The Bodhisattva may say:
"It shall be as you wish.
Then he asks again:
"What is the power of this jewel you have given me?
The dragon replied,
"This jewel can rain down everything one requires for four thousand yojanas."
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"This jewel is indeed superior; though it is exquisite, it does not yet satisfy my wishes.
The dragons, both great and small, escorted him outside the gate, each harboring feelings of longing and regret.
"Then, after parting, they proceeded further and saw a golden city; its color was radiant and exceedingly magnificent, and the Bodhisattva went toward it."
Seeing that outside the city there were likewise seven layers of moats, and that within these moats were filled with venomous snakes, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"These venomous snakes have also received this poisonous form because, in previous lives, their habits of hatred, envy, anger, and malice were so rampant. He sat upright and entered the state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), applying his thoughts with the utmost affection. Once his heart of compassion had reached its full measure, the snake venom was entirely dispelled; he then stepped forward, treading upon them as he passed over.

Upon reaching the city gate, he saw two nāgas coiling their bodies around the walls with their heads joined at the threshold. Having seen the Bodhisattva, they looked up at him in astonishment; the Bodhisattva, according to the Dharma, entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). The poison of the nāgas was thereby dispelled, and they lowered their heads to look down. He then stepped forward upon them and crossed into the city.
At that time, there was also a dragon king within the city who resided in a jeweled palace. Seeing the Bodhisattva from afar, he was struck with amazement and thought to himself:
"Beyond these city walls of mine, there are seven layers of moats filled with venomous snakes; no other dragons or yakṣas are able to cross them."
"Who is this person who has been able to come here?

Thinking this with great wonder, he immediately descended to meet him and inquire, paid his respects with a bow, invited him up to the palace, provided him with a bed of the seven precious gems, and yielded it to him to sit upon. Once he was seated, he prepared various kinds of delicious food for him; when he had finished eating, he slowly asked the purpose of his visit.
The Bodhisattva replied:

"The people of Jambudvīpa are of meager virtue and live in poverty and suffering; they exhaust their bodies and weary their minds, committing murder, killing, and deception for the sake of food and clothing, thereby completing the ten unwholesome paths of action. After their lives end, they fall once again into the three most grievous sufferings. My heart is deeply moved by compassion, and I wish to rescue and deliver them."
"O Dragon King of the Sea, you possess a wish-fulfilling jewel; therefore, I have traveled through these vast and perilous regions solely in hope of obtaining it.
The Dragon King replied, "The wish-fulfilling jewel is a thing difficult to obtain. Since the Great Being has come for this purpose, I shall grant it to you."
"If you wish to obtain [this], please remain for four months and accept my humble offerings, while also receiving my instructions.
The Bodhisattva immediately consented.

The Dragon King was filled with joy; day after day he prepared a hundred flavors of exquisite delicacies, personally serving the sweet foods with his own hands. He also ordered the performance of various kinds of music, while the Bodhisattva constantly analyzed the names, origins, and endings of all phenomena, extensively proclaiming their meanings.

The Dragon King revered him with devotion and listened attentively. Morning and evening he paid his respects without missing the proper time. Regarding whatever was required at any given moment, the dragon himself made the necessary arrangements. When various dragons and yakṣas came wishing to appear before him, he established his own limits for when they might advance or retreat. Having served him for four months, he understood perfectly what was appropriate for the occasion.
When the fourth month had ended, the Bodhisattva took his leave.
At that time, the dragon immediately untied the wish-fulfilling pearl from within her topknot and offered it to him, making this vow:

"Great Being, with your vast vows and compassionate heart, you universally save all beings and do not shrink from toil; you will surely attain Buddhahood and rescue those suffering in the weeds of affliction. I pray that you take me as your attendant and disciple, entrusted with the power of dhāraṇī."
The Bodhisattva consented.
He was asked again:
"As for the pearl you intend to give as a gift, what is its power like?"
The Dragon King replied,
"This jewel can rain down whatever seven treasures are required for eight thousand yojanas.
The Bodhisattva rejoiced and thought to himself:
"The land of Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas in extent; the virtue of this jewel accords with my expectations.
Having obtained three such jewels in all, he fastened them to the corners of his robe and immediately rose to depart the city.
The dragons, both large and small, escorted him outside the city; each harboring feelings of sorrow and longing, they finally took their leave together.
When the Bodhisattva reached the front, he grasped the jewel and made this aspiration:
"If this is truly a *cintāmaṇi*, may my body be able to fly through the void."
Having finished his prayer, he immediately raised his body and was able to fly away, departing beyond the sea.
Once he had crossed the perils of the ocean, he slept for a short while to rest. At that time, there were various dragons within the sea who deliberated among themselves, saying:
"In our seas, there are only these three jewels; their merit is exceedingly great and difficult to match. Yet this man has been able to seek them all out and carry them away."
"It is a pity that this treasure should be taken back; it must be recovered.
Having finished speaking thus, he secretly untied it and took it away.
When the Bodhisattva woke from his sleep and saw that the jewel was not there, he reflected to himself:
"There is no human here; it must be a sea dragon that has taken my treasure.
For the sake of this jewel, I have traversed distant and perilous lands; now that I am about to return to my kingdom, my heart's desire is nearly fulfilled."

"Though you take my pearl, I shall never let it go; I will surely exert all my strength to drain this sea water. With a solemn vow and resolute will, I shall devote my life to this task; if I do not obtain the pearl, I shall never return empty-handed."

Having thus resolved his thought, he went immediately to the seashore and obtained a tortoise shell. Grasping it with both hands, he was just about to bale out the ocean when the Sea God, knowing his intention, came and asked him:
