"The waters of the sea are deep and vast, extending for three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand li. Even if all classes of human beings were to come together to bale them out, they could not diminish them; how much less can you, with your single body, hope to accomplish this?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"If a person possesses a sincere heart and desires to accomplish something, there is nothing that cannot be achieved.
Having obtained this jewel, I shall use it to benefit all living beings; by means of this merit, I shall seek the path to Buddhahood."
"My mind is unwearied; why should I not be able [to succeed]?

At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven saw from afar that the Bodhisattva was single-minded and focused, alone enduring such diligent toil, desiring thereby to provide for, sustain, and bring peace and happiness to all beings.
"How can we not go to assist him?
they said, speaking to one another as they proceeded to his location.

The Bodhisattva set down the vessel, and all the devas took their celestial robes and together covered the water within it. When the Bodhisattva lifted the vessel, the devas raised their robes and cast them aside in another place; with a single stroke of the oar, he drained forty *li* from the sea.
After he had drawn out the water twice, it was reduced by eighty *li*;
after he had drawn it out thrice, it was reduced by one hundred and twenty *li*.
The dragon, terrified and alarmed, came to where he was and spoke, saying:
"Stop, stop!
Do not drain the ocean any further!
The Bodhisattva immediately ceased his efforts.
The dragon came and asked,
"For what purpose do you seek this treasure?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I wish to use it to provide relief and succor for all sentient beings.
The dragon asked again, "According to what you say, there are many sentient beings like us in the ocean; why do you not give it to them, but insist on taking it away?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"The creatures within the ocean are also sentient beings, yet they do not endure such extreme suffering as the people of Jambudvīpa,
who for the sake of wealth and profit commit killing, harm, and deception, performing the ten unwholesome deeds and falling into the three miserable realms upon death."

"Because I am a human being who understands the transformation of the Dharma, I have come to seek these treasures; first I shall satisfy their deficiencies, and afterwards I will exhort them with the ten wholesome deeds."
Upon hearing these words, the dragon brought forth the pearl and returned it to him.
At that time, the Sea God, witnessing the power of his diligent effort and what he had accomplished, made this vow:
"Since you are now thus, practicing diligence without ceasing, you shall surely attain the Way of the Buddha; I vow to become your disciple in diligent practice."
"Once the Bodhisattva obtained the jewel, he flew away once more.
Upon arriving, he first asked his fellow merchants who had entered the sea, and immediately descended to the ground.
When his companions saw him, they were filled with immeasurable joy and surprise, and they all sighed in admiration together, saying:"
"How most marvelous! How most extraordinary! Thinking thus, he proceeded further until he reached the city of Kapila.

Hearing that the Bodhisattva had returned safely from his journey across the ocean, the Brahmin Kapila was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He went out to meet him, inquired after his welfare, and invited his companions as well. He prepared a guest feast, providing various kinds of delicacies and food; when they had finished eating, they conversed regarding the hardships and experiences of their journey.

At that time, the Bodhisattva took his precious jewel and pointed it toward the house; within the Brahmin’s home, all the treasuries became completely full. Those assembled who witnessed this marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

At that time, Kapila adorned his daughter with various kinds of jewels to embellish her body; he personally took a golden jeweled pitcher in his own hand, first washed his hands himself, and then led the girl by the arm and presented her to the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva accepted her.

Kapila was filled with joy; he selected five hundred skilled and talented courtesans and prepared five hundred white elephants adorned with various jewels, making them most extraordinary, to escort his daughter to him.

The Bodhisattva commanded his companions and set out on the road; the people of the city, both great and small, escorted him to the roadside, performing various musical performances as they returned to the kingdom in procession.

"The Great Donor and his parents, having parted from their child, were overcome with grief and confusion; they wept with such excessive sorrow that both their eyes grew dark and blind, leaving them unable to see."

The son returned to his kingdom, paid his respects, and inquired after their welfare. When his parents heard his voice and stroked him with their hands, they realized for certain that the Great Giver had returned to the land. Overwhelmed by alternating waves of grief and joy, they rebuked their son severely:
"You have truly acted without propriety! You abandoned us to enter the sea, causing us such hardship and distress that our fragile lives barely survive."
"What kind of things did you obtain from within the great ocean?
The Bodhisattva took out the jewels and presented them to his parents. His parents took them in their hands and said to themselves:
"In our own treasuries, there are no fewer such stones as these."
"Why must you undergo such hardship to obtain this?

The Bodhisattva took the jewel and pointed it toward his parents' eyes; their vision suddenly became clear and pure, like clouds being swept away by the wind. Having regained their sight, they were filled with joy and, moved by the virtue of this jewel, exclaimed:
"How marvelous!"
"Though you have undergone such hardship, your merit shall not be in vain.
The Bodhisattva again took hold of the jewel and made this aspiration:

"If this is indeed a *cintāmaṇi*, may there spontaneously appear beneath my parents' bodies seven kinds of precious, wondrous, and extraordinary jeweled seats, with a magnificent and pure canopy of the seven treasures above them."
As soon as he had finished speaking, it was accomplished, and everyone rejoiced.
The Bodhisattva again took hold of the jewel and made this aspiration:
"May my parents, the king, his ministers, and the common people—may all their treasuries be filled to overflowing."
He then took the jewel and traveled in all four directions; everything was fulfilled exactly as he had spoken, and everyone was filled with wonder and joy.
He immediately dispatched men riding eight-thousand-li elephants to announce to all the people of Jambudvīpa:

"Mahāsāgarakṣa has returned safely from the sea and obtained a wish-fulfilling jewel. Its virtue is extraordinary; seven days hence, this jewel shall rain down all manner of precious treasures, clothing, and food. Let each person take whatever they require as much as they desire. All must observe the fasts and purify yourselves, storing up provisions in anticipation."

"Once the proclamation had been made throughout the land, the day of the seventh day arrived. The Bodhisattva Mahādāna bathed his body, donned new and clean garments, and went to a level piece of ground. He then took the jewel and placed it atop a high banner; holding an incense burner in his hand, he prayed toward the four quarters:

'The people of Jambudvīpa suffer from poverty and hardship; I wish to provide for them so that they lack nothing. If this is truly a Candra-maṇi, may it then rain down, in due order, all that is required.'"
Once the prayer had been completed, dark clouds gathered from the four quarters, and immediately a wind arose that blew away all impurities, defilements, and refuse, clearing them all away.

Next, a fine rain fell to settle the dust; next, a rain of food and drink fell, exquisite with a hundred flavors; next, a rain of the five grains fell; next, a rain of clothing fell; and next, a rain of the seven treasures and various rare jewels fell, so that the interior of Jambudvīpa was filled to overflowing with all manner of precious things.

The people took whatever they desired at will; exquisite food and clothing were so abundant that they remained in surplus, and they regarded precious jewels as if they were mere shards of pottery or stones.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva observed that the people were well-sustained, he immediately dispatched his ministers and officials to the four quarters to proclaim throughout Jambudvīpa, so that all might hear and know:
"O you, the multitudes of my subjects!..."

First, driven by poverty, they seek clothing, food, and various treasures; they deceive one another, kill for their own benefit with utmost intent, and forget righteousness. Disregarding both sin and merit, at the end of their lives they all fall into the three miserable realms, passing from darkness into darkness, suffering punishment for many kalpas.

We have always felt deep compassion for you, yet had no means to provide relief; therefore, disregarding our own physical suffering, we traversed perilous terrain and entered the sea to obtain this precious jewel, which we now bring to rescue you.

Since you are now free from all lack and deficiency, you should mindfully exert yourselves and diligently cultivate the ten wholesome actions; restrain body, speech, and mind; be compassionate, benevolent, filial, and obedient; be vigorous in governing the mind, and harbor no negligence.

"Using various skillful means, he extensively exhorted them to practice virtue; he then composed written documents and informed all the kings and ministers, disseminating these teachings so that they might all hear and know them, and further urging one another to refrain from committing wrongful acts."
At that time, throughout all of Jambudvīpa, having been moistened by the pervasive grace of his great benevolence, each person pondered how they might repay such supreme virtue.

Furthermore, having received his excellent instructions and being exhorted to cultivate goodness, they all admired righteousness and devoted themselves to practicing kindness and respect. They restrained their bodies, speech, and minds, refraining from any arbitrary transgression or wrongdoing; after their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.
"In this way, Śāriputra!
If you wish to know who that Brahmin father Niṅgūḍha was at that time, he is none other than my own father, King Śuddhodana, now present here."
The mother at that time is now my own mother, Mahāmāyā.
The Great Benefactor of that time is now my own self.
The nāga within the silver city is now Śāriputra.
The nāga in the city of Vaiḍūrya was Maudgalyāyana in this life;
the nāga in the golden city was Ānanda in this life;
and the sea deity at that time was Rāhula in this life.
"When Ānanda was a dragon king, he served me, skillfully knowing the proper timing; even until this day, he naturally knows the time.
If Ānanda wishes to obtain these three vows, I shall comply with his intention."
Upon hearing this, Ānanda was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; rising from his seat, he knelt on his right knee and addressed the Buddha:
"I shall serve as the Buddha’s attendant for as long as I live."

At that time, those present in the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were moved by his great kindness. With single-minded diligence, they contemplated the Four Noble Truths and the essential means of deliverance from all phenomena. Some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat*; some planted the roots of merit for the path of a *pratyekabuddha*; some resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; and some attained the stage of non-retrogression. All rejoiced together, receiving the teaching with reverence and putting it into practice.
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume Eight;
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume Nine.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Yuan Wei Dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.
36. Chapter on the Śuddhāvāsa Devas Inviting the Buddha to Bathe (41). Chapter Thirty-Six: The Śuddhāvāsa Devas Invite the Buddha to Bathe.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven descended to Jambudvīpa and went to where the World-Honored One was. He invited the Buddha and the Sangha to bathe and receive offerings.
The World-Honored One remained silent, thereby granting his consent.

He immediately prepared food and drink, as well as washing implements; he provided warm water in a heated room, adjusted it to be comfortable for the body, and ensured that ghee, oil, and cleansing herbs were all fully available.
Having completed the preparations, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "The meal is ready; may the Holy One know the time.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus accepted his offerings; they all bathed together and partook of the food and drink. That food was sweet and delicious, such as was rarely found in the world.
When the meal was finished and they had rinsed their mouths, each returned to his original seat.
At that time, Ānanda knelt with palms joined and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"What meritorious deeds did this deva perform in the past, such that his form is so exquisite, his majestic appearance so extraordinary, and his radiance so brilliant, like a great mountain of jewels?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively and hold this well!
I shall explain it for you.
In the distant past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, this deva was in that world as the son of a poor family; he constantly performed manual labor to provide for his own body and mouth."

Having heard the Buddha Vipaśyin speak of the merit of bathing the Saṃgha, his heart was filled with joy and he thought to provide an offering. He diligently applied himself to his labors and obtained a small amount of money and grain, which he used to purchase bathing implements as well as food and drink; he then invited the Buddha and the assembly of monks and offered them everything he possessed.
"By virtue of this meritorious conduct, after his life came to an end, he was reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, and thus possesses these radiant signs.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This deva did not only invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha today; during the time of Śikhin Buddha, he also came to this world to make offerings to the World-Honored One and the assembly of monks, and it was likewise so during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This deva has not only made offerings to the seven Buddhas; in the future, during the Bhadrakalpa when the thousand Buddhas appear, she shall likewise wash each of those Buddhas and their Saṅghas, no different from what she does today."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having received this prophecy from the deva, declared:

"In a future age, after the completion of a hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śuddhakāya (Pure Body), fully endowed with the ten titles; the sentient beings you shall transform will be beyond measure."
At that time, Ānanda and the fourfold assembly, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced immeasurably and all spoke these words:
“The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world brings such great benefit; even with such a small gift, one obtains a reward that is far more abundant.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said.”
For the sake of the assembly, he extensively expounded the sublime Dharma.

Among those who heard the Dharma, there were those who attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna), Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), Non-returner (anāgāmin), and Arhat (arhat); others resolved their minds upon the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna). Each was filled with joy, received the teaching with reverence upon the crown of their heads, and practiced it accordingly.

Chapter 37: The Prince Sudhana Enters the Sea (42). Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Prince Sudhana Enters the Sea. In the Danben (Dunhuang) edition, this chapter appears in Volume Nine as the forty-second. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus, preaching the Dharma.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda saw that Devadatta constantly harbored jealousy toward the Tathāgata; by means of various expedients, such as driving a drunken elephant to attack him and pushing down a mountain to crush the Buddha, he sought to cause him harm.
However, the Buddha’s compassionate mind is ever filled with pity and concern; toward Rāhula and Devadatta, he regards them as equals without any distinction.

When the Venerable Ānanda observed this, he harbored resentment within his heart and reflected upon it. Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and sighed while speaking of these matters.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Devadatta has not only brought evil upon me today; he also harmed me in past lives. Nevertheless, I have always maintained thoughts of loving-kindness toward him."
The venerable Ānanda then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not know for certain what occurred in a previous life when Devadatta likewise attempted to cause him harm; at that time, how was it that he felt such compassion?"
"I pray that you will explain this in detail.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, incalculable, immeasurable, inconceivable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Rāṇavaṃśa (in the Jin language, 'Jewel Armor'), who ruled over five hundred minor kings. He had five hundred wives and court ladies, yet none of them had any sons."

The king then offered prayers and sacrifices to the various heavens, the sun and moon, the mountains and seas, and the deities of the trees; yet after years and cycles had passed, he still did not obtain offspring.
The king became deeply distressed and anxious, thinking to himself:
"I now have no son; if I should perish this very day or tomorrow, the kingdom will have no successor, and the world will surely fall into chaos."

Why is this so? Because if these five hundred ministers do not submit to one another, they will inevitably contend by force; the strong will oppress the weak, the innocent will be unjustly killed, and the ruin of the state and the loss of the people will all stem from this.
Having reflected on these matters, his agitation and distress increased all the more.
At that time, there was a deva who, knowing the king’s earnest intent, spoke to him within a dream, saying:

"In the grove outside the city, there are two rishis. Of these, the first rishi has a golden body; his merit, wisdom, and eloquence are such that none can equal them. If you truly require a son, you should go and entreat him; he will surely change his mind and come to be born into your royal house."

The king was immediately startled into realization; his countenance showed a trace of joy as he immediately ordered his carriage prepared. Accompanied by only a few attendants, he traveled everywhere to search for her until he finally found her. He then implored her for mercy, recounting variously how the kingdom lacked an heir and that his grief and anxieties were profound.
"Great Seer, please condescend to be born into my family to succeed to the royal lineage and remove my anxieties and sufferings.
If you do not find this shameful, I only pray that you will deign to look upon me with favor."
At that time, seeing the king’s earnestness, the seer could not bear to refuse him and immediately consented.
The second seer then spoke again to the king, saying:
"I, too, shall go to be born into the royal family."
The king was greatly delighted and took his leave to return to the palace.
After some time had passed, the golden-hued seer reached the end of his life.
The king’s chief queen, named Soma, then perceived that she was pregnant.
An intelligent woman, being able to attain this wisdom and knowing what she carries in her womb, distinguishes between male and female, and then says to herself:
"What I carry in my womb will certainly be a boy."
When the king and those within the palace heard these words, they were filled with immeasurable joy.

The king commanded the palace ladies and court attendants to serve him together, seeking to please his every wish; he provided him with bedding and food that were exceedingly fine and soft, and attended to his movements with care, ensuring he never encountered any peril.

When the ten months were complete, the chief queen gave birth to a son who was exceptionally handsome and extraordinary; his body was the color of purple gold, his hair was deep blue-black, and he was endowed with all the marks of a great man. Both the king and those within and without gazed upon him without ever being satiated.
He summoned a physiognomist and ordered him to examine the child's features.
The physiognomist arrived immediately and, having observed his appearance from head to toe, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness as he addressed the king:
"The auspicious marks of this child are rare among men; his intelligence and merit are unsurpassed."
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly pleased and again addressed the physiognomist, saying, "You may now establish a name for him.
The physiognomist asked the king,
"Since the time this crown prince first entered the womb, what extraordinary signs have occurred?"

The King replied: "This mother of the Prince was envious and malicious from the time she conceived; she delighted in the faults of others and falsely accused them of wickedness. Seeing the goodness of others, her heart felt no joy.

Since her pregnancy, her character has changed completely: she has become compassionate and benevolent, taking pity on the ignorant and loving the wise; she delights in practicing charity and bestows gifts with an impartial mind to protect and nurture all."
Upon hearing this, the physiognomist praised him, saying:
"Excellent! This is the child's resolve; he has entrusted his aspirations to his mother."
He then established a name for him, calling him Kalyāṇakārī, which in the Jin language means "One of Good Deeds.

As for the second wife, named Pṛthā, the second seer likewise passed away and was reborn within her womb. When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose physical form and features were no different from those of the other.
He summoned the physiognomists again to examine the prince's features.
Upon inspecting him, the physiognomists said to him:
"This crown prince is merely an ordinary man; his merit, fortune, wisdom, and capability are sufficient for him to manage his own affairs."
The king commanded him again to establish a name for him.
The physiognomist spoke once more:
"What extraordinary signs are there?"
The King said to the physiognomist:
"This mother of the crown prince is by nature loyal and virtuous; she is compassionate and submissive toward others, delighting in proclaiming the goodness of men.
Yet, since she became pregnant, she has instead come to delight in evil, becoming envious of the worthy and capable, and taking no pleasure in seeing what is good."
The physiognomist spoke again:
"This too is the child's own intent; it was entrusted to his mother, and thus it has come to be so.
Thereupon, he established a name for him: Pāpaka, which in the Jin language means "Evil Deeds."

At that time, the king focused his heart on loving and cherishing Kālaṇāgari; never failing in his intention, he immediately issued an edict to have three seasonal palaces built for him: a warm palace for the winter, a central palace for spring and autumn, and a cool palace for the summer, where musical performances were provided to entertain him.

As the Prince gradually grew up, he became exceptionally intelligent and eloquent; he studied the various worldly classics and the eighteen divisions of the scriptures, reciting and retaining them with complete fluency, and was well-versed in their underlying principles.

Later, when he took his leave to go on a journey, the King immediately granted him permission and ordered the roads and streets to be repaired and all impurities removed. He mounted a great white elephant adorned with gold and silver, escorted by thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of horsemen leading and following him. As he traveled through the streets and thoroughfares, all the people lined both sides of the road, and countless spectators atop the various pavilions and towers all said of the Prince:
"He resembles Brahmā; his majestic marks and physical appearance are rare among men."

At that time, the Prince saw the beggars, their bodies emaciated and their clothing tattered and torn; with a broken vessel in their left hands and a splintered staff in their right, they spoke in humble tones and sought pity, begging for food from others.
The Crown Prince asked,
"Why is it so? The ministers replied:

"Such people as these may have no parents; they are orphaned, destitute, and solitary, with nothing upon which to rely. Afflicted by chronic illness or madness, they are unable to perform labor and possess not a single coin in savings; it is the pressing needs of their very bodies and mouths that drive them to such actions."
The Prince, moved by compassion, felt a deep and increasing sorrow in his heart.
Continuing further on his way, he saw several butchers slaughtering livestock, cutting them into pieces and weighing them for sale.
The Prince asked, "Why have you done this?
and they each replied immediately:
"I need not take pleasure in this; it has been our family occupation since my grandfather's time. If I were to abandon this work, I would have no means to support myself.
Upon hearing these words, the Prince sighed deeply and departed.

Turning back, he went to the fields and saw several farmers tilling the soil; as they worked, insects emerged from the earth and were picked up and swallowed by frogs. He further saw a snake that was swallowing the frogs, when a peacock flew down and pecked at and ate the snake.
The Prince asked the people,
"What is this being done? The plowmen replied:
"This is my work: I sow the seeds within it, and later I shall obtain grain to provide for my own food and to pay to the royal house.
The Prince sighed and said, "It is because of food and drink that people slaughter living beings and exhaust their bodies and strength to such bitter toil."

Proceeding further on, he saw several hunters rushing toward a flock of birds, drawing their bows and intending to shoot them; he also saw nets spread out upon the ground, in which various birds and beasts had fallen, shrieking and struggling in terror, unable to escape.
The Crown Prince asked,
"What are you all doing? and they all replied:
“Capture various birds and beasts to provide for our own sustenance.
Upon hearing this, the Prince sighed deeply and departed.

Arriving at the edge of a river and pond, he saw a fisherman spreading his net to catch fish; they lay scattered upon the ground, leaping, struggling, and stretching their bodies, with countless dead among them.
The Prince questioned them again, and they each replied,
"We rely on these fish to provide for our food and clothing.
The Prince heaved a long sigh, feeling compassion for all living beings.
"For the sake of food and clothing, one should indeed act in this way, killing sentient beings to provide for body and mouth;
yet as calamities and sins increase daily, what will the retribution be in the future?"
He then returned to the palace, filled with anxiety and finding no joy; he went to his father, the king, and said:
"I pray you, grant me one wish.
The king replied to him:
"Grant you whatever you desire; I shall not oppose you.
The Prince addressed the King, saying:

"While traveling abroad for sightseeing, I observed those various classes of beings who, for the sake of food and clothing, deceive and kill one another, thereby accumulating sins day by day. My heart is deeply moved with compassion, and I wish to provide for and relieve them."
"I pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission to draw from the royal treasury to give as I wish, so as to satisfy the needs of those among the people who lack anything.
The King’s affection for his crown prince redoubled upon hearing these words; unable to go against his son's intent, he immediately granted his request.
Thereupon, the Crown Prince immediately issued a proclamation to the people, saying:

"The Crown Prince Kalyāṇakāri is bestowing gifts upon those who are destitute and in need; let everyone come and take what they require. If there are those who desire gold, silver, precious objects, clothing, food, drink, or anything else they may need, it shall be given to them."
He immediately opened the royal treasury, brought out various precious objects, placed them at the city gates and in the marketplace, and provided everything to all people according to their needs.

At that time, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas from various countries, along with the poor, the orphaned, the elderly, the infirm, and the sick, arrived one after another, supporting the weak and the strong. To those who needed clothing, he gave clothing; to those who needed food, he gave food; and as for gold, silver, and precious objects, he gave them as they desired.

At that time, the people spoke to one another in succession until the news spread throughout Jambudvīpa; they all assembled together and, using the king’s treasury, divided it into three parts and took two for themselves.
At that time, the minister in charge of the treasury entered and addressed the king, saying:

"Great King, you preside over five hundred minor kingdoms; envoys from these various states will surely come and go, and for their affairs they shall require precious objects to be sent back as gifts."
The Crown Prince’s acts of giving have drawn from the royal inner treasury, consuming two-thirds of its contents.
Your Majesty should reflect upon this and ensure that no cause for regret arises later.
When the king heard these words, he said to his ministers:

"This crown prince delights in giving; his resolve is so fierce and intense that it cannot be turned back. If we were to restrain him and thwart his intent, causing him distress and sorrow, what would become of us?"
"Let him dispose of his will as he pleases; none shall oppose or obstruct him.
After this had been done several times, the Prince practiced giving, and of the remaining treasures in his storehouse, two-thirds were expended.
The minister spoke again to the king:

"Regarding the remaining items from the previous [donation], which were distributed as alms day after day, two-thirds have already been spent. Only a small residue remains; it should await the arrival of the messenger's gift and must not be exhausted."
"I pray that Your Majesty will reflect deeply on this, so that you may not later incur blame.
The king then reflected and said to his ministers:

"I love this son more than any other; I cannot bear to openly oppose his wishes. If he comes to demand the treasure, I shall avoid him slightly as he approaches; but if he demands it urgently, I shall simply grant it to him."
"Sometimes we may obtain them and sometimes not; this can be used to delay the matter for days and months.

At that time, having received the King's instructions, whenever the Prince came later to request treasures, the minister would make excuses and travel elsewhere. Thus, at times he obtained what was requested and at times he did not, unable to provide everything according to his requirements.
The Crown Prince perceived this and thought to himself:
"What power does this minister of the treasury possess that he dares to disobey and neglect me, failing to carry out my commands?"
"It must be because of the King's intention that this has come to pass.
Furthermore, according to the etiquette of a son, one should not exhaust the treasury of one's parents until it is empty.
Now, with so little remaining in this storehouse, how can I obtain wealth and treasures to provide for all beings so that none lack anything?"
Having had this thought, he immediately asked the people:
"In this world today, what occupation can one pursue to acquire great wealth to use as one pleases?"
One person said:
"By braving great hardships and traveling far to trade, one can acquire much wealth.
Another person said:
"By tilling the fields and avoiding neither cold nor heat, and by sowing the five grains extensively, one may acquire great wealth.
Another person said:
"By raising many domestic animals, caring for them according to the seasons, and allowing them to multiply in their proper time, one may acquire great wealth."
One person said:

"Only by disregarding one's own life can one enter the great ocean and reach the palace of the Dragon King to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel; once this task is accomplished, one will obtain the greatest amount of wealth."
At that time, having heard the words of the multitude, the Prince thought to himself:
"Engaging in trade, farming, or raising livestock is not suitable for me; the profits gained are but meager."
"Only by entering the great ocean and going to the palace of the Naga King will my heart's desire be fulfilled; I shall diligently seek this matter.
Having formed this thought, he went to inform his royal father:
"I wish to enter the sea to seek precious jewels, which I shall bestow upon all sentient beings so that they may use them without end."
“I only pray that my father and mother will grant me your permission.
When the king and queen heard the prince’s words, they were filled with deep anxiety and distress, and asked the prince:
“What is your intention that you wish to enter the sea?”
If you truly wish to practice giving and fulfill your original aspiration, I shall give you all that remains within my household treasury for you to use in your acts of charity.
Why do you abandon yourself, saying you wish to go out to sea?

Furthermore, I have heard that within the ocean there are many extreme perils: black winds, rākṣasas, surging waves and eddies, the great makara fish, and mountains of colored water. Among such manifold dangers, those who emerge safe and sound are few; though a hundred companions may set out together, only one returns at any given time.
"Why are you in such haste to cast yourself into danger?
Both I and your mother are filled with the utmost anxiety, and all the kings, ministers, and subjects harbor a burning fear."
"Renounce this thought and do not cause further turmoil.

Thereupon, the Prince, hearing these words from the King, set his mind upon the great enterprise and resolved to bring about deliverance. Although the King detained and obstructed him, his resolve remained unshakable; he intended to offer up his very life to accomplish the task. He prostrated himself upon the ground, striking his belly against the King’s feet, and addressed the King, saying:
"I pray only that you will show me compassion!"
"I shall thus fulfill my original intention.
If you must refuse and will not grant me permission, I shall prostrate myself upon this ground and never rise again.

When the King, the Queen, and everyone inside and outside the palace saw that the Prince’s resolve was irreversible and that he had sworn to die rather than move, they all together attempted to console him, pleading with him to get up.
His words remained as they were at first, and his resolve did not waver, continuing from the first day through the second, and so on until the sixth day.
The King and the Queen Consort consulted with one another, saying:
"The Prince has not eaten for six days already; when the seventh day dawns, his life will surely not be sustained."
Whatever this child intends to do from beginning to end must necessarily be accomplished; it cannot be turned back.
If he were allowed to enter the sea, there would still be a possibility of his return;
but now, if we go against his will, we shall utterly sever his hope.
"You should simply listen to this and set aside your worries for now.
After the King and his consort had reached an agreement, they both came forward together, each grasping one of his hands, their tears flowing freely as they spoke to him:
"We grant you permission to enter the sea; please rise and return to eat."
At that time, having heard the King’s words, the Prince rose with joy and exhorted his parents:
"Though I enter the sea, I shall return before long; I only pray that you do not worry about me too greatly."
Having prepared various kinds of delicacies and food and drink, he went outside and issued a proclamation far and wide:
"Kalyāṇakārī now wishes to go to sea; who among you wishes to go?"
"Let us proceed together.
At that time, five hundred merchants gathered from within the kingdom, all declaring their desire to depart.

There was a blind guide in the kingdom who had previously traveled to the sea many times; when the Prince heard of him, he went immediately to his side and addressed him with earnest and gracious words, seeking his understanding:
"You should enter the great ocean with me and show me what is beneficial or harmful, what should be pursued or avoided.
The guide replied, "I am already old and blind, seeing nothing; though I wish to go myself, it is extremely difficult for my private circumstances."
The King loves the Crown Prince with a devotion that exceeds the ordinary; should he be separated from his sight for even a moment, he would feel deep anxiety and longing.
Now, hearing that you have been given to me to enter the great ocean together, if he should again refuse, the blame will not fall lightly upon me.
At that time, having heard these words, the Prince immediately returned to the palace and addressed his father, the King:
"In this kingdom, there is a blind guide who has previously traveled back and forth many times and reached the great ocean. I pray that Your Majesty will command him to accompany me."
Upon hearing these words, the king went to him in person and said to the guide:

"This crown prince of mine is determined to enter the sea. Though I have exhorted him with various counsels, his resolve remains firm and he will not turn back. Having no other recourse, I now grant him permission to depart."

Considering that you are young and have not yet grown weary of hardship, and knowing from your previous journey that you understand the ways of the sea, I hope you will change your mind and endure the toil to go with me.
At that time, the guide, having heard these words from the king, immediately addressed him, saying:
"I regret that I am advanced in years and blind, seeing nothing; yet how would I dare disobey the command of the Great King?"
Upon receiving these words, the king immediately returned to his palace.
At that time, the crown prince, together with the guide, deliberated and fixed the date for their departure.
Upon returning to the king's presence, the king asked his attendants:
"Whoever loves and honors me may go with the Crown Prince to gather treasures.
Pāpāgāli immediately addressed the King, saying,
"I wish to accompany my elder brother and together cross the great ocean."
Upon hearing these words, the king thought to himself:
"If my younger brother goes with me now into this perilous and distressing place, he might be able to save us where others could not."
Having formed this thought, he was permitted to depart.

At that time, the Prince took out three thousand taels of gold: one thousand taels were used to provide provisions, one thousand taels to procure a ship, and another one thousand taels for all other necessities.
When the preparations were completed, he was about to depart.
The king, the queen, and all the princes, ministers, and subjects followed him weeping, bidding him farewell by the wayside.
Thereupon, the Prince, together with his companions, proceeded on his way.

Upon reaching the seashore, he had his ship securely constructed with seven layers. Waiting for the proper season of the wind, he pushed it into the water and moored it to the shore with seven great cables. Shaking a bell, he proclaimed to the multitude, saying:
"Listen all of you!

Within the ocean there are many perils: surging waves and eddying currents, malevolent nāgas and rākṣasas, black winds that swirl overhead, mountains of sea-hues, and the great makara fish; such other dangers as these are still numerous.
"Those who have previously entered the sea and returned safely are few.
If you harbor doubts, you may return here.

Who among you can resolve their will, sacrifice their very lives, disregard their parents, and have no longing for wife or children? Such as these shall enter the sea together to reach the place of treasures. If we obtain precious jewels and return in safety, our descendants for seven generations shall never exhaust their use of them."

Having given these instructions, he then cut one rope. He did this every day for seven days. Once the proclamation was finished and the seventh rope had been severed, they raised the sails against the wind; the ship sped like an arrow and went straight with the others to that island of jewels.

The Crown Prince was intelligent and wise, thoroughly versed in the secular classics, and possessed the discernment to recognize the characteristics of precious gems and know their values. He demonstrated to the multitude the superior and inferior qualities of the various treasures and commanded the merchants to take whatever they desired.

He again addressed the merchants, instructing them to take a moderate amount: "If you take too much, the boat will be overloaded with the danger of sinking; if you take too little, the journey will be arduous and the hardship will not be compensated."
Having finished his exhortation, he took the guide alone in a separate small boat, parting from the merchants and proceeding further.
The guide asked, "There should be a white mountain ahead; do you see it?"
The prince replied,
"I see them.
The guide said:
"This is the Silver Mountain.
As they proceeded further, the guide asked again:
"There shall be a mountain of deep blue color; have you seen it yet?"
The prince replied,
"I have already seen it.
The guide said to him:
"This is a mountain of dark-blue lapis lazuli.
As they proceeded further forward, he asked the Prince again:
"There ought to be a yellow mountain here; have you seen it yet?"
The Prince replied,
"I see them.
The guide said to him:
"This is the Golden Mountain.
Upon reaching the foot of the Golden Mountain, he sat upon the golden sand, and the guide said:

"I am now so weak and frail that my life will surely not be sustained. Having shown you the directions and the path for your advance and retreat, you should depart from here; ahead there shall be a city, a most wondrous one, interspersed with the seven treasures."
When you reach the city gate, if the gate is closed, there will be a vajra near it; you should then take the vajra and strike the gate with it.

Within the city, there shall be five hundred celestial maidens, each carrying a precious jewel, who will come to offer them to you. Furthermore, there is one maiden who is most exceptionally noble and eminent; the precious jewel she carries is deep blue in color and is named Candra-maṇi.
This wish-fulfilling jewel, once obtained, should be firmly held so as not to lose it; as for other things given, they may also be accepted.
Guard your sense faculties and do not engage in further conversation.
I am now at the very end; my remaining life is but a little while. After my death, if you should remember my kindness and feel sorrow for me, please bury me in this sand.
When the guide had finished speaking, his breath ceased and he passed away.
[The travelers] were overcome with grief and sorrow in his presence; they buried him and then proceeded forward as he had instructed.

Upon reaching the city of seven treasures, the city gates were firmly closed; seeing a vajra at the side of the gate, he took it as instructed and struck the gate with it, whereupon the city gates opened.
Five hundred celestial maidens each held a precious jewel and came to offer them to the Prince.
The foremost maiden held a jewel in her hand that was as deep blue as the color of sapphire; he took it up in succession, wrapped it in the corner of his robe, and then turned back.
After the former prince had departed, Pāpaka again said to the multitude:
"Traveling back and forth is no easy matter; you should simply take as much as possible.
Greedy for the jewels, the people took them in excess.

When the Crown Prince returned, his boat was already full; as he released it to come back, the boat immediately sank. The merchants were now sinking and now floating, but because the Crown Prince possessed the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), his body did not drown.
Pāpāgiri called out from afar to the Prince, saying, "Please rescue me; do not abandon me!
Hearing these words, the Prince immediately pulled him along to float together; through their strenuous mutual efforts, they were able to emerge from the sea.
After they had set sail, the younger brother said to his elder brother:
"We brothers have left our parents to enter the great ocean, hoping to return home without our hopes being in vain."
"Since our fortunes have not aligned and we have lost our wealth and treasures, it would be most shameful to arrive here alone and empty-handed.
Kālaṇāgari, being by nature loyal and upright, immediately said to his younger brother:
"I have indeed obtained the treasure."
The younger brother said to his elder brother,
"Please show me what you have.
He immediately untied his garment and showed him the pearl.

When the younger brother saw the pearl, he harbored resentment, thinking: "I have long felt that my father the King’s benevolence was not impartial, as he showed partial favor toward my elder brother; I did not mind this before.
Now, though we two came together to enter the sea, my brother has obtained extraordinary treasures while I alone return empty-handed."
From this point forward, they will treat me with contempt; what shall I do?

Taking advantage of his sleep, I shall secretly kill my elder brother, take his jewels, and return to tell our father the king that my brother has perished at sea; in this way, he will surely regard me with exceptional affection.
Having formed this thought, he secretly devised a plan and said to his elder brother:
"The human village is drawing near; we brothers should not both sleep together. It would be better for one of us to remain seated and guard the precious jewel."
The elder brother immediately agreed, and they took turns guarding him constantly.
It was Pāpāgāli’s turn to rest; he lay on the ground for a long time, exceeding his usual duration by far, before finally rising.
The elder brother lay down again; because he had sat for so long, he fell into a deep sleep.

Pāpaka arose and entered the forest. In the forest there was a tree with extremely sharp thorns; he immediately took two of them, each fifteen inches long, and brought them to his brother’s side. His brother slept very heavily; [Pāpaka] grasped a thorn with one hand and thrust it into the socket of his eye, piercing it through until the thorn was buried. He then gathered the treasure and departed.
In intense agony, the Prince cried out in a loud, urgent voice: "Pāpaka! Pāpaka!"
"There is a thief here.
He called out several times, but there was no response.
At that moment, the tree deity spoke to the prince, saying:
"Upacāru is your thief; having gouged out your eyes, he has taken your jewels and fled.
Thereupon, the Prince, writhing in agony, crawled forward on his hands and knees, gradually advancing until he reached the kingdom of Rājagṛha.

Upon reaching the marshy ravine, he encountered five hundred oxen approaching him. There was a bull king who, seeing the Prince, felt both pity and reverence; he extended his tongue and licked him, while the remaining oxen all gathered around, standing in awe as they gazed upon him together.

At that time, a cowherd came forward to investigate and beheld the Prince lying upon the ground; seeing that there was such a long thorn in his eye, and observing his physical features, he knew him to be no ordinary man. He immediately extracted the thorn, took him to his dwelling, and constantly applied ghee and milk to the wound, providing him with food and drink, attending to him with constant care.
After several more days had passed, the eye abscess gradually healed; the host continued to serve him without ever becoming negligent or weary.
At that time, the Prince asked the cowherd, "While you reside here, what means of livelihood do you have?"
The cowherd replied, "I have no estate here;
I rely solely on milk and curds, selling them to support myself.
The Prince thought to himself:
"I have troubled you, my host, by suffering through this affliction while you constantly provided for me.
Now that my wound has healed and I am able to walk about a little, I shall seek out another, more suitable location."
Having reflected on these matters, he said to his host:
"Throughout this period of time, you have exerted yourself for my sake; I am deeply grateful to you, my host, and your kindness is difficult to repay."
"I wish to go forward into the city to wander from house to house begging for alms so that I may support myself.

When the cowherd Śāla heard the prince's words, he feared that his wife, children, or servants within the house might have uttered some further words of weariness that reached the prince's ears; "If it were not so," he thought, "for what reason would he have taken his leave?"
Having had this thought, he first asked those within the house:
"What is it that you all find so unsatisfactory that you would cause these honored guests to take their leave and wish to depart?"
The members of the household all said, "We have been like brothers to one another here; we do not know for what reason you wish to abandon us and depart?
Then the head of the household spoke to the prince, saying:
"I have served you with such devotion that I have never failed to meet your expectations; you must not abandon me to go begging elsewhere.
At that time, the Prince heard the householder’s words and, seeing his earnestness, constantly respected his intent and paused for a short while.
After several more periods of time had passed, he said to his host:
"You have attended to me with hospitality, providing for my every need without lack; all within your household have treated me with great generosity."
"But in my own mind, I wish to travel on ahead to the city; I hope you will send someone to take me along.
At that time, seeing his earnestness and fearing that by refusing him he would become sorrowful, the cowherd personally escorted him and went together with him into the city.
Having reached that city, they were about to part ways and return;
the Prince said to him, "If you have pity for me, buy a lute for me so that I may amuse myself."
Then the cowherd immediately gave him the rope in exchange for the price, and after they had mutually expressed their thanks, they parted ways.

At that time, the Prince was naturally possessed of many skills; his songs, verses, and literary compositions were exceedingly clever and refined. He then sang with a resonant voice upon the crossroads, accompanied by the lute, his tone being exceptionally pure and elegant. All the people in the city who heard his voice delighted in listening and watching, never tiring of it; each brought food and drink, vying with one another to give them to him.
At that time, there were five hundred beggars in the city who all came to depend upon him, relying on him for their full meals.
King Līśavaskanda had a park keeper who served as the king’s guardian over an orchard of mangoes.
There were ripe mangoes, which a parrot came to eat; as his physical strength was insufficient, he could not be startled away or stopped.

At that time, the garden superintendent carried some mangoes to the king; among them were fine mangoes that the parrot had pecked at and ruined. When the king saw this, he became enraged and intended to inflict punishment.
The park superintendent was terrified and addressed the king, confessing:
"It was only because our household lacked manpower that this occurred; I pray only for your clemency and pardon regarding the punishment. We shall seek guards and ensure it does not happen again."
The king then pardoned him and did not question him regarding his crime.
Having escaped, the park superintendent went out to search for someone; seeing Kālaṇāgāri sitting by the roadside, he observed his appearance and, finding him to be a loyal man, spoke to him, saying:
"Can you keep watch over my garden for me?"
"If you are able to do so, I shall provide for whatever you lack.
The Prince replied, "My eyes cannot see; how can I guard it?"
The park keeper said:

"If you truly wish to watch them, even though you have no eyes, you must employ a skillful means. Make many fine ropes and tie them to the tops of the trees, connecting them all together with small bells so that they are linked in succession. You should grasp one end;
if you hear a sound, pull the rope taut, and the parrot, being terrified, will have no way to remain."
Upon hearing these words, the Prince replied,
"If such a thing is possible, I am able to do it.
After they had reached an agreement, he immediately went there to serve as a guard.
At that time, Pāpāgāri arrived at his father the king’s realm. The king, marveling that he had come alone, immediately asked for news.
Pāpāgāri spoke to the king, saying: "We were ill-fated;
our ship became heavily laden and sank. Kalyāṇakāri, along with all the merchants and all the precious treasures, have perished entirely in the great ocean."
"I exerted all my strength to swim and managed to reach safety.

Upon hearing these words, the king and his consort fainted for a long time; they were unconscious and unaware of their surroundings until water was sprinkled on their faces, whereupon they finally regained consciousness.
Among the various princes, ministers, and subjects, both inside and outside the palace precincts, there was none who did not mourn upon hearing this news.
The King and the Queen said to Pāpākāli:
"Prince Kāli has perished at sea; why have you come?"
"Why not die together with him in the great ocean?
The people of the entire land were all filled with grief and regret; morning and evening they wailed and longed for him, as if they had lost their own parents.
While the Crown Prince was in the palace, he was always fond of a wild goose. The King said to the goose:
"The Prince raised you; now he has entered the great ocean and suddenly vanished without returning. Why do you not go to see him and learn where he is?"
Thereupon, he wrote a message and tied it to the crane's neck.

The crane immediately soared high and traveled far in search, arriving above that garden. Recognizing the sound of the singing, it descended to investigate and beheld the Prince; its cries were a mixture of grief and joy, beyond its own control.

Upon hearing this and recognizing the voice, the Prince immediately took the letter; however, his eyes being sightless, he was unable to read it. He therefore requested paper and a brush to write a reply to the King, detailing the circumstances of how Pāpaka had gouged out his eyes, as well as the bitter and painful events he had experienced along his journey.
A tether was fastened around the goose's neck, and the goose immediately flew away.
"At that time, King Līśavatsa had a daughter who was exceptionally beautiful and rare in the world; the king cherished her deeply and never went against her wishes."
At that time, the woman took leave of the king and went out to stroll through the gardens; the king granted her permission to go.

Upon arriving in the garden, she saw the crown prince Kalyāṇakāri, his hair disheveled and his face soiled, his eyes sightless, wearing tattered and ruined garments, sitting amidst the trees of the grove.
The girl observed him, and seeing his appearance and demeanor, her heart was drawn toward him; she did not leave his side, but sat beside him and conversed with him.
When the time for the meal had arrived, the king sent someone to summon her; the woman, in turn, sent someone back to inform the king, saying:
"I pray that you send the food here, for I wish to eat it right here."
The food was then brought out, and the woman said to the prince,
"I wish to sit and eat together with you.
The prince replied:
"I am a beggar, and you are the daughter of a king; how can we eat together?
If the King were to hear of this, my punishment would not be small.
The girl spoke earnestly to the Prince, saying:
"If you are unwilling, I shall not eat.
Thus he repeated this several times, pressing her incessantly until they finally ate together.
Their conversation became sincere and earnest; their hearts gradually drew closer, and her eyes never left him.
As the sun was turning toward dusk, the king sent a messenger to summon his daughter. The daughter, in turn, sent someone back to inform the king, saying:
"I wish only to be the wife of this gardener; I do not desire any other prince among the kings. Now my mind is focused and my devotion is as earnest as this."
"I only pray, O Father King,
that you do not go against my wish.
The messenger went to the king's presence and related the matter in full detail.
Having heard this, the king could not suppress his feelings and said to himself:
"This is a calamitous omen; this daughter is unworthy.
Even so, the Great King Ratnavarman has come to seek her for his eldest son, Kalyāṇakāri."
"Now that this prince has entered the sea and not yet returned, you wish to take a wife for this beggar; this brings great dishonor upon our family name.
Where shall I hide my face and conceal myself?"
Having spoken these words, he again sent a messenger to summon her;
the woman spoke as she had before, her resolve unshakable.

At that time, the king cherished her so much that he could not go against her will, so he took her along with him and placed her within the palace, immediately ordering them to unite and become husband and wife.
After several more days had passed, the wife would always leave during the day and only return at night. The husband, finding this strange, questioned her:
"You say you are my wife, yet you leave in the morning and return at dusk; your heart is not here with me. Is it because you have set your affections elsewhere that you act in this way?"
The wife then made a vow:
"I now pledge my heart to serve you together with complete devotion; I have no other intent, not even as much as a hair or a speck of dust.
If this be truly so, and my sincerity be not false, may your one eye be restored to its former state, whole and perfect."
Once he had finished speaking these vows, his eye immediately returned to its former state.
He asked the Prince again:
"In what country do your parents reside?"
The Prince said to his wife,
"Have you heard the name of the Great King Leṇyavatī?
She replied:
"I have heard it. "He was my father.
Have you also heard of that prince, Kalyāṇakāri?"
He replied, "I have heard of it. [The Buddha said,] "It was my very self."
The wife was immediately startled and asked,
"Why are you again enduring such hardship?
The Prince then explained the beginning and end of the matter to her.
Upon hearing these words, the wife sighed deeply and said to the prince:
"Pāpaka harbors malice toward you; from antiquity until now, there has never been such a thing."
"If you were to capture him, how would you deal with him?
He replied,
"Although Pāpaka has harmed me, I harbor no resentment toward him whatsoever."
The wife spoke again, saying, "This matter is difficult to believe; you have tormented me so much, how could you not be angry?
Kāliṅgagiri then made this vow to himself:
"If I harbor not even a hair’s breadth of resentment toward Pāpaka, and my words are sincere and not false, may this one eye be restored to its former state."
Having finished this self-vow, his eyes became completely clear and bright.
When the wife saw her husband, his two eyes were restored and pure; his upright and majestic appearance was such as she had never beheld before.
Overjoyed beyond measure, she went to inform her father: "Does Father the King know Prince Ratnavarman Kalyāṇakāri?"
The king replied,
"I recognize her.
The woman then said:
"Do you wish to see him now?
The king said,
"Where is he now?"
The woman said,
"My husband is that very man.
The king laughed at her and said:

"This woman is deluded and insane; her mind is disordered and she has lost her senses. Because Kāliṅgagiri has entered the sea and not yet returned, she sees this blind beggar and mistakes him for him."
The woman spoke again, saying, "I pray that Your Majesty will go and look.

The king immediately went to see; upon confirming it was indeed the prince, his hair stood on end with horror, and shame and fear intertwined within him. He struck his chest before him and addressed this repentance:
"Truly we were unaware of this; we pray you will forgive our transgression.
They then secretly returned the Prince to the border and proclaimed aloud:
"Great King!"
"The Crown Prince Kalyāṇakāri has returned from the great ocean.

Having made the necessary preparations and adorned elephants and horses, he personally went with his ministers to welcome him. Upon returning to the kingdom, he hosted a grand assembly of guests and elaborately adorned his daughter, intending to offer her in marriage to him.

"At that time, the goose returned and carried the letter to the kingdom. When the Great King saw the goose, he opened and read it; only then did he receive news and learn that the crown prince was still alive, gaining full knowledge of all the bitter hardships he had endured."

The king and his consort were alternately sorrowful and joyful; throughout the inner and outer palace, there was no one who did not mourn, lament, and feel resentment and indignation. They seized Pāpāgāli, bound his body with shackles and manacles, and cast him into prison.
An imperial edict was issued to King Līśavara, commanding him:
"The Crown Prince is undergoing hardships in your kingdom; why do you remain silent and fail to come forward to represent him?
When this letter arrives, you must escort him back with elephants and horses. Should there be any violation of these instructions, I shall come in person."
The messenger then took the letter and traveled directly to that kingdom.
King Līśavatsa received it respectfully and read it; thereupon, the prince said to King Līśavatsa, "The cowherd has been kind to me.
I am now thinking of him and wish to see him; you may dispatch a messenger to summon him on my behalf."
The king summoned him at once.

The prince said to the king, "My eye was pierced, and I relied entirely upon this man to provide for me and nourish me as my own parents. If Your Majesty has any regard for me, you should grant him a reward in my stead."

The king was greatly delighted and immediately bestowed upon him famous garments and superior robes, elephants, horses, and carriages, gardens, fields, and houses, gold, silver, and precious objects, as well as male and female slaves and servants, along with the oxen under his charge; he gave them all to him.
The man was filled with joy, exceeding all his expectations; he immediately attained peace and happiness, and became wealthy and noble for the rest of his life.
He then returned to report to the messenger, explaining the circumstances:
"The Prince is here; I truly did not know of this. Regarding his various hardships and sufferings, I humbly imagine you are already fully informed of the details."

The Crown Prince has now regained his sight; we have betrothed our humble daughter to be the Prince’s wife, prepared all the necessary ornaments and provisions, and shall personally escort her to him.

He then issued orders to prepare five hundred white elephants, adorned with gold and silver until they were most exquisite; he selected five hundred men to serve as attendants for the Prince, and further commanded that five hundred handmaidens be chosen—those of the utmost beauty and skill—who were then decorated with various precious objects.
Five hundred chariots, adorned with precious treasures and made exceedingly magnificent, were sent to escort his daughter.

King Liśāvara himself, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of ministers and chariots, also attended the procession; surrounded before and behind by musicians and singers offering hymns of praise, they celebrated boundlessly as they traveled the road back to their kingdom.
At that time, the messenger went to the Great King’s presence, opened and read the letter, and with great joy and exultation, announced to the subordinate kings:
"All of you must assemble here."

He immediately prepared his elephants and horses, with the ministers and officials, the queen, and the court ladies leading and following in procession before and behind, personally going out to welcome the Prince as far as the border pass.

At that time, the Prince saw his father, the King, from afar; he descended from his carriage and approached on foot, prostrating himself with his head at the ground to pay homage and inquire after his parents' well-being.
The parents also descended, and they embraced one another; having longed for their son during their separation, they were moved simultaneously by sorrow and joy upon seeing him.
When the kings, ministers, and subjects saw this, their feelings of joy and gratitude were beyond description.

Having finished their brief conversation, they immediately returned to their carriages; bells were struck and drums beaten as various musical performances were played. Amidst great joy and cries of "Excellent!", the procession led the way back toward the city.
Upon arriving outside the city gate,
the Prince asked the King, "Where is Pāpaka now?
The King replied to him:
"Such an evil person as this is not fit for the world to shelter; I cannot bear to see him, so I have already brought him here to be confined within prison.
The Prince said to the King:
"He should now be released and sent back."
The king replied to him, saying, "His offense is profound and grave;
before it has even been investigated, how could he possibly be released?
The prince spoke again:
"If you do not release Pāpaka, I shall never enter the city.
The King immediately issued an order for his release, telling him to come out.
Having been freed, he came to see the Prince.
The Crown Prince took him in his arms and comforted his mind; only then did he enter the city and proceed to the palace.

At that time, the parents, the various kings, ministers, and citizens—men and women, old and young—all beheld the Crown Prince as they would look upon an enemy, yet they regarded him as they would their own infant. Although Pāpaka had gouged out his eyes, the Prince harbored not even a hair’s breadth of resentment; instead, his reverence, love, and compassionate sympathy increased manifold beyond what they had felt before.
The entire assembly together praised him, exclaiming that it was most extraordinary!
Truly, there is no one to compare with him among gods or men.
When the Prince arrived at the palace, his intimate and affectionate feelings toward Pāpaka were as loving and kind as before; he calmly asked him where the pearl was now located.
Pāpāgāli replied to the prince,
"When we came, we buried it in the earth by the side of the road.
He ordered him to go back and retrieve it, but though they searched for it, they could not find it.
The Crown Prince went with him; upon arrival, he saw it and took the precious jewels, returning together to the palace.
He gave five hundred precious jewels to the various kings, instructing each to take one, while keeping the remaining wish-fulfilling jewel for himself.
Grasping the jewel in his hand, he immediately made this aspiration:

"If this is truly a wish-fulfilling jewel, let there appear for my parents where they sit thrones made of the seven treasures, and above their heads let there be great canopies made of the seven treasures."
As soon as he had finished speaking, it was accomplished exactly as he had said.
He then took hold of the jewel and made this aspiration:
"May all the treasuries within my parents' palace, as well as all the treasuries belonging to the kings and ministers, which were previously exhausted by acts of giving, be restored to fullness."
Immediately, he took hold of the pearl and traveled in all four directions; all the treasuries were then completely refilled.
He further commanded his ministers to proclaim throughout the various kingdoms:
"Seven days from now, Prince Kālaṇāgari shall cause a rain of the seven treasures."
Immediately, he issued the proclamation, which was heard and known by all.

At that time, the Prince bathed in fragrant water, erected a great banner, placed a jewel upon his head, donned fresh and clean garments, and holding a censer in his hand, prostrated toward the four directions and spoke these words himself:
"If this is indeed a wish-fulfilling jewel, then let it rain down everything that is required."

When his prayer was completed, clouds and mists arose from the four quarters, and a wind immediately blew forth, sweeping away the filth and all other impurities, so that they were entirely removed of their own accord.
Next, rain falls to cover the dust and soil.

Then, rain falls as food and drink of a hundred flavors and various delicacies; next, it rains the five grains; then, it rains clothing; and finally, it rains the seven treasures, which fill the world beneath heaven.
At that time, the people rejoiced immeasurably; they regarded all precious treasures as if they were mere shards of pottery or stones.
Then the Prince issued a proclamation far and wide:

"Now that you have obtained everything necessary for your sustenance and lack for nothing, if you can recognize such kindness, you should restrain your body, speech, and mind to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action."

At that time, throughout all of Jambudvīpa, people were moved by the Prince’s boundless generosity. Upon hearing his command, they exerted their minds to practice the ten wholesome deeds and refrain from all evils; after their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who the Prince Kalyāṇakāri was at that time, it is my own self here now.
At that time, my father, King Renabhadra, is the present King Śuddhodana, my father."
The mother at that time is now my mother, Mahāmāyā.
King Liśavardhana was Mahākāśyapa.
The wife at that time is now Gopī.
At that time, Pāpāgāli was none other than Devadatta.
Those people of Jambudvīpa who have received my grace are such as the eighty thousand devas and my disciples who were granted the prediction of enlightenment when I first attained the Way.
Ānanda! At that time, although I was harmed by him and suffered to the utmost degree, I still regarded him with compassion and affection.

How much more so now, when I have attained the Way of Buddhahood, my afflictions are entirely eliminated, and my kindness and compassion are widely diffused; if I am slightly harmed by him, would I not surely feel pity and compassion?

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, those assembled there, having heard what the Buddha taught, were moved to reflect upon the World-Honored One; for the sake of all living beings, he had endured extreme hardships without ever withdrawing or desisting. They marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, their hearts filled with a mingling of sorrow and joy, as they disciplined their minds and resolved their wills to contemplate the wondrous Dharma.

There were those who attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat; those who planted the roots of goodness for Pratyekabuddhahood; and those who resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment—all of whom paid him reverent homage and joyfully practiced his teachings.
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume Nine (43). Chapter Forty-Eight: The Story of Mahānāman. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Kapilavastu at the Nyagrodha Monastery.

When the Buddha first returned to his kingdom, the Śākyas beheld the Buddha’s majestic deportment; his marks and signs were extraordinary, his body was golden in color, and he possessed the thirty-two major characteristics. Gazing upon him, they could never tire of doing so. Gathering together in groups throughout the streets, lanes, markets, and villages, they praised the Tathāgata with one voice: "Among this assembly, there is no peer; he is truly worthy of veneration!"
When the bhikṣus had heard this discourse, they all together addressed the Buddha, recounting the words of praise and eulogy uttered by those people.
At that time, the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
"You should know that in the past, I was the most honored and most sublime among this assembly, not only today."
Then the bhikṣus each addressed the Buddha:
“We do not understand, World-Honored One!
What were the circumstances regarding that which was most honored and most sublime among this assembly in a past life?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively! Listen attentively!
Keep this well in your hearts; I shall fully explain for you the events of past lives.”
He replied,
"Indeed, I wish most earnestly to hear it.
The Buddha then spoke for him:

"In the past, immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Lingnu. That king ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kings, ten thousand ministers, five hundred princes, and a total of twenty thousand queens and court ladies."

The chief queen, named Devavatī, was in her final pregnancy when she gave birth to a crown prince. The child was handsome, with a body the color of purple-gold and hair of deep blue-black. On the palms of both his hands were the marks of thousand-spoked wheels; on the sole of his left foot was the mark of a horse, and on the sole of his right foot was the mark of a white elephant.
That son possessed such merit that he was a most extraordinary and honored being among men; thus, following his parents' wishes, they gave him the name Devadatta.

As he grew up on milk and was raised to adulthood, King Devadatta suddenly contracted a seasonal illness. His life was drawing to a close, and the minor kings, ministers, and crown princes all came to inquire after his health.
He then asked the Great King,
"Should he eventually pass away, which of the kings' sons should succeed him?
At that time, the king replied:
"If among my sons there is one who can be fully endowed with ten virtues, he shall be established as king.
What are these ten virtues?
First, his body is of purple-gold color, and his hair is deep blue-black."
Second, the palms of both hands bear the mark of the golden wheel, complete and without deficiency.
Third, the sole of his right foot bears the mark of the white elephant.
Fourth, beneath his left foot, there is the form of a horse.
Fifth, he put on the royal garments, which were well-suited to his body, being neither too large nor too small.
Sixth, as he sat upon the royal throne, his majestic virtue was towering and sublime, and his sitting was peaceful and secure.

Seventh, the kings and their ministers rejoiced and paid him homage, praising him boundlessly; upon entering the inner palace, the queens and court ladies leaped for joy and prostrated themselves with reverence.
Eighth, if he goes to a celestial shrine, he bows in reverence to all clay and wooden images of the gods.
Ninth, through the power of his merit and majesty, he can cause the seven treasures to rain down, providing for all as they desire.
Tenth, as for his mother, he was born of Queen Devavatī.
If one is endowed with these ten merits, then he shall be established and appointed as the Great King.
Having finished his instructions, impermanence arrived and he passed away.
Among the kings, ministers, and subjects, the eldest of his five hundred sons, together with ten others, examined the features of his body.

These princes did not possess golden complexions, nor did their hair have a deep blue-black hue; their palms lacked the mark of the wheel, and the soles of their feet were devoid of the signs of elephants and horses.
They wore royal garments that were ill-suited to them;
when they sat upon the imperial throne, the wooden lions there leaped up in alarm and stood erect, as if wishing to seize and bite them.
The kings, ministers, and subjects all failed to pay him respect;
when he was about to enter the palace, the ladies and court attendants were all displeased and showed no reverence;
even when he entered a temple, he would personally prostrate before the deity image, yet he would not pay homage to any other images made of clay or wood.
He commanded that it rain jewels, yet this too he could not do;
furthermore, he was not even born of Queen Devavatī.
Thus, among the five hundred great princes, he lacked even a single one of the ten qualities.

The youngest son was of a purple-gold complexion, with hair as deep blue-black as sapphire; his two hands were observed to be fully endowed with the mark of the wheel, and the soles of his feet were seen to display the signs of the elephant and the horse, as vividly clear as if painted.
He wore royal robes that were perfectly suited to his body;
seated upon the imperial throne, his merit and virtue were most majestic.
Among the kings, ministers, and subjects, there were none who did not pay him respectful homage;
when he entered the inner palace, the ladies and court maidservants respectfully attended to him and performed their salutations;
as he was about to reach the celestial shrine, even the clay and wooden images of the gods all rose to pay him homage.
He instructed him to cause rain-jewels to fall; at the mere utterance of the words, they fell.
When asked, "By whom were they produced?
he replied, "They were produced by Queen Devavatī."
When he was fully endowed with these ten qualities, the kings, ministers, and subjects immediately prostrated themselves and enthroned him as king.
On the fifteenth day, at the moment the sun first rose, the precious golden wheel appeared from the east; the wheel had a thousand spokes and measured one yojana in length and breadth.
The king immediately descended from his seat, knelt with his right knee touching the ground, and said:
"If I possess the merit to be a king, may the wheel proclaim my name."
Immediately, as he had said, he came before the palace and stood in mid-air.

As for the precious white elephant, it came from Mount Gandhamādana; its hair and tail were threaded with pearls. When the king mounted it, the elephant could fly, traveling throughout the four continents from morning until noon. If it were to walk on foot, the ground touched by its feet would instantly turn into gold sand.
