As for the precious dark-blue horse, its body is a deep azure color; its mane and tail are entirely the color of pearls, and they rain down the seven treasures.
If the king mounts it, he can travel across the four continents in the time it takes to eat a single meal, without becoming weary or fatigued.

As for the divine jewel, it arrives spontaneously; its radiance constantly illuminates one hundred and twenty *li* day and night, and within it, it can further rain down the seven treasures to provide for all as required.
As for the Jewel of the Woman, she arrives spontaneously; she is upright and exceptionally beautiful, perfectly suited to the King's wishes.
As for the Minister of the Treasury, whenever the King requires the seven treasures, he provides them in full according to his desire, never failing or becoming exhausted.

As for his minister in charge of the military, whenever the king requires the fourfold army, within the mere blink of an eye, all the troops assemble; their battle arrays are strictly orderly, and their prowess is extraordinary.
Once the seven treasures were complete, he sat and reflected to himself:

"That I enjoy this position is entirely due to the meritorious karma sown in previous lives; it is for this reason that I have attained it. Now I must ensure its succession so that it does not come to an end."
He immediately bathed his body with fragrant water, donned fresh and clean garments, and holding a censer in his hand, faced the eastern direction, knelt, and said:
"Noble beings of the East, come and accept my invitation."
Immediately, twenty thousand pratyekabuddhas came to the royal palace;
having been invited from the south, west, and north as well, sixty thousand pratyekabuddhas then arrived to accept the king’s invitation.

The king and his ministers provided them with offerings of the four requisites; after these eighty-four thousand minor kings had been away from home for a long time, they addressed the great king, wishing to take their leave and return to their own countries, and the king granted their request.
He then addressed the King, saying:

"The number of noble beings here is exceedingly great; I pray that Your Majesty will show compassion and reduce [the offerings] slightly, granting a small portion for me to provide as an offering, so that we may share in this merit together in the future."

At that time, the Great King immediately provided the Pratyekabuddhas from the four directions with offerings appropriate to the occasion, together with the minor kings, for eighty-four thousand years.
"All the kings, ministers, and subjects, after their lives ended, were reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who was the King Let-servant at that time, it is my father, King Śuddhodana, who is he now."
The lady Devavatī at that time is now my mother, Mahāmāyā.
The king Dāsaka whom Deva commanded at that time is my present self.
Those five hundred princes at that time are these five hundred Śākyas here today.
At that time, I was the most honored and sublime among all people;
now that I have attained Buddhahood, fully endowed with all the marks, I am the most wondrous and extraordinary among this assembly.

At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat; some planted the causal conditions for Pratyekabuddhahood; and some gave rise to the bodhicitta and became non-retrogressive. The gathered multitude rejoiced and, receiving it upon their heads, practiced it accordingly.
(44) Chapter Forty-nine: On the Conditions for Seeking the Auspicious and the Inauspicious. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, although Devadatta had renounced the world, his mind was obscured by gain and honor; he committed three of the heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma): he pushed down a mountain to crush the Buddha, injuring the Buddha’s toes; he further released a black elephant, intending to harm the Buddha; he caused a schism in the Sangha into two factions; and he killed a bhikṣuṇī who had attained the exhaustion of outflows (kṣīṇāsrava).
Because he had killed living beings, he was filled with doubt and fear regarding his retribution in future lives.
At that time, there were six teachers; he went to them and questioned them, and the six teachers immediately expounded various heterodox views for him, saying:
"Committing evil incurs no sin, and performing good brings no merit. To give rise to a mind of faith and reverence is to destroy and sever one's roots of goodness."
At that time, Ānanda, his body trembling with deep affection and his grief profound, choked with sobs and filled with distress, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Devadatta is foolish!
"He has committed unwholesome deeds, destroyed his roots of goodness, and brought disgrace upon the sons of the Śākya clan.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"Devadatta did not only destroy his roots of goodness for the sake of gain and offerings in this present life; in past lives as well, he lost his body and forfeited his life out of greed for gain and offerings."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding Devadatta, how did he lose his life out of greed for profit in a past existence? What were those events?"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen well; I shall speak!"
In the past, immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a caravan leader named Mahānāman; his wife became pregnant, and she was naturally benevolent and virtuous, with a gentle and mild disposition.

When the moon was full, a son was born with a handsome and well-proportioned form. His parents cherished him dearly and prepared exquisite delicacies. They invited their relatives as well as various physiognomists to enjoy themselves together; they took the child in their arms to show him to the assembly and conferred a name upon him.
The physiognomist asked,
"Since this child was conceived, what auspicious signs have occurred?
His father replied:
"From the moment of conception, the wife was naturally compassionate, harmonious, and kind.
The physiognomist then gave him a name, calling him Śubhavyūha (Good Seeking).
As he grew up on milk and nourishment, he delighted in accumulating various virtues and felt compassion for all sentient beings.
Thereafter, she conceived, but her condition naturally became wretched; when the term was fulfilled, she gave birth to a boy whose physical form was hideous.
She immediately invited a physiognomist to bestow a name upon him.
The physiognomist asked,
"Regarding this child conceived in her womb, what auspicious signs or responses have occurred?
She replied:
"Since she conceived this child, her disposition has been wicked and evil.
At that time, the physiognomist immediately gave her a name, calling her Akṣamālā (Evil-Seeker).
As she grew up on milk and nourishment, she delighted in committing evil deeds; she constantly harbored greedy thoughts and maintained a mind of jealousy.

“As we have all grown to adulthood, we wish to travel together as merchants into the sea to seek precious treasures. Each of us has five hundred attendants, and we set out with them in front and behind.
The road is vast and remote; midway, our provisions ran short, and after seven days had passed, we were not far from death.”

At that time, Shanqiu and all the merchants, with sincere hearts, offered prayers to the various deities, desiring to alleviate the famine; then, in the midst of the empty wilderness, they saw from afar a tree with lush and flourishing branches and leaves, and they immediately headed toward it.
There was a spring of water, and Shanqiu and the multitude all joined together with sincere hearts, seeking compassionate protection.
Their sincerity moved the divine response, and [the deity] manifested its form and spoke to them:
"Cut off one branch, and what you require shall emerge."
The people were filled with joy; they then cut off one branch, and a delicious drink flowed forth.
When they cut off the second branch, various kinds of food emerged, complete with a hundred flavors. They all received it together, and each was fully satiated.
When he cut the third branch, various exquisite garments emerged, complete in every variety.
When he cut the fourth branch, all manner of precious objects appeared, fully provided and perfectly adorned; everything required was entirely prepared.
Pāpabhikṣu arrived later, and as before, the multitude all obtained their fill. He then thought to himself:
"If these branches of this tree can produce such various excellent things, how much more so its roots?"
"Now we shall cut it down; we will surely obtain things of the utmost excellence and beauty.
Having thus resolved with a firm mind, he ordered men to cut it down.
At that time, Kalyāṇabhadrika, hearing these words, was filled with resentment and distress, and spoke to Pāpabhadrika:
"We are famished and our lives hang by a thread; it is by the grace of this tree that we have been able to preserve our remaining lives.
Why, then, do you harbor such a wicked and evil intent as to wish to cut it down?"
At that time, Evil Seeker did not heed his words and immediately dug up the roots.
Good Seeker was deeply moved and could not bear to see it; he led his followers back home.
Once the felling of the trees was completed, five hundred rākṣasas seized this wicked seeker and the merchants, devouring them all; their wealth, goods, and companions were entirely lost.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"He who was the seeker at that time is my very self today.
He who was the father at that time is my current father, King Śuddhodana."
The mother at that time was none other than my present mother, Mahāmāyā.
The one who was wicked and greedy then is now Devadatta. Ānanda!
Devadatta has not only committed unwholesome deeds today; for the sake of gain and offerings, he has constantly created them throughout every lifetime.
In the past, I was always encountered by him, and though I constantly taught him the wholesome Dharma, he did not employ it, but instead treated me as an enemy.

At that time, Ānanda and the fourfold assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were filled with a mingling of sorrow and joy; they all exhorted themselves to diligence and reverently accepted and practiced it.
*Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Northern Wei Dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.
38. Chapter Thirty-Eight: Ānanda’s Dhāraṇī (45). Chapter Thirty-Eight: Ānanda’s Dhāraṇī; in the Dan edition, this is Chapter Forty-Three.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt.
“Worthy Ānanda, what practices did you perform in the past to obtain this dhāraṇī, such that upon hearing what the Buddha has spoken, you do not lose a single word?
They all went together to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
“Worthy Ānanda, what merit did you originally cultivate to attain such immeasurable dhāraṇīs?”
“May the World-Honored One please grant us an exposition!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively and fix your minds!
This *dhāraṇī* is entirely due to the power of merit.

In the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a bhikṣu who kept a śrāmaṇera. He constantly issued strict commands, instructing him to recite the sūtras. He set a daily course of study; if the student completed the required portion of the sūtra, the bhikṣu would rejoice, but if he fell short, he would reprimand him with harsh severity."

Thereupon, the śrāmaṇera was constantly filled with distress; though he had mastered the recitation of the sūtras, he lacked the means for food. If he went out to beg for alms and obtained food quickly, his recitation would be sufficient; but if he returned late from begging, his recitation would be incomplete. Fearing that if the recitation were insufficient he would be rebuked, he walked about weeping, his heart burdened with sorrow and vexation.
At that time, there was an elder who, seeing him weeping, approached and called out, asking:
"Why are you so distressed?
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"Householder, you should know!

My teacher is stern and difficult to please; he commands me to recite the scriptures with a daily quota. If I fulfill it, he is pleased; if I fail to complete it, he reprimands me with harsh severity."

When I go out to beg for alms, if I obtain food quickly, my recitation of the sutras is sufficient; however, if I beg and receive it late, my recitation falls short, and if I fail to obtain any sutras at all, I am subjected to reprimand.
"It is for this reason that I am sorrowful.
At that time, the elder said to the śrāmaṇera, "From now on, you shall come to my house regularly;
I will provide you with food and drink so that you have no cause for worry. After eating, apply yourself single-mindedly and diligently to reciting the sūtras."

At that time, having heard these words, the śrāmaṇera immediately attained single-minded focus and applied himself diligently to his recitation and study; he did not fall short of his assigned quota, completing his daily lessons every day. Consequently, both teacher and disciple were filled with mutual joy.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The teacher at that time was Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
The śrāmaṇera at that time was my own self in this present life."
The great elder who provided the food at that time was none other than Ānanda.
Because he performed such deeds in the past, he has now attained dhāraṇī and is free from any forgetfulness or loss.
At that time, having heard this teaching, the bhikṣus rejoiced, accepted it with faith, and respectfully put it into practice.
39. Chapter on the Brother Killed by Upasī (46). Chapter Thirty-Nine: The Brother Killed by Upasī. (In the Danben edition, this is the forty-fourth chapter. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there were two merchant brothers living together in one place.
The elder brother sought the daughter of a wealthy man to be his wife; however, the girl was young and not yet of marriageable age.
At that time, her elder brother went with a group of merchants far away to another country; after many years had passed, he remained there and did not return in due time.
As the girl grew up and reached a marriageable age, she said to her younger brother:
"Your elder brother has traveled afar and has not returned despite his efforts; you should now take me as your wife."
The younger brother replied,
"How could such a thing be?
As long as my elder brother is alive, I dare not disobey him."
At that time, the elder brother spoke repeatedly, yet his younger brother’s resolve remained firm and he never wavered.

The elder brother, not ceasing his efforts, forged a letter from afar and entrusted it to various merchants, stating that the elder brother had died. Upon hearing of his brother's death, the younger brother was struck with utter astonishment.
The elder went back again and said to him, "Your brother has already died; what will you do with your daughter?
If you do not take her, you must consider another plan."
Urged by this pressing necessity, the younger brother married his sister; after some time had passed, she became pregnant.
Subsequently, the elder brother returned from another country.
At that time, when his younger brother heard that his elder brother had returned to the kingdom, he was filled with shame and fear and fled to Śrāvastī.
After he had departed, his relatives and friends pressed his wife's belly and caused her to have a miscarriage.
Thus, passing from one to another, they arrived before the Buddha; overcome by a sense of shame and remorse, they sought to leave the household life.
Knowing they were ready for deliverance, the Buddha immediately granted his permission.

Having received the Buddha’s permission, he immediately became a śramaṇa named Upasīva. He upheld the disciplinary precepts with diligent and tireless effort, and in due time attained the path of arhatship; his six supernormal powers were pure and penetrating, and he was fully endowed with all forms of wisdom.

When the elder brother arrived home, he saw that his younger brother had already married the woman; filled with jealousy and inner rage, he went in pursuit intending to kill him. Upon searching and questioning others, they were told that the younger brother had gone to Śrāvastī.
With a mind poisoned by anger and affliction, he immediately issued a heavy reward, proclaiming:
"Whoever can obtain my younger brother's head shall be granted a reward of five hundred taels of gold.
At that time, there was a man who came forward to respond to this call.
"I can go and take his head.
The elder brother immediately produced gold to recruit such a man; they set out together and reached Śrāvastī.
Upon arriving there, he saw his younger brother sitting in meditation and contemplation. At that moment, the man was suddenly moved by a heart of loving-kindness and thought to himself:
"How shall I kill this bhikṣu?
If I do not kill him, he will take my gold.
Drawing his bow, he intended to shoot; as he drew it toward the bhikṣu, when he released the arrow, it instead struck his elder brother.

His elder brother, harboring resentment and dying in a state of bitter anguish, subsequently took rebirth in the form of a venomous serpent. He was born within the pivot of that practitioner’s door; his poisonous intent unabated, he plotted to harm him.
As he opened and closed the door, the snake struck his body and killed him.

After his death, he was unable to reform his conduct; instead, he vowed to become a small venomous insect and dwell within the room of that practitioner. While the practitioner sat in meditation, the insect descended from the rafters, alighted upon the crown of his head, and with its fierce and virulent poison, immediately killed the bhikṣu.
At that time, Śāriputra, having witnessed this event, went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"By what prior conditions did that deceased bhikṣu now attain the Way and yet die from poison?"
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to reveal it to me.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Listen well and bear it in mind!
I shall explain this to you in full detail.
In the past, countless eons ago, there was a Pratyekabuddha who appeared in the world; dwelling in the mountain forests, he cultivated his aspirations."
At that time, there was a hunter who constantly captured birds and beasts; he devised various stratagems, watching and waiting in hopes of catching them.

On this occasion, the Pratyekabuddha startled the birds and beasts, causing the hunter to fail in his pursuit. Thereupon, the hunter harbored malice, becoming vexed and filled with resentment, and immediately shot the Pratyekabuddha with a poisoned arrow.

At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, feeling compassion for this man and wishing to cause him to repent and reform, manifested his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), namely: flying through the air, extending and contracting his limbs, appearing and disappearing at will, and various other transformations of supernormal power.

At that time, having witnessed these events, the hunter felt deep reverence and admiration; overcome with fear and self-reproach, he returned in sincerity to apologize for his transgressions, seeking mercy and repentance.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted his repentance; once the repentance was completed, he died from the poison.

When that man’s life ended, he fell into hell. Having emerged from hell, for five hundred lifetimes he was constantly killed by poison. Even until today, though he has attained the path of an Arhat, he is still bitten to death by poisonous insects whenever they see him.
Having given rise to an evil thought, he immediately repented and made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, encounter a holy teacher and attain supernormal powers just like those of the present."
"Therefore, having now encountered me, you have received and attained the Way and its Dharma.
At that time, Śāriputra and the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter 40: The Son Who Accidentally Killed His Father (47). Chapter Forty: The Son Who Accidentally Killed His Father. According to the Dan-ben, this is Chapter 45. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was an old man who had lost his wife early in life and lived alone with his son; being destitute of wealth and realizing that the world is impermanent, he conceived the desire to leave the household life and immediately went to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek entry into the Path.
At that time, the Buddha, out of compassion, immediately granted him permission to leave the household life.

Thereupon his father became a bhikṣu, and since the son was young, he became a śrāmaṇera. He constantly accompanied his father into the village to beg for food, returning to their dwelling in the evening.
At that time, there was a village that was most remote; having gone there to beg for alms, he intended to return by dusk.

His father was old and his gait was slow; the son, fearing wild beasts, hurriedly supported his father, pushing him forward along the path. Because he did not hold him firmly, he pushed his father until he fell to the ground, and at that very moment, his father died from the blow of his hand.
After his father had died, he went alone to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the bhikṣus asked the śrāmaṇera, "This morning you went with your teacher to the village for alms; where is he now?"
The śrāmaṇera replied:

"Just now I went with my teacher to that place to beg for alms. When we returned at dusk, the teacher walked somewhat slowly; I was terrified at the time and therefore pushed him in haste. My hand was so forceful in the push that I knocked my teacher to the ground, and he died right there on the road."
At that time, the bhikṣus rebuked the śrāmaṇera:
"You are a most wicked man!
You have killed your father and killed your teacher!"
He immediately reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha told him:
"Although this teacher has died, he did not do so with an evil intention."
He then asked the śrāmaṇera,
"Did you kill your teacher?
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"I truly pushed him; it was not with an evil intent that I killed my father.
The Buddha approved of his words, saying, "It is so, śrāmaṇera!"
"I know that your mind harbors no ill intent.
In past lives as well, it was just the same; you had no ill intent, yet you killed one another.
When the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s words, they immediately addressed the Buddha together:
“I do not understand, World-Honored One!
During a past life, what karmic conditions existed between this man and his father that led them to kill one another?
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall now explain it to you.
In the past, during immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there lived a father and son together in one place."

At that time, his father’s illness was extreme; he lay in bed asleep when many gadflies and flies came repeatedly to disturb him. The father then ordered his son to drive away the flies, hoping to obtain peaceful sleep so as to relieve his exhaustion.

At that time, the boy hurriedly tried to ward it off, but the fly continued to come back again and again; as it did not stop returning, the boy became enraged and, seizing a large staff, waited for the fly to strike and kill it.
At that time, various flies and gnats vied with one another to land on his father’s forehead; he struck them with a staff and thereby killed his father.
At that moment, it was not out of any malicious intent.
"Monks, you should know!
He who was the father at that time is this very śrāmaṇera.
He who was the son who struck his father on the forehead with a staff is now that deceased monk."
Because at that time he had no evil intent when he struck his father with a staff and killed him, it was not done with malice; now, as he returns the favor, it is likewise not a deliberate killing.
At that time, the śrāmaṇera gradually practiced and studied with diligent and tireless effort, and eventually attained arhatship.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, all the bhikṣus believed and understood it in their hearts; they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter 41: Sudatta Erects a Monastery (48). Chapter Forty-one: Sudatta Erects a Monastery. [In the Danben edition, this is Chapter 46. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove.

At that time, King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī had a high minister named Sudatta. His household was immensely wealthy, possessing boundless treasures and riches; he delighted in practicing generosity, providing relief to the poor, the destitute, the orphaned, and the elderly. Because of his conduct, people of the time gave him the title "Givaka," meaning "The Provider for the Lonely."
At that time, the elder fathered seven sons; when they had each grown up, he arranged their marriages in succession until the sixth.

As for the seventh son, who was exceptionally handsome and distinguished, the father cherished him with particular affection. When it came time to find a wife for him, he desired a girl of exquisite beauty, perfect countenance, and auspicious marks, and sought one for his son.
He then spoke to the brahmins, saying, "Who has a daughter of excellent appearance and endowed with all auspicious marks? You should go and seek one for my son.
The brahmins then set out to search for her, traveling from place to place in search of alms until they reached the city of Rājagṛha.
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a great minister named Ghoṣila, whose wealth was immeasurable and who had faith and reverence for the Triple Gem.
At that time, a brahmin went to his house and begged from him.
According to the laws of the kingdom, when giving alms to others, young maidens were required to personally carry the offerings.

At that time, the householder Pūrṇa had a daughter whose dignified appearance was upright and whose complexion was exceptionally beautiful; she immediately took food out and gave it as alms to a brāhmaṇa.
When the brahmin saw her, his heart was filled with great joy:
"The one I have been seeking, I see her today!
He then asked the girl:
"Has anyone come to ask for you? He replied, "No."
He asked, "Young woman!
Is your father at home?"
The girl replied,
"I am here. The brāhmaṇa said:
"Tell him to come outside; I wish to see him and converse with him.
Then the daughter went inside and said to her father, "There is a beggar outside who wishes to see you."
The father then went outside.
At that time, the brahmin inquired after his well-being, asking:
"Do you know the chief minister of King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī, whose name is Sudatta?"
He replied, "I have not seen him; I have only heard his name.
He [the other] said:
"Do you know?
That man is the foremost in wealth and status in that city of Śrāvastī, and you are the foremost in wealth and status here.
Sudatta has a son who is exceptionally handsome, marvelous, and endowed with many extraordinary qualities; he wishes to seek your daughter as a wife—is this acceptable to you?"
He replied, "So be it.
It happened that there was a merchant intending to go to Śrāvastī; at that time, the brāhmaṇa wrote a letter and sent it with him to Sudatta, detailing the matter in full.
Sudatta was filled with joy; he went to the king to request leave so that he might marry a wife for his son.
The king granted his request immediately.

He loaded a great quantity of precious treasures and set out for Rājagṛha. Along the way, he relieved the poor and destitute. Upon arriving at Rājagṛha, he went to the house of Ghoṣila to seek a wife for his son.

The householder Ghoṣila welcomed him with joy and reverence, provided him with bedding and seating, and had him stay overnight at his home; the household bustled about as they prepared food and drink.
Sudatta thought to himself:
"This elder has prepared such a vast array of offerings; what does he intend to do?
Is he perhaps inviting the king, the crown prince, ministers, elders, householders, and his marriage-related kin to hold a great assembly?"
Reflecting on the reason for this, yet unable to understand it, he asked him:

"Householder, why is it that at this late hour you have personally taken up such labor, attending to affairs and preparing these offerings? Is it because you wish to invite the King’s crown prince or a great minister?"
He replied, “No.
[The other asked,] “Are you planning a marriage or a gathering of relatives?”
He replied, “No.
[The Buddha asked: “What then will you do?”
He replied, "I invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
At that moment, upon hearing the names of the Buddha and the Saṅgha, Sudatta’s hair stood on end as if he had attained something; his heart and mind were filled with joy, and he asked again:
"What is meant by 'Buddha'?
I pray that you will explain its meaning.
The elder replied:
“Have you not heard?

The prince of King Śuddhodana, named Siddhārtha, on the day of his birth, thirty-two auspicious omens descended from heaven; ten thousand deities attended him, and he immediately took seven steps, raising his hand and saying:
‘In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored.’”
His body was golden in color, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; as a Wheel-Turning King, he ruled over the four continents.

Having witnessed the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, he took no pleasure in the household life, renounced his home to practice the Way, and after six years of asceticism, attained all-knowledge (sarvajñā), exhausted all fetters, and became a Buddha.

Having subdued eighteen hundred million hosts of Māras, he is titled "The Capable One" (Nengren). Possessing the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities, his radiance shines brilliantly and his threefold penetration gazes afar; therefore, he is called a Buddha.
Sudatta asked, "What is meant by 'Saṃgha'?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:

"After the Buddha had attained enlightenment, Brahmā entreated him to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma. He went to the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī and, for the sake of the five men including Kauṇḍinya, turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths. Their outflows were exhausted and their fetters untied; they immediately became śramaṇas, endowed with the six supernormal powers, and fully trained in the four foundations of mindfulness, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path. In the sky above, eighty thousand devas attained the stage of srotāpanna, and immeasurable devas and humans resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
Next, he converted the thousand brothers of the Kāśyapa clan, including Uruvilvākāśyapa; their outflows were exhausted and their minds were liberated, just as those five had been.
In succession, he converted the followers of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, numbering five hundred, who likewise attained arhatship.

"Those such as these possess mastery over the supernormal powers (ṛddhi) and can act as a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) for the benefit and protection of sentient beings; therefore, they are called the Saṃgha.
Having heard of such wondrous matters, Sudatta leaped for joy with great exultation. Moved by deep faith and reverence, he looked forward to the break of dawn, intending to go and see the Buddha.

The sincere response of the deity was clearly manifest; having gained clear understanding, he sought out the light and proceeded toward the gate of Rājagṛha. The gate opened during three periods of the night: the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch—these are called the three periods.

At midnight he went out the gate and saw a deva temple; he immediately prostrated himself there, but suddenly forgot to recite the Buddha’s name. His mind returned to darkness, and he thought to himself: "It is very dark tonight;
if I go further, I might be harmed by evil spirits or fierce beasts. I shall return to the city for now."
"I shall go at dawn.
At that time, there was a friend who had passed away and been reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; seeing that [the householder] wished to repent, he descended and said to him:
"Householder!..."
Do not regret it!

Go to see the Buddha; you will obtain immeasurable benefit. Even if you were to obtain a hundred carts of precious jewels today, it would not equal the profound benefit gained by taking a single step toward the World-Honored One, which far surpasses the former.
"Householder!
Go, and do not regret it!
Even if you were now to obtain a white elephant and precious jewels, it would not equal taking a single step toward the World-Honored One; the benefit of that would surpass them."
"Householder!
Go now and do not regret it!
Even if you were to obtain all the precious jewels filling the entire Jambudvīpa, it would not equal the vast benefit gained by taking a single step toward the World-Honored One."
"Householder!
Go, and do not regret it!

Even if you were to obtain the seven precious jewels filling an entire four-continent world-system, it would not equal the profit gained by taking a single step toward the World-Honored One; the latter exceeds the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of times."

Having heard these words spoken by the deva, Sudatta’s joy increased all the more; he paid reverent homage to the World-Honored One, and the darkness immediately turned to light. He then followed the path until he arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Sudatta was approaching, went outside to practice walking meditation.

Then Sudatta, seeing the World-Honored One from afar, perceived him as being like a mountain of gold; his marks and signs and majestic countenance were solemn and brilliantly manifest, surpassing by ten thousand times what Pūraṇa had described. Beholding him, his heart was filled with joy, yet not knowing the proper etiquette, he asked the World-Honored One directly:
"I wonder, Gautama!"
"How are you faring?
The World-Honored One immediately commanded him to take a seat.

At that time, the deva of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven saw Sudatta from afar; although he beheld the World-Honored One, he did not know the proper manner for prostrating and making offerings. He transformed himself into four men who approached in a procession.

Arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground to inquire after his well-being, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Sudatta, seeing this, was struck with amazement and thought to himself:
"The manner of showing reverence ought indeed to be like this."

He immediately rose from his seat, paid his respects as was customary, inquired after the World-Honored One’s well-being, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand at one side.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for him—the subtle and wondrous Four Noble Truths of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
Having heard the Dharma with joy, he was immediately imbued with the noble Dharma and became a *srotāpanna*, just as a clean, white cloth is easily dyed.
Kneeling long and joining his palms, he asked the World-Honored One:
"In the city of Śrāvastī, are there others like my companions who are so easily imbued by hearing the Dharma, or are there any more like me?"
The Buddha told Sudatta:
"There is no one else like you.
In the city of Śrāvastī, many people believe in heterodox teachings and are difficult to lead to the Holy Dharma."
Sudatta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to manifest his divine power and descend to Śrāvastī, so that the sentient beings therein may abandon heterodoxy and turn toward the Right Path."
The World-Honored One said:
"The way of those who have left the household life differs from that of the laity; their places of residence ought to be distinct. Since they have no vihāras, how can they go there?"
Sudatta addressed the Buddha, saying, "Your disciple is able to rise; I pray that you will grant me permission.
The World-Honored One remained silent.
Sudatta took his leave and went to take a wife for his son.
Having finally bid farewell to the Buddha and returned home, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I return to my native country, I intend to establish a vihāra; do you not know the method for its construction?"
"I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will send one disciple with me to go and give instructions.
The World-Honored One reflected:
"Within the city of Śrāvastī, the assembly of brahmins holds false and perverted views; if any other person were to go there, they would certainly be unable to accomplish the task.
Only Śāriputra, being of brahmin descent, possessing innate intelligence from his youth, and endowed with supernormal powers, will surely be of benefit if he goes."
He immediately gave the order, and they went together with Sudatta.
Sudatta asked,
"How many *li* can the World-Honored One travel on foot in one day?"
Śāriputra said, “Half a yojana [per day], according to the practice of a wheel-turning monarch traveling on foot; the World-Honored One shall do likewise.

At that time, Sudatta immediately established a guest house every twenty li along the route; he calculated the labor required, paid money to hire workers, settled the laborers there, and ensured they were fully provided with food, drink, and bedding.

From Rājagṛha to Śrāvastī, and returning again to Śrāvastī, he traveled together with Śāriputra, inspecting various sites to find a place that was level and spacious where a vihāra could be built; yet after searching everywhere, they found no site to their liking.
Only Prince Jeta possesses a garden; its ground is level and even, its trees are lush and flourishing, and it is neither too far nor too near, being situated in the perfect location.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Sudatta:

"Now, a vihāra should be built within this garden. If it were built at a distance, begging for alms would be difficult; if it were close by, the clamor and bustle would obstruct and hinder one's practice of the Path."
Sudatta was filled with joy; he went to the prince’s residence and said to him, “I now wish to erect a vihāra for the Tathāgata. Your park is excellent, and I wish to purchase it.”
The Prince smiled and said, "I lack for nothing;
this garden is lush and flourishing, and it is intended for my pleasure, recreation, and the relaxation of my mind.
Though Sudatta was earnest and repeated his request up to three times, the Prince remained reluctant to part with it.
He doubled the price, saying, "This price is too high; you will not be able to buy it.
He then said to Sudatta, "If you can cover the ground with gold coins so that there is no empty space between them, I shall give it to you."
Sudatta said, "Agreed;
let it follow its price.
Prince Jeta replied:
"I was only joking. Sudatta replied, "According to the law for a crown prince, one should not speak falsely.
How can one succeed to the throne and care for the people while practicing deception through lying?"
He then went together with the prince, intending to settle the dispute.

At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, because he was destined to build a vihāra for the future Buddha, feared that the ministers would be partial toward the prince; he therefore manifested as a man and descended to adjudicate the case.
He said to the prince, "According to the law for princes, one should not speak falsely; since you have already promised a fixed price, it is improper to regret it midway.
Thereupon, he cut the piece and gave it to him.
Sudatta was filled with joy and immediately commanded his attendants:
"Load the elephants with gold and bring it out.
Within eighty *qing* of land, it was nearly full in an instant, with only a small portion remaining.
Sudatta reflected:
"What storehouse of gold will suffice?
I shall take exactly what is needed—neither more nor less—to fulfill my requirement."
Jeta asked, "Are you dissatisfied with the price and thus leaving it?
He replied:
"No. Thinking of my own store of gold, what could possibly suffice?
I shall simply fill it to completion."
Jeta thought to himself:
"The Buddha must possess great virtue, for he has caused this man to regard his treasures as so insignificant.
He then commanded him to stop at that point.
"Do not pay any more gold. The garden grounds belong to you, but the trees belong to me; I shall offer them to the Buddha, and together we shall establish a vihāra.
Sudatta was delighted and immediately agreed. He then returned home to prepare for the construction work.
When the six teachers heard this, they went to inform the king:
"The elder Sudatta has purchased Prince Jeta’s Grove, intending to build a vihāra for the śramaṇa Gautama."
"Let my disciples compete with yours in a contest of skills; if the śramaṇas prevail, they may then rise up, but if they do not, they shall not rise.
Let the followers of Gautama remain in Rājagṛha, while our own followers shall remain here."
The King summoned Sudatta and asked him:

"Now these six masters say that you have purchased Prince Jeta’s Grove, intending to erect a vihāra for the śramaṇa Gautama, and they seek to compete with the śramaṇa’s disciples in their various arts and skills; if you prevail, you may establish the vihāra, but if you do not, you shall not be allowed to build it."
Sudatta returned home wearing soiled and greasy clothes, distressed and unhappy.
Then, when the time came the following day, Śāriputra put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to Sudatta’s house.
Seeing that he was unhappy, [the Buddha] immediately asked him,
"For what reason are you unhappy?
Sudatta replied:
"The vihāra we have set out to build, I fear will not be completed; that is why I am sorrowful.
Śāriputra said, "For what reason do you fear it will not be accomplished?"

He replied, “Now these six teachers have come to the King seeking a contest. If our honored guest wins, he shall be permitted to establish a vihāra; if he does not prevail, it shall be forbidden and he shall not be allowed to build.”
"These six teachers have been practitioners for a long time; they have long been sincere and steadfast, and there is no one who can equal them in the skills they have mastered.
I do not yet know whether your venerable self’s arts and crafts can compete with theirs."
Śāriputra said:
"Even if this assembly of six heretical teachers were to fill Jambudvīpa, as numerous as a grove of bamboo, they could not move even a single hair on my foot."
"As for what they wish to contest, let them do as they please.
Su-datta was delighted; he changed into new clothes, bathed in scented water, and immediately went to inform the king:
"I have already questioned them. The six masters wish to compete; let their will be followed as they desire."
At that time, the king addressed the six teachers, saying,
"I now permit you to compete with the śramaṇa. Thereupon,
the six teachers made an announcement to the people of the country:
"Seven days from now, I shall engage in debate with the śramaṇa in a spacious area outside the city. Within the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there were eighteen hundred million people.

According to the laws of that country, when the drum was beaten to assemble the masses: if the bronze drum was struck, eight hundred million people would gather; if the silver drum was struck, one billion four hundred million would gather; and if the golden drum was struck, everyone would assemble. When the seven-day period had ended, they arrived at the level and spacious site. The golden drum was struck, and everyone gathered; the followers of the six masters numbered three hundred million.
At that time, the people all prepared high seats for the king and his six teachers.
Then, Sudatta prepared a high seat for Śāriputra.

At that time, Śāriputra was beneath a tree, serenely absorbed in meditative concentration. His faculties were tranquil and silent as he traversed various dhyānas with unimpeded mastery, and he thought to himself:
"The great assembly in this gathering has practiced in error for a long time; they are arrogant and self-exalting, regarding all living beings as mere weeds. By what virtue shall I subdue them?"
Having reflected thus, one should establish a vow based on two virtues:

"If, throughout incalculable eons, I have been compassionate and filial toward my parents and have revered śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, then as I first enter this assembly, the entire multitude shall pay homage to me."
At that time, when the six masters saw that the assembly had already gathered but Śāriputra alone had not yet arrived, they addressed the king, saying:
"The disciple of Gautama, knowing himself to be without skill, falsely sought to compete in ability; now that the assembly has gathered, he has failed to come out of fear."
The King said to Sudatta, "The time for debate has arrived; you and your teacher’s disciple should come to discuss it.
At that moment, Sudatta went to where Śāriputra was and, kneeling with his right knee on the ground, addressed him:
"Venerable One!
The great assembly has gathered; we pray that you will come to the gathering.

Then Śāriputra arose from his meditative concentration, adjusted his robes, placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his left shoulder, and proceeded slowly and deliberately toward the assembly, like a lion king.

At that time, when the multitude saw that his appearance and dharma-robes were extraordinary, they and the six masters suddenly rose up and, like grass bending in the wind, unconsciously paid him homage.
Then Śāriputra ascended the seat spread out by Sudatta.

Among the assembly of the six heretical teachers was a disciple named Raudrākṣa, who was skilled in the arts of illusion. Before the great multitude, he cast a spell and produced a tree that grew naturally large, its canopy covering the entire assembly; its branches and leaves were lush and thick, and its flowers and fruits were each distinct.
The multitude all said,
"This transformation was wrought by Raudrākṣa.
Thereupon Śāriputra, employing his supernormal powers, conjured up a whirlwind that uprooted the trees, casting them to the ground and pulverizing them into fine dust.
Everyone said,
"Śāriputra has prevailed!
Now, Rādhagupta is indeed inferior."
Furthermore, he used incantations to create a pond; its four sides were all made of the seven treasures, and within the waters of the pond grew various kinds of flowers.
Everyone said, "This was created by Raudrākṣa."

Then Śāriputra transformed himself into a great white six-tusked elephant. Upon each tusk were seven lotus flowers, and upon each flower were seven jade maidens. The elephant proceeded slowly toward the edge of the pond and, taking up its water with its trunk, the pond immediately vanished.
The multitude all said,
"Śāriputra is victorious!
Raudrākṣa is not his equal."
He further created another mountain, adorned with the seven treasures, where springs, ponds, trees, flowers,
and fruits flourished in abundance. Everyone said,
"This was made by Raudrākṣa."
Thereupon, Śāriputra immediately manifested as a Vajrapāṇi and, with a vajra, pointed at it from afar; the mountain was instantly shattered, leaving nothing behind.
The entire assembly said:
"Śāriputra is victorious!
Raudrākṣa is not his equal."

He further manifested another dragon with ten heads, which rained down various treasures from the midst of the sky; its thunder and lightning shook the earth, startling and agitating the great assembly.
The multitude all said,
"This too was done by Raudrākṣa. Thereupon,
Śāriputra transformed himself into a golden-winged garuḍa king, who tore him apart and devoured him.
The multitude all said:
"Śāriputra is victorious!
Raudrākṣa is not his equal."
Again, he manifested another ox, its body massive and tall, fat, strong, and powerful; with coarse hooves and sharp horns, it scraped the ground and bellowed loudly as it charged forward.
Then Śāriputra transformed himself into a lion king and tore the [elephant] apart to eat it.
The people said,
"Śāriputra has won!"
"Laudouxu is not his equal.

He then transformed his body, becoming a yakṣa ghost with a massive form; flames blazed from his head, his eyes were red as blood, and his four fangs were long and sharp. Fire issued from his own mouth as he leaped and rushed forward.

At that time, Śāriputra transformed his own body into that of King Vaiśravaṇa; the yakṣas were terrified and immediately sought to flee, but flames erupted on all four sides, leaving them no place to go.
Only at the side of Śāriputra was it cool and without fire; he immediately prostrated himself, casting his body to the ground in five limbs, seeking mercy to save his life.
Once the sense of shame had arisen within him, the fire was instantly extinguished.
The assembly all cried out:
"Śāriputra has won!
Raudrākṣa is no match!"

At that time, Śāriputra ascended into the air and manifested the four dignified postures—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. Water issued from his upper body while fire issued from his lower body. He vanished in the east and reappeared in the west; he vanished in the west and reappeared in the east; he vanished in the north and reappeared in the south; he vanished in the south and reappeared in the north. Sometimes he manifested a massive body that filled the void of space, and then again appeared small. Sometimes he divided his single body into hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of bodies, and then merged them back into one. While in the air, he suddenly descended to the ground; he walked upon the earth as if upon water, and walked upon water as if upon the earth.
Having performed these transformations, he withdrew his supernormal powers and sat upon his original seat.
At that time, the great assembly, witnessing his spiritual power, all felt profound joy.

Then Śāriputra preached the Dharma for them, according to their original practices and the causes and conditions of their past merit; each attained the fruits of the path—some becoming stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), or arhats. Furthermore, three hundred million disciples from the following of the six heretical masters went forth from home to study the Way under Śāriputra.
When the contest of skills was concluded, the fourfold assembly dispersed and each returned to their respective quarters.

The elder Sudatta, together with Śāriputra, went to survey the site for the vihāra; Sudatta held one end of the measuring line in his own hand, while Śāriputra held the other end, as they walked together along the perimeter of the vihāra.
At that time, Śāriputra smiled joyfully.
Sudatta asked,
"Venerable sir, why do you smile?"
He replied, "At this very spot where you have begun this sutra, palaces have already been completed within the six heavens of the desire realm.
He then lent him the divine eye, and Sudatta saw all the magnificent and pure palaces within the six heavens of the desire realm; he then asked Śāriputra:
"Among these six heavens of the desire realm, which place is the most blissful?
Śāriputra replied:

"In the lower three heavens, sensual desire is deep and thick; in the two upper heavens, there is arrogance, indulgence, and self-indulgence; in the fourth heaven, however, there is little desire and contentment, and a Bodhisattva bound to one more birth (ekajātipratibaddha) constantly comes to be born therein, so that the instruction of the Dharma never ceases."
Sudatta said, "I am destined to be reborn in the fourth heaven. As soon as these words were spoken,
all other palaces vanished, and only the palace of the fourth heaven remained serene and resplendent.
As they continued along the cord, Śāriputra’s face turned somber with grief.
He immediately asked the Venerable One,
"For what reason do you have such a sorrowful countenance?"
He replied,
“Do you now see the ants in this ground?
He answered:
"I have seen it.
Then Śāriputra said to Sudatta:
"In the past, during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin, you also built a vihāra for that World-Honored One on this very spot; it was there that these ants were born."
During the time of Śikhin Buddha, you were a patron for that Buddha and likewise constructed a vihāra within this very spot, and these ants were born therein.
During the time of Viśvabhū Buddha, you were a patron for the World-Honored One and erected a vihāra upon this ground, and these ants were also born therein.
When Krakucchanda Buddha was in the world, he too was a World-Honored One who erected a vihāra upon this very spot; these ants were also born here at that time.
During the time of the Buddha Kanakamuni, you were the World-Honored One; you erected a vihāra upon this very spot, and these ants were born within it as well.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you were also a Buddha; you constructed a vihāra on this very spot, and these ants were born therein as well.
From then until today, for ninety-one kalpas, they have received this same kind of body and have not attained liberation.
"Birth and death are long and far-reaching; merit alone is essential, and one must not fail to plant it.
At that time, Sudatta was filled with compassion and pity.

Having finished surveying the ground, he erected a vihāra and constructed a cave for the Buddha, using exquisite sandalwood as fragrant plaster. There were twelve hundred separate rooms for dwelling, and at every one hundred and twenty locations, a *ghanṭā* (gong) was struck individually.
Having completed the preparations, he wished to go and invite the Buddha, and further reflected to himself:
"There is a king above; I ought to inform him, lest he should become resentful if I do not announce it."
He immediately went to inform the king, saying:
"I have already constructed a vihāra for the World-Honored One; I only pray that Your Majesty will dispatch a messenger to invite the Buddha."
When the king had heard this, he immediately dispatched a messenger to Rājagṛha to invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha,
saying: "I pray only that the World-Honored One will deign to visit Śrāvastī."

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the fourfold assembly before and behind him, emitted a great radiance that shook the great earth. He arrived at the kingdom of Śrāvastī, halting at every guest-house along the way, and on his journey he delivered countless people. Gradually drawing near to the outskirts of Śrāvastī city, the entire great assembly, bearing various offerings, came out to welcome and await the World-Honored One.

When the World-Honored One arrived at the country and reached a vast open space, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm. Pressing the earth with his toe, the ground shook everywhere; the musical instruments within the city sounded spontaneously without being struck. The blind saw, the deaf heard, the mute spoke, the hunchbacked straightened, and those who were crippled, lame, or afflicted by chronic ailments all attained full physical restoration.

All the people—men and women, great and small—seeing this auspicious response, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they came to where the Buddha was, and eighteen hundred million people gathered there in total assembly.

At that time, the World-Honored One administered medicine according to their ailments and preached the sublime Dharma for them. Through the influence of their past conditions, each attained the fruits of the Path: some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat; some planted the causal conditions for Pratyekabuddhahood; and some resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment. Each was filled with joy and reverently practiced the Buddha’s words.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This parkland was purchased by Sudatta; the groves, trees, flowers, and fruits belong to Jeta. Since these two have joined their hearts together to establish this vihāra, it should be named 'Prince Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. This name shall be widely circulated and transmitted to future generations."
At that time, Ānanda and the fourfold assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, received it upon their heads and practiced accordingly. 42.

Chapter on Mahāprabha’s Initial Resolve for the Unsurpassed Mind (49). Chapter Forty-two on Mahāprabha’s Initial Resolve for the Unsurpassed Mind. [In the Danben, this is Chapter Forty-seven. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of the Kalandakas.
At that time, Ānanda was sitting in quiet meditation among the trees and groves, when this thought suddenly arose in him:
"The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, is endowed with all the sense faculties; his merit and wisdom are luminous, exquisite, and immeasurable."
World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions did you, in the distant past, first resolve upon this unsurpassed mind of the Mahāyāna?
What practices did you cultivate to attain such supreme and wondrous benefits?
Having formed this thought, he immediately arose from his meditation and went to where the Buddha was. Prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As for all the World-Honored Ones, among all the humans and devas in the world, they are the most honored and most sublime; their merit, wisdom, and radiance are majestic and immeasurable.”
"I do not understand, World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions did he previously give rise to this unsurpassed mind of the Mahāyāna?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If you wish to know, reflect upon it well;
I shall explain it to you in full detail.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Very well, listen attentively!
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Mahāprabhasa (in the Jin language, ‘Great Radiance’), who ruled over five hundred minor kingdoms.”

At that time, the Great King went out on a hunting excursion together with his ministers. The elephant upon which the King rode was overcome by a fierce lustful desire; it bore the King away at full speed, pursuing a female elephant and gradually drawing near to a great forest, where it burst into the midst of the trees.
The elephant trainer said to the king,
"If you grasp the tree and stand firm, we shall surely be saved.
The king followed his words, and they all together grasped the tree.
After the elephant had departed, the king was filled with great rage;

he severely rebuked the elephant trainer and intended to put him to death immediately, saying, "Because you trained this elephant contrary to the prescribed regulations, you have nearly brought peril to my person."
The elephant trainer said to the king:

"I have trained it according to the proper methods; however, this elephant is now deluded by desire, and its lustful mind is difficult to subdue. This is not my fault, and I pray that you will grant me your pardon."
"In three days' time, the elephant will surely return of its own accord; let Your Majesty observe my trial, and I shall have no regrets even if I were to die ten thousand deaths.
He then set it aside. When the three days had passed according to the schedule, the elephant returned to the palace.

At that time, the elephant trainer heated seven iron balls until they were glowing bright red and forced the elephant to swallow them; the elephant did not dare disobey, and as soon as it had swallowed them all, it died.
The king’s mind was opened and understood, and together with his ministers, they marveled at what had never occurred before.
He asked him again, saying:
"Who is able to tame such a mind of desire?"
At that time, a deva moved the elephant trainer to enlightenment, prompting him to reply to the king:
"The Buddha can tame it.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately gave rise to a resolute thought and said:
"Such stubborn and difficult-to-subdue dharmas can only be eliminated by a Buddha.
He then made a vow:
"I pray that I may attain Buddhahood."
"Exerting himself with diligence through kalpas without ever ceasing or flagging, he has today finally obtained the fruit of his retribution.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who the Great King of that time was, it is I myself who am he now."

At that time, the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; they leaped for joy with such exuberance that they could not contain themselves, receiving his words upon the crowns of their heads and reverently putting them into practice.
Chapter 43: Raṇajaya (50). Chapter Forty-three on Raṇajaya; in the Danben it is the forty-eighth. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Monastery.

At that time, the Śākyas beheld the World-Honored One’s radiant supernormal transformations as he proclaimed his wondrous edification; it was most marvelous and extraordinary, majestic and sublime, such that none could equal it.
Furthermore, he praised Kauṇḍinya and the others, saying:
"What auspicious merit did you possess in your past lives?

That the Tathāgata has appeared in the world and the drum of the Dharma has first resounded, that you were the very first to hear it, and that as the nectar of immortality first descended, you immediately received its blessing, forever departing from defilement so that the essence of your minds attained the profound and essential truth."
"In the cities, camps, villages, and towns, crowds follow one another, praising You with one voice and countless voices.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at His feet, and addressed Him, saying:

'Now the people of this realm have all gathered together, praising the World-Honored One with one voice for His various virtues. Furthermore, what past merit did these five men possess that they alone were first granted deliverance?'"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"It is not only today that I first delivered these five; in the distant past, I likewise rescued them. Using my own body as a boat, I saved those who were drowning, preserved their lives, and enabled each of them to attain peace and reach the other shore."
"Now that I have attained Buddhahood, I shall first rescue them.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We do not understand, World-Honored One!"
In times past, how were they rescued and delivered so that each might find peace and security?
We pray only that the World-Honored One will explain this for us.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to hear it, I shall speak for you.
They all replied: [We do.]
“Yes, indeed,” [the bhikṣus replied]. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“In the distant past, in this Jambudvīpa at the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta.”

At that time, there was a great caravan leader in the kingdom named Renajaya who went out on a journey and arrived among the forest trees. There he saw a man weeping bitterly and piteously, having tied himself to a tree with a rope and thrust his head into the noose, intending to hang himself.
He approached him and asked, "Why have you done this?"
"A human body is difficult to obtain, and life is fragile; there are countless transformations and decays, and one is constantly in fear that they will arrive.
Thus, he used various exhortations to instruct him to renounce his pursuit."
The man replied to him:
"I am of meager merit; my poverty is extreme and my debts have accumulated until they are beyond counting.
These creditors vie with one another to strip me of everything, pressing me day and night so that my mind cannot find release from anxiety."
"Though heaven and earth are vast, there is no place to hide my body; I now wish to drown myself to escape this suffering.
Though you, O Benevolent One, have exhorted me, living is not better than death.
At that time, the Sārthavāha immediately granted his permission, saying:
"Simply release your bonds; however much you owe, I shall repay it all for you.

Having spoken these words, the man immediately ceased his efforts, leaping for joy with immeasurable gratitude. He followed the Sārthavāha to the marketplace together, where he proclaimed to everyone that he intended to pay off the debts.
At that time, his creditors gathered together in great numbers, vying with one another to collect what was owed to them; those who came were limitless, and they exhausted his wealth.
When his goods and riches were spent, the debt was still not fully repaid; his wife and children were left destitute and freezing, surviving only by begging for alms.
His kinsmen and the people of the city all reproached and despised him, saying:
"This man is a madman; he is destroying his own family estate.
At that time, there was a group of merchants who urged the caravan leader (sārthavāha), wishing to go into the sea together with him, to which he immediately replied:
"For the sake of the caravan leader's dharma, one must prepare the ship's equipment;
I am now impoverished and possess nothing further—by what means could I possibly follow?
The multitude replied:
"We are five hundred people in all; let us open our hearts and contribute funds to procure the necessary equipment for the ship.
Having heard these words, he immediately gave his consent.
The multitude agreed, and they obtained a great quantity of gold and treasures.

At that time, the Sārthavāha used three thousand taels of gold: one thousand taels to procure the ship, one thousand taels to procure provisions, and one thousand taels for the various necessities required on board; there remained a great surplus with which he could support his wife and children.

He then had a great ship constructed by the seashore; the ship had seven decks, and once it was fully prepared and finished, he pushed it into the water and moored it to the shore with seven great ropes. He struck a large golden bell and proclaimed to all:
"Whoever desires to enter the sea to obtain great, wondrous jewels and rare treasures for inexhaustible use, may now gather like clouds and proceed together to the place of treasure."
He spoke to them again, saying:
"Only those who do not cherish their parents, wives, children, the pleasures of Jambudvīpa, or even their own lives may go.
This is because within the great ocean there are many hardships and perils—whirling waves, violent storms, massive fish, and malevolent spirits; such various dangers cannot be fully described."
Having spoken these words, he immediately cut one rope;
doing so day after day, by the seventh day all the ropes were severed, and the ship sped away.

Then, while on their way, they were suddenly overtaken by a violent storm that shattered their ship. The people cried out for rescue, but had no one to turn to for refuge; some managed to save themselves by seizing planks, masts, or floats, while others fell into the water and drowned.
Among them were five men who spoke together to the caravan leader:
"We followed you here and now face death; danger is imminent, so we pray that you will save us."
The Sārthavāha replied:
"I have heard that the great ocean does not harbor corpses.
You all must now each seize me; for your sake, I shall take my own life to relieve your distress, vowing to seek Buddhahood."
"When you later attain Buddhahood, you shall use the vessel of the unsurpassed True Dharma to ferry you across the suffering of the great ocean of birth and death.
Having spoken these words, he cut himself with a knife.
"After their lives had ended, the sea deity raised a wind that blew them to the opposite shore; they crossed the great ocean and all attained peace and security.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who Lerañjaya was at that time, it is I myself who am he now."
The five individuals at that time were Kauṇḍinya and his companions.
In a previous life, I saved those people from the cycle of birth and death;

now that I have attained Buddhahood, I have enabled these five to be the very first to obtain the untainted True Dharma and to depart from the great ocean of the outflows, fetters, and latent tendencies.

At that time, all the bhikṣus together praised the Tathāgata’s great compassion, which is profound, subtle, and immeasurable; they all applied themselves with diligent effort, and having heard what the Buddha had taught, they joyfully practiced it.
44. Chapter on Kapila with a Hundred Heads (51). Chapter Forty-four on Kapila with a Hundred Heads. [In the Danben, this is the forty-ninth. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the Bamboo Grove in the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, set out for Vaiśālī and arrived at the banks of the River Līlaja.
At that moment, there were five hundred cowherds and five hundred fishermen by the river.
Those who catch fish employ three kinds of nets of varying sizes: the smallest is pulled by two hundred men, the medium by three hundred men, and the largest by five hundred men.
At that time, the Tathāgata sat down to rest not far from the river, and the bhikṣus also all sat together with him.
Then a fisherman caught a large fish in his net; five hundred men pulled at it, yet could not bring it out.

He then called for a group of cowherds, totaling a thousand men, who joined their strength to pull it out. It was a massive fish with a hundred heads, consisting of various species: donkeys, horses, camels, tigers, wolves, pigs, dogs, monkeys, foxes, and other such creatures.
The multitude was greatly astonished and gathered together in competition to see what was happening.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"What matter is there such that the great assembly has all gathered?"
“Go and examine it.
Ānanda, having received these instructions, went immediately to look.
He saw a large fish with a hundred heads on its body, and returned to report to the World-Honored One exactly what he had seen.
At that moment, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, went to where the fish was and asked it,
"Are you Kapila? It replied:
"It is indeed so.
He asked with great earnestness three times:
"Are you Kāpilīya or not?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
He asked again:
"Where is the one who instructed you now?
He replied,
"He has fallen into the Avīci Hell."
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, not knowing the reason for this, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"For what reason now do you call these hundred fish 'Kāpilī'?"
"I only pray that you will show compassion and grant me instruction.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall now explain it for you.

Long ago, in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a brāhmaṇa who fathered a son named Kapila (translated into Chinese as 'Yellow Head'). He was intelligent and widely learned; among his peers, he was foremost in erudition, yet he still fell short of the śramaṇas."
As his father was approaching death, he earnestly instructed him:
"You must be careful never to debate the principles of the Dharma with the śramaṇa Kāśyapa Buddha. Why is this?"
"Śramaṇa Zhishen, you will certainly not be his equal.
After her father passed away, his mother asked him:
"You were originally lofty and brilliant; is there now anyone who surpasses you?"
He replied,
"The śramaṇa is superior to me.
His mother asked again:
"What makes you superior?
he asked. He replied, "I have some doubts and went to question a śramaṇa; what he expounded caused me to attain understanding."
"If he were to question me, I would be unable to answer.
For this reason, I know for myself that I am not his equal.
The mother spoke again, saying:
"Why do you not go to study their Dharma?
He replied, "To study their Dharma, one must become a śramaṇa; I am a layperson (avadātavasana), so by what means could I study it?"
His mother spoke again, saying, "Pretend to be a śramaṇa; once you have mastered your studies, return home.
Following his mother’s instruction, he became a śramaṇa.
After a short time, he had read and recited the Tripitaka and mastered its principles and meanings.
His mother asked him, "Have you attained victory yet? He replied:
"Among the various forms of learning, the excellence of scholarship is not equal to that of seated meditation.

How do we know this? When I questioned those scholars, they were all able to provide detailed explanations; [yet their understanding remained inferior to that of one who has realized through practice]."
"That person questioned me, yet I could not know [the answer].
Because of this matter, I am not equal to others.
The mother spoke again, saying:
"From this day forward, if we engage in discussion and you happen to fail to respond appropriately,
you may then revile and insult me. Kapila replied,
"For a renunciant śramaṇa, there can be no further transgression or fault."
"How should one revile him? He replied,
"Simply revile him, and you shall achieve victory."
At that time, Kāpilī could not bear to disobey his mother; on a subsequent day, when they debated again and his reasoning was defeated, he immediately reviled them, saying: "You fools!"
"Lacking any discernment, they are worse than beasts; what dharma could they possibly understand?
All the leaders of the various hundred beasts compared him to them in this way, repeatedly and not just once or twice.
"Due to this karmic retribution, he has now received the body of a fish with a hundred heads.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"When shall he be able to escape from this fish body?"
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Within this Bhadrakalpa, though a thousand Buddhas have passed, he has still not been liberated.
At that time, Ānanda and the great multitude, hearing what the Buddha had said, were despondent and unhappy; grief and sorrow filled their hearts, and with one voice they spoke these words:
"One must be careful in the conduct of body, speech, and mind.
At that time, the fisherman and the cowherd simultaneously joined their palms toward the Buddha and requested to leave the household life to purely cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The Buddha then said, "It is well; come, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
At that time, World-Honored One!

For their sake, he preached the sublime Dharma with various exhortations on suffering; their outflows were exhausted and their fetters untied, and they became Arhats. He then further expounded the various dharmas extensively for the assembled multitude, analyzing the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
There were those who attained the first fruit up to the fourth fruit, and there were many who gave rise to the mind of the Great Vehicle.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume Ten;
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume Eleven.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Northern Wei Dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.
45. Chapter on Aṅgulimāla (52). Chapter Forty-Five on Aṅgulimāla. According to the Danben (Dunhuang manuscript), this is chapter fifty-one.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a king named Prasenajit.

The king had a minister who was both intelligent and immensely wealthy. His wife became pregnant and gave birth to a son whose features were upright and handsome, and whose physical form was exceptionally sublime.
At that time, the prime minister, seeing his son’s joy, immediately summoned a physiognomist and ordered him to examine the boy's features.
Upon seeing him, the physiognomist spoke with delight:
"This child possesses the marks of merit; he is preeminent among men, endowed with intelligence and eloquence, and possesses virtues that surpass those of others."
Upon hearing this, the father was greatly pleased and ordered that a name be given to the child.
The physiognomist asked,
"Since the child was conceived, what extraordinary events have occurred?"
The prime minister replied:

"Her mother’s natural disposition was not virtuous; however, since she became pregnant, her character has become exceptionally so—she is respectful and compliant, delights in proclaiming the virtues of others, takes pity on those in distress, and does not take pleasure in speaking ill of anyone."
The physiognomist said, "This is the child's own aspiration;
we shall establish a name for him, calling him A-xin-ze-qi, which in the Jin language means 'Free from Affliction' (Ananda).

As the boy gradually grew up, he became peerlessly heroic and possessed the strength of a great athlete; one man could match a thousand, he could leap as high as a soaring bird, and his speed in running surpassed that of a galloping horse. His father, the Prime Minister, cherished him exceedingly."

At that time, in the kingdom, there was a brahmin who was intelligent and profoundly learned, possessing vast knowledge and extensive erudition; he had five hundred disciples who followed him and studied under him.
At that time, the prime minister took his son and went to entrust him [to the brahmin], commanding him to pursue his studies.
The brahmin agreed, accepting him and undertaking to instruct him.

A-xinzeqi applied himself diligently day and night; what he learned in a single day of consultation and instruction surpassed that of others after a whole year. Although his studies had not lasted long, he attained universal and thorough mastery.

The Brahmin teacher treated him with exceptional courtesy; whether walking, coming, going, or stopping, he was always accompanied by him, and his fellow students all looked upon him with devoted respect.

At that time, the wife of the brahmin teacher saw that he was handsome and his talents were so preeminent that they far surpassed those of ordinary men; she conceived a lustful attachment, and her love for him would not leave her mind.

However, as he was constantly accompanied by his disciples, never remaining alone in his movements or stillness, he had no opportunity to speak with them; his heart's desire remained unfulfilled, and he was perpetually sighing in melancholy.
There was a donor who came to invite his teacher and his disciples for a period of three months.
The Brahmin teacher consulted with his wife:
"I must now go to accept this invitation for three months; I shall leave one person behind to manage affairs in my absence."
At that time, the wife was inwardly delighted and secretly devised a plan. She said to the Brahmin:
