"This matter should indeed be so; however, the affairs of my household are important and require capable talent. You may stay here without distress, and I shall entrust you with future matters."
At that time, the brahmin immediately commanded Anupama:
"I am now going to attend to the invitation of that donor; there are many subsequent matters that require someone to manage them."
"You possess great talent; you shall serve as my successor.
Unmada accepted this instruction and immediately remained there without departing, while the teacher and his disciples led the way and departed.
The wife was filled with immeasurable joy and delight; she adorned herself to the utmost, assumed many seductive gestures, and engaged him in conversation to disturb his mind.
Yet, his will remained firm and undisturbed, and he had no intention of complying.
His lustful mind grew even more intense, and he spoke to her with sincere words:
"I have long cherished a mutual affection for you; it was only because of the presence of others that I restrained myself and did not let my feelings be known."
"When your teacher was about to depart, I intentionally detained you; now that we are alone and in quietude, you should follow my wishes.
Anuruddha apologized and said, "In the dharma of our brahmins, one does not violate the wife of a teacher; were I to transgress this, I would no longer be a brāhmaṇa."
"I would rather die together with you than ever do such a thing.
At that time, the teacher’s wife, hoping to avoid a grave violation of her heart, felt both shame and indignation, and devised another secret plot.
Anticipating that the Master was about to arrive, he tore his clothes, gashed his face, covered his body in dust and dirt, and lay prostrate on the ground in a state of exhaustion, unable to speak.
At that time, the Brahmin master and his disciples arrived together; the master immediately entered the inner quarters and, seeing the wife’s appearance and condition, asked her the reason:
"For what cause has it come to this?"
The wife wept as she spoke:
"It is not fit for you to ask.
Then the Brahmin questioned her once more:
"What is your business?
You should tell me; why do you not speak?
The woman wept and said:

"Regarding that Arhat whom you so highly esteem and praise, since you departed, he has constantly harassed and oppressed me; just now, when I did not comply with him, he tore my clothes and mangled my head and body."
"You have taken on disciples; how could you have acted in such a manner?
Upon hearing this, the brahmin was filled with great resentment and anger, and said to his wife:
"This Ananda is a man whose strength rivals a thousand men; he is the son of a prime minister and his lineage is powerful. Although we wish to discipline him, we should do so gradually."
Having thus deliberated, he went to see Aśoka and, employing appropriate skillful means, comforted him, saying:
"After I departed, you have endured great hardship and toil."
Furthermore, you have served me with complete loyalty from beginning to end; I have always been moved by your devotion and have long desired to repay you.
There is a secret dharma that I have never previously disclosed; if you can accomplish it, you will be reborn directly in the Brahma Heaven.
Unnābha knelt down and asked, "What is this?
He replied,
"If one takes the heads of a thousand people within seven days and takes a finger from each, obtaining a total of a thousand fingers, these are used to fashion a garland for adornment."
"At that time, the Brahmā descended of his own accord; after his life ended, he was certain to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
Hearing this, Anala felt hesitant and again addressed his teacher, saying, "This cannot be right—that by killing sentient beings, one is reborn in the Brahma Heaven."
The Master spoke again:
"You are my disciple; do you not believe these most essential words of mine?
If you do not believe them, our bond is severed; follow your own path and do not dwell here any longer."
He again performed a mantra and thrust the sword into the ground.
When the recitation of the mantra was finished, an evil intent arose within him.
The master, perceiving his intention, immediately handed the sword to him.

Taking up his sword, he ran outside; whenever he encountered a person, he would kill them immediately and take their fingers to make a garland. People saw him and called him Aṅgulimāla, which in the Jin language means "Finger-Garland.

He traveled about committing slaughter for seven days until he finally obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine fingers; he was lacking only one finger, so he killed another person, and the count of fingers was complete.
Everyone hid away and dared not go out; though they searched everywhere, they could find nothing.
For seven days he had no food or drink. His mother, feeling pity for him, sent others to bring it, but all were filled with fear and none dared to go.
His mother took the food and went there in person; when the son saw his mother from afar, he ran toward her intending to kill her.
At that time, the mother spoke, saying:
"O you, unfilial creature!"
"Why do you harbor such rebellious intent and wish to harm me?
The son then spoke, saying,
"I have received my teacher's instruction that within seven days, once I have obtained a full thousand fingers, I shall then fulfill my vow to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven."
When the days had already expired and he could obtain nothing more, he said to himself, "Since I have no other recourse, I must kill my mother.
His mother spoke to him again, saying, "If this matter must indeed be so, simply take my finger; do not see me harmed or killed."
At that time, the World-Honored One beheld him from afar; knowing he was ready for deliverance, he manifested as a bhikṣu and walked by his side.
Upon seeing the bhikṣu, Aṅgulimāla abandoned his mother, leaped up, and rushed toward him with the intent to kill.
When the Buddha saw him approaching, he walked slowly and departed.
Aṅgulimāla ran with all his might but could not catch up, so he called out from afar:
"Bhikṣu, stop for a moment!"
The Buddha answered from afar:
"I always abide in myself; it is only you who do not abide.
Aṅgulimāla asked again:
"How is it that you abide while I do not?
The Buddha replied,
"My faculties are tranquil and stilled, and I have attained mastery."

Following an evil teacher, you have received perverted and inverted teachings that have transformed your mind, preventing it from abiding in stability; day and night you commit slaughter, creating boundless transgressions.
Upon hearing these words, Aṅgulimāla was suddenly awakened; he cast his sword far away and prostrated from a distance to take refuge.
Thereupon the Tathāgata waited for him and manifested his Buddha-body once more, its radiance like the bright sun and its thirty-two marks clearly manifesting in wondrous splendor.
Seeing the Buddha’s radiant marks and majestic demeanor, Aṅgulimāla threw himself to the ground, repenting his transgressions and reproaching himself.
The Buddha briefly expounded the Dharma, whereby he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; his mind became purely faithful, and he sought to leave the household life.
The Buddha granted his consent, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!

His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and the Dharma robes were donned upon his body. According to what was appropriate for him, the Buddha preached the Dharma again; his mental defilements were completely exhausted, and he attained the path of Arhatship.
The Buddha then took him back to the Jeta Grove.

At that time, when the people of the land heard the sound of Aṅgulimāla, they were all struck with terror; even those among humans and animals who were pregnant were so afraid that they could not give birth.
At that time, there was an elephant that could not give birth to its offspring. The Buddha commanded Aṅgulimāla to go and speak these truthful words:
"Since my birth, I have never killed a single person."
Aṅgulimāla said to the Buddha, “I have killed many since long ago; how could it be that I have not killed?
The Buddha told him:
"Within the Noble Dharma, this is what it means to be newly born.
Thereupon, Aṅgulimāla adjusted his robes and went to deliver the message as instructed; immediately upon hearing these words, they were all born anew and attained peace and security.
He returned to the vihāra and sat within a single room.

At that time, King Prasenajit had assembled a great host of troops and was personally intending to go and subdue Aṅgulimāla; his route passed through the Jetavana as he was about to launch the attack.

At that time, within the Jeta Grove, there was a bhikṣu whose physical form was extremely haggard and ugly, yet his voice was exceptionally wonderful. As he raised his voice in a loud chant, the sound was exceedingly harmonious and flowing; the military multitude leaned their ears toward him, never tiring of it, while the elephants and horses pricked up their ears, standing still and refusing to move.
The king was astonished and asked his charioteer,
"Why has it come to this?
The charioteer replied:
"Because of hearing the sound of the chanting, these elephants and horses have halted their steps to stand and listen.
The King said,
"If even animals delight in hearing the Dharma, why should we humans not go to listen?"
He then returned with the multitude to the Jetavana for a moment.

Upon reaching the elephant stable, he dismounted, unsheathed his sword, and set aside his parasol; proceeding directly to where the Buddha was, he paid his respects and offered greetings. At that moment, the chanting of the bhikṣu had ceased.
The king first asked:

"Just now I heard the sound of your chanting; it was pure, wondrous, harmonious, and flowing. My heart is filled with joy and admiration, and I wish to meet you and know you, so I offer you one hundred thousand coins."
The Buddha told him:
"First give him the money, and only then may you see him.
If you have already seen him, you will no longer have the heart to give even a single coin."
He was about to show it to him.
Upon seeing its form, it was twice as hideous and loathsome; unable to bear the sight of it, he had no desire to give even a single coin.
The king rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This bhikṣu here has an extremely short and ugly form, yet his voice is so deep and far-reaching that its sound penetrates even to this extent."
"What kind of deeds did he perform in his past lives to bring about this retribution?
The Buddha told the king,
"Listen well and fix your mind!"
In the past, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa who, having completed his work of delivering sentient beings, entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the king of that land, named Kṛkin, collected his relics with the intention of erecting a stūpa for them.
At that time, the four dragon kings transformed themselves into human form, came to see the king, and inquired about the matter of building the stupa:
"Are you using jewels to construct it,
or are you using earth?"
The king then replied:
"I wish to make the stupa large, yet I have no abundant treasures; how can it be completed?
I now wish to build it of earth, making it five li square and twenty-five li high, so that it is exceedingly lofty and magnificent to behold."
The Dragon King replied, "We are not humans;
we are all dragon kings. Having heard that Your Majesty is building a stupa, we have come to inquire about it. If you truly wish to use these jewels, we shall assist you."
The king said with joy,
"It would be wonderful if you could do so.
The dragon spoke again, saying:
Outside the four city gates, there are four great springs. The spring water from the east of the city is taken to make bricks, which, once formed, become dark-blue lapis lazuli.
The spring water from the south of the city is taken to make bricks; once these bricks are formed, they all become pure gold.
The spring water from the west of the city was taken to make bricks; once the bricks were completed, they transformed into silver.
The spring water from the north of the city was taken to make bricks; once those bricks were completed, they transformed into white jade.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s joy redoubled, and he immediately established four supervisors, each to oversee one side.
While the work undertaken by three of the supervisors was nearly complete, the work of one supervisor remained unfinished due to his negligence and indolence.
The king saw him walking and rebuked him with reason, saying, "You have failed to apply your mind; you shall be subject to punishment.
The man harbored resentment and addressed the king, saying:
"This stupa is too large; when will it be completed?
After the king had departed, he commanded all the laborers to work diligently day and night, and in a single session, the work was entirely finished.
The stupa was exceedingly high and steep, adorned and embellished with various jewels that shone brilliantly; it was a most extraordinary sight.
Having seen it, he felt great joy and repented of his past transgressions. Taking a single golden bell, he hung it upon the pinnacle of the stupa and made this vow:

"May the sound of my voice be exquisite in every rebirth, such that all sentient beings will delight in hearing it. When the future Buddha named Śākyamuni appears, may I behold him and be delivered from birth and death."
"Thus it was, Great King!
If you wish to know who that supervisor of the work who grumbled about the stupa being too large was at that time, it was this very bhikṣu.
Because of those resentful words and his dislike of the stupa’s size, for five hundred lifetimes he has always been extremely humpbacked and ugly."

Because he joyfully offered a bell to the top of a stūpa and prayed for a beautiful voice as well as for the sight of me, for five hundred lifetimes he possessed an exquisite voice; now, having seen me again, he has attained liberation.
Having heard this, the king took his leave and wished to depart.
The Buddha asked the Great King,
"Where do you intend to go?"
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In my kingdom there is an evil bandit, Aṅgulimāla, who injures and kills the people, committing violent atrocities wherever he goes. I now wish to lead my troops to attack and subdue him."
The Buddha told the king:
"Aṅgulimāla, as he is now, he cannot even kill an ant, much less anyone else.
The king thought to himself:
“Has the Blessed One already gone and subdued him?
The Buddha said to the king:
“Aṅgulimāla has now left the household life to enter the Way and attained arhatship; all evils are forever exhausted. He is currently in his room; do you wish to see him?”
The king said, "I wish to see him.

He immediately rose and went outside the monk's cell, where he heard the sound of Aṅgulimāla coughing. Remembering the vast extent of harm caused by that violent and evil man, he fell down in terror and remained unconscious for a long while before reviving. He returned to the Buddha’s presence and reported the matter to him.
The Buddha said to the king:
"It is not only today that you fell to the ground and were cut off upon hearing his voice; in past lives as well, it was the same when you heard his sound."
"Listen well, Great King!
Long ago, in the distant past, there was a great kingdom in this Jambudvīpa named Vārāṇasī.
At that time, within that kingdom, there was a poisonous bird that would catch various venomous insects and constantly eat them for sustenance."
Its form was extremely venomous and could not be approached; wherever it passed over, all sentient beings died and all trees withered.
At that time, this bird encountered a forest and perched upon a tree, clearing its throat in preparation to cry out.
At that time, in that forest, there was a king of white elephants who, while beneath a nearby tree, heard the cry of the poisonous bird; he fell to the ground, his life-force severed, unable to move.
Thus it is, Great King!
"The poisonous bird of that time is now this very Aṅgulimāla.
The white elephant king of that time is now your majesty's own body.
The King spoke again to the Buddha:
"Aṅgulimāla was exceedingly violent and harmful; he killed so many people until, fortunately, he was tamed and converted to practicing virtue by the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the king:
"Aṅgulimāla has not only killed these many people today and then been tamed and converted by me."
"In past lives as well, these were killed; I too have subdued and transformed them, and they shall again contemplate the good.
The King addressed the Buddha again with reverence:
"I do not understand how it was that these were harmed in previous lives, and how the World-Honored One subdued and transformed them. Pray, tell me of those matters."
“I pray that you will explain this for me.
The Buddha told the king,
“Listen well and fix your mind!”
In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī; at that time, the king’s name was Paramada.
At that time, the king, leading the fourfold army, entered the mountain forest to roam and hunt for sport.
Upon reaching a marshy plain, he pursued wild beasts until, riding alone on a single carriage, he reached a deep forest. The king was then utterly exhausted and dismounted to rest for a short while.

At that time, there was a male lion in the forest whose lustful desire was intense; he went about seeking a mate but, being exhausted, could not find one. While wandering through the woods, he saw the King sitting alone. His lewd intent grew even more fervent, and wishing to pursue the King, he drew near to his side and stood with his tail raised over his back.
The king understood his intention and reflected to himself:
"This is a fierce beast whose strength could kill me; if I do not comply with his wish, I might suffer harm."
Out of fear, the king immediately followed the lion; once the act of desire was completed, the lion departed.
When the host of soldiers and attendants returned, the king and his people immediately went back to the palace city.
At that time, the lion became pregnant; when the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son whose form was entirely human, except for his spotted feet.
The lion remembered and recognized that this was the king's possession; he then carried it in his mouth and brought it before the king.

The king also reflected and recalled past events, realizing it was his own son. He immediately took him in to raise him, and because his feet were mottled, he named him Kalmāṣapāda—translated into Chinese as Bōzú (Mottled Feet).
As he grew up, his heroic talent and fierce ambition became manifest. When his father, the king, passed away, Khara succeeded him in the governance of the realm.
At that time, King Khara had two queens: one of royal lineage and the other of Brahmin lineage.
At that time, King Kalmāṣapāda went out of the city one day to roam in the gardens and parks, and he commanded his two wives:
"Follow behind me; whichever of you arrives first shall enjoy my company for an entire day to her heart's content, while I shall not even look upon the one who follows after."
After the king had departed, his two queens adorned themselves most elaborately and prepared their carriages; they set out together at once.

Upon reaching a celestial shrine along the road, they saw a member of the Brahmin caste and alighted from their carriages to pay him homage. Having finished their prostrations, they hurried forward, yet they still arrived behind him.
The king, adhering to his original words, did not proceed further.
Thereupon, the lady, filled with anger and resentment, reproached the deity:
"Because of my worshiping you, I have been slighted by the King; if you possess divine power, why do you not protect me?"
Filled with resentment, hatred, and indignation, he secretly devised a plan.
After the king returned to the palace, he served him with even greater devotion; the king, in turn, treated him with renewed favor. Thereupon, he requested a boon from the king:
"Grant me the freedom to rule over my own kingdom for one day."
Taking advantage of the king’s partiality, he immediately obtained permission for this.
He went outside and ordered men to destroy the celestial shrine, leveling it until it was even with the ground, and then returned to the palace.

The deity who guarded the celestial shrine was filled with grief, suffering, and anguish; he went into the palace intending to cause harm, but the deities of the royal palace blocked him and would not allow him entry.

"There was a rishi who dwelt in the Mountain of Rishis; King Kalmāṣapāda constantly made offerings to him, and every day at mealtime, he would fly into the palace. He did not eat delicacies, but partook only of coarse food and simple offerings."
Once, on a day when the seer did not come, a celestial deity learned of this and transformed himself into his likeness, intending to enter the palace.
The guardian spirit of the palace still recognized him and would not allow him to proceed inside.

Standing far outside the gate, he addressed the king, requesting an audience. When the king heard that the seer was outside seeking to be seen, he marveled at the reason for his arrival and urgently ordered him to be admitted.
At that moment, the palace deity, hearing the king’s command, immediately ceased obstructing him.
He proceeded directly forward and entered, sitting upon the seat where the rishi usually sat, and prepared his regular food to offer as an act of hospitality.
However, the transformed rishi was unwilling to partake of the meal and spoke to the king, saying:
"This food is coarse and poor; furthermore, it lacks meat and fish. How can it be eaten?"
The king immediately replied, "Great Seer, you have always come here yourself and have always eaten pure, simple food; therefore, I have not prepared meat, fish, or savory delicacies.
The transformed seer spoke again:
"From this day forward, do not prepare coarse offerings; provide only meat for food.
They prepared it exactly as instructed, and after eating, he departed.
When the next day arrived, the former seer flew back. The king provided him with various kinds of meats as a meal, which caused the seer to become enraged and to harbor resentment toward the king.
The king said,
"Great Seer, yesterday you commanded that this be done.
The seer spoke, saying:
"Yesterday I was ill and fasted for one day, so I did not come here; who told you all this?
You were merely mocking me, which is why it happened as it did."
"Let the King, for the twelve years thereafter, constantly eat human flesh.
Having finished these words, he flew back to the mountains.

Subsequently, the head cook forgot to prepare meat; when the time arrived and having no other plan, he went outside to seek it. Seeing a dead infant, plump and white, lying on the ground, he thought, "This will suffice for the emergency," and immediately severed its head and feet, carried them to the kitchen, added various fine medicinal herbs, prepared the food, and gave it to the King.
When the king ate it, he found it twice as delicious as usual, and he immediately asked the chief cook:
"In all my years of eating meat, I have never tasted anything so exquisite; what kind of meat is this?"
The kitchen superintendent was terrified and beat his breast before the king, saying:
"If Your Majesty would pardon my offense, I would dare to speak the truth.
The king replied to him:
"Speak only the truth; I shall not question you regarding your offense.
The chief cook addressed the king:
"The other day, due to certain circumstances, I was unable to procure meat. I found a dead child and used it to satisfy the requirements of the moment."
"I did not expect that Your Majesty would notice this.
The King said, "This meat is exceptionally delicious; from now on, provide it for me in this manner whenever it is requested."
The chief cook addressed the king:
"Previously, we happened upon a small child who had died of its own accord, but it is impossible to find another.
Those who prepare the food fear the laws of the state."
The king spoke again, saying:
"You need only take them secretly; if anyone should discover it, the decision regarding the punishment shall rest with me.
Following these instructions, the chief cook captured them in secret and supplied them to the king day after day.
At that time, the people within the city each wept as they went about, lamenting the loss of their young children, and asked one another in turn:
"How has this come to pass?
The ministers gathered to deliberate, deciding that they should observe discreetly; they immediately stationed people in every street and quarter.

Seeing the king’s kitchen supervisor dragging away another’s young child, he waited until he had captured him, bound him, and brought him before the king, reporting in full detail all the previous instances of children being lost.
Upon hearing these words, the king remained silent and gave no answer.
The three ministers addressed the White King, saying:
"Now that the thief has been captured and his crimes have been exposed, the matter must be adjudicated; why do you remain silent?
The King then replied:
"This was my teaching," [the king said].
The ministers, harboring resentment, each departed and deliberated together outside:
"The king is a thief; he eats our children. How can we govern together with a king who devours men?"
"We must join together to eliminate this calamity.
With one mind, they all deliberated together:
"In the garden outside the city, there is a fine pond where the king goes every day to bathe."
The ministers had stationed their troops in ambush within the garden.
When the king came out to bathe and reached the pool, the hidden soldiers simultaneously surrounded him on all four sides; they then besieged the king, intending to seize and kill him.
When the king saw the troops gathered, he was struck with alarm and fear, and asked:
"For what reason do you surround and press upon me?
The ministers replied:
"Now, for one who is a king, the nurturing of the people is his primary duty.
Yet you are presiding over the kitchen, slaughtering people for food.
The masses cry out in lamentation, having nowhere to appeal their grievances; unable to endure such bitter cruelty, they wish to kill you, O King."
The king said to his ministers:
"I have indeed acted improperly; from this day forward, I shall never do so again. I beg only for your forgiveness and release, and I shall reform and exert myself."
The ministers said, "We will never let you go;
even if it were to rain black snow today, or if a black venomous snake were to grow upon your head, we still would not grant you leave—there is no need for further talk."
When King Kharaṅga had heard the minister’s words, he knew for certain that he would die and saw no way to escape.
He then said to his ministers, "Even though you must kill me, delay for a brief moment and let me stay a little longer."
The ministers set him down gently, and the king immediately made this vow:

"By all the virtuous deeds I have cultivated since time immemorial, by my righteous governance as a king, by my offerings to the rishis, and by the accumulation of all these merits, may they be dedicated so that today I may be transformed into a flying rākṣasa."
As soon as he had finished speaking, it was accomplished by his word; he immediately flew into the air and addressed the ministers, saying:
"You all joined your forces, wishing to kill me by force, but by my great good fortune, I have been able to extricate myself."
"From this day forward, you must endure well; your beloved wives and children shall be my next meal.

Having spoken these words, he flew away and settled among the mountain forests, where he would swoop down upon people from the air and carry them off as food. Consequently, the human population lived in terror, hiding themselves to escape him.
After this, he killed and devoured many people.
Various rākṣasas joined him as his followers; his retinue gradually increased, and the harm he caused became ever more widespread.
Thereafter, the rākṣasas said to King Pādaśṛṅga:
"We serve you and act as your attendants; we pray that you will grant us a banquet."
Then King Kalmāṣapāda immediately granted his word, saying:
"I shall take one thousand kings and provide them for you and your companions to hold a banquet."

Having granted his permission, [the king] went one by one to fetch them and confined them in the deep mountains; he had already captured nine hundred and ninety-nine kings, lacking but one person, so that the number was not yet complete.
The kings thought to themselves:
"We are in dire straits; where shall we turn?
If they capture Sudassana, he possesses great skillful means and can deliver us."
Having made this plan, he said to the Rākṣasa King:
"Your Majesty wishes to hold a great assembly; let it be made truly extraordinary. Take only kings, and do not include commoners;
Sutasoma possesses most excellent virtue—if you can have him come, the King’s assembly will be perfect."
The Rākṣasa King asked,
"What great virtue do you possess?
and immediately he soared into the air, intending to seize him.
"Encountering Sudassana, who was leading his court ladies out of the city at dawn intending to go to the park to bathe, he saw a brahmin on the road and begged from him for alms."
The king said to the brahmin, "Wait until I have finished bathing and returned; then I shall bestow a gift upon you.
Having reached the garden, the king entered the pond to bathe.
At that time, the Rākṣasa King flew through the air to seize him and carried him to the mountains.
Sudāsa-mi was filled with grief and wept bitterly.
Then King Kalmāṣapāda asked him:

"I have heard that your reputation and virtue are supreme and foremost; as a man of great resolve, you ought to accept both poverty and success. Why then do you grieve so excessively, weeping like a small child?"
Sudāsaṃmi addressed the Rākṣasa King, saying:

"I do not cherish my body nor do I covet my life; however, I reflect that since birth I have never spoken falsely. This morning, as I was leaving the palace, I saw a Daoist standing before my carriage who begged from me."
"I promised to wash it and return it, and I intended to give it to you.

On my way out, I encountered the Great King carrying me here; I thought to myself that I would now be guilty of lying and thus violate my word of honor. It is for this reason that I am sorrowful, not because I cherish my own body."
"I pray that you will show me compassion and grant me seven days to bestow [my body] upon that ascetic; I shall then return to face my death.
When Pādaśṛṅga heard this, he said to him, "If you are now permitted to go, would you truly return of your own accord to face your death?"
He then asked again,
"Even if you do not return, I myself shall obtain it.
He immediately released him and let him go.
When the king returned to his kingdom, the ascetic was still there; the king joyfully made offerings and bestowed gifts upon the Brahmin.

At that time, seeing that the king would soon have to return to his death, the Brahmin feared that the king might feel sorrowful out of attachment to his country, and so he spoke these verses for the king:
"When the kalpa reaches its ultimate end, heaven and earth will burn through and through; Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans—
All have been reduced to ashes and embers.
Among them, devas, dragons, humans, and ghosts have perished; even the two polarities of heaven and earth have met their end—how can there be any constancy in a kingdom?
Birth, old age, sickness, and death revolve without end; Matters run contrary to one's wishes, and grief and sorrow bring harm.
Desires are deep and calamities heavy; like sores and ulcers, there is nothing outside of them. The three realms are entirely suffering—what reliance can there be in this world?

That which exists has originally been non-existent; all things are formed through causes and conditions. That which flourishes must inevitably decline; that which is substantial must inevitably become empty.
Sentient beings, in their restless turmoil, are all like those dwelling in an illusion. The three realms are entirely void; even the lands are likewise so.
The conscious spirit has no form; it merely rides upon the four serpents. With the precious elephant of ignorance, it makes its pleasure-carriage.
The body has no permanent master, and the spirit has no permanent home. Since even the body and spirit are separated, how could there be a kingdom?

At that time, Sudāsaṃmi, having heard these verses and contemplated their meaning, felt immeasurable joy. He immediately established his crown prince as regent to succeed him as king, took leave of his ministers, and set out to fulfill his promise.
The ministers spoke with one voice to the king, saying:

"May Your Majesty simply remain here; do not worry about Khara. We shall devise plans and take precautions, forging iron for a dwelling where Your Majesty may stay. Even though Khara is fierce, what can he possibly do?"
The king addressed his ministers and the people:

"When a person is born into this world, sincerity and faithfulness are its foundation. To exist through falsehood and hypocrisy is something my heart cannot tolerate; it would be better to die with integrity than to live by speaking falsely."
He further expounded for them in various ways the benefits of sincerity and faith, and extensively analyzed the transgressions of falsehood.
The ministers were choked with grief and remained speechless for a long while.
The king arose and departed from the city; everyone followed him out, wailing and lamenting along the way until they collapsed, only to regain consciousness.
After the king had finished exhorting them, he proceeded on his journey.
At that time, King Kalabha thought to himself,
"Sutasoma should arrive today.
He sat upon the mountain peak and waited, looking out from afar, until he saw him approaching along the path toward him.
Having arrived and seen him, his countenance was serene and joyful; he was so delighted and relieved that it surpassed anything from before.

The Rākṣasa King asked: "It is wonderful that you have been able to arrive. In this world, there is no one who does not cherish their life. You were now to die, yet you are twice as joyful as usual. Upon returning to your own country, what beneficial merit will you obtain?"

Sudāsa replied: "Great King, may Your Majesty’s grace extend to me for seven days to allow me to practice giving, so that I may fulfill my sincere vow and hear the sublime Dharma. My mind shall then be opened and liberated; my aspirations will be fully satisfied as they are today, and even though I am destined for death, my heart will rejoice as if still living."
King Khara said:
"What Dharma have you heard?
Try to explain it to me."

Sudāsa recited the original verses for him, and employing further skillful means, he extensively expounded the Dharma, analyzing the sin of killing and its evil retribution, while also explaining the merit of a compassionate mind that refrains from killing.

Kalmāṣapāda was filled with joy and paid him respectful homage; he accepted his teachings and no longer harbored any intent to harm. He immediately released the various kings, each returning to his own kingdom.

Sudassana then gathered his troops and returned Kalmāṣapāda to his own country. Once the twelve-year period vowed by the former seer had been fulfilled, Kalmāṣapāda never again ate human flesh. He subsequently returned to the throne as king and governed the people as before.
"Thus it was, Great King!
If you wish to know who the King Sutasoma was at that time, he is none other than my own self.
As for King Kalmāṣapāda, he is now Aṅgulimāla."
The people who were devoured by King Kharaṇāda during those twelve years are these very people who have now been killed by Aṅgulimāla.
"These people have been constantly killed by Aṅgulimāla throughout their successive lives, yet I, too, have treated them with kindness life after life.
I recall that in the past, when I was still an ordinary person, I transformed them so that they would not kill;
how much more so now that I have become a Tathāgata, fully endowed with all virtues and forever stilled of all evils—how could I not be able to transform and subdue them?"
The king spoke again to the Buddha:
"What karmic conditions did these people have in their past lives that they are constantly being killed by him throughout every successive lifetime?"
The Buddha said to the king:
"Listen attentively!
Long ago, in the distant past, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī. At that time, the king’s name was Paramada."
The king had two sons, both possessed of heroic talent and were exceptionally handsome; the king loved them dearly.
At that time, the younger son thought to himself:

"Should my father pass away, my elder brother shall succeed him in ruling. Since I am still young, I have no hope of the throne. Having been born into this world and already failing to become king, what is the point of remaining in it?"
"It would be better to seek the Way of the Immortals in secluded tranquility.
Having formed this thought, he went to inform his father the King:
"I long for the deep mountains to seek the Way of the Immortals; I pray that you will grant me leave so that I may fulfill my aspiration."
Thus, with such earnestness, his resolve could not be shaken; his father then granted him permission and immediately allowed him to enter the mountains.
After he had been gone for several years, his father the king passed away, and his elder brother succeeded to the throne and ruled over the people.

Before long, the elder brother fell ill and passed away; as he had no son and there was no one left to succeed him, the ministers gathered for consultation, not knowing to whom the succession should go.
A certain minister said:

"The King has a young son who previously petitioned Your Majesty to enter the mountains to study the arts of the immortals; he shall soon return, and we should go to welcome him back to succeed to the royal throne."
The ministers rejoiced and said,
"This must certainly be so.
They immediately led one another into the mountains to invite him, and upon arriving, they explained their intentions in detail according to the circumstances:
"Only we pray that you show compassion and accept our kingdom!
The seer replied:
"This matter is to be feared; in this tranquility and joy of mine, there shall forever be no sorrow or affliction.
Yet the people of the world are fierce and evil, delighting in mutual slaughter; were I to become king, I might well fall victim to their plots and harm."
"Now I am so deeply attached to this that I cannot do it.
The ministers addressed him again:
"The King has passed away and the lineage is severed; there is no one else to succeed him, and only the Great Seer is of the royal bloodline."
The land and its people must not be left without a ruler.
We only pray that you will look upon us with compassion and deign to protect us!
Thus, with utmost sincerity and earnest entreaty, his heart could not bear it, and he finally returned with him to the kingdom.

The rishi was young and had never practiced the affairs of desire; yet once he came to govern the state, he gradually became drawn to female beauty. His lustful passions grew deep, and he became dissolute and profligate, indulging in debauchery day and night, unable to restrain himself.
He then issued an edict throughout the kingdom that all women, when wishing to go abroad, must first come to him; only then would he permit them to go and follow their husbands.
Furthermore, whenever beautiful women from various countries entered his mind, he would humiliate them all.
At that time, a certain woman stood naked and urinating upon a public road amidst a great crowd; everyone was shocked and laughed, coming together to rebuke her:
"How can you be so shameless as to reach such an extreme?"
The woman immediately replied:
"Among women, what is there to be ashamed of?
Since you yourselves stand in the water without feeling shame, I am no different from you; why should I feel ashamed?"
The people replied,
"What does this speech mean?
The woman spoke again, saying:
"Only the King alone is a man; all the women of the kingdom have been shamed by him.
If you were men yourselves, would you allow such a thing?"
Thereupon, those people felt mutual shame and began to consult one another, saying, "What this woman says is indeed logical.
They secretly adopted her words, whispering among themselves in private; with one mind and a single plan, they sought to conspire against the king.

In a garden outside the city, there was a cool pond where the king would regularly go with his attendants to bathe. While the ministers and commoners remained settled within the garden, they encountered the king coming out to wash; the hidden soldiers then all emerged, surrounding him on every side, intending to seize and kill him.
The king was startled and asked,
"What do you wish to do?
The ministers replied:
"The King governs with injustice; his lust and dissipation are excessive, he has subverted the constant customs, and he brings disgrace upon all families.
We, your ministers, having witnessed this, could not bear it; therefore, we wish to remove the King and seek out one who is worthy and capable."
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly alarmed and said to his ministers:
"I truly did not intend to bring trouble upon you; I pray you will reform yourselves and henceforth never dare to act in such a manner again."
"We pray that you will grant us clemency and allow us to begin anew with the people.
The ministers replied again:
"Even if it were to rain black snow today, or if venomous snakes sprouted from our crowns, we would never release you; why need you say so much?"

Upon hearing this, the king realized he was certain to die; filled with rage and indignation, he said to his ministers, "I originally lived in the mountains and had no concern for worldly affairs, yet they forcibly came to constrain me and made me their king."
"You have not yet committed a great offense, yet you conspire with one mind to plot against me.

I am now solitary and weak, lacking the power to extricate myself; I swear that in a future life I shall always kill you, and even when I am on the verge of attaining the Way, I will still not let you go."
"Although he made this vow, he nevertheless killed him.
Thus it was, Great King!
If you wish to know who that royal seer was at that time, he is now Aṅgulimāla."
Those subjects and citizens who at that time conspired together to kill the king are these very people now being killed by Aṅgulimāla.
From that time onward, they have constantly been his victims, and even until today, he continues to harm them.

At that time, the king knelt down on his right knee and addressed the Buddha again, saying, "The bhikṣu Aṅgulimāla killed many people; now that he has attained the Way, will he still have to undergo retribution?"
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Every action must have its retribution. Now this bhikṣu is in his room; the fires of hell issue from his pores, and he suffers such extreme agony that its piercing intensity is beyond words."
At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to make the assembly understand that performing evil deeds inevitably brings retribution for one's sins, commanded a bhikṣu:
"Take this door-bolt, go to Aṅgulimāla’s cell, and insert it into the keyhole."
The bhikṣu immediately went there and, following the instructions, pushed it inside the door; it melted away instantly.
The bhikṣu was struck with amazement and returned to inform the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣu, “Such is the retribution for one’s actions.”
The king and the entire assembly were all moved to faith and understanding.
At that time, Ānanda knelt on his right knee and addressed the Buddha:

“What auspicious merit did Aṅgulimāla possess in his past lives such that his physical strength is so magnificent, possessing the power of a champion, and being so agile and swift that he can outrun even flying birds?”
Furthermore, how may they encounter a Buddha and transcend birth and death?
We only pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for the sake of the assembled multitude.
The Buddha told Ānanda: “Listen well!

In the distant past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who served as an administrator for the Saṃgha. He was transporting grain and rice belonging to the monks when he encountered rain on the road; having no place to take shelter, the bags of grain and other goods were all soaked through.”

At that time, the bhikṣu, wishing to pass through quickly, found his strength insufficient and his progress slow; unable to act according to his will, he felt dejected and delayed, and immediately made this vow:

"May I, in a future life, possess strength equal to a thousand men, with a light body and swift movement, running faster than a flying bird; and when the Buddha Śākyamuni appears in the future, may I be able to see him and forever escape birth and death."
"Thus it was, Ānanda!
The bhikṣu who served as the administrator at that time is now Aṅgulimāla.

Because he left the household life and upheld the precepts during that era, and because of the vow he made while attending to the affairs of the Saṃgha, from then until now, in birth after birth, he has been handsome, possessed of fierce strength, and swift of foot—exactly according to his wish. Furthermore, having encountered me, he has attained liberation from birth and death."

At that time, Ānanda, the bhikṣus, the king, the ministers and the common people, and all those present in the assembly, having heard the Buddha’s discourse on the causes, conditions, and retributions of actions, were all moved to profound inspiration. They contemplated the Four Noble Truths; some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat; some planted the roots of goodness for the path of a Pratyekabuddha; some resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; and some attained the stage of non-retrogression. All guarded their bodies and speech, disciplined their minds, and followed what was wholesome. Having heard what the Buddha taught, they joyfully accepted and practiced it.
46. Chapter on Dhanyākara (53). Chapter Forty-six on Dhanyākara (in the Danben [Dunhuang manuscript], it is the fifty-second). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, within the kingdom, there was a brahmin named Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja. His wife was ugly and her two eyes were blue; she had seven daughters alone and no sons. The family was impoverished, and the daughters were likewise destitute.

The wife was of a wicked nature and constantly reviled her husband; whenever his daughters came one after another to ask for what they needed, she would glare at them and weep if their requests were not immediately granted.

When the husbands of these seven daughters gathered at their home, she attended to them with great hospitality, fearing they might lose their favor. There was ripe grain in the fields that had not yet been harvested; she borrowed oxen from others and led them there to tread it. However, she was not careful in guarding the oxen, and they were lost in a marsh.
At that time, the brahmin sat down and reflected to himself:
"What sin have I sown that such bitter and poisonous calamities have converged upon me?

Internally, I am reviled by my wicked wife and tormented by my seven daughters; when their husbands gather, I have nothing with which to receive them; furthermore, I have lost another's ox, and I do not know its whereabouts."

He searched extensively, until his body was exhausted and his mind weary; filled with grief, distress, and agitation, he happened upon a grove where he encountered the Tathāgata sitting beneath a tree, his faculties serene and stilled, dwelling in tranquil peace and bliss.
At that time, the brahmin rested his chin upon his staff and stood gazing at them for a long while, whereupon this thought arose in him:

"The śramaṇa Gautama is now most peaceful and happy; he has no wicked wife to scold or quarrel with, nor daughters to torment him, nor the distress and suffering caused by poor husbands. Furthermore, he has no concern over ripened grain in the fields, as he does not borrow others' oxen, and thus he knows no grief over loss."
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, spoke to him, saying: "It is as you have thought.

As for me now, I am tranquil and free from all afflictions. Truly, there is no wicked wife who curses or reviles me; there are no seven daughters who torment me; nor do sons-in-law flock to my house in competition. Furthermore, I do not worry about the ripening grain in the fields, I do not borrow oxen from others, and I have no anxiety over lost property."
The Buddha asked him,
“Do you wish to leave the household life?
He immediately replied to the Buddha:

"As I now view my home as a cemetery and the various conditions of women as being among enemies and bandits, it would be most fitting for my humble wish if the World-Honored One, out of compassion, would grant me permission to leave the household life."
The Buddha then said to him,
“Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and the garments he wore were transformed into saffron robes.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and at that very seat, his various defilements were forever exhausted, and he became an Arhat.
Hearing this, Ānanda sighed in praise, saying:
"Excellent!"
The Tathāgata’s skillful guidance is truly inconceivable.
What auspicious merit did this brahmin plant in past lives that he has been freed from all afflictions and attained such wholesome benefit?
He is like a clean cloth, which easily takes on any dye.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This brāhmaṇa has not only received my grace today to be freed from suffering and attain peace;
in a past life as well, he relied upon my grace to escape various calamities and again obtain well-being.”
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“I do not understand, World-Honored One!
How did you rescue and deliver them from suffering in a past life?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in detail.”
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
“Yes, I shall listen attentively!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a great king named Aparājitamukha—translated in the Jin language as 'Upright'—who governed through the transformation of the Way and did not oppress the people or their property."

At that time, in the king’s realm, there was a brahmin named Dhanika whose household was destitute and impoverished; his food did not suffice for his mouth, and having only a small amount of ripened grain, he was unable to process it. He borrowed an ox from another and led it away to trample the grain.
Having finished threshing the grain, he drove the oxen back to their owner.
When he reached another's gate, he forgot to entrust them to someone; thus, he returned home.
Although the owner saw the oxen, he thought they were still being used and did not take them back.
The two families abandoned one another and consequently lost the ox.
Later, when they went to demand it back, each claimed, "I have already returned it to you," as they insulted and reviled one another.
At that time, the owner of the ox took Dhanika and went before the king to claim his ox.
Just as he went outside, he encountered a man from the royal household who was tending horses; at that moment, the horse bolted, and the man called out to Dhanyākṣa, saying, "Stop the horse for me!
Then Dhanyākṣa reached down and picked up a stone, which he hurled at it, and by chance, the horse's leg was broken.
The groom then seized him, and they both went together before the king.
Next, they proceeded to the water, but not knowing where to cross, they encountered a woodworker who was crossing by lifting his clothes while holding a wooden adze in his mouth.
At that time, Dhanika asked the man,
"Where can one cross?"
As soon as he answered with these words, his mouth opened and the axe fell into the water; though they searched for it, they could not find it.
They came back to seize him and together led him before the king.

At that time, Dhanika was being urgently pressed by his creditors; moreover, being afflicted by hunger and thirst, he went to a wine-seller along the road and begged for a little white wine. He drank it while lying on a bed, unaware that a young child was sleeping beneath him; the child’s abdomen was crushed and ruptured.
At that time, the child’s mother again seized him and would not let go, crying out, “You are devoid of the Way;
you have unjustly murdered my son!
They held him fast together and led him to the royal palace.
Arriving at the side of a wall, he thought to himself:
"I am unfortunate; my many transgressions have converged upon me. If I go before the king, he might perhaps kill me;
if I flee now, I may yet escape."
Having had this thought, he leaped over the wall himself; beneath it was a weaver who died instantly upon his falling onto him.
At that time, the weaver’s son seized him and, together with the crowd, led him to the king.
Proceeding further on, he saw a pheasant perched upon a tree; calling out from afar, he asked it, "O Dhananjaya!
Where do you intend to go now?"
He immediately recounted these circumstances to the pheasant, who replied:
"When you reach that place, speak to the king on my behalf: 'While I was in other trees, my song was not pleasing; but when I am in this tree, my song is mournful and beautiful.'"
"For what reason is this so?
If you see the king, ask him for me.
Next, he encountered a venomous snake, which also questioned him:
"O Dhanika! Where are you going now?
He then related the preceding events in detail to the snake.
The snake replied again:

"When you reach the king's presence, speak on my behalf to the king: 'In the morning, when I first emerge from my hole, my body is supple and free from all pain; but in the evening, when I return to enter it, my body becomes coarse and stiff with pain, making it difficult for me to pass through the opening.'"
At that time, Dhanika also accepted her entrustment.
He then saw a woman and asked her,
"Where do you wish to go?"
She then related all these matters in detail to him.
The woman said:

"When you reach the king's presence, speak on my behalf to the king: 'I do not know for what reason, when I am with my husband's family, I long for my parents' home; yet when I dwell in my parents' home, I long for my husband's family.'"
He also accepted their entrustment.
"At that time, the creditors all surrounded and guarded him, leading him before the king.
Then the owner of the ox stepped forward and addressed the king, saying:"
"This man borrowed my ox and departed; when I went to him to reclaim the ox, he refused to repay me.
The King asked him, "Why did you not return the ox?"
Dhanika said: "I am truly poor and destitute;

there was ripened grain in my field, and out of kindness, he lent me an ox. I used it until the work was finished and drove it back to its owner. The owner saw it as well, so although he did not say anything, the ox was right at his gate when I returned home empty-handed. I do not know how that ox was ever lost."
The king said to those men:

"Both of you are at fault. Because Dhanika did not deliver [the ox] due to his mouth, you shall cut out his tongue; because you saw the ox and failed to restrain yourselves, you shall have your eyes gouged out."
That man said to the king, "I beg you to let go of this ox;
I do not wish to gouge out its eyes or cut off its tongue.
The king then granted permission for them to reach a peaceful settlement.
The groom spoke again:
"He was devoid of the Way; he broke my horse's leg.
The King then questioned Dhanika, saying:
"This is the king's horse; why did you recklessly break its leg?
He knelt and addressed the king, saying: "A creditor led me along this road.

That man called out to me, ordering me to stop the king's horse. The horse bolted and could not be restrained; I reached down and seized a stone that was there and threw it, but by mistake I broke the horse's leg. It was not done intentionally."
The king said to the groom:
"Because you summoned him, your tongue shall be cut off;
because he struck the horse, his hand shall be cut off."
The groom said to the king, "I shall prepare the horse myself; please do not carry out the execution.
Thus, they reached a mutual reconciliation.
The carpenter came forward again and said,
"Dhanika has lost my adze.
The king then asked:
"Why have you also lost another adze?
He knelt and addressed the king, saying, "When I asked for the crossing point, he answered me;
at that moment, the adze fell from my mouth into the canal water. I searched for it but could not find it; truly, I did not do it intentionally."
The king said to the carpenter:

"Because you called out [the elephant], its tongue must be cut off; as for the manner of carrying loads, one ought to use one's hands. Since you caused it to fall into the water by holding it in your mouth, I shall now strike your two front teeth until they break."
Upon hearing this, the carpenter came forward and said to the king,
"I would rather cast away my adze than undergo such punishment. Thus,
they reached a mutual reconciliation.
At that time, the mother of the tavern owner again led [her son] before the king.
The king asked Dhanika:
"Why have you thus unjustly killed his child?"
Kneeling, he addressed the king, saying:
"A creditor is pressing me, and I am further afflicted by hunger and thirst; I begged for a little wine, climbed onto the bed to drink it, and did not realize there was a small child lying beneath."
The drinking has been completed and the child’s life has already ended; this is not what Your Majesty desires.
I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me your pardon and consideration.
The king said to the woman:
"You run a tavern and have many guests; why did you lie your child down in his seat and cover him so that he was not visible?"
"You two now both have faults.
Since your son has died, we shall give you Dhanika as a son-in-law so that you may have a son again; only then will we release him to go."
At that time, the woman bowed her head and said, "My son is already dead;
please allow us to reconcile with one another. I have no need for this famished brahmin to serve as my husband."
Thereupon, each understood that they had attained reconciliation with themselves.
Then the weaver’s son came forward again and said to the king:
"This man was violent and impetuous; he trampled my father to death."
The king asked,
"For what reason have you unjustly killed your father?
Dhanika replied:
"Various debts press upon me; I was filled with great terror and leaped over a wall to flee, only to accidentally fall upon it—this was truly not what I desired.
The King said to that man:
"Both of you are at fault. Your father has already died, and I have appointed Dhanika to serve as your official."
The man said to the king, "My father has already died; I will never accept this brahmin as my father.
[The king] granted permission for each to resolve the matter according to their own understanding, and the king then consented.
At that time, Dhanañjaya, having completed all his worldly affairs, stood before the king with immeasurable joy.
He saw two women disputing over a single child and approaching the king to present their case.
At that time, the king was wise and shrewd; employing a clever stratagem, he said to the two mothers:
"Now there is but this one son, whom both of you summon. I grant you both permission to each pull at one of his hands; whichever of you can get him shall have this son."
"The one who is not his mother has no affection for the child; she pulls him with all her might and without hesitation, fearing no injury or harm.
The mother who gave birth to him possesses deep affection for the child; she follows and protects him, unable to bear pulling or dragging him."
The king, discerning the true from the false, spoke to the one who had exerted force:
"This is truly not your son; you have forcibly dragged another child. Now, before the king, speak the truth of your matter."
He then confessed to the king:
"I have indeed been false; I falsely claimed another's son as my own.
O Great King, you are wise and sagacious!"
"I beg you to forgive my empty transgression.
He returned the child to his mother, and each was released.
Again there were two men who disputed over a white goat; they came before the king in a tumultuous quarrel, and the king again used his wisdom to settle it as he had done above.
Then Dhanika addressed the king, saying:
"When these creditors brought me here, by the side of that road there was a venomous snake. It earnestly entreated me to convey its message to Your Majesty:

'I do not know for what reason it is when I emerge from my hole that I am supple and easy to move, yet when I return to my hole, I am obstructed and suffer great pain; I myself do not know by what cause this is so.'"
The king replied to him, saying:
"The reason for this is that when emerging from the cave, I was free from all afflictions; my mind and feelings were harmonious and gentle, and my body was likewise."

Because the snake has been outside for a long time, various birds and beasts have irritated its body; its anger having become intense, its body becomes coarse and large. Therefore, when entering, it is obstructed by the hole and finds it difficult to move forward.
"You may say to him:
'If you remain outside and maintain a mind free from anger, just as it was when you first went out, then you will have no such affliction.
He then spoke again to the king, saying:
"The Daoist saw a woman and asked me to inform the King:
'While I am in my husband's household, I long for my parents' home; when I am in my father's home, I again long for my husband's household. I do not know what karmic conditions cause this to be so.'"
The king replied again: "You may say to her:
'It is because of your own depraved mind that you kept a paramour in your parents' house, and while living in your husband's home, you thought of that other man.'"
"Having reached that place, she became slightly weary and returned to thinking of her rightful husband;
that is why this has happened. You may say to her:
'If you maintain your resolve, abandoning the heterodox and returning to the orthodox, then you shall have no such affliction.'"
Again, he addressed the king, saying:
"By the side of the road, upon a tree, I saw a pheasant who requested me to inform Your Majesty:
'When I am on other trees, my cry is not pleasant; yet when I am on this tree, my cry is mournful and harmonious. I do not know for what reason it is thus.'"
The king said to that person:
"The reason for this is that beneath that tree there is a large cauldron of gold; therefore, when perched upon it, the sound is mournful and beautiful.
In other places there is no gold; therefore, when staying upon them, the sound is not beautiful."
The King said to Dhanika, "Your many transgressions have already been pardoned by me.
Since your family is in extreme poverty and distress, the gold in the cauldron beneath the tree rightfully belongs to me; I shall give it to you, so you may dig it up and take it."
Having received the king’s command, he answered each point in turn.
He excavated that gold and traded it for land and property; all his necessities were provided without lack, and he thus became a wealthy man, enjoying happiness throughout his life.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As for that great king Aparājitamukha at that time, could he have been anyone else?
It was I myself."
The Brahmin Dhanika of that time is now the Brahmin Piṇḍola-bharadvāja.
In the past, I delivered him from his many calamities and bestowed upon him precious treasures to bring him joy;
now that I have attained Buddhahood, I have again extracted him from suffering and bestowed upon him the treasure-wealth of the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury.
When the Venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Eleven;
*The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Twelve.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Northern Wei Dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.
Chapter 47: The Son of the Master, Mātṛceṭa (54). Chapter Forty-seven: The Son of the Master, Mātṛceṭa.
[In the Dan edition, this is Chapter Fifty-four. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a brahmin in the country named Śreṣṭhin; his household was very wealthy, yet he had no children. He went to the six teachers and asked them about the causes and conditions for this.
The six teachers replied, "Your physiognomy shows that you will have no son.
Thereupon, Śreṇika returned home; wearing soiled and greasy clothes, he was filled with grief and discontent, thinking to himself:
"I have no offspring; once my life comes to an end, my household wealth and property shall pass to the king.
Having reflected thus, his grief and distress increased all the more.
A Brahmin woman was close friends with a certain bhikṣuṇī.
When the bhikṣuṇī happened to go to her house, she saw her husband looking distressed and emaciated, and asked him,
"For what reason is your husband so sorrowful and haggard?"
The Brahmin’s wife replied to him immediately, saying, "Our household has no children;
we went to consult the Six Teachers, and their divination and physiognomy indicated that we would have no son."
"For this reason, I am sorrowful and find no joy.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī spoke to him again, saying:
"The disciples of the Six Teachers are not omniscient; how could they know the causes and conditions of a person's karmic actions?"

While the Tathāgata is in the world, he clearly understands all phenomena; regarding the past and the future, he is without obstruction. You may go and question him, and he will surely know them thoroughly.
After the bhikṣuṇī had departed, the wife informed her husband of what she had heard.
Upon hearing this, the husband’s mind was immediately awakened; he changed into new clothes, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him:
“According to my signs and destiny, will I have a son?”
The World-Honored One said, "You shall have a son who is fully endowed with merit and virtue; once he has grown up, he will delight in leaving the household life.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin was filled with immeasurable joy and spoke these words:
"If I simply have a son, what hardship would there be in studying the Way?
At that time, he invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to a meal at his home the following day; the World-Honored One silently granted his consent.

When the time arrived the following day, the Buddha and the assembly of monks went to his house; once the assembly was seated, the Brahmin couple, with single-minded devotion and shared purpose, respectfully served them food and drink.

When the assembly had finished eating, the Buddha and the community of monks returned to their lodgings. On the way, they passed through a marsh where there was a spring of water that was exceptionally clear and delicious; the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus then stopped there to rest.
While the assembly of bhikṣus was each washing their bowls, a monkey came to Ānanda and sought his bowl; fearing it might break, Ānanda did not wish to give it to him.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Give it to him quickly; do not worry.
Following these instructions, he gave it to him.
The monkey took the bowl, went to a honey tree, filled it to the brim, and returned to offer it to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said,
"Remove the impurities from within."
The monkey immediately picked away the bees and insects until it was perfectly clean.
The Buddha then said to him,
"Add water to it."
As instructed, he added water until it was properly mixed, then presented it to the World-Honored One.
Having accepted it, the World-Honored One distributed it among the Saṃgha; they all drank of it together until it was completely exhausted.
The monkey was filled with joy; it leaped and danced, fell into a great pit, and immediately passed away. Its consciousness then entered a womb in the household of Sāketi.

At that time, Sāketi’s wife perceived that she was pregnant; when the months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose countenance and features were so handsome as to be rarely equaled in the world.
At the time of his birth, the household vessels were spontaneously filled with honey; the parents, Śreṣṭhin and his wife, were overcome with joy beyond measure.
They invited various physiognomists to divine his fortune and misfortune.
When the physiognomist had finished his divination, he declared to them:
"This child possesses virtue that is exceedingly good and beyond compare.
He then gave him a name, Mātṛceṭa; in the Jin language, this means "Honey-Superior" (Misheng). Because honey served as an auspicious omen on the day of his birth, he was named accordingly.

When the boy had grown older, he sought to leave the household life; however, his parents, out of affection and attachment, were unwilling to let him go. The boy again earnestly addressed his parents:
"If you must oppose and obstruct me so as not to grant my wish, I shall take my own life; I cannot remain in the secular world."
The parents deliberated and said:
"In the past, the World-Honored One already predicted this in advance, saying he would renounce the world.
If we now insist on keeping him here, he may even choose death; therefore, we should grant his wish."
Having reached a decision together after deliberation, they said to their son, "Follow whatever you desire.
The son was greatly overjoyed;
he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in salutation, and requested to leave the household life. The World-Honored One said to him:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!

At these words, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the Dharma robes appeared upon his body; he immediately became a śramaṇa. Thereupon, [the Buddha] extensively expounded for him the sublime Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and various principles. His mind was opened and his fetters were exhausted, and he attained arhatship.

Whenever he traveled among the people for the purpose of teaching with his monks, if they were thirsty or exhausted, he would toss his alms bowl into the air; it would naturally fill with honey, which everyone would drink together, and all would receive sufficient nourishment.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What merits has Māthuraśreṣṭhin accumulated such that, not long after leaving the household life, he attained arhatship, and whatever his mind requires, he obtains it at will?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you remember the occasion when you accepted the invitation of the teacher's son?
He replied:
"Remember this," the Buddha said. "Ānanda!"

Upon returning from that meal, you arrived at a desolate marsh. At that time, a monkey approached you asking for your bowl; you filled it with honey and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha accepted it, and the monkey, filled with joy, began to dance, fell into a pit, and died immediately—do you remember this?
He replied, "I remember it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"That monkey was none other than Mātulaśreṣṭhin; because he joyfully offered honey upon seeing the Buddha, he was reborn into that family with a handsome and upright appearance, whereupon he left the household life to study the Way and swiftly attained the state of being free from outflows."
Ānanda knelt with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha again, saying,
“By what further causes and conditions was he born among the monkeys?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a young bhikṣu who saw another śramaṇa leap across a stream and said:
'That man is as swift and agile as a monkey.'"
At that time, having heard these words, the śramaṇa asked him:
"Do you know me? He replied:
"I recognize you.
You were a śramaṇa during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha; why do you not recognize me?
Then that śramaṇa spoke to him again, saying:
"Do not call me a 'nominal śramaṇa'; I have fully accomplished all the fruits of a śramaṇa.

Upon hearing this, the youth’s body hair stood on end; he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, seeking mercy and repenting. Because of this confession of his transgression, he did not fall into hell;
however, because he had disparaged an arhat, he was reborn as a monkey for five hundred lifetimes.
"Because he previously left the household life and observed the prohibitive precepts, he is now able to see me; having bathed in my pure transformation, he shall bring all sufferings to an end.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The young bhikṣu at that time was none other than Mātulaśreṣṭhin here."
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had said, were filled with a mixture of grief and joy, and all spoke these words:
"The actions of body, speech, and mind must not fail to be guarded; it is because this bhikṣu failed to guard his speech that he received such a retribution."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is as you have said.

Thereupon, for the sake of the fourfold assembly, he expounded upon all dharmas extensively. Their bodies, speech, and minds were purified; the defilements of their hearts were removed and cleansed, and each attained the fruits of the Path. Some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat; some resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment; and some dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.
The assembly, having heard the Dharma, all rejoiced together and received it with reverence, practicing it accordingly.
48. Chapter on Damila (55). Chapter Forty-Eight on Damila; in the Dan edition, this is the fifty-fifth. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kosala, there was an elder named Dharmagupta, who was noble, influential, and immensely wealthy, yet he had no children.
He offered prayers to all the deities within the kingdom, seeking to obtain offspring; his sincere devotion moved the gods, and his wife soon became pregnant.

When the months of her pregnancy were complete, she gave birth to a son whose physical form was so dignified and handsome that it was rarely seen in the world; she summoned various physiognomists to examine his features and divine his fortune.
An astrologer examined him and, recognizing his virtuous qualities, bestowed upon him a name, calling him Dāmilī.
When he had grown to adulthood, his father passed away; at that time, King Prasenajit conferred upon him his father’s rank and title.
Having received the royal investiture, his father’s former residence transformed into the seven treasures, and all the storehouses became completely filled with every variety of possession.

At that time, Prince Vidūḍabha was afflicted with a purely feverish illness until he became extremely emaciated and distressed; the physicians prescribed medicine, stating that his body must be anointed with ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*) for him to recover.
The king immediately issued an edict, proclaiming throughout the kingdom:
"Whoever possesses ox-head sandalwood, let them bring it to the royal palace;
I shall purchase it for a price of one thousand taels of gold."
When the proclamation had been made throughout the entire city,
yet no one brought anything, a certain man addressed the king, saying:
"The householder Cunda of the Kosalas possesses great wealth within his home."
When the king heard this, he mounted his carriage and went in person to seek him out, arriving at the gate of the householder Cāṇḍa-mi-li.
At that time, the gatekeeper entered and announced:
"King Prasenajit has arrived and is standing outside the gate."
The elder was filled with joy and immediately went out to welcome him, inviting the king to enter his palace.

Upon approaching the outer gate, he saw that it was made entirely of white silver. Inside the gate was a woman of exquisite and peerless beauty, sitting upon a silver couch spinning silver thread, attended on both sides by ten young girls.
Then the king asked,
"Is this your wife?
She replied:
"No, she is a gatekeeper's maidservant.
The King continued to question her:
"What use have you for such lowly women?"
Mili replied, "I shall convey the message.

He then entered the middle gate, which was made of pure, deep-blue lapis lazuli. Inside the gate was a woman whose countenance was dignified and beautiful, even more so than the one before; her attendants on both sides were twice as numerous as those previously mentioned.
Entering the inner gate, which was made entirely of gold, there was a woman within the gate whose countenance was upright and beautiful, surpassing all others.
She sat upon a golden couch spinning golden thread, while her attendants on both sides were twice as numerous as those previously mentioned.
The king also asked him,
"Is this woman your wife? He replied:
"No," he replied.

Upon entering the palace, he saw a floor of lapis lazuli, as transparent and clear as water. Carved into the ceiling were various animal forms and images of aquatic creatures; when the wind blew, their reflections appeared upon the ground, shimmering and swaying. Seeing this, the king was struck with doubt and fear, thinking it was actual water, and asked:
"There is no other land here; have you made a pond before the palace?"
Mili replied, "This is not water; it is dark-blue lapis lazuli.
He then removed a ring and bracelet of the seven precious gems from his finger and cast them upon the ground; he proceeded directly to the edge, where he stopped, obstructed by the wall.
The King, seeing this, was filled with joy; they immediately entered the inner quarters together and ascended the palace of the seven treasures.
There, Lady Mili sat upon a throne made of dark blue lapis lazuli, and she invited the King to sit upon another exquisite couch.
Lady Mili’s eyes immediately filled with tears.
The King asked her,
"Why are you weeping?"
"Do you not rejoice?
The lady replied,
"It would be most excellent if the King were to come!"
"However, there is a slight scent of smoke from the King's garments that causes me to shed tears;
it is not that I harbor any ill will toward you. The King then asked, "Is no fire being lit within your home now?"
He replied, "No. The king asked:
"With what do you cook your food?
He replied,
"When I wish to eat, meals of a hundred flavors appear spontaneously before me."
The king asked again:
"In the darkness of night, what serves as light?
He replied:
"Use the maṇi jewel.
Thereupon, he closed the doors and all the windows and brought forth the maṇi jewel; its brilliance surpassed that of the midday sun.
At that time, Dhanamitra knelt and addressed the king, saying:
“Great King!
Why have you troubled yourself with such an arduous journey?
The king replied to him:
