"My son has been exiled and is gravely ill; he requires ox-head sandalwood, and so I have come to seek it.

Mili was overjoyed and led [the king] into the various treasuries to point out the goods. There were seven precious jewels, brilliant and pure as the sun, and piles of sandalwood beyond measure or calculation.
He then said to the king, "Take whatever you require."
The king replied, "I require two *liang*.
He then broke off and gave it to him; the amount was exactly sufficient.
Even though his attendants first escorted him back to his own country,
the king, out of deep respect and mindfulness, spoke to him, saying:
"You must go to see the Buddha."
Mili replied, "What is meant by 'Buddha'?
The king said:
“Have you not heard?

The son of King Śuddhodana from Kapilavastu, having become weary of old age, sickness, and death, left the household life to study the Way. Having perfected the Way, he is titled Buddha. Possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, with supernatural powers and wisdom so preeminent and peerless that he is honored as the Most Venerable among gods and men, he is therefore called Buddha.”
Having heard this, Mili conceived a heart of profound reverence and asked the king,
"Where is he now?
The king replied to him:
"I am staying at the Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha.

After the king had departed, he went immediately to see the Buddha; beholding the Buddha’s majestic countenance, which surpassed that praised by the king ten thousandfold, his heart was filled with joy. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and inquired after his well-being.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna. He knelt upright with palms joined and requested ordination.
The Buddha immediately granted his permission, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!"

His beard and hair fell away, and the dharma robes clothed his body; the Buddha again preached for him the True Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and with all mental defilements utterly exhausted, he became an Arhat.
At that time, Ānanda and the bhikṣus joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, asking the World-Honored One:
"What meritorious virtues did the bhikṣu Dāmilī possess that, though born among humans, he enjoyed celestial blessings and emoluments yet took no pleasure in worldly delights;
and how was it that not long after leaving the household life, he immediately attained the fruits of the Path?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Listen well, for I shall speak!

In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin. After his parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka), there were five bhikṣus who made a solemn covenant together, seeking a secluded place where they would practice the Path in unison."
They saw a forest grove where the spring water was clear, sweet, pure, and delightful; at that time, all the bhikṣus raised their voices in unison and exhorted one man, saying:
"This place is far from the city, and begging for alms here is laborious and exhausting; you should perform a meritorious deed by making offerings to us."
At that time, one person immediately gave his consent.
He went among the people of the world and exhorted the donors to provide food daily.
The four men’s bodies became at ease, and they applied themselves single-mindedly to practicing the Way; within ninety days, they attained the fruits of the Path.
Then, with one mind, they said to this bhikṣu:
"Because of you, we have found peace; that which our original hearts intended, we have now attained."
"What wish do you seek?
Seek it as you please.
At that time, the bhikṣu’s heart was filled with joy, and he spoke these words:

"May I, in the future, naturally attain wealth and honor among devas and humans; may all things I desire arise without the application of effort; may I encounter a holy teacher who surpasses those such as you by hundreds of thousands of millions of times; and having heard the Dharma, may my mind be purified so that I swiftly attain the fruit of the Way."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The bhikṣu at that time was none other than this present Dāmali.

Because he provided for those four bhikṣus, for ninety-one kalpas he was born among gods and humans, noble, wealthy, and dignified, never dwelling in poor or lowly households; now he has been able to see me and attain the Way, crossing over into liberation."

At that time, Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, each exhorted themselves to diligence and applied themselves with vigor to the cultivation of the Path. Some attained the first fruit up to the fourth fruit; others gave rise to the mind of universal salvation and abided in non-retrogression. All were filled with joy, receiving the teaching upon their heads and practicing it accordingly.
Chapter 49: On the Protection by the Elephant (56). Chapter Forty-nine on the Protection by the Elephant. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in the kingdom of Magadha, there was an elder who fathered a son endowed with perfect features, whom all held in great affection and respect.
On the day of his birth, a golden elephant spontaneously emerged from within his storehouse; the parents were filled with joy and invited a physiognomist to bestow a name upon him.
At that time, the physiognomists, seeing the child's merit and virtue, asked his parents:
"What auspicious signs occurred on the day this child was born?
They immediately replied to them, saying:
"There was a golden elephant born together with the boy.
Because of this auspicious omen, he was given the name Elephant Protector (Hastipāla).

As the boy gradually grew up, the elephant likewise grew; whenever the boy could walk, the elephant could also walk, and whether entering or leaving, advancing or stopping, they were never separated from one another.
If the elephant does not wish to go out, it remains inside.
Its excrement and urine consist solely of fine gold.
The elephant's keeper constantly accompanies five hundred sons of elders on excursions and plays, and they each recount the extraordinary events within their own households.
Some might say:
"The houses, dwellings, couches, and seats in my home are all made of the seven treasures.
Others might say of themselves:
"My house and its gardens are likewise made of various jewels," another said;
yet another declared,
"The treasuries of my house are perpetually filled with wondrous jewels."
There were many such instances of various kinds.
At that time, Hastipāla spoke again of his own accord:
"On the day of my birth, a golden elephant appeared spontaneously within my home."
"As I have grown older, I am capable of traveling on foot; the elephant is likewise so, and it does not hinder me.
I constantly ride it as I travel east and west to observe the sights, moving at whatever speed I desire, which is most agreeable to my disposition."
"Their excrement and urine are pure, high-quality gold.
At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru was also among them; hearing what Hastipāla said, he thought to himself:
"If I become king, I shall seize this for myself."
Having succeeded to the throne, he summoned Elephant-Protector (Hastipāla) and instructed him to lead an elephant to the king’s presence.
At that time, Elephant-Protector’s father said to his son:
“King Ajātaśatru is cruel, violent, and unrighteous; he is greedy and stingy, inflicting such tyranny even upon his own father, let alone others.”
"I have summoned you now because I wish to covet your elephant;
perhaps it might be seized from you. His son replied, "This elephant of mine cannot be plundered."
At that moment, father and son together mounted the elephant and went to see the king.
Then the gatekeeper entered and informed the king:
"Gajapāla and his son have mounted the elephant and are at the gate."
The king told him, "I permit you to enter riding the elephant.

Thereupon, the gatekeeper returned and reported this; the father and son, Elephant-Protector and his son, rode the elephant straight forward. Once they had reached the interior of the palace, they dismounted from the elephant and prostrated themselves before the king, inquiring after his well-being.
The king was greatly delighted and commanded him to take a seat, granting him food and drink. After they had conversed briefly for a short while, he took his leave of the king and wished to depart.
The king said to Khaṇḍa: "Keep Khaṇḍa here; do not let him go out."
Hastipāla was delighted and, following the instruction, left him there and departed from the palace on foot.
Before long, the elephant sank into the ground and then leaped back out through the palace gate; Hastipāla was able to mount it again and return home.
After a short while, he thought to himself:
"The king is unrighteous and his punishments are unjust; because of this elephant, I may perhaps be harmed."
"Now that the Buddha is in the world, his grace moistens all living beings; yet this does not compare to leaving home to cultivate the pure life (brahmacarya).

He then addressed his parents, seeking permission to enter the Way. His parents gave their consent, whereupon he took his leave and departed, riding upon his golden elephant, until he arrived at the Jetavana.
Having seen the World-Honored One, he prostrated himself in worship and set forth his original aspiration. The Buddha immediately granted him permission, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!

His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and with the dharma-robes upon his body, he became a śramaṇa. The Buddha then preached for him the essential Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; his spirit attained transcendent awakening, and he immediately realized arhatship.
Whenever he was with the bhikṣus, meditating on the path under trees in the forest, that golden elephant would always appear before his eyes.
When the people of Śrāvastī heard there was a golden elephant, they gathered in competition to see it; the sudden clamor and lack of stillness hindered and obstructed their practice of the Way.
At that time, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha of the matter with their minds. The Buddha told Khaṇḍadravya:
"Because of this elephant, there has arisen such disturbance; you should now quickly dispatch the elephant so that it may depart."
Gajapāla said to the Buddha,
"I have long wished to send him away, yet he is unwilling to go.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"You should say to him:
'My life-portion is now exhausted; I no longer require you.
Say this three times, and the elephant shall perish."
At that time, Gajapāla, having received the instruction of the World-Honored One, addressed the elephant three times, saying:
"I have no need for you.
Thereupon, the golden elephant immediately entered into the earth.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with wonder and said to the World-Honored One:
"What virtues did the bhikṣu Hastipāla originally cultivate? In what field of merit did he plant these roots of goodness, such that he has obtained such a magnificent retribution as this?"
The Buddha told Ānanda and the bhikṣus:
"If there are sentient beings who plant even a small amount of goodness within the field of merit of the Triple Gem, they shall obtain an infinite fruit."
In the distant past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the lifespan of the people of that world was twenty thousand years.
When that Buddha had completed his work of teaching and transformation and passed away into parinirvāṇa, his sacred relics were distributed and many stupas and temples were erected.
At that time, there was a stupa containing an image of the Bodhisattva as he descended from Tuṣita Heaven riding upon an elephant and entered his mother’s womb;
at that time, the body of the elephant had a small abrasion.
At that time, there was a man who happened to be circumambulating the stupa and saw that the elephant’s body was wounded; he then thought to himself:
"This is the elephant upon which the Bodhisattva rides; since it is now damaged, I shall repair it."
He took mud to patch it and smeared it with yellow orpiment, then made this vow:
"May I, in the future, always dwell in a position of honor and nobility, never lacking in wealth or resources."

When that person’s life ended, they were reborn in the heavens; having exhausted their celestial lifespan, they descended to be born among humans, always being born into families of noble rank, wealth, and happiness. Their countenance was upright and handsome, surpassing that of the world, and they were constantly attended by golden elephants at all times.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who that elephant trainer was at that time, it is this very Elephant-Protector (Gajapāla).
Because he trained elephants in that world, from that time forward, throughout his lives among devas and humans, he has received natural rewards."

Because of his reverent heart and his devotion to the Triple Gem, he has now encountered me and received my sublime transformation; the defilements of his mind are entirely exhausted, and he has attained the state of an Arhat.

The Venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all enlightened and attained their respective goals. Some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat; some resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path; and some realized the stage of non-retrogression. All were filled with joy, reverently upholding and practicing the teaching.
Chapter 50: Pāpā (57). Chapter Fifty: Pāpā. [In the Dan-ben edition, this is Chapter 57. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty venerable disciples.

At that time, there was a king of Vārāṇasī named Paramada. The king had a chief minister who fathered a son endowed with the thirty-two marks and fully possessed of all the secondary characteristics; his body was the color of purple-gold, and his appearance was exceptionally distinguished.
When the Prime Minister saw his son, his joy redoubled; he immediately summoned a physiognomist and ordered him to examine the boy's marks.
The physiognomist inspected him and exclaimed:
"How extraordinary!
His marks and signs were fully perfected, his merit was exceptionally complete, and his wisdom and eloquence were thoroughly penetrating, surpassing those of all men.
The prime minister was even more joyful and consequently gave him a name. The physiognomist asked again:
"Since his birth, what extraordinary events have occurred?"
The prime minister replied:

"This is most extraordinary and unprecedented. Her mother’s natural disposition was never virtuous; yet since she became pregnant, she has felt compassion for those in distress and has protected and nurtured the common people with equal kindness."
The physiognomist joyfully said,
"This is the child's own aspiration.
Thereupon he conferred a name upon him, calling him Maitreya.
The parents were filled with joy and their hearts knew no bounds.
The boy’s extraordinary reputation spread throughout the land; when the king heard of it, he was seized with fear and said, "I am mindful of this child, whose marks and features are so magnificent.
Should he possess such high virtue, he will surely seize my throne."
"While he is still young, he should be eliminated in advance; if allowed to grow old, he will surely become a source of calamity.
Having made this plan, he immediately commanded his chief minister:
"I have heard that you have a son whose appearance is extraordinary; you may bring him here, for I wish to see him."
At that time, when the women of the palace heard Prince Kāśyapa’s inquiry and learned of the King’s plot, they were consumed by inner anguish as if in boiling water or fire.
The Prince had an uncle named Pāpali, who resided in the kingdom of Pāriyātra as its state preceptor;
he was brilliant, profoundly learned, possessed of exceptional talent and penetrating wisdom, and five hundred disciples constantly followed him to seek instruction.
At that time, the Prime Minister, out of affection for his son and fearing he might be harmed, devised a secret plan and sent someone on an elephant to deliver him to his maternal uncle.
When the uncle saw Maitreya, observing his handsome appearance, he took special care to nourish him and held him in high esteem, cherishing him as if he were his own heart.

As he grew older, his grandfather taught him to study; in a single day of instruction, he excelled more than others would in an entire year, and before a year had passed, he was proficient in the common scriptures.

At that time, Pāpali saw that his nephew had mastered all the books despite his short period of study. Desiring to hold a gathering to celebrate his excellence, he sent a disciple to Vārāṇasī to speak with the prime minister regarding the boy's learning, requesting precious treasures to provide for the assembly.

On his way, the disciple heard people speak of the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues and, longing to see him, set out for the Buddha. Before he had even reached him, he was devoured by a tiger along the way.
Riding upon that virtuous mind, he was reborn in the first of the four heavens.

Pāpali exhausted all his possessions and gathered together his wealth to organize a great assembly; he invited the brahmins, and when they had all assembled, he prepared and provided various kinds of delicious and sweet delicacies.
When the assembly had concluded, he bestowed a great *dakṣiṇā* (alms-offering), such that each person received five hundred gold coins.
Once the giving was finished, his wealth and goods were completely exhausted.
There was a brahmin named Raudrākṣa who arrived last of all; seeing Pāpali, he said:
"I have come from afar; even though I have received no food, you should give me five hundred gold coins as a matter of course.
Pāpali replied, "My goods are exhausted; truly, I have nothing I wish to give you."
Raudrākṣa said: "I have heard of your charitable offerings and came here with hope; why do you see me in vain and fail to bestow your bounty?
If you persist in refusal and do not grant me anything, in seven days your head shall split into seven pieces."
At that time, having heard these words, Pāpali reflected to himself:
"In this world there are evil spells and other forms of sorcery; such matters must not be taken lightly, for it is possible that such a thing exists."
When his wealth was completely exhausted and he had no means left, he became anxious with grief and felt deep fear.

His former disciple, who had been reborn in heaven, saw from afar that his teacher was distressed and helpless; he immediately descended from heaven, came before him, and asked his teacher, "For what reason are you so sorrowful?"
The Master related the circumstances and causes in detail.
Upon hearing his words, the deity immediately addressed the Master, saying:
"Laudakṣa does not yet recognize the Summit Dharma; he is a person of folly, delusion, and evil heterodoxy—what, after all, can he possibly achieve?"
"And yet you worry about this.
Now there is only the Buddha, who most thoroughly understands the supreme Dharma; he is the unsurpassed Dharma King and is uniquely worthy of taking refuge in.
At that time, Pāpali, having heard the deva speak of the Buddha, immediately asked him again:
"Who is this Buddha? The deva then replied:

"The Buddha was born into the house of King Śuddhodana in Kapilavastu; he emerged from his mother’s right side and immediately took seven steps, proclaiming himself the Honored One among gods and men. He possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor excellencies, and his radiance illuminates heaven and earth. Brahmā and Śakra attend upon him, while thirty-two auspicious omens manifest and shake the world."

The physiognomist observed him and made a prediction regarding two possibilities: that if he remained at home, he would become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin rājā*); if he left the household life, he would attain Buddhahood.

Witnessing old age, sickness, and death, he took no pleasure in the position of kingship; he leaped over the palace walls and departed the country. After six years of ascetic practice, beneath the Bodhi tree, he defeated eighteen billion Māras. During the latter part of the night, he fully perfected the Buddha-dharma, becoming complete in the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

Upon arriving at Vārāṇasī, he first turned the Wheel of Dharma; Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the other four attained the exhaustion of outflows, eighty thousand devas obtained the purity of the Dharma-eye, and countless devas and humans resolved their minds upon the Great Way.

He then proceeded to Magadha, where he converted Uruvilvā, along with Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, bringing forth twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus as his followers; they were designated as the Saṃgha, and their merit and wisdom were beyond measure or calculation.
"In short, he is named Buddha, and he is currently at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
When Pāpali heard this praise of the Buddha's virtues, he reflected to himself:
"There must surely be a Buddha."
"In the records I have written, it was foretold that when a Buddha appeared beneath the stars, heaven and earth would shake greatly, and a sage would be born.
Now all these signs are present; it seems this must indeed be so."
He then commanded Maitreya and sixteen others:
"Go to see Gautama and observe his physical marks and signs.
If he is endowed with all the marks, think of ways to challenge him."
"My teacher Pāpali—how many marks does he possess?
"As for me now, my body possesses two marks:
first, hair that is deep blue-black; second, a broad and long tongue."
If he recognizes him, he will again find it difficult in his mind to ask:
"How old is my teacher Pāpali now?
For one of my age, he would now be one hundred and twenty years old.
If he were to know this, he would further think to himself:
"What is the caste of my teacher, Pāpali?
I wish to know his lineage; it is that of a Brāhmaṇa."
If he answers regarding his disciples, you should again challenge him with this thought:
"How many disciples does my teacher Pāṭali have?
To which he will reply, "As I do now, he has five hundred disciples."
"If he answers that he knows the number, he must surely be the Buddha; you must all become his disciples and send one person to bring me news.

Then Maitreya and the others proceeded toward Rājagṛha and approached Vulture Peak Mountain. There they saw the Buddha’s footprints, the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel shining as clearly as a painting.
They immediately asked the people, "Whose tracks are these?"
Someone replied, "This is the footprint of the Buddha.
Thereupon Maitreya and the others conceived a sense of longing and reverence; they paced back and forth beside the footprint, filled with profound veneration and thirsting for the sight.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Kṣānti who took a dead insect and placed it at the site of the Buddha’s footprint, showing it to Maitreya and the others, saying:
"All of you gaze upon this footprint with such reverence, admiration, and longing; yet you trample and kill living beings—what is so extraordinary about that?"
Maitreya and the others all stepped forward to examine it; observing its form and features closely, they saw it was a dead insect, and they immediately asked the bhikṣuṇī, “Whose disciple are you?”
The bhikṣuṇī replied,
“She is a disciple of the Buddha.
Then Maitreya and the others each spoke:
“Among the disciples of the Buddha, there is indeed such a person as this.

He gradually approached the place where the Buddha was; seeing the World-Honored One from afar, his radiance shining brightly and his various marks resplendent, he immediately began to count those marks, yet he could not find a second.
The Buddha then extended his tongue for him to cover his face, and further, by means of his supernormal power, caused him to see the male organ concealed within a sheath.
Seeing that the marks were complete in number, he was filled with even greater joy; he then followed his teacher’s instruction and mentally questioned him from afar:
"How many marks does my teacher, Pāpali, possess?"
The Buddha replied from afar:
"Your teacher Pāpali possesses only two marks:
first, his hair is deep blue-black; second, he has a broad and long tongue."
Having heard these words, he again questioned himself in his mind:
"How old is my teacher, Pāpali?
The Buddha answered from afar:
“Your teacher Pāpali is one hundred and twenty years old.
Having heard this, he again thought to himself with difficulty:
“What is the lineage of my teacher Pāpali?”
The Buddha replied from afar:
"Your teacher, Pāṭali, is of the Brahmin caste.
Having heard this, he again reflected with doubt in his mind:
“How many disciples does my teacher Pāṭali have?
The Buddha replied from afar:
“Your teacher Pāṭali has five hundred disciples.”
At that time, those present in the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had said, were greatly astonished that the Tathāgata spoke these words alone.
Then the disciples knelt with their right knees on the ground and asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!...”
"For what reason did you say those words?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"There was one named Pāpali in the kingdom of Pāpali-pudraka, who sent sixteen disciples to come to my place to examine my physical marks. Because they harbored doubts in their minds, I answered each of them in turn."

At that time, Maitreya and the others, having heard the Buddha’s answers to their challenges, found that every matter was exactly as it truly is, without the slightest discrepancy. They conceived a deep sense of reverence and admiration, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and those sixteen people attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Each rose from their seat and requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha said, "Welcome!"

Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, and dharma robes appeared upon their bodies; they immediately became śramaṇas. The Buddha again employed skillful means to preach the Dharma for them, and those fifteen people attained the state of arhat.
At that time, Maitreya and the others deliberated among themselves, saying:
"The teacher Pāpali is far away and waiting in anxiety; we should immediately dispatch someone back to inform him of the news."
Among the sixteen men, there was one named Piṅgiya, who was the nephew of Pāpali; the group immediately dispatched him to deliver the message.
He returned to his own country to the place where Pāpali was and recounted in detail everything he had heard and seen.
Upon hearing this, Pāpali felt joy arise in his heart; he immediately rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined toward Rājagṛha, and spoke these sincere words:

"To be born in an age of sages is extremely rare to encounter. I long to behold the Honored One’s countenance and receive his pure transformation. Yet, my years have already advanced and my physical strength is no longer robust; though I possess sincere devotion, there is no means by which it may reach him on its own."
“World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
You already know the minds of men in advance; I only pray that you will deign to come and grant me relief.

At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing his intention from afar, arrived before him in the mere twinkling of an arm’s extension and contraction. Having paid homage, the man raised his head and immediately beheld the World-Honored One. Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, he prostrated himself, offered greetings, invited the Buddha to take a seat, and attended upon the Buddha with reverent solemnity.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
At that time, the World-Honored One returned to Vulture Peak Mountain.

King Śuddhodana, hearing that the Buddha had realized the Way and was traveling about to teach and transform others, saving many, felt a deep longing and yearning, desiring to behold him. He addressed Udāyin:
"Go to the Buddha's presence and convey my intent, saying to Siddhārtha: 'You previously made a vow that you would return once you had attained the Way.
I pray that you will honor your former word and come to see me at this time.'"
When Udāyī arrived, he fully conveyed the King’s intention; the Buddha immediately granted his consent, saying he would go in seven days.
Udāyī was delighted and returned to report the news.
When King Śuddhodana heard this, he addressed his ministers, saying:
"Udayin has arrived and says that the Buddha is about to return.

Adorn the city within and ensure it is made utterly clean; smear the streets and roads with fragrant paste, erect banners and streamers everywhere, and stock up abundantly on flowers and incense so that we may await him for offerings."
When the preparations were complete, he went forty *li* outside with his various ministers to welcome the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Tathāgata was together with the great assembly; eight Vajrapāṇi spirits stood at the eight sides, and the Four Heavenly Kings each led the way in front.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the various devas of the desire realm, attended upon his left;
at that time, Brahmā, King of the Gods, together with the devas of the form realm, attended upon his right;
and the assembly of bhikṣus stood in a line behind him.

The Buddha was amidst the assembly, emitting a great radiance that illuminated heaven and earth; his majesty surpassed that of the sun and moon. Together with the great multitude, he traveled through the void, gradually drawing near to the king until he descended level with the heads of the people. The king, along with his ministers, subjects, consorts, and court ladies, beheld the vast assembly shining brilliantly and clearly, with the Buddha at their center like the moon among the stars.

The King was filled with great joy and, without realizing it, descended to prostrate himself before him. Having completed his prostrations, he exchanged greetings and returned to the kingdom with him, staying at the Nyagrodha Monastery.

At that time, according to the laws of the land, there was a distinction between men and women; the King, along with his ministers and subjects, listened to the Dharma daily. Hearing the Dharma, they attained awakening, and many were delivered.
However, the women among them each harbored resentment, thinking:

"Although the Buddha and the great assembly have returned to the kingdom, the men there have the good fortune to behold him and hear his teaching, while we women do not receive such grace and protection."
The Buddha, knowing his intention, spoke to the king:
"From this day forward, let the men and women of the kingdom take turns attending the Dharma for one day and one watch."
From that time forward, he brought many to liberation.

At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī, after the Buddha had already left the household life, personally spun and wove a single bolt of golden cloth, maintaining it in her thoughts and waiting only for the Buddha.
Having seen the Buddha, her joy reached the very marrow of her heart; she immediately took this rice gruel and offered it to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to Gautamī, "Take this rice gruel and go offer it to the Saṃgha."
Then Mahāprajāpatī addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Since the Buddha went forth into homelessness, my mind has been constantly preoccupied with him; therefore, I have spun and woven by hand, intending my heart to wait for the Buddha."
"I only pray that you will look upon me with compassion and accept it from me!
The Buddha said to him:
"I know my mother’s single-minded desire to give it to me;
however, because of her affectionate attachment, the merit would not be vast. If she were to give it to the Sangha, the reward she would obtain would be far greater."
"I know this matter, and for that reason I exhort you.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"If there is a donor who makes sixteen kinds of full-scale individual invitations, although they obtain a karmic reward, it is not yet considered much."
What are the sixteen?

There are eight classes each of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; yet, as in the case of the Saṃgha, if one were to invite four people at random, the merit obtained would be greater than that [of the former], such that the latter does not equal even a sixteenth part of the former.

In the future, at the end of the age when the Dharma is about to perish, even if there are bhikṣus who keep wives and harbor sons, and groups of four or more who bear the name of the Saṃgha, you should regard them with reverence as you would Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī’s mind was opened and she attained understanding; she immediately offered her robes to the assembly of monks. As they were passed through the ranks of the Sangha, no one wished to take them, until they reached Maitreya, who then accepted them.
Thereafter, the World-Honored One, together with the community of bhikṣus, traveled to Vārāṇasī, proceeding there to teach and transform beings.

At that time, Maitreya, wearing a golden-colored robe, was upright in appearance; his complexion was purple-gold, and his inner character accorded perfectly with his outward form. His deportment was composed and orderly as he entered the city of Vārāṇasī, intending to go on his almsround.

Arriving at the great crossroads, he stood holding his alms bowl. When the people beheld his physical appearance, they gathered around to gaze upon him, never tiring of the sight; though they all held him in deep reverence, none could bring themselves to offer him food.

There was a pearl-drilling artisan who happened to arrive at the monastery and saw Maitreya; feeling profound reverence and admiration, he immediately asked the Venerable One, "Have you received food yet?"
He replied, "I have not yet attained it.

He then invited [the monk] to return home, prepared food and drink, and after [the monk] had eaten and rinsed his mouth, he preached the sublime Dharma for him; the words were lofty and beautiful, and [the listener] never grew weary of hearing them.

At that time, there was a great elder who, wishing to marry off his daughter, first gave him a pearl and hired him to bore it, saying, "If you succeed in boring it through, I shall give you one hundred thousand coins."
At that time, the elder sent a messenger to request [the jewels]. Having heard the Dharma, the jeweler’s five faculties were filled with joy and contentment, and he said:
"Go for now! I shall polish them later."
The man spoke again:
"It is urgently needed now; think of it and apply yourself to it immediately.
Having given these instructions, he departed and related everything to the elder.
After a short while, he was sent out again to fetch him, yet [the man] continued to listen to the Dharma and had not yet made a hole.
He returned and told the elder, who spoke with resentment:
"Since I have hired you repeatedly and your services were not in vain, why do you now procrastinate and fail to meet my needs?"
He sent another person again, providing him with money and instructing him: "If he has not yet pierced them, bring the pearls back.
When the messenger arrived and inquired, the man was still listening to the Dharma; knowing the pearls had not been pierced, he urgently demanded them back.
When there was no other recourse, he immediately took it and returned it to him.
The pearl-stringer remained before Maitreya, listening to the Dharma in successive order, his mind free from weariness or retreat.
His wife became angry and reproached her husband, saying:
"With a mere moment's labor, you could have earned a hundred thousand coins to provide for our family's lack of food and clothing;
yet you merely listened to the flowery talk of that śramaṇa and lost such a profit of wealth."
Upon hearing these words, the man felt regret and remorse in his heart.
Maitreya, knowing his thoughts, spoke to him, saying:
"Would you now be willing to go with me to the vihāra?"
He replied, "So be it.
Immediately they went together to the monastery; having brought him into the midst of the Sangha, he asked the assembly of monks:
"If there is a donor who invites a single śramaṇa of pure precepts to their home for offerings, how does the profit gained from this compare to someone obtaining one hundred thousand coins?"
Then Kauṇḍinya immediately spoke, saying:

"Suppose there were a person who obtained the precious treasures of a hundred chariots; even calculating its merit and benefit, it would not equal the vast and great gain of inviting a single śramaṇa of pure precepts to one's home for offerings."
Śāriputra said:

"Suppose there were a person who obtained precious jewels filling the entirety of Jambudvīpa; this would still not equal the immense benefit gained by inviting one who maintains pure precepts to one's home for offerings."
Maudgalyāyana said:

"Even if someone were to obtain seven treasures filling two intermediate world-systems, it would truly not be as beneficial as inviting a single pure śramaṇa to provide offerings at one's home, for the profit gained from that would be far greater."
The other bhikṣus likewise each cited analogies from various quarters to compare their respective benefits, finding that theirs were all far greater than his.
Then Aniruddha spoke again of himself:

"Even if one were to obtain the treasures filling the four continents of the world, the benefit would still not equal the manifold and extraordinary gain of inviting a single pure śramaṇa to one’s home to provide offerings."
The reason for this is that I am its witness.
I recall that ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin; after his parinirvāṇa, the sutras and the Dharma were completely extinguished.
At that time, in Jambudvīpa, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī.
At that time, within that kingdom, there was a caravan leader whose family was immensely wealthy and lacked for nothing.
He had two sons, both of whom were handsome; the elder was named Teḷa, and the younger was called Ateḷa.
As his life drew to a close, the father instructed his two sons:
"I shall certainly not escape death; I am about to pass into the next world."
"You, brothers, should mindfully support one another; with unified hearts and combined strength, be careful not to live apart. Why is this so?
It is like a single strand of thread, which cannot bear the weight of binding an elephant; only when many strands are gathered together can they restrain an elephant."
For example, a single reed cannot burn by itself; however, when held together as a bundle, it burns so fiercely that it cannot be extinguished.

You brothers are just like this: if you rely upon one another, outsiders will not be able to harm you, and with internal harmony and diligence at home, your wealth and enterprises will increase day by day.
After these instructions were given, he passed away.
His brothers followed his teachings and lived together for some time. Later, Ārṭīṭa’s wife thought to herself:
"Now that we live together, it is difficult to visit my brother's household; guests and acquaintances cannot be received there."
"If we were to separate and each strive for our own ends, since there would be no obstacles to our individual pursuits, we could each establish our own households.
Having reflected on this matter, she related it in full to her husband.
When Ārta heard what his wife said, he considered it unacceptable; yet his wife urged him persistently, citing extensive principles and reasonings.

Ārta’s mind was turned, and he reported the matter to his elder brother. The elder brother, in turn, cited the words his father had uttered at the time of his death, providing broad analogies and demonstrating the reasons why it was impossible.
At that time, the wife of Arita repeatedly urged her husband, but he was resolute and urgently sought a separation from his household;
seeing his intent was firm, the elder brother divided the property and established separate households for them.

After the division of the estate, Ārdraka and his wife gave rein to their passions and indulged their whims; they gathered a following, lived in luxury and excess, and disregarded all rules of propriety. Before several years had passed, the family wealth was exhausted, and they were utterly destitute with no means left.
He went to his elder brother to beg for it.
His brother took pity on him again and gave him one hundred thousand coins.
When these were exhausted, he asked for more; this happened six times, and in total, his brother gave him six million coins.
Later, he came again to request [his share].
His elder brother rebuked him once more:
"Your deceased father gave you instructions and admonitions which you did not follow; before even a short time had passed, you have come to ask for a division of the property."
The funeral expenses have been beyond measure and cannot be fully provided; previously I gave you six hundred thousand coins, yet you were not content and came again to beg for more.
Now I give you another one hundred thousand coins; whether you have enough or not, do not come to solicit further.

Having received this reprimand, the younger brother felt ashamed and took back the money. The husband and wife reformed their conduct, being careful in their personal lives and frugal in their expenditures. They applied themselves diligently to their household affairs, and their property increased daily; subsequently, they gradually became wealthy and were no longer in want.

His elder brother, Teṭa, had met with successive misfortunes; his estates were ruined and destroyed, his wealth scattered, and his household affairs were suddenly brought to utter destitution. Having no means of support, he went to his younger brother’s side and recounted their hardships, requesting a small amount of money, but his needs could not be fully met.
His younger brother, feeling resentment and disdain, said to his elder brother:
"In looking toward your family, you do not realize there is poverty; why have you come again to beg from me?"
Having spoken these words, he refused to share the food.
His elder brother then returned home, struck with amazement, thinking:
"In the midst of birth and death, what is there to fear?"
"If even brothers born of the same body do not recognize the kindness of their upbringing, how much less so others?

When he reasoned thus, his mind became weary of the world; he left his home to enter the mountains, where he sat in meditation contemplating the arising and ceasing of all phenomena. His mind then attained awakening, and he became a Pratyekabuddha. His dignified demeanor was worthy of admiration as he entered the city to beg for alms.
Later, during a time of famine when the people were destitute and hungry, it was difficult for the Pratyekabuddha to obtain almsfood.

At that time, his younger brother Arita became increasingly impoverished; encountering yet another year of scarcity, his supply of grain could not sustain them. Every day he went to gather firewood and sold it to purchase *priyaṅgu* seeds, providing for himself and his wife and children.

One morning at dawn, he went early to enter the marsh; there, within the city gate, he saw a pratyekabuddha whose dignified demeanor was worthy of admiration as he entered the city to beg for food, whereupon [the man] immediately went to gather firewood.
Returning to the gate, he saw the Pratyekabuddha coming out with an empty bowl and thought to himself:
"This is a noble being; I saw him enter the city this morning, yet now he comes empty-handed. If I were to accompany him back to his dwelling, I should share my food with him and offer it as a gift."
Having formed this thought, he abandoned them and departed.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, immediately perceiving his intention, followed after him and went to the gateway.

When Arita saw this, his heart was filled with joy; he immediately prepared a seat and invited him to enter and sit. He then requested his own portion of millet porridge and, holding it with his own hands, offered it to the Pratyekabuddha.
Then the Pratyekabuddha said to Aṭṭhaka, "You too are hungry and thirsty;
we should eat together. Aṭṭhaka replied:
"We are people of the mundane world, eating at no fixed hour, whereas you, Venerable One, eat but once a day; we only pray that you will accept our offering.

Having finished receiving the food, he was moved by their utmost sincerity: "In the midst of this year's famine, when fathers and sons cannot even save one another, they have been able to cut from their own bodies to offer as alms to me. I shall manifest a transformation for them to bring them joy."
He immediately flew into the air, emitting water and fire from his body, extensively manifesting his supernormal powers, and then returned to stand before him, saying to Aṭṭhaka:
"What wish do you seek?"
"Do as you wish.
Seeing this transformation, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately stepped forward with a sincere heart and made this vow:
"May all sentient beings, who seek wealth through many means, never lack anything in life after life; may whatever they desire arrive according to their wishes."

Furthermore, I pray that in the future I may encounter a Superior Being whose merit exceeds yours by a hundred thousand millionfold, so that under him I may realize the exhaustion of outflows and attain supernormal powers and transformations no different from yours.
Having finished making his vow, he was redoubled in joy.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha returned to his dwelling.
Then Ārṭīṭa immediately went back into the marsh to gather firewood.

Upon arriving, he saw a rabbit and intended to capture it. As he pursued it, drawing closer, he cast a sickle from afar; it struck the ground instantly. Just as he was about to go forward and seize it, the rabbit transformed into a dead man who sat upon his back and gripped his head tightly. Though he pushed with all his might, he could not dislodge him.
Filled with fear, trembling and distressed, he wished to enter the city with his wife to remove [the burden], yet he feared that people might see them and prevent their entry.
Waiting until sunset, he covered it with a garment, carried it upon his back, and entered the city to go to his house.
Having arrived inside the house, it naturally fell to the ground and transformed into a single mass of Jāmbūnada gold, its brilliance so dazzling that it illuminated the entire neighborhood.
This news spread by word of mouth until it reached the ears of the king.
The king immediately dispatched a messenger to go and investigate the matter thoroughly.
Upon arrival at the site, the messenger saw that it was indeed a corpse, and he returned at once to inform the king:
"It is merely a dead man."
The king questioned others, and they likewise said it was gold.
Finding this deeply strange, he sent people to investigate again.
This occurred seven times, yet their reports remained inconsistent.
The king immediately went there in person to look at it; seeing that it was a dead man whose body was gradually beginning to stink, he asked Ārdraka:
"What do you see here?"
He replied,
"Upon inspection, it is indeed gold.
He then took a small amount and presented it to the king.
When the king saw the golden color, he had never before seen such a thing; he asked where it came from:
"By what cause was this obtained?
At that time, Arita related the matter from beginning to end to the king, saying, "It must surely be due to having given alms to a Pratyekabuddha."
When the king heard these words, he sighed in admiration and said: "Excellent!
You have attained great benefit by encountering such a superior person."
He was immediately granted further rewards and appointed as a high minister.
Thus it was, O Venerable Ones!
That Aṭṭhaka was none other than myself.

In that past life, I offered a small portion of millet gruel to a Pratyekabuddha and made a vow for myself; because of this, throughout ninety-one kalpas since then, I have been born among gods and humans without any lack, excelling in three matters: I have been praised for my physical beauty and comeliness, and whatever I desired would arrive according to my wish.
"Even until this present life, while I was still living as a householder, I always lived in leisure and took no pleasure in worldly affairs;
my elder brother Mahānāma, however, was constantly full of grievances."
My mother said,
"My son possesses great merit.
Mahānāman replied:
"I alone labor with anxious concern over the management of the household and the fields;
while you lie in leisure, eating and sleeping, what merit or virtue can there be in that?
His mother, wishing to test him, sent him to the fields to supervise the sowing and planting, ordering that no food be sent to him.
I was surprised that the meal was being served so late, so I sent someone to inquire about it. My mother sent someone to tell me, "There is nothing.
I returned and reported this to my mother.
"I only wish that you would send me 'nothingness'.

At that time, his mother, hearing these words from her son, immediately took a precious table, prepared various vessels and implements, covered them with a cloth, and sent them to me, instructing Mahānāman to follow and observe them.
Once they had reached my presence, he opened his bundle, and it was found that the trays and vessels were entirely filled with food and drink of a hundred flavors.

Thus, at other times, whatever one’s heart desired—be it the filling of the four continents with jewels—even if such things were obtained, they would naturally perish when the kalpa comes to an end and could not endure for long.

Thus, because I offered a small portion of gruel to a Pratyekabuddha, for ninety-one kalpas my merit and benefit have not diminished; furthermore, by virtue of this merit, I have now encountered a Buddha and am being delivered from suffering.
"For this reason, you should know that by inviting a single bhikṣu of pure precepts to receive offerings in one's home, one gains more merit than the treasures of those four continents.
When Anuruddha had finished speaking these words, the World-Honored One entered from outside; hearing Anuruddha recounting past events, he addressed the bhikṣus: "O bhikṣus!"

Having spoken of past events, I shall further speak of the future world: this Jambudvīpa will have lands that are square, level, and vast, with no mountains or rivers; the ground will grow soft grass, just like celestial garments.

At that time, the lifespan of the people was eighty-four thousand years, and their height was eight zhang. They were upright and exceptionally beautiful; by nature they were harmonious and benevolent, fully practicing the ten wholesome deeds.

At that time, there shall be a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Śaṅkha (in the Jin language, "Complete"); at that same time, a son shall be born into a Brahmin family named Maitreya, his body the color of purple-gold, endowed with the thirty-two marks and all the secondary characteristics, and radiating a most brilliant light.
Having left the household life to study the Way, he attained supreme perfect enlightenment and extensively turned the sublime Wheel of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
At his first great assembly, he delivered ninety-three billion classes of sentient beings;
at his second great assembly, he delivered ninety-six billion.
At the third great assembly, nine hundred and ninety million were delivered.
Thus it is, O Bhikṣus!

Those who have attained deliverance through the Dharma teachings of these three assemblies are all sentient beings who have planted merit within my bequeathed Dharma; they are those who have made offerings during the restoration of the Triple Gem, those—whether monastics or laypeople—who have observed the fasts and precepts, and those who have burned incense, lit lamps, and performed prostrations; all of them shall be present within those three assemblies.
"In three assemblies, you shall deliver the remaining sentient beings left by my legacy, and only then will you transform those disciples with whom you share a common affinity.
At that time, Maitreya, having heard these words from the Buddha, rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I vow to become that World-Honored One, Maitreya."
The Buddha told him:
"As you have said, you shall be born there as Maitreya Tathāgata; all those who were taught by you above are indeed yours."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly named Āśīta, who knelt with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha:
"I vow to become that Wheel-Turning King."
The Buddha said to him:
"Have you merely been indulging in the pleasures of birth and death throughout the long night, without intending to escape from them?

At that time, the entire assembly gathered there, seeing the World-Honored Buddha bestowing upon Maitreya the prediction of his future attainment of Buddhahood while he was still named Maitreya, each harbored doubts and wished to know the full details from beginning to end.
Venerable Ānanda immediately rose and addressed the Buddha:
"When Maitreya attains Buddhahood, he will again be named Maitreya; I wonder from what source this name was derived?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively and take this to heart!

In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Dharmaruci. He ruled over eighty-four thousand kingdoms, sixty thousand mountains and rivers, eight billion villages, twenty thousand ladies of the court and handmaidens, and ten thousand high ministers."
There was a small kingdom, prosperous and joyful, whose ruler was a king named Prasenajit.
At that time, when the Buddha Puṣya first appeared in the world, he resided in this kingdom to transform and guide sentient beings.

At that time, King Prasenajit, together with his various ministers, was exclusively engaged in making offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks; they had no leisure to go and pay their respects to the Great King, and even the sending of tributes and news was entirely suspended.
At that time, the Great King, marvelling at this sudden interruption, immediately dispatched a messenger to inquire as to the reason.
Upon arrival, the messenger proclaimed the King’s decree:
"In recent years, both people and their faith have been cut off; as a subject, why do you deviate from the norm?"
"Will you harbor a different mind and intend to act in rebellion?

At that time, Pāseṇadi, having received the Great King’s command, realized he had failed his duty and did not know where to turn; he immediately went to see the Buddha and reported these matters to him.
The Buddha told the king:
"Do not worry. Simply send a messenger back with this sincere message:
'The Buddha is in my kingdom, and because I attend upon him morning and evening, I have no leisure to go and pay my respects to Your Majesty.'"
"The wealth within my kingdom has been offered to the Buddha and the Sangha; there is nothing remaining that can be presented as an offering.
Having received the Buddha's instruction, King Prasenajit immediately returned the message to the envoy exactly as the Buddha had spoken.
The messenger arrived and saw the king, fully explaining his purpose.
Upon hearing this, the Great King was filled with intense anger; he immediately assembled his ministers to deliberate together on the matter.
The ministers all said, "That king is arrogant and haughty, and he arbitrarily cites principles of logic; we ought to assemble our troops and go to attack him.
The king agreed with this, assembled his forces, and went there in person.
When the vanguard drew near, the king realized it and was seized with fear; he hurried to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the king:
"Do not worry; simply go yourself and deliver my previous message."
King Prasenajit, together with his ministers, went to the border and, upon seeing the Great King, completed his salutations and inquiries, then stood to one side.
The Great King questioned him, saying:
"Upon what do you rely that you have become so insolent and negligent as to fail to come for audience?
Pāśr̥kī replied:

"A Buddha appears in the world but rarely; it is exceedingly difficult to behold him. Because he has recently been in our country, transforming and guiding the people and all things, we have attended upon him morning and evening, which caused us to neglect our duties."
At that time, the Great King again rebuked him severely:
"Even if you were commanded to do so, why did you stop the offering? Posaṅki replied:
"The Buddha has a retinue called the Sangha, whose precepts and virtues are pure; they are the world's excellent field of merit.
All that exists within the kingdom is constantly used for their offerings, leaving nothing in surplus that could be presented as a tribute."
Having heard these words, Dharmaruci said: "Wait!
I must first see the Buddha;
once I have returned from seeing the Buddha, I shall then inquire about your offense."
He immediately went with his ministers to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Tathāgata was surrounded by a great assembly, all of whom sat quietly and upright, having entered meditative concentration.
There was a bhikṣu who entered the samādhi of loving-kindness and emitted a golden light like a great mass of fire.

Dharmaruci saw the World-Honored One from afar; his radiance was so brilliant and dazzling that it surpassed the sun, and he was surrounded by a great multitude like the moon among the stars. He paid homage to the Buddha and inquired after his well-being in accordance with the Dharma.
Seeing this bhikṣu’s radiance so exceptionally manifest, he addressed the World-Honored One:
"In what meditative concentration has this one bhikṣu entered, that his brilliance is thus?"
The Buddha told the Great King:
"This bhikṣu has entered the meditative concentration of universal loving-kindness.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s admiration and veneration increased all the more, and he said:
"This concentration of loving-kindness is so sublime; I shall surely practice this samādhi of loving-kindness.
Having made this vow, he aspired to the concentration of loving-kindness; his mind became exceedingly gentle and tender, and he was free from any thought of harm.
He immediately entreated the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus, saying, "I only pray that you will turn your steps and proceed to the great kingdom."
The Buddha immediately granted permission and set a date for his departure.
When King Prasenajit heard that the Buddha intended to go to the kingdom of the Great King, he felt profound longing and regret; overcome with anxiety and despondency, he thought to himself:
"If I were that Great King, the Tathāgata would remain permanently in my own country. Because I am but a minor ruler, I cannot have him stay at will."
Having reflected on this matter, he immediately asked the Buddha,
"Among all kings, which one is the greatest?
The Buddha told him:
"O Great Wheel-Turning King!
King Prasenajit, having made a vow himself, said:
"May I, from this time forth, by virtue of the merit I have gained through making offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha, vow that in all future lives I shall always become a wheel-turning monarch."
"Thus it was, Ānanda!
That Great King Dharmaruci at that time is none other than Maitreya now.
It was in that world that he first gave rise to this mind of loving-kindness; from that time forward, he has always been named Maitreya."

That King Prasenajit is none other than Jeta here today; he has constantly served as a wheel-turning monarch within those realms, and from that time until now, he has done so in every lifetime. His merit remains inexhaustible even unto this day, and for this reason, he seeks to become one once more today.
At that time, having heard this teaching, the pearl-drilling master immediately resolved his mind upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

As for the rest of those in the assembly who heard what the Buddha had said, some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat*; some resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; and some attained the station of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). All of them paid homage with reverence and joyfully practiced what they had been taught.
51. Chapter Fifty-one: The Two Parrots Hearing the Four Noble Truths (in the Danben [Dunhuang manuscript], this is Chapter Fifty-eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the elder Sudatta, who revered and had faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, served as a patron (*dānapati*) for the Saṃgha, providing everything they required.
The bhikṣus, according to their needs, came and went daily, preaching the Dharma and offering instruction.
In the house of Sudatta, there were two parrots:
one named Lūtī and the other named Śalūtī;
they were naturally clever and wise, and were able to understand human speech.
Whenever the bhikṣus came and went, they would always inform the household in advance so that everyone would know; they would then sweep and arrange their bedding, welcoming them with joy.
At that time, Ānanda went to the house and saw that the bird was clever and wise; taking a liking to it, he spoke to it, saying:
"I wish to teach you the Dharma."
The two birds were filled with joy; he bestowed upon them the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and instructed them to recite and practice it, speaking these verses:
*Dūka* (豆佉) *Sammutiya* (三牟提耶) *Niruddha* (尼樓陀) *Maga* (末加) [In the language of Jin: "Suffering, Origin, Cessation, and the Path.

Before the tree, the two birds heard the Dharma and, filled with delight, recited and practiced it. They flew toward the tree, ascending and descending in succession, passing through this seven times, chanting the sublime Dharma of the Four Noble Truths they had received.
That evening, they stayed in a tree and were eaten by a wild civet. Because of this wholesome mind, they were immediately reborn in the Four Heavenly Kings' realm.

When the time arrived the following day, the Venerable Ānanda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Hearing that two parrots had been killed by a civet, he felt a sense of compassion and returned to inform the Buddha, saying:
"In the house of Sudatta, there were two parrots. Yesterday, I instructed them in the recitation of the Four Noble Truths; they passed away that night."
I do not know where the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*) dwells when it is born;
I only pray that the Tathāgata will look upon me with compassion and reveal this to me.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Take this well to heart; I shall speak for you so as to bring you joy.”
Because you received the Dharma from me and joyfully upheld it, after the end of your life, you were reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

Fifty years in this Jambudvīpa constitute one day and night in that heaven; thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year. The lifespan in that Heaven of the Four Great Kings is five hundred years.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"Having passed away there, where will they be reborn?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"When one is born in the second heaven above, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, one hundred years here in Jambudvīpa constitute one day and night in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Furthermore, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year; the lifespan in that Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is one thousand such years."
Ānanda asked again,
“When they pass away from there, where will they be reborn?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"One shall be born in the third heaven, the Yāma Heaven.

Two hundred years in this Jambudvīpa constitute one day and night in the Yāma Heaven; likewise, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year. The lifespan in that Yāma Heaven is two thousand such years."
Ānanda asked again:
"When their life there comes to an end, where will they be reborn?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"He shall be reborn in the fourth heaven, Tuṣita.

Four hundred years in this Jambudvīpa constitute one day and night in that heaven; likewise, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year. The lifespan in that Tuṣita Heaven is four thousand such years."
Ānanda asked again:
"When their lives there have ended, where will they be reborn?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"One shall be born in the fifth heaven, the Heaven of No-Contention (Abṛha).

Eight hundred years in this Jambudvīpa constitute one day and night in that fifth heaven; likewise, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year. The lifespan in that fifth heaven is eight thousand such years."
Ānanda asked again:
"When their lives there come to an end, where will they be reborn?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"One shall be born in the sixth heaven, the Heaven of Made-by-Others' Transformations (Nirmāṇarati).

One thousand six hundred years in this Jambudvīpa constitute one day and night in the sixth heaven. Thirty such days make a month, and twelve months make a year; the lifespan in that sixth heaven is sixteen thousand years."
Ānanda asked again:
"Having passed away from there, where will they be reborn?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"He was reborn again in the fifth heaven above.
Following this sequence, he proceeded down to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Thus, ascending and descending seven times among the six heavens of the desire realm, he enjoyed his blessings at will, living out the full lifespan of each heaven without meeting an untimely death."
Ānanda asked again:
“When the lifespan of those in the six heavens is exhausted, where will they be reborn?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Having descended into Jambudvīpa and been born among humans, he left the household life to study the Way.

Due to his previous recitation and upholding of the Four Noble Truths during his time as a bird, his mind was spontaneously enlightened, and he became a Pratyekabuddha—first named Dharma and second named Sudharma."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"All Buddhas, as well as the multitude of worthy sages, devas, humans, and all classes of beings—the extent of the blessings they receive—all stems from planting the causes of goodness through the Dharma, which subsequently leads each to obtain their wondrous fruits."
At that time, Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter 52: The Bird Who Heard the Dharma of a Bhikṣu and Was Reborn in Heaven (59). Chapter Fifty-two according to the Danben (Dandan edition), which is the fifty-ninth. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, amidst the forest trees, there was a bhikṣu who sat in meditation and practiced the Way; after his meal, he walked in contemplation and subsequently recited a sutra, his voice being pure, elegant, and wondrously beautiful beyond compare.
At that time, there was a bird that cherished its own song; it flew up into a tree to listen to its own resonance. Then a hunter shot and killed it with an arrow.

By virtue of this wholesome mind, the bird was immediately reborn in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Suddenly appearing upon the knees of his parents, he grew to the size of an eight-year-old boy. His countenance was upright and handsome, and his extraordinary radiance was so brilliant as to be without peer.
He then thought to himself:
"By what merit have I been born here?"

Through the karmic fruit of heavenly merit, he immediately recognized his past lives; observing his former body, he saw that it had originally been a bird, which, by virtue of the merit from hearing a bhikṣu recite the sūtras, had now attained birth among these beings.

He then took celestial flowers and went to Jambudvīpa; arriving at the place where the bhikṣu was, he paid his respects, inquired after his well-being, and scattered the celestial flowers and incense upon him as an offering.
The bhikṣu asked,
“What deity are you? He replied:
"I was originally a bird who loved the sound of the Venerable One's voice and came here to listen to the sutras.
Having been killed by a hunter, I have been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven because of this wholesome mind."

The bhikṣu was filled with joy and immediately invited him to sit; he then preached various kinds of sublime and wholesome Dharma for him. The deva attained understanding, realized the fruit of srotāpanna, and leaping for joy, he returned to the heavens.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Tathāgata’s appearance in the world brings immense benefit; the various dharmas he has taught are truly profound and subtle.

Even flying birds that encounter the sound of the Dharma obtain immeasurable merit—how much more so for those among humans who, with firm faith, receive and uphold them? The karmic rewards they obtain are difficult to compare with anything else."
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Twelve;
*The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Huijue and others of Liangzhou during the Northern Wei Dynasty at Gaochang Commandery. 53.
Chapter Sixty: Five Hundred Geese Hearing the Buddha-Dharma and Rebirth in Heaven (Chapter Fifty-three in the original; Chapter Sixty in the Danben).
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst a grove and marshland, expounded the sublime Dharma for the sake of the fourfold assembly of devas and humans.

At that time, there were five hundred flocks of geese in the sky; hearing the Buddha’s voice, they felt deep affection and joy, circling and wheeling about as they sought to descend to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, there was a hunter who had spread out a net; a flock of five hundred geese fell into it and were killed by the hunter.

They were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where they suddenly grew upon the laps of their parents, appearing like eight-year-old children. Their bodies were upright and majestic, their countenances peerless, and their radiant features so bright and pure as to resemble mountains of gold.
He then thought to himself:
"By what cause have I been born in this heavenly realm?

With a mind that was sharp and a spirit of divine understanding, he immediately recognized his past lives; having attained birth in heaven as the fruit of his attachment to the sound of the Dharma, he felt he ought to repay its kindness.

At that very moment, carrying celestial flowers and incense, they descended to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī in Jambudvīpa and arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was. Their celestial radiance shone like a forest of jewel trees; simultaneously, they bowed their bodies to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One and, with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
"Having been born in this wondrous place by virtue of the sound of the World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma, we pray that you will again take pity on us and reveal the essentials of the Path."

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded for them the wondrous Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. The devas and humans attained awakening and realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*; they immediately returned to the heavens, no longer falling into the three miserable realms, and through seven births according to their conditions, they exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Last night, there was a celestial light shining brilliantly as they paid homage to the World-Honored One.
I do not know the cause of this."
"I pray that you will instruct me.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Reflect upon this well!"
I shall explain this for you.

Yesterday, while the World-Honored One was in the forest groves expounding the sublime Dharma for the assembly of gods, humans, and the fourfold community, there were five hundred flocks of wild geese who, out of love and reverence for the sound of the Dharma, felt joy and celebration in their hearts.
They immediately flew together toward my location, intending to reach where I was, but they fell into the net of a hunter.
At that time, the hunter immediately killed him.
Because of this virtuous mind, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; recognizing his own past lives, he has come here to repay his debt of gratitude.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had said, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence, he spoke these words:
“The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is truly marvelous!”

The rain of the Dharma was poured forth and spread, such that there were none who did not receive its moisture; even birds and beasts heard the sound of the Dharma and obtained such merit. How much more so for humans who, with faith, accept and uphold it—their karmic retribution will exceed that of the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, beyond all comparison.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said.”

The Tathāgata appears in the world to provide abundant benefit and nourishment, raining down nectar everywhere to soak and sustain all living beings; for this reason, you should all with one mind believe in and revere the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter 54: The Lion of Firm Vows (61) The Lion of Firm Vows, Chapter Fifty-Four (in the Danben [Dunhuang manuscript], it is Chapter Sixty-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, Devadatta constantly harbored an evil mind toward the World-Honored One, desiring to harm the Tathāgata and claiming for himself the title of Buddha;
he instructed Ajātaśatru to kill his father and seize the throne as king.
"Would it not be a joy for a new Buddha and a new king to govern the world?
Believing these words, the prince killed his father and established himself as king.
At that time, the people of the world all harbored evil intentions toward the bhikṣus and detested even the sight of them.

When the bhikṣus entered the city to beg for food, the populace, filled with resentment and anger, would not speak to them at all; they returned with empty bowls. Returning to the mountains, they said to the World-Honored One:
"Devadatta has committed unwholesome deeds, causing the fourfold assembly to each give rise to malice toward the śramaṇas."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"If there are sentient beings who give rise to an evil mind toward any śramaṇas who wear dyed robes, you should know that such persons, with their evil minds, are directed toward the past Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats; they are directed toward the future Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats; and they are directed toward the present Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats."
Because one has given rise to an evil mind toward the worthies and sages of the three periods of time, one shall immediately incur the retribution of immeasurable sinful karma. Why is this?

Dye-dyed robes are the insignia of the worthies and sages of the three periods; if there are sentient beings who shave their hair and beards and don these dyed robes, you should know that such persons will before long attain liberation from all sufferings, obtain untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and act as great protectors for all sentient beings.
"If there are sentient beings who can give rise to faith toward those who have left the household life and wear dyed robes, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It was because I, in the past, gave rise to deep faith and held those who had left the household life and wore dyed robes in profound reverence that I attained Buddhahood."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What was the matter regarding your profound mind in the past, when you revered those who wore dyed robes?”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen well; I shall speak."
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Tivi who ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kings. At that time, the Buddha-dharma did not exist in the world; however, there were *pratyekabuddhas* dwelling among the mountains and forests, practicing meditation and cultivating the Way, manifesting supernatural transformations, and bringing blessings and salvation to sentient beings."
At that time, all the wild beasts came to him in affectionate submission.

There was a lion named Rṣigālava (translated into Chinese as Jiānshì, "Firm Vow"), whose body was golden in color and whose radiant marks were so brilliant they seemed to burst forth with light; he fed on fruits and ate grass, never harming living creatures.
At that time, a hunter—shaven-headed and wearing a *kāṣāya*, yet with a bow and arrows concealed within—was walking through the marsh when he saw a lion. Filled with great joy, he thought to himself:
"I have now attained a great benefit; having seen this beast, I can kill it to take its skin and present it to the King, which will surely enable me to escape poverty."
At that time, the lion happened to be asleep when the hunter struck it with a poisoned arrow.
Startled awake, the lion was about to charge and kill him, but seeing that he was wearing the *kāṣāya*, he thought to himself:
"A person such as this will not remain long in the world; he will surely attain liberation and be freed from all suffering and calamity."

Why is this? This dyed robe is the distinguishing mark of the noble ones of the three periods of time—past, future, and present. If I were to harm it, I would be directing an evil mind toward all the worthy and holy ones of the three periods of time.
Reflecting thus, his malevolent thoughts subsided.
With two rows of poisoned arrows piercing him and his life lasting but a short while, he spoke these verses: “Yarala, vaśaśa, svāhā.”

When these words were spoken, heaven and earth shook violently, and rain fell from a cloudless sky. The devas were filled with grief and alarm; they immediately looked down upon the world with their divine eyes and saw the hunter killing the Bodhisattva lion. Thereupon, they rained down celestial flowers from the void to make offerings to his corpse.
At that time, the hunter skinned the lion, took it home, and presented it to King Tīva, seeking a reward.
Then the king thought to himself:
"The scriptures say:..."
"If there is a beast with a body of golden hue, it must surely be a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
How then shall I reward such a person?
